title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
6.2 A stylized coal-to-clean reform
Consider a reform that retires 2 gigawatts (GW) of coal-fired capacity ten years early and replaces it with procured clean power. The numbers are stylized and chosen for round arithmetic. The plants run 6,000 hours a year at 0.95 tCO₂ per megawatt-hour, so retirement avoids 11.4 MtCO₂ a year. The government’s net cost (compensation to plant owners, transition support for coal regions and a higher tariff while the replacement is built, less domestic benefits) is $100 million a year for ten years, $772 million in present value at 5 percent, or about $9 per tonne avoided. Take \(q_1 - q_0 = 1\), the most favorable case for every instrument, so the required reward equals \(K\).
Figure 1 and Table 3 compare the rewards. A step-down of 100 basis points on a $1 billion loan for ten years is worth $77 million, a tenth of the cost and less than $1 per tonne avoided. Matching the cost at that step needs a $10 billion loan. Even waiving all interest at 6 percent on $1 billion for ten years is worth $463 million, short of the cost; by Proposition 3 the loan would have to exceed $1.7 billion and carry no interest at all. Policy crediting at $10 per tonne would be worth $880 million, enough to pay for the reform, at a cost in cash of the same amount (Stretton 2026c).

Guarantee capacity reaches the reform’s cost for a small fraction of the funder’s outlay. Capacity of $3.3 billion on borrowing that saves 300 basis points is worth $772 million to the government. If the guarantor’s losses match development banks’ sovereign record, the series’ base case, its expected cost is about $10 million and the buffer behind it is $16 million, which donors hold rather than spend. Each dollar of guarantor cost buys about 80 dollars of incentive. If calls are as frequent as 3 percent a year and lose 10 cents per dollar, the cost is $77 million and the ratio 10; if they lose 37 cents, the average haircut in sovereign restructurings, the cost is $286 million, the buffer $310 million and the ratio 2.7. Even in that stress case the funder pays less than two-fifths of the reform’s cost. Charging the buffer a 2 percent a year carry cost lowers the ratio to 63 in the base case and 2.3 in the stress case.
The leverage depends on the spread saved and the risk of a call, and it disappears for distressed borrowers. Figure 2 shows \(\lambda\) at a 300 basis point spread across annual call probabilities from 0.5 to 5 percent, for losses per call of 4.9, 10 and 37 percent. With development banks’ recovery record it stays above 12 even at a 5 percent call probability. At a 37 percent loss it falls from about 16 to about 1.6, and at 150 basis points it is 1.4 at a 3 percent call probability and falls below 1 above 4 percent, where guarantee capacity offers no advantage over cash. A saving of 200 basis points, the World Bank’s reported expectation for Kenya’s guaranteed loan (Muiruri 2026), needs $5.0 billion of capacity to match the reform’s cost; the funder’s expected cost is then $15 million in the base case and $429 million in the stress case, ratios of 53 and 1.8.






Figure 2: Guarantee capacity multiplies the incentive per dollar most for countries with high spreads and low default risk. Incentive value per dollar of guarantor cost, by annual probability of a call on the guarantee, for three losses per call; 300 basis points saved, buffer held in safe assets at no net carry, full use. Points mark the base case (development banks’ record), the middle case and the stress case. Source: author’s calculations, 2.Source/make_wp_figures.py.



Three assumptions deserve scrutiny, and Section 8.1 takes the most important. A 300 basis point saving assumes that a guarantee from a highly rated guarantor removes most of the spread on a sub-investment-grade sovereign’s green borrowing, which holds only if the guarantee is credible and covers the risk investors price. The base case assumes the guarantor’s losses look like development banks’ own sovereign record. And full use of capacity assumes a pipeline of eligible borrowing; a government with no projects to finance gains little from guarantees.

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
7.1 The trusted intermediary
The intermediary in the SLIDI design is a small, specialized development bank (Estevão et al. 2024). It borrows by issuing fixed-coupon bonds backed by guarantees from a coalition of advanced economies, lends to governments as codified sustainability-linked loans at a higher fixed rate, and pays interest refunds when verified KPIs are met. The spread covers its operating costs and expected losses; the coalition’s guarantees cover the tail. Development agencies monitor the indicators and help governments meet them. The intermediary could be a financial intermediary fund managed by a multilateral development bank or a separately capitalized vehicle. Lending to many countries also answers Svensson’s commitment problem: a funder that has committed a reward pool to a group of countries and published the price per unit of outcome can pay the countries that perform without being tempted to rescue those that do not (Svensson 2003).
The refunds need a funder, and they should come from outside the lender’s existing envelope. Uruguay’s rebate is paid by a dedicated World Bank fund rather than by other borrowers (World Bank 2023a). That is the right principle. If a government undertakes a difficult reform and receives climate finance that is offset by less concessional finance elsewhere, it has been paid nothing, and the incentive loses its credibility for everyone watching (Stretton 2026h).
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
section: 7.2 From rebate to guarantee capacity and collateral
text:
7.2 From rebate to guarantee capacity and collateral
The step from a codified loan to scale is to let the same verified indicators earn a larger prize. Under the notional capitalized value, a country’s climate balance, credited for carbon stocks and low emissions and debited for business-as-usual emissions, sets its guarantee capacity on eligible green borrowing (Stretton 2026e). Meeting a KPI from the codified menu would add to the balance at the published price. Under the Climate Investment Trust, meeting a KPI would credit the country’s beneficiary account, which can be pledged as collateral now and withdrawn after 2050 (Stretton 2026g). In both, the reward arrives in a form the government can use immediately, which also eases the timing problem of Section 4.4.
The two routes fit together in one contract. The sustainability-linked loan supplies the agreed indicator, the baseline, verification and a price. The guarantee supplies the size. One verification report can trigger both the interest refund and the increase in guarantee capacity. The refund is then a visible, annual signal, and the guarantee capacity the incentive. Kenya’s reported program, a sustainability-linked loan with a World Bank credit enhancement (Muiruri 2026), would be a first step toward this combination, with the guarantee lowering the price of the whole loan rather than serving as the reward for performance.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
section: 7.3 Relation to policy crediting and conditional de-risking
text:
7.3 Relation to policy crediting and conditional de-risking
Sustainability-linked lending, policy crediting and conditional de-risking reward the same thing in different currencies. Policy crediting pays cash per tonne cut by a policy, measured as a carbon-price equivalent (Stretton 2026c, 2026b). It is the most direct and the most expensive, because every dollar of incentive is a dollar of donor cash, and it faces the counterfactual problem of measuring tonnes against what would have happened. Sustainability-linked lending pays in interest and measures outturns against a pledge-based target, which sidesteps part of the counterfactual problem at the cost of rewarding some outcomes the policy did not cause (a high \(q_0\)). Conditional de-risking pays in guarantees for a specific clean power pipeline in return for specific reforms (Stretton 2026a). The codified pricing schedule of Section 4.5 connects them: it states every reward per tonne-equivalent, so a funder can compare a dollar spent through each.
The guarantee capacity earned under Section 7.2 can stand behind the structures of series 3. A country that meets its indicators gains capacity that multilateral development banks can use for the payment intermediary of Stretton (2026a), so the incentive and the de-risking draw on one balance sheet.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
section: 8.1 The strongest objection: the leverage rests on preferred-creditor treatment
text:
8.1 The strongest objection: the leverage rests on preferred-creditor treatment
The strongest objection is that the base case mixes two populations. The 300 basis point saving is a market spread: what investors charge a sub-investment-grade sovereign. The base-case expected loss, 0.038 percent a year, is development banks’ record on their own sovereign loans, 1984–2024 (European Investment Bank 2025), and that record reflects preferred-creditor treatment: governments in distress keep paying the banks while they restructure other debt. A guarantee of market debt is a claim of the kind the market prices at 300 basis points. If governments treat a guarantor’s claim like a market claim, its losses will look like the stress case, 3 percent of exposure called a year and 37 percent lost, an expected loss of 1.1 percent a year. A spread of 300 basis points against that expected loss gives a ratio of 2.7, roughly what the evidence on high-yield spreads implies (Huang and Huang 2012).
The objection is right about the stress case and does not overturn the conclusion. First, even on market-like losses guarantee capacity beats cash, 2.7 to 1 at 300 basis points, although at 200 basis points the multiple falls to 1.8 and at 150 basis points it reaches 1 at about a 4 percent call rate. Second, the base case is attainable when the guarantor is a development bank, or is backed by one, and the guaranteed government signs a counter-indemnity that makes a called guarantee a debt to that bank, which is how development bank guarantees work. The government’s own exposure then does not disappear: it becomes smaller, contingent and contracted (Stretton 2026a). Third, a new facility can price on the development banks’ record but hold the stress-case buffer, $310 million in the coal example rather than $16 million, until it has a record of its own; the Climate Investment Trust exists to hold it (Stretton 2026f). A buffer held in safe assets costs nothing net, so the multiple stays at about 80; if holding it costs 2 percent a year, the funder’s cost rises to $58 million and the multiple falls to about 13. What the objection does establish is that the multiple of 80 is an upper end, and that the stress case must be reported wherever 80 is.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
section: 8.2 Guarantees move risk; they do not remove it
text:
8.2 Guarantees move risk; they do not remove it
Expected loss is an average; in a correlated global shock several guaranteed sovereigns default together and the guarantor’s loss can be many times the expected loss. The buffer cost in Proposition 4 is the price of holding capital against that tail, and the leverage stays above one unless the buffer is very large or very expensive. With the base-case parameters, \(\lambda\) stays above one as long as the buffer cost \(b\,r_b\) is below 296 basis points of capacity a year, and in the stress case below 189; a 2 percent carry on the stress-case buffer of 9.3 percent costs 19. The leverage figure is only as good as the default and correlation assumptions behind it, which should be stress-tested before any guarantor commits.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
8.3 Weak targets and greenwashing
A codified menu can still carry soft targets if the margin over the pledge is small or the pledge is weak. Corollary 1 shows the cost: with \(q_0 = 0.6\), the funder pays three dollars for each dollar of policy cost it induces. The defenses are a peer-based floor on targets (Section 4.2), a published margin by indicator, and verification by a named third party from the national inventory.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
section: 8.4 Indicators that move for other reasons
text:
8.4 Indicators that move for other reasons
Outturn indicators move with weather, commodity prices and growth as well as policy. Uruguay’s KPI uses a truncated five-year average to smooth weather (Ministry of Economy and Finance, Uruguay 2023), and because it divides by output, a smaller herd does not by itself count as success. Every indicator in the menu should be normalized and smoothed in the same way. Residual noise raises \(q_0\) for some countries and lowers it for others; across a portfolio of countries it is partly diversified, which is another reason to pay rewards through an intermediary.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
8.5 Accounting and fiscal treatment
A KPI-linked rate creates contingent flows that accounting rules may treat differently from fixed-rate debt. For the borrower, the debt is recorded at its contractual terms and the rebate as a contingent reduction in interest; for the lender, the rebate is a cost that must be funded, which is why Uruguay’s is pre-funded by a dedicated fund. Guarantee capacity creates a contingent liability for the guarantor and, through counter-indemnity, for the government. These treatments should be settled once, at the level of the codified instrument, rather than deal by deal.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
8.6 Moral hazard and reversal
A government could meet its indicators, collect guarantee capacity and then reverse the policy. Rewards paid annually for continued performance, as in Uruguay’s loan, limit this: the rebate stops when the indicator falls back. Guarantee capacity can be made to decline with the indicator, as the notional capitalized value is debited for emissions (Stretton 2026e). Capacity already used cannot be withdrawn without hurting investors, so the intermediary should release it gradually.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
8.7 Fairness
Rewarding outperformance of pledges rewards countries that pledged little and then did more over countries that pledged much. Peer-based floors reduce this, and the pricing schedule can pay for the level of an indicator as well as for outperformance. Guarantee capacity is worth most to countries that borrow; low-income countries with little market access gain more from beneficiary-account credits than from guarantees.
crumbs: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
Footnotes


The fixed-coupon, third-party-reward design in Section 4 and Section 5 (Sustainability-Linked Intermediated Debt Instruments, or SLIDIs) was developed jointly with Marcello Estevão and Nils Zimmermann (Estevão et al. 2024), building on Estevão’s earlier unpublished note on bonds with key performance indicators. The propositions, the size analysis and the link to guarantee capacity are new here, and any errors are mine. The paper uses only public documents to describe World Bank practice.↩︎

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text: Working paper, version 0.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.1.1
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
section: 4.1 Definition: a balance that the stock opens and emissions draw down
text:
4.1 Definition: a balance that the stock opens and emissions draw down
A country’s notional capitalized value is a climate balance held for it by an international arrangement. It opens at the value of the country’s carbon stock and moves each year with its emissions:
\[B_0 = p_s S_0, \qquad B_{t+1} = B_t + p_e\,(A_t - E_t), \qquad B_t \ge 0. \tag{1}\]
Here \(S_0\) is the verified carbon stock at entry in tonnes of CO₂ (forest carbon, and optionally fossil reserves legally retired), \(p_s\) is the stock price in dollars of opening balance per tonne of stock, \(E_t\) is the country’s emissions in year \(t\) from all sources including land use, \(A_t\) is its allowance, an agreed benchmark path, and \(p_e\) is the debit price in dollars per tonne. Emitting above the allowance debits the balance; emitting below it credits the balance. Deforestation enters through \(E_t\) as land-use emissions, so the forest stock is not revalued each year; every tonne emitted, from a chimney or a cleared hectare, costs the same \(p_e\).
The balance is notional. Nobody claims that Guyana’s forests could be sold for \(p_s S_0\); the number is an agreed basis for an entitlement (Stretton 2026j, ch. 21). The idea has a mirror image in liability law: an emission inflicts damage on identifiable people in the future, so the prudent response is to provision for it, which makes it a capital requirement rather than an expense (Stretton 2026i, ch. 7). The NCV applies the same accounting to the country that holds a stock: an unreleased stock is notional capital, and each tonne released is a withdrawal from it.
The balance sets guarantee capacity:
\[G_t = \lambda_t B_t, \qquad X_t = \min(G_t, D_t), \tag{2}\]
where \(\lambda_t\) is the capacity ratio (dollars of guarantee capacity per dollar of balance, possibly declining over time), \(D_t\) is the country’s outstanding eligible green borrowing, and \(X_t\) is the exposure actually guaranteed.
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text:
4.2 Four formulations, reconciled
Earlier drafts contain four versions of the idea. Table 1 sets them side by side.

The four versions agree on the core and differ on three choices, which this paper settles.
Reward form: guarantee capacity, not interest. Interest paid into an account is cash, deferred; it costs donors a dollar per dollar of incentive. Guarantee capacity costs a fraction of its value (Proposition 1). It also arrives when a government needs it, as cheaper borrowing for the investments the policy requires, rather than years after the result. Interest into a trust account remains the right form for countries that do not borrow in volume, such as small island states without bond market access or a country whose oil revenue makes borrowing unnecessary.
Capacity is a cap on outstanding exposure, not a flow of new guarantees. The original arithmetic did not say which, and the difference is a factor of ten (Section 6.2). A cap on outstanding exposure is the natural reading of a balance, matches how MDBs manage guarantee limits, and gives the debit a clean meaning: every dollar debited is a dollar less of exposure the country can have guaranteed from then on.
The debit is per tonne emitted, against an allowance, at its own price. “Used up by business-as-usual emissions” could mean a fixed draw-down set by a forecast. That would have no effect on behavior (Proposition 2). The debit must move with actual emissions. Setting the debit price separately from the stock price is the main change from all four drafts.
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
section: 4.3 Why the stock and the debit need different prices
text:
4.3 Why the stock and the debit need different prices
A single price cannot both size the balance and price the margin. Suppose \(p_s = p_e = p\). For the debit to bite, capacity must bind: the country must want more guarantee capacity than it has, so \(\lambda B_t < D_t\). With Guyana’s stock of 19.5 billion tonnes and eligible borrowing of, say, $5 billion, a binding balance requires \(p < \$0.26\) per tonne, and the marginal tonne is then worth about $0.15 to the country (Section 6.3). At the $100 per tonne of the original proposal, the balance is $1.95 trillion, capacity never binds, and the marginal tonne is worth nothing.
The two prices do different jobs. The stock price decides how much capacity each country starts with, which is a question of distribution and of what the country stands to lose. The debit price decides what each tonne costs, which is the question of incentives. Separating them lets the stock reward large forest countries without paying them for tonnes they were never going to emit, and lets the debit price be set high enough to change behavior without creating a balance no guarantor could stand behind.
The stock still matters at the margin, for a reason the separation makes clear. An international feebate between countries founders on negative transfers, because no sovereign will write a check for exceeding its benchmark; a deduction from a balance held in trust is enforceable where a payment is not (Stretton 2026i, ch. 5). The opening balance is what the debit is deducted from. Without a stock there is nothing to debit; with one, a country that emits loses something it already counts as its own.
Fixing the opening balance at entry also answers the hold-up problem of Harstad (2016). In a market for conservation the owner is paid more the more credibly it threatens to exploit, so threats pay. Under the NCV the opening balance depends on the verified stock at entry, not on the threat to it, and the reward for not emitting is the uniform debit price, the same for every country and every tonne. A country cannot raise either by threatening to clear.
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text:
5.1 Setup
A country holds balance \(B_t\) under equation 1 and capacity \(G_t\) under equation 2. Guaranteed borrowing pays the guarantor’s rate rather than the market rate, saving \(\Delta s\) per dollar of guaranteed exposure per year. The guarantor’s annual expected loss per dollar of exposure is \(\pi L\), the probability of a call times the loss per call. Behind the guarantees sits a buffer fund holding \(k\) dollars of capital per dollar of exposure; holding it costs \(\varphi\) a year per dollar, the donors’ opportunity cost of funds net of what the buffer earns. The guarantor may charge a fee \(f\) per dollar of exposure. Time is discrete in Proposition 1 and continuous in Propositions 2 and 3, with discount rate \(r\) and discount factor \(\delta = 1/(1+r)\).
The incentive value to the country is the present value of spread saved, net of fees:
\[V = \sum_t \delta^t (\Delta s - f) X_t. \tag{3}\]
The cost to the guarantor and donors is expected loss plus buffer carry, net of fees:
\[C = \sum_t \delta^t (\pi L + k\varphi - f) X_t. \tag{4}\]
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
section: 5.2 Proposition 1: a guarantee is worth several times what it costs
text:
5.2 Proposition 1: a guarantee is worth several times what it costs
Proposition 1 (incentive-to-cost ratio). Let \(\Delta s\), \(\pi L\), \(k\), \(\varphi\) and \(f\) be constant over the life of the exposure.
(a) For any path of guaranteed exposure,
\[\frac{V}{C} = R \equiv \frac{\Delta s - f}{\pi L + k\varphi - f}. \tag{5}\]
A guarantee delivers more incentive per dollar of donor cost than a grant (\(R > 1\)) if and only if \(\Delta s > \pi L + k\varphi\). A fee \(f = \pi L + k\varphi\) makes the scheme self-financing while the country keeps \(\Delta s - \pi L - k\varphi\) a year per dollar of exposure.
(b) Suppose the market spread is the market’s expected default loss plus a risk premium \(\rho\), and the country, which counter-indemnifies the guarantor, gives up its option to default on the guaranteed debt except to the extent the guarantor itself loses. Then the country’s economic gain per dollar of exposure a year is \(\rho + \pi L - f\), and
\[\frac{V_e}{C} = R_e \equiv \frac{\rho + \pi L - f}{\pi L + k\varphi - f} \;\le\; R . \tag{6}\]
The proofs are in Appendix A. Part (a) is the budget ratio: what a finance ministry sees each year as lower interest bills. It does not depend on the size or timing of the exposure, so it is the right statistic for comparing a guarantee with a grant, for which \(R = 1\). Part (b) is the economic ratio. Under market debt a country in distress imposes a haircut on its creditors; under a guarantee backed by its counter-indemnity it owes the guarantor instead, and on the MDB record repays almost all of it. The part of the spread that paid creditors for bearing default is therefore not a gain to the country, only the risk premium and whatever loss the guarantor still bears. Part (b) is a lower bound, because it ignores the output and access costs of a market default that the country also avoids (Cruces and Trebesch 2013).
Why should the spread saved exceed the guarantor’s cost? Because the market prices the sovereign’s risk to all creditors, plus a premium, while the guarantor bears only the sovereign’s risk to it. MDBs are senior creditors in practice (Schlegl et al. 2019) and, for guarantees with a sovereign counter-indemnity, hold a claim the government has strong reasons to honor. Their record bears this out: sovereign and sovereign-guaranteed loans defaulted at 0.77 percent a year over four decades and recovered 95.1 percent (European Investment Bank 2025). The resource being spent is the gap between the risk the guarantor actually bears and the risk the market charges for (Stretton 2026j, ch. 21). It needs no appropriation, but it is not free: losses will occur, and a buffer must stand behind the exposure.
This paper takes that record as its base case, shared with the companion papers on the Climate Investment Trust and sustainability-linked lending (Stretton 2026h, 2026b): a 0.77 percent annual probability that a guarantee is called and a 4.9 percent loss when it is (one minus the 95.1 percent recovery), for an expected loss of 0.038 percent a year (European Investment Bank 2025). A buffer of 0.5 percent of exposure then keeps the annual chance of exhausting it at 1 percent across 20 guaranteed programs with asset correlation 0.2; it covers two calls in the same year. The buffer is invested in safe assets and earns the rate used to discount, so its carry cost is zero (\(\varphi = 0\)). With \(\Delta s\) = 3 percent, \(R\) = 3/0.038, about 80. With a risk premium of a third of the spread (Longstaff et al. 2011), \(\rho\) = 1 percent and \(R_e\) = 1.038/0.038, about 27.
The record is not a promise that a new facility can keep. It reflects the MDBs’ preferred-creditor status: governments in distress keep paying the development banks while they restructure other debt. A climate guarantee facility might not inherit that status, especially if its guarantees cover market debt rather than MDB loans. So the paper reports two less favorable cases with the same correlation, number of programs and exhaustion target. In a middle case, a call is about four times as likely (3 percent a year) and loses 10 percent; \(R\) = 10 (\(R_e\) = 4.3), and the buffer is 2.5 percent of exposure. In a stress case, calls occur at 3 percent a year and lose 37 percent, the average investor haircut in sovereign restructurings over 1970–2010 (Cruces and Trebesch 2013), an expected loss of 1.11 percent a year, nearly 30 times the MDB record; the buffer is 9.3 percent of exposure and \(R\) = 2.7 (\(R_e\) = 1.9) (Stretton 2026h). Charging the buffer a 2 percent carry cost lowers \(R\) to 63 in the base case and 2.3 in the stress case. Because a buffer invested at the discount rate costs nothing net, a facility can price its guarantees on the record and still hold the stress-case buffer until it has a record of its own. That holds only at zero carry: if the buffer costs 2 percent a year to hold, pricing on the record while holding the stress-case buffer gives a ratio of about 13, not 80. The ratios also assume the exposure is held indefinitely, so the buffer is consumed only by losses (Stretton 2026h).

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
section: 5.3 Proposition 2: the debit must be per tonne, and capacity must bind
text:
5.3 Proposition 2: the debit must be per tonne, and capacity must bind
The marginal incentive is what changes behavior. Let capacity bind on an interval of time, meaning \(0 < \lambda_t B_t < D_t\), so every extra dollar of capacity is used and every dollar lost reduces guaranteed exposure. Let the capacity ratio decline at rate \(\theta \ge 0\), \(\lambda_t = \lambda_0 e^{-\theta t}\).
Proposition 2 (incentive compatibility and the carbon-price equivalent).
(a) If capacity binds from time \(s\) onward, a tonne emitted at \(s\) costs the country, in present value at \(s\),
\[\tau(s) = \frac{\lambda_0\, p_e\, (\Delta s - f)}{r + \theta}\, e^{-\theta s}. \tag{7}\]
This is the carbon-price equivalent of the scheme: the uniform carbon price that gives the same reward for cutting a tonne.
(b) If the debit is fixed in advance from a forecast of business-as-usual emissions rather than charged per tonne emitted, the marginal incentive is zero.
(c) The allowance path \(A_t\) does not enter \(\tau(s)\). It changes the level of the balance, and so who gains, but not the reward per tonne.
(d) If capacity does not bind, because \(\lambda_t B_t \ge D_t\) (the country has more capacity than borrowing) or \(B_t = 0\) (the balance is exhausted), the marginal incentive in those years is zero.
The proof is in Appendix A. Part (a) gives the conversion rate from notional to effective price: with no decline in capacity and \(\lambda_0 = 1\), each dollar of debit price is worth \(\Delta s/r\) dollars of carbon price, 60 cents at a 3 percent spread and a 5 percent discount rate. A government that cuts emissions until the marginal cost of a cut equals its marginal reward makes the same cut under the NCV as under a uniform carbon tax of \(\tau\), so \(\tau\) is the carbon-price equivalent in the sense of the series’ Total Effective Carbon Price (Stretton 2026e), and the NCV can be compared directly with a tax, a feebate or policy crediting. The donors’ cost per dollar of carbon-price equivalent is \((\pi L + k\varphi)/\Delta s\): about 1.3 cents in the base case and 37 cents in the stress case.
Part (a) also states its conditions, and both matter in practice. The formula assumes capacity binds from \(s\) for ever. If the scheme ends at a fixed date, the price falls as the date approaches: at a $50 debit price, a tonne emitted in 2027 under a scheme that ends in 2050 costs $20 rather than $30, and one emitted in 2040 costs $12. The scheme must therefore be open-ended, or its balance must end in something the country still values, such as a beneficiary account.
Part (b) is the reason the debit must be per tonne emitted. A schedule that draws the balance down by business-as-usual emissions whatever the country does is a declining transfer, and a transfer changes nothing at the margin. “Used up by business-as-usual emissions” must mean that business-as-usual emissions would use it up, not that they are assumed to.
Part (c) turns the hardest dispute in results-based finance, the baseline, into a question of distribution. A generous allowance gives a country more balance, but each tonne still costs \(p_e\). Negotiators can trade allowance against participation without weakening the incentive. That is not true of crediting against a baseline, where an inflated baseline pays for tonnes that were never at risk, nor of HFLD crediting, where the stock reward is delivered by inflating the baseline.
Part (d) gives two design rules. Capacity must be sized to the country’s borrowing, so that it binds; surplus balance above \(D_t/\lambda_t\) should flow somewhere it still has value, such as a beneficiary account in the Climate Investment Trust (Stretton 2026g). And the allowance must keep the balance positive along a path the country can reach, because a country that expects to exhaust its balance has no incentive in the years after exhaustion and a weaker one before.
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text:
5.4 Proposition 3: paying for acting now
A government chooses when to adopt a policy, such as a coal-retirement program or a forest-enforcement regime. Adopting at time \(T\) costs \(K_0 e^{-gT}\) up front, a cost that falls at rate \(g\) as technology improves, and cuts emissions by \(\Delta E\) tonnes a year from then on. The country values each tonne abated at \(b\) (domestic co-benefits, such as cleaner air) and bears an ongoing cost of \(\omega\) per tonne (for example, agricultural rent forgone on protected forest). Under the NCV each tonne abated at time \(s\) is worth \(m(s)\) to the country, the carbon-price equivalent of equation 7, written here in the general declining form \(m(s) = m_\infty + (m_0 - m_\infty)e^{-\theta s}\) with a floor \(m_\infty \ge 0\). The net present value of adopting at \(T\) is
\[W(T) = \int_T^\infty \Delta E\,[m(s) + b - \omega]\,e^{-rs}\,ds \;-\; K_0 e^{-(r+g)T}. \tag{8}\]
Proposition 3 (early action). Suppose the persistence condition \(m_\infty + b \ge \omega\) holds and the incentive declines no faster than technology costs, \(\theta \le g\). Then acting now (\(T = 0\)) is optimal if and only if
\[\Delta E\,(m_0 + b - \omega) \;\ge\; (r + g)\,K_0. \tag{9}\]
The minimum initial incentive is \(m_0^* = (r+g)K_0/\Delta E + \omega - b\). Holding \(m_0 = m_0^*\), the donor cost of the incentive falls as \(\theta\) rises, so among schedules satisfying the conditions the cheapest declines at \(\theta = g\) toward the floor \(m_\infty = \max(\omega - b, 0)\).
The proof is in Appendix A. The condition has a plain reading. Waiting a year saves interest on the up-front cost (\(rK_0\)) and lets the cost fall (\(gK_0\)); acting a year sooner earns a year of net benefit from the abated tonnes. Falling technology costs raise the hurdle: the faster solar or storage costs fall, the more a government gains by waiting, and the bigger the early incentive must be. Without an incentive, a government whose co-benefits do not exceed its ongoing costs (\(b \le \omega\)) never acts. One whose co-benefits do exceed them acts, but late: only once the cost has fallen to the point where \(\Delta E\,(b - \omega)e^{gT} = (r+g)K_0\), that is at \(T^* = \tfrac1g \ln\left[(r+g)K_0/(\Delta E(b - \omega))\right]\). The incentive’s job is to bring \(T^*\) forward to zero.
The persistence floor separates two cases. For an energy transition, the ongoing cost of keeping clean capacity is close to zero once it is cheaper than coal, so \(\omega \approx 0\) and the incentive can phase out: the reward is needed to start, not to continue. For forests, the opportunity cost of standing forest persists as long as there is demand for land, so \(\omega > 0\) and the floor stays: a forest needs a permanent price, an energy transition a temporary early one. A single scheme can serve both because the floor and the decay are parameters, not constants.
Uncertainty raises the hurdle further. If the up-front cost follows a driftless random walk, the standard result is that the trigger rises by a factor \(\beta/(\beta - 1) > 1\), where \(\beta\) depends on volatility and the discount rate (Dixit and Pindyck 1994, ch. 5). With a 5 percent discount rate and volatility of 15–20 percent a year, the factor is 1.6–1.9 (author’s calculation, Appendix B), so the initial incentive in equation 9 must be 60–90 percent larger. The decaying schedule is the instrument for this: a government that knows capacity per tonne falls each year it delays faces a cost of waiting that the market alone does not impose. This is the early-action premium of the series, built into the release schedule.
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text:
5.5 Three quantities, kept apart
The framework keeps apart three quantities that discussions of climate finance often merge (Stretton 2026f). Mitigation effectiveness is \(\Delta E\): the emissions cut that a policy produces. The sovereign incentive required is \(m_0^*\) in equation 9: the reward per tonne that makes acting now worth more than waiting. The resource cost to MDBs and donors is \(m_0^* (\pi L + k\varphi)/\Delta s\) per tonne: what it costs to create that incentive through guarantees. A grant makes the third quantity equal to the second; a guarantee divides it by \(R\).

text:
6.3 A forest country
Take a stylized forest country with Guyana’s verified stock: 19.5 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent on about 18 million hectares, an average of about 1,080 tonnes per hectare (Government of Guyana 2022). Give it $5 billion of eligible green borrowing (stylized), a stock price that opens the balance at that level (\(p_s\) = $0.26 per tonne), a debit price of $50 per tonne, and emissions of 15 MtCO₂ a year from all sources against an allowance that falls from 12 Mt in 2027 to zero in 2050 (stylized).
Incentive and cost. With capacity fully used, the country saves $150 million a year, $1.87 billion in present value over 20 years. On the MDB record, donors hold a buffer of $25 million and bear an expected annual cost of about $2 million; in the stress case the buffer is $0.47 billion and the cost $56 million. While capacity binds in an open-ended scheme, each tonne emitted costs the country $30 in lost spread savings ($50 × 3% ÷ 5%), and each hectare cleared about $32,500. Donors’ cost per tonne of that carbon-price equivalent is about 40 cents in the base case, $3 in the middle case and $11 in the stress case, against the $15–20 per tonne Hess pays in cash for credits against a reference level.
Business as usual drains the balance; action keeps it. Under business as usual the debit grows as the allowance falls, and the balance is exhausted in 2042 (Figure 1). A country that cuts emissions from 15 to 3 Mt by 2037 keeps its balance near its borrowing need throughout. The present value of spread savings over 2027–2050 is $2.11 billion if the country acts and $1.13 billion if it does not; acting is worth about $1 billion to it. From 2037 the acting country’s balance exceeds its $5 billion borrowing need, and by Proposition 2(d) a further tonne would then cost it nothing unless the surplus flows into a beneficiary account. That is why the surplus rule is part of the design, not an option.






Figure 1: A per-tonne debit drains the balance under business as usual. Stylized forest country: opening balance $5 billion, debit $50 per tonne of CO₂ against an allowance falling from 12 Mt to zero in 2050. Capacity above the $5 billion borrowing line is unused, so in the action case the surplus should flow to a beneficiary account. Source: author’s calculations (Appendix B).



Comparison with existing instruments. Table 4 puts the scheme beside the Guyana–Hess sale and the TFFF, converting each to a price per tonne at Guyana’s average carbon density. The TFFF’s $4 per hectare a year is about $0.004 per tonne of stock a year, equivalent to a stock price of $0.07 per tonne capitalized at 5 percent, under a third of the stock price used here. Its deforestation deduction of $400–800 per hectare is $0.37–0.74 per tonne released. The Hess price pays for avoided flow against a reference level and only for the credits sold. The NCV at a $50 debit price gives the stock a balance of the same order as the TFFF’s capitalized value and prices each tonne released at 40–80 times the TFFF’s deduction.



Table 4: Three ways of rewarding a forest country, at Guyana’s carbon density of about 1,080 tCO₂e per hectare. Note: The TFFF row multiplies $4 by 18 million hectares and assumes full eligibility; payments depend on fund returns. 6.4 How big must the scheme be?
The incentive scales with guaranteed borrowing, not with the stock. Proposition 1 makes the arithmetic linear: at a 3 percent saving, each $1 billion a year of incentive needs $33 billion of outstanding guarantee capacity. On the MDB record that capacity needs a buffer of $0.16 billion and costs donors about $13 million a year in expected losses; in the stress case the buffer is $3.1 billion and the cost $370 million (Table 5).

These numbers explain why the guarantee form matters. The largest sovereign sustainability-linked loan to date, Uruguay’s $350 million World Bank loan of 2023, can save the country at most about $12.5 million over its life (Stretton 2026a). Multilateral REDD+ funds pledged about $6.4 billion from 2008, about $400 million a year (Government of Brazil 2025), so a results-based payment of $1 billion a year would be more than twice their average. A guarantee scheme delivering $1 billion a year of spread savings needs donors to accept about $13 million a year of expected losses on the MDB record, and about $370 million in the stress case. The buffer, $0.16 billion on the record and $3.1 billion in the stress case, is capital donors keep and which earns. Holding it is the job of the Climate Investment Trust (Stretton 2026g, 2026h).
The binding constraint is borrowing, not donor money. A country can only save spread on debt it actually issues, so the scheme delivers big incentives to countries that borrow a lot at high spreads: large, lower-rated forest and coal countries. For small or lightly indebted countries, the ceiling on the guarantee form is low, and the interest-on-balance variant or a link to the trust’s accounts must carry the reward.
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text:
6.5 A coal-reserve country
Fossil reserves raise the same question from the supply side: should a country be rewarded for coal it leaves in the ground? Indonesia had 34.9 billion tonnes of proved coal reserves at the end of 2020 (BP 2021), about 78 billion tonnes of CO₂ at IPCC default carbon contents (IPCC 2006). Valuing the whole reserve even at $1 per tonne would open a balance of $78 billion, and would reward the country for owning coal rather than for keeping it unburned.
Crediting the whole reserve would be a mistake. It rewards the largest fossil holders most, invites countries to report larger reserves, and pays for coal that would never be mined at today’s prices. The right base is narrower: credit only reserves that are legally and verifiably retired, by canceling concessions or mining licenses, and debit combustion emissions at the debit price as for any other country. Retiring 2 billion tonnes of bituminous coal, about 4.9 billion tonnes of CO₂, at a stock price of $1 per tonne would open $4.9 billion of capacity.
What that capacity is worth depends on the spread. For an investment-grade sovereign saving 1 percentage point, it is worth $49 million a year and each $1 of debit price converts to only 20 cents of carbon price; at a 3-point saving it would be worth $146 million a year. Guarantees are a strong incentive for countries that borrow at high spreads and a weak one for investment-grade emitters. For the latter, the same balance is better delivered as access to the trust’s collateral, or as a reward linked to sustainability-linked lending (Stretton 2026a).
Supply-side credits also leak. Retiring Indonesian reserves raises the world coal price and draws supply from elsewhere, so the emissions avoided are smaller than the carbon in the reserves retired (Harstad 2012). The debit on combustion emissions does not leak in this way, because it prices what the country burns. A coal country’s reward should therefore come mainly from the debit on its own emissions, with reserve retirement credited at a low stock price to reflect leakage.
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text:
6.6 Early action in numbers
Take a stylized energy reform: retiring coal capacity and replacing it with renewables at a net up-front cost of $1 billion, falling 5 percent a year as technology improves, cutting emissions by 5 MtCO₂ a year, with no domestic co-benefit counted and no ongoing cost. The minimum initial incentive from equation 9 is \((0.05 + 0.05) \times \$1\text{bn} / 5\text{ Mt} = \$20\) per tonne; with the option-value factor of 1.6–1.9 it is $32–37 per tonne. Below that level the government gains by waiting, and without any incentive it never acts (Figure 2). Counting a co-benefit of $5 per tonne, it would act without an incentive, but only after about 28 years.






Figure 2: Below the minimum incentive, delay beats acting now. Net present value of adopting a stylized reform in each year, for incentives at 120 percent, 60 percent and zero of the minimum in equation 9. Reform costs $1 billion up front, falling 5 percent a year, and cuts 5 MtCO₂ a year; the incentive decays at 5 percent a year; discount rate 5 percent. Source: author’s calculations (Appendix B).



The decaying schedule halves the donor cost. To give $20 per tonne at the start with capacity that does not decline needs a debit price of $33 per tonne and costs donors $25 million in present value on the MDB record ($740 million in the stress case). With capacity declining at 5 percent a year, matching the fall in technology costs, the debit price must be $67 per tonne to deliver the same $20 at the start, but donors’ present-value cost falls to $13 million ($370 million in the stress case), because the incentive is concentrated where it changes the decision. Delivered as cash on results, the same incentive would cost $1 billion.
crumbs: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text:
6.7 Sensitivity






Figure 3: A guarantee is worth many times what it costs. Ratio of incentive value to guarantor cost (Proposition 1) against the guarantor’s expected loss, for three spread savings, on log scales. Solid lines: budget ratio \(R\). Dashed line: economic ratio \(R_e\) at a 3-point spread with a risk premium of 1 point. The buffer earns the discount rate, so cost equals expected loss. Dotted lines mark the base case (the MDB sovereign record: 0.77 percent annual calls, 4.9 percent loss), the middle case (3 percent, 10 percent) and the stress case (3 percent, 37 percent). Source: author’s calculations; European Investment Bank (2025); Longstaff et al. (2011); Stretton (2026h); Cruces and Trebesch (2013).



The ratio of value to cost is most sensitive to the spread saved, to whether the guarantor keeps preferred-creditor treatment, and to whether MDB capital is charged (Figure 3). Halving the spread to 1.5 points halves the budget ratio, to 40 in the base case and 1.4 in the stress case. Losing preferred-creditor treatment moves it from 80 toward 10 or 2.7; that is the main risk to the scheme’s cost, and the reason the stress case is reported throughout. Counting only the economic gain lowers it to about 27, and to 1.9 in the stress case, where a guarantee is barely better than a grant. If the guarantees were instead carried on an MDB balance sheet that holds capital at IBRD’s minimum equity-to-loans ratio of 18 percent (World Bank 2024), at a 2 percent carry, the base-case budget ratio would be about 7.5: still well above one, but a tenth of the headline. That is the case for holding a dedicated buffer in a trust rather than consuming MDB capital. The carbon-price equivalent is proportional to the debit price and the spread and inversely proportional to the discount rate plus decay, so a country with a 4.5-point spread gets half as much again per tonne as one with 3 points. On the budget measure, the guarantee form delivers more incentive per donor dollar than a grant unless expected losses exceed the spread saved, 3 percent a year, nearly 80 times the MDB record and almost three times the stress case.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text: Working paper, version 0.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.2.1

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
5.1 Setup
The Trust holds capital \(K\) in safe assets and stands second-loss behind guarantee exposure \(G\). Exposure is spread over \(n\) equal guaranteed programs, one per participating country. In a year, country \(i\) fails to honor its first-loss indemnity with probability \(p\). Failures are correlated through a one-factor structure: country \(i\) fails when \(X_i = \sqrt{\rho}Z + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_i < \Phi^{-1}(p)\), where \(Z\) and \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent standard normal and \(\rho\) is the asset correlation. When country \(i\) fails, the Trust pays the amount called and ultimately loses a share \(L\) of the program’s exposure \(G/n\), the loss given call. The expected loss rate on exposure is \(\lambda = pL\).
The borrower saves a spread \(s\) a year on guaranteed debt; the Trust may charge a guarantee fee \(f \le s\). The incentive value to the country is the present value of \(s - f\) on the guaranteed debt. The buffer earns a safe yield \(r_s\) and incurs running costs \(c\), both as shares of \(K\). Donors discount at \(d\); the carry \(\kappa = d - (r_s - c)\) is what holding a dollar in the buffer costs them each year, and it is zero when the buffer earns what donors would otherwise earn. A fund that pays rewards out is the benchmark: it delivers a dollar of incentive per dollar of capital.
The Trust targets a probability \(\alpha\) that guarantee losses in a year exceed its capital. That event is the one in which the AAA entity behind the Trust is called, so \(\alpha\) is the AAA backer’s attachment probability. The buffer ratio \(b = K/G\) is the smallest that meets the target.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
section: 5.2 Proposition 1: the leverage of a buffer
text:
5.2 Proposition 1: the leverage of a buffer
Proposition 1 (Leverage of a buffer). (a) With \(n\) equal exposures, the buffer ratio is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of the annual loss rate \(\ell = (L/n)\sum_i \mathbf{1}\{X_i < \Phi^{-1}(p)\}\). As \(n \to \infty\) it converges to \[
b_\infty = L\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(p) + \sqrt{\rho}\,\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right),
\tag{1}\] which rises with \(p\) and \(L\), falls with \(\alpha\), and rises with \(\rho\) whenever \(\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha) > \sqrt{\rho}\,|\Phi^{-1}(p)|\), which holds for all \(\rho\) when \(\alpha \le p < 1/2\). A buffer of \(K\) supports exposure \(K/b\).
(b) Suppose the Trust keeps exposure at \(G = K/b\) as its capital changes, and donors discount incentive flows at \(d\). Then the present value of interest savings delivered per dollar of initial capital is \[
M = \frac{s - f}{\lambda - f + \kappa b}
\tag{2}\] when the denominator is positive. With no carry (\(\kappa = 0\)), \(M = (s - f)/(\lambda - f)\), which does not depend on \(b\). A payout fund delivers 1. At no carry the buffer delivers more than a payout fund if and only if \(s > \lambda\): the spread saved exceeds the Trust’s expected loss rate.
(c) If the assets in which the buffer is held lose a share \(k\) of their value in the states that exhaust it, the buffer ratio must rise to \(b/(1-k)\).
(d) If each call requires the Trust to pay a share \(m\) of the program’s exposure in cash before it recovers anything, the buffer that keeps the chance of running out of cash at \(\alpha\) is \(\max(L, m)/L\) times the buffer in part (a), for finite \(n\) as well as in the limit.
The intuition is that a buffer is consumed only by losses, while the incentive it supports is paid every year. A dollar paid out is gone. A dollar held behind guarantees supports \(1/b\) dollars of exposure each year, on which the borrower saves \(s\), and it shrinks only at the expected rate \((\lambda - f)/b\). With no carry, equation 2 is the ratio of the incentive flow to the rate of consumption, and it does not depend on \(b\): the buffer ratio decides how much exposure a given capital supports at a moment, not how much incentive it delivers over its life. The condition \(s > \lambda\) is the series’ central claim in precise form. The market charges a sovereign a spread that covers its expected loss to market creditors plus a risk and liquidity premium; the Trust bears only its own expected loss, which is lower again if, as a preferred creditor with recovery rights on the sovereign’s obligation, it loses less than market creditors do.
The carry is what makes a thick buffer expensive. When the buffer earns less than donors could earn elsewhere, each dollar held costs \(\kappa\) a year whether or not it is ever called, and that cost is proportional to the buffer. The term \(\kappa b\) in equation 2 is the same carry that the companion paper adds to the guarantor’s cost (Stretton 2026h). It matters little for a thin buffer and a great deal for a thick one, which is why the cost of prudence is the cost of holding the stress-case buffer when losses turn out to follow the banks’ record.
Part (c) is why the buffer must not be invested in clean power. Construction-stage equity in clean energy loses value in the same crises, a sovereign debt crisis or a currency collapse, that trigger guarantee calls. A buffer half-invested in such equity, with a 40 percent fall in a stress, would need \(b/(1-0.2) = 1.25b\). Holding the buffer in high-grade bonds of other issuers sets \(k\) near zero. This resolves a tension in earlier drafts, which described the Trust both as capital “held, not spent” and as an investor in blended project equity (Stretton 2026j, ch. 20): the buffer is held; the investment function uses private capital and the Trust’s surplus.
Part (d) separates solvency from liquidity. A government that misses a payment on a guaranteed loan triggers a call for the debt service due, and recoveries come later; on the banks’ record almost all of it comes back. A buffer sized for ultimate losses can be solvent and still unable to pay. The remedy is either a thicker buffer or a liquidity line from the AAA backer that funds calls until recoveries arrive, which leaves the buffer sized for losses alone.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
5.3 Proposition 2: growth and self-funding
The Trust’s capital evolves with its yield, fees, expected losses, costs and the fee on private returns. Let private investors commit equity \(E_p\) to the investment function, earning a gross return \(r_e\), of which a share \(\varphi\) goes to the Trust. In expectation, \[
\dot K = \big(r_s - c - (\lambda - f)/b\big)K + \varphi\, r_e E_p + C,
\tag{3}\] where \(C\) is new contributions. Define the net burn rate \(\beta = c + (\lambda - f)/b - r_s\).
Proposition 2 (Self-funding). (a) Without private co-investment or contributions, the Trust’s capital grows if and only if \(\beta < 0\), that is, if the guarantee fee satisfies \[
f \ge \lambda - b\,(r_s - c).
\tag{4}\] In particular it grows with no fee whenever \(\lambda < b(r_s - c)\): the buffer’s net yield exceeds its expected losses.
(b) With constant private equity \(E_p > 0\), no contributions and \(\beta > 0\), capital converges monotonically to \[
K^* = \frac{\varphi\, r_e E_p}{\beta},
\tag{5}\] and its growth rate \(g_t = \varphi r_e E_p/K_t - \beta\) falls as it grows. The Trust funds itself (its capital does not fall) if and only if \(K_0 \le K^*\), and it grows at a target rate \(g\) only while \(K_t \le \varphi r_e E_p/(g + \beta)\).
(c) Private investors with a required return \(r_p\) participate only if \((1-\varphi) r_e \ge r_p\). The fee income available to the Trust is therefore at most \((r_e - r_p)E_p\): the excess of the investment return over what private investors require.
The proposition settles the growth claims of earlier versions. A buffer is not a money machine. At high leverage its safe yield cannot cover expected losses unless borrowers pay most of the expected loss as a fee, and every point of fee is a point of incentive taken back from the borrower. A thick buffer earns more than it loses if losses are low, which is the case that matters for a prudent Trust (Section 6.3). Beyond that, the Trust grows because it earns a share of returns on capital that is not its own. That income is fixed by the size of the private pool, not by the size of the Trust, so growth is fastest at launch and slows as capital catches up with what the fee income can sustain. Part (c) gives the fee rule a foundation: a 25 percent fee is acceptable to private investors only if three-quarters of the gross return clears their hurdle. It is the same arrangement as the earlier dynamic incentive in which returns above an agreed cap pass to countries and dilute the original investors down to their agreed maximum (Stretton 2026j, ch. 18).
Country stakes financed by borrowing carry a cost the accounts must repay. In the indicative structure, $4 billion of the Trust’s $5 billion launch capital comes from developing countries that finance their stakes through long-term development policy lending (Stretton 2026j, ch. 20). Each such country owes the loan and owns an account of the same size. Its net position improves only if the account’s safe yield, its allocations and the value of the guarantees and collateral it secures exceed the loan rate \(i_L\). With a stake \(S_i\), the annual carrying cost is \((i_L - r_s)S_i\). The stake raises the country’s gross debt, which a debt sustainability assessment will record; the matching asset is real but not liquid until 2050.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
5.4 Proposition 3: an allocation rule
The Trust allocates its distributable surplus by a rule that pays for joining and for performance. Let participating countries \(i = 1, \dots, N\) produce output \(Y_i\) in a covered sector (power, to start) at emissions intensity \(e_i\), with output share \(s_i = Y_i/\sum_j Y_j\). Let \(\bar e = \sum_j s_j e_j\) be the output-weighted average intensity. Each year country \(i\)’s account receives \[
A_i = \frac{a}{N} + \tau\,(\bar e - e_i)\,Y_i,
\tag{6}\] a base allocation from the surplus \(a\) the Trust distributes, plus a feebate at rate \(\tau\) per tonne: a credit for intensity below the benchmark and a deduction above it. Account balances \(B_i\) earn the Trust’s yield. Let \(V_i\) be the annual value to country \(i\) of the guarantees it receives as a participant and \((i_L - r_s)S_i\) its carrying cost.
Proposition 3 (Allocation). (a) Budget balance: the feebate terms sum to zero, so total allocation equals the surplus distributed, \(\sum_i A_i = a\). (b) Performance: a country that cuts its emissions by one tonne through lower intensity raises its allocation by \(\tau(1 - s_i)\). A leave-one-out benchmark, the average of the other participants, raises it by exactly \(\tau\), at the cost of exact budget balance. (c) Feasibility and participation: deductions can be enforced only up to the balance, so the rule is feasible in a year if \(\tau \le \min_{i:\, e_i > \bar e} (B_i + a/N)/((e_i - \bar e)Y_i)\). A country above the benchmark joins in a static comparison only if \(a/N + V_i - (i_L - r_s)S_i \ge \tau(e_i - \bar e)Y_i\). (d) Early action: a cut of \(\Delta\) in intensity made \(k\) years later than it could have been forfeits allocations of \(\sum_{j=0}^{k-1} \tau_{t+j}(1-s_i)\Delta Y_i/(1+\delta)^j > 0\). Waiting is never free, and a declining schedule of rates \(\tau_t\) raises the cost of waiting relative to a flat schedule at the later rates.
The rule is the series 1 feebate applied between countries, and its properties carry over. Part (b) is the dominant-firm result for feebates with a current-average benchmark: a country that is a large share of the covered output partly sets its own benchmark and sees only part of the rate (Stretton 2026c). Part (a) is what makes the rule affordable: the feebate moves money between accounts but needs no net money from the Trust. Part (c) is the binding constraint, and it shows why the international feebate needs a trust. Without balances to deduct from, any positive \(\tau\) requires the most carbon-intensive participants to pay their peers, which sovereigns will not do (Stretton 2026i, ch. 5). With balances, \(\tau\) is limited by the size of the accounts relative to the deviations from the benchmark. Part (d) answers the additionality problem. A payment for cuts measured against a baseline is worth as much, or more, if the cut is made later, so it rewards waiting. A feebate is a flow earned every year a country is below the benchmark, so delay forfeits it.
Participation and strength pull against each other, and a transitional benchmark resolves the conflict. Part (c) shows that a high feebate rate drives the most carbon-intensive countries away, because their deduction exceeds what they gain from joining. Two remedies are available. The Trust can start the rate low and raise it as balances grow. Or it can give each entrant a transitional benchmark that starts at its own intensity on entry and converges to the common average on a published schedule. That is a baseline, but one fixed at entry and not a counterfactual, so it does not reward delay before entry as long as the convergence schedule is the same for every entrant, whenever it joins.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
6.2 Buffer and leverage
On the development banks’ loss record a buffer of 0.5 percent of exposure keeps the annual chance of exhaustion at 1 percent, so on paper $5 billion could support about $1 trillion of guarantees. The expected loss rate is \(\lambda = 0.0077 \times 0.049 = 0.038\) percent of exposure a year. With 20 programs a single call costs 0.25 percent of exposure in the end, and the buffer of 0.49 percent covers two calls in the same year, a leverage of about 200 times. With many small programs equation 1 gives 0.3 percent.
That trillion is a ceiling, not a forecast, and the Trust should start well below it. Exposure is limited by the green borrowing that participating governments actually undertake, and by what the AAA backer will accept. More important, the record belongs to the development banks. It reflects their preferred creditor treatment, which is informal (G20 Expert Panel on Multilateral Development Banks’ Capital Adequacy Frameworks 2022), and a new trust standing behind guarantees of market debt might not inherit it. Table 3 and Figure 1 therefore show two less favorable cases with the same correlation and number of programs. In a middle case, calls occur at 3 percent a year and lose 10 percent; the buffer is 2.5 percent and $5 billion supports $200 billion. In a stress case, calls occur at 3 percent a year and lose 37 percent, the average sovereign haircut; the buffer is 9.25 percent, a leverage of 10.8 times, and $5 billion supports about $54 billion. A prudent Trust would hold the stress-case buffer until its own record shows which case it is in. A tighter exhaustion target of 0.5 percent raises the base buffer to 0.7 percent and leaves the other two unchanged at 20 programs, because the loss distribution moves in steps of one failure.

Solid lines: 20 equal programs (steps reflect single failures). Dashed lines: many small programs, equation 1. Source: author’s calculation, 2.Source/make_wp_figures.py.



Paying calls in cash before recoveries cuts the base-case ceiling from about $1 trillion to about $390 billion. If a call costs a year’s debt service on a 10-year loan at 5 percent, 13 percent of the program, the Trust must find 0.65 percent of total exposure for each call even though it will lose only 0.25 percent in the end. Under Proposition 1(d) the buffer that keeps the chance of running out of cash at 1 percent is then 1.3 percent of exposure on the banks’ record and 3.2 percent in the middle case, and $5 billion supports about $390 billion and $150 billion. The stress case is unchanged, because there the ultimate loss per call (37 percent) exceeds a year’s debt service. A liquidity line from the AAA backer, drawn only to pay calls and repaid from recoveries, restores the solvency figures at little cost, since on the banks’ record almost all of what is called comes back.
Each donor dollar held as a buffer delivers about 80 dollars of interest savings in the base case, 10 in the middle case and 2.7 in the stress case, when the buffer earns what donors would otherwise earn. From equation 2 with no fee and no carry, the incentive per donor dollar is \(0.03/0.00038 \approx 80\) on the banks’ record and \(0.03/0.0111 = 2.7\) in the stress case. In the stress case the $54 billion of exposure saves borrowers $1.6 billion a year at a 3-point spread; paid out in cash, $1.6 billion a year would use up $5 billion in about three years. A guarantee fee of half the expected loss raises the ratios to about 160, 19 and 4.4, because the borrower pays part of the cost and the capital lasts longer (Figure 2). The parameter that matters most is whether the government’s first-loss obligation to the Trust ranks like its obligations to development banks or like its market debt.
A carry, a horizon and prudence each cut the multiplier, and the third cuts it most. At a 2 percent carry the three ratios are 63, 8.6 and 2.3; at 0.5 percent, the running costs alone, they are 75, 9.6 and 2.6. Counting only interest savings to 2050, at no carry, they are 68, 9.5 and 2.6. The large cut comes from the policy the paper recommends. A Trust that holds the 9.25 percent stress-case buffer while its losses follow the banks’ record supports $54 billion, not $1 trillion, and consumes its capital at only 0.4 percent a year. At no carry it still delivers 80 dollars per dollar in the end, but over centuries: by 2050 it has delivered 7.7 dollars per dollar and still holds 90 percent of its capital. At a 2 percent carry the ratio is 13.5. Prudence costs about four-fifths of the incentive until the Trust’s own record lets it hold less, which is the case for building that record fast, with many small programs and published calls and recoveries.

A payout fund delivers 1. Log scales. Spread saving 3 percentage points. Source: author’s calculation, 2.Source/make_wp_figures.py.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
6.3 Growth
A Trust levered to its base-case buffer must charge a guarantee fee to hold its capital steady: about 0.02 percent of exposure a year on the banks’ record, and 0.8 percent in the stress case. At the base leverage of about 200 times, expected losses consume \(0.00038/0.0049 = 7.7\) percent of capital a year, against 3.5 percent of net yield. From equation 4, the fee that stops the buffer shrinking is \(0.00038 - 0.0049 \times 0.035 = 0.02\) percent of exposure, 55 percent of the expected loss, and the borrower keeps almost all of the 3-point saving. In the stress case the fee is \(0.0111 - 0.0925 \times 0.035 = 0.79\) percent, 71 percent of the expected loss, and the borrower keeps 2.2 points. A Trust that charges no fee and has no other income shrinks by about 4 percent a year in the base case and 8.5 percent in the stress case. That is a legitimate choice, a subsidy that spends the capital slowly, but it is spending, not holding.
A Trust that holds the stress-case buffer grows on its own yield if its losses follow the banks’ record. With a 9.25 percent buffer and expected losses of 0.038 percent of exposure, losses consume 0.4 percent of capital a year against a net yield of 3.5 percent, so capital grows by 3.1 percent a year with no fee and no other income, to $10.7 billion after 25 years (Figure 3). The condition after equation 4 holds: the buffer’s net yield exceeds its expected losses. If losses are at the stress level, the same Trust shrinks by 8.5 percent a year without fee income. The self-funding question is therefore answered by the losses the Trust actually suffers, which it will observe within a few years.
Fee income on private co-investment makes the Trust grow faster, quickly at first and then more slowly. With $95 billion of private equity at a 10 percent gross return and a 25 percent fee, the Trust earns $2.4 billion a year. Holding the stress-case buffer with no guarantee fee, it grows by about half in its first year. If losses follow the banks’ record it reaches $34 billion after 10 years and $98 billion after 25, by which time it supports about $1.1 trillion of guarantees. If losses are at the stress level, the net burn rate is 8.5 percent, capital reaches $18.5 billion after 10 years and levels off near \(K^* = 2.4/0.085 \approx 28\) billion (equation 5). With only $10 billion of private co-investment the Trust reaches $9.7 billion after 10 years on the banks’ record and, in the stress case, falls toward $2.9 billion, below its launch capital.






Figure 3: With the stress-case buffer held, the loss record decides whether the Trust grows. Trust capital over 25 years from $5 billion at launch, no guarantee fee, exposure kept at capital divided by 9.25 percent. Stylized parameters in Table 2. Source: author’s calculation, 2.Source/make_wp_figures.py.



Earlier versions computed growth at full leverage on the banks’ record, which implies more guarantees than developing countries have debt. At a 0.49 percent buffer and no guarantee fee, capital levels off near $57 billion; but at 200 times leverage that capital would stand behind about $11.5 trillion of guarantees, more than the $8.9 trillion combined external debt of all low- and middle-income countries in 2024 (World Bank 2025). Long before that, exposure is limited by demand, and a Trust whose capital outgrows its guarantee book is a Trust holding a thicker buffer than it needs, which grows. This paper therefore reports growth with the stress-case buffer.
The largest uncertainty is whether $95 billion of private equity will co-invest on these terms. It is 19 times the Trust’s launch capital and more than 100 times what Climate Investor One raised for development and construction equity (FMO 2019). A 7.5 percent net return is also low for construction-stage equity in developing countries, where the cost of capital for solar power is well over twice that in advanced economies (International Energy Agency 2024); under Proposition 2(c), investors who require more will not come, and the fee raises nothing. The calibration treats $95 billion as an upper case and $10 billion as a lower one. The growth result does not depend on the number, only on its sign: without fee income, a Trust that holds a thin buffer must charge most of its expected loss as a fee, and one that holds a thick buffer grows only if its losses are low.
The country stakes cost about $40 million a year to carry. At a 5 percent policy loan rate and a 4 percent buffer yield, the $4 billion of borrowed country stakes costs participants 1 point, or $40 million a year in total, $4 million for each of ten countries. The guarantees the Trust supports save them $1.6 billion a year at the base spread even with the stress-case buffer, and up to $30 billion on the banks’ record, so the condition after Proposition 2 holds by a wide margin in aggregate. It may fail for a country that borrows to contribute but receives little guarantee exposure, which argues for linking each country’s guarantee capacity to its stake as well as to its notional capitalized value.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
6.4 One set of numbers
Earlier versions of the proposal used two sets of numbers, and this paper uses one. The May 2024 proposal and Time and Chance charge private investors about 25 percent of investment returns and assume a 10 percent return, so that $800 billion of equity across eight funds pays the Trust $20 billion a year; the same chapter also uses a 10 percent fee on a 15 percent return, $1.5 billion a year on $100 billion (Stretton 2024; Stretton 2026j, ch. 20). The two give similar fee income per dollar of private equity, 2.5 and 1.5 percent a year. This paper uses the 25 percent fee and 10 percent return throughout. Private investors then keep 7.5 percent, which is the hurdle the fee must respect under Proposition 2(c). The earlier claims that the Trust doubles “every two years” or “every three years” describe launch growth only.
The headline of $2 trillion a year of investment from eight funds is gross leveraged investment, not the Trust’s capacity, and is not carried forward. It assumes a global fund and seven regional funds of the same size, $800 billion of equity in total, debt of four times equity and a two-year construction cycle (Stretton 2026j, ch. 20). Each step is plausible, but together they require $760 billion of private equity on the Trust’s terms. The earlier list of regional funds also included North America, Europe and Central Asia, and China, which sits oddly with beneficiaries who are the future populations of participating developing countries. This paper restricts the regional funds to regions with participating developing countries.
Profit allocations cannot pay a full carbon price, and the calibration shows why the design does not depend on them. Earlier drafts sized the incentive at $100 per tonne on a 10 percent cut in about 10 billion tonnes a year, or about $100 billion (Stretton 2026j, ch. 20). That is about 40 times the Trust’s fee income in the upper case. The large rewards come elsewhere: from the guarantees the buffer supports, worth $1.6 billion a year to borrowers at launch with the stress-case buffer, more as the record allows a thinner buffer and as the Trust grows, and from the feebate between accounts, which costs nothing net.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
6.5 The feebate between accounts
Account balances, not the Trust’s income, limit the strength of the feebate between accounts. In a stylized power sector of ten participating countries, each producing 200 terawatt-hours a year at intensities spread evenly from 0.3 to 0.9 tonnes of CO₂ per megawatt-hour, the benchmark is 0.6 and the most carbon-intensive country is 60 million tonnes above it. A feebate of $10 per tonne moves at most $0.6 billion a year to or from any one account and nets to zero. If a $5 billion Trust were divided equally among the ten accounts, a single year’s deduction could not exceed the balance at any rate above about $8 per tonne; this ignores the year’s base allocation, so it is the conservative version of Proposition 3(c). After 10 years of growth with the stress-case buffer and $95 billion of co-investment, the limit is about $31 per tonne in the stress case ($18.5 billion of capital) and $57 per tonne on the banks’ record ($34 billion).
Participation binds earlier, and how much earlier depends on the buffer the Trust holds. With a base allocation of $100 million a year per country and a carrying cost of $4 million, the most carbon-intensive country gains from joining at rates up to about $4 per tonne while the Trust holds the stress-case buffer, because $54 billion of guarantees saves each country only $162 million a year. Once its record allows the middle-case buffer the limit rises to about $12 per tonne, and on the banks’ record, with guarantee savings of up to $3 billion a year per country, to about $53 per tonne. That is why the transitional benchmark of Section 5.4 is needed until the Trust’s own record is known.

title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength

Footnotes


The proposal was first written as the Climate Incentives Trust in May 2024 (Stretton 2024) and developed in the book manuscript Time and Chance (Stretton 2026j, chs. 14, 18–20). The regional fund design and the design questions draw on joint work on two-stage clean energy project finance with Jasper Zimmermann. Errors are the author’s own.↩︎

title: 4. Sovereign Incentives
text:
The benefits of cutting emissions are global and the costs national, so incentives for national climate policy have to come from outside. Cash transfers on the scale needed are politically impossible. This section of papers argues that the international system should instead reward governments with what it can supply cheaply and they value highly: cheaper borrowing, delivered through guarantees and collateral. A guarantee saves the borrower the full credit spread but costs its provider only expected loss and the carry on a buffer, so on the development banks’ own sovereign loss record each dollar of donor cost delivers about 80 dollars of interest saving, and 2.7 in a stress case where a new facility does not inherit their preferred-creditor status. Net of the default option the borrower gives up, the country’s gain is about 27 per dollar (1.9 in the stress case), and the ratios fall when the guarantor’s capital carries a cost or calls must be met in cash, so the institution behind the guarantees matters. Three instruments follow: a notional capitalized value that turns a country’s carbon stock into guarantee capacity, debited for every tonne emitted above an allowance; a Climate Investment Trust that holds the capital behind those guarantees instead of spending it; and codified sustainability-linked lending, which delivers the reward but is too small on its own. Capacity that declines as clean technology gets cheaper pays a premium for acting now.
