title: 4. Sovereign Incentives
section: 4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
text:
4.1 Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow: Notional Capitalized Value and Guarantee-Based Climate Incentives
Turning carbon stocks and low-emission paths into cheaper borrowing
Climate finance pays for tonnes avoided against baselines nobody can observe, and almost nothing for carbon stocks never released. This brief proposes crediting each country with a notional capitalized value: a balance opened by its carbon stock, debited for every tonne emitted above an agreed allowance, and used as guarantee capacity on green borrowing rather than paid out. A guarantee is worth the full spread to the borrower but costs only the expected loss, so on the development banks’ record each dollar of expected loss buys about 80 dollars of interest saving (2.7 in a stress case). For a forest country with Guyana’s stock, a $5 billion balance prices emissions at about $30 a tonne.

title: 4. Sovereign Incentives
section: 4.2 The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
4.2 The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
A buffer fund that insures policy guarantees, invests in clean energy and holds national climate accounts
International rewards for national climate policy fail because donors will not vote for large cash transfers and governments cannot borrow against promises. This brief proposes a Climate Investment Trust that holds capital instead of spending it. One pool stands second behind the guarantees that reward policy, earns fees by co-investing in clean energy, and holds national accounts that countries pledge as collateral now and draw after 2050. On the development banks’ sovereign loss record, each donor dollar delivers about 80 dollars of interest savings; without their preferred-creditor status, 2.7. Holding the cautious buffer, the Trust grows on its own yield if losses follow the banks’ record.

title: 4. Sovereign Incentives
section: 4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
4.3 Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
Standard indicators, verification and pricing, and why the reward must be bigger than an interest margin
Sustainability-linked debt lowers a government’s interest rate when it meets agreed climate targets, but it remains rare, bespoke and small: Uruguay’s 2023 World Bank loan, the first of its kind, can save the country at most $12.5 million. This brief proposes codifying the instrument, with standard indicators, verification from published data and a published price per tonne. The reward should come from outside, through an intermediary, because a bond whose coupon moves with results makes the government pay for its own reward. Even then an interest margin is too small to pay for major reforms. Guarantee capacity as the reward gives it scale.

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The proposal builds on a policy brief on regional payment intermediary facilities written with Nils Zimmermann and on the solar payments intermediary proposal developed by Evie Davey. The full analysis, with the model, proofs and calibration, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Clean power in developing countries is cheap to build and dear to finance. The same solar plant sells power 80 percent dearer when its capital costs 12 percent a year rather than 4, and the cost of capital for solar in emerging and developing economies is well over twice that in advanced economies.
The risk investors price most directly is the buyer. A loss-making state distribution company that pays late and recovers little adds about 11 percent to the tariff in a stylized case.
Put a creditworthy payment intermediary between generators and distribution companies. It buys under one standard contract, pays generators whatever the buyer does, and collects arrears behind a guarantee waterfall agreed in advance.
Guarantee the contract, not the debt. A contract guarantee removes the whole premium for about half its value in expected cost; a debt guarantee removes under a third of it and puts the whole loan at risk.
Pair the facility with utility reform, and record the guarantee. Without better collection and fewer defaults the facility only moves risk to the state, as India’s experience shows.


Clean power costs too much because its finance does
Solar power is a bond with panels attached. Almost all of its cost is paid up front, and the tariff repays the capital. Table 1 shows a representative utility-scale plant costing $800 per kilowatt, running at a 20 percent capacity factor for 25 years; only the cost of capital changes from column to column. At a 4 percent real weighted average cost of capital (WACC) the plant needs 3.6 US cents per kilowatt-hour. At 12 percent it needs 6.5 cents, 80 percent more for the same hardware.



Table 1: The same solar plant costs twice as much at 15 percent as at 4 percent (stylized). $800/kW, capacity factor 20 percent, operation and maintenance $12/kW a year, 25-year life, capital spent at commissioning. “Return on capital” is the capital charge above straight-line depreciation. Source: working paper, Table 1.

Developing countries pay far more for capital than rich ones. The International Energy Agency’s survey of financiers finds that the cost of capital for utility-scale solar in emerging and developing economies is well over twice that in advanced economies, and that financing can be half or more of the cost of the power. It estimates that narrowing the gap by one percentage point would cut clean energy financing costs in these economies by about $150 billion a year (International Energy Agency 2024).


The buyer of the power is the risk
A finished solar plant carries little operating risk; the company that buys its power carries a lot. In most developing countries that buyer, the offtaker, is a state-owned distribution company that sells below cost and collects badly. A World Bank study of 39 Sub-Saharan African countries found only two, Seychelles and Uganda, with a financially viable electricity sector (Trimble et al. 2016). The IEA ranks payment risk among the three sector risks that investors price most in these economies (International Energy Agency 2024).
Long arrears and poor recovery cost far more than lateness. Suppose a distribution company falls into a year of unpaid bills once every six or seven years and eventually pays back 60 percent of what it withheld, and investors charge for that risk at twice its expected loss. The generator then needs a tariff 11 percent above its cost, the same as 1.4 percentage points on the cost of capital. A buyer that is late as often but pays back 90 percent adds only 0.4 points; one that pays back 30 percent adds 2.6 (stylized; working paper, the premium).


A payment intermediary removes the risk at source
The fix is to change whom the generator is exposed to. A payment intermediary facility is a creditworthy institution that buys power from generators under one standard power purchase agreement, sells it on to distribution companies, and pays generators in full and on time whatever the distribution companies do. Their arrears become a debt to the facility, a repeat creditor with more patience and more leverage than any single developer.
A guarantee waterfall, agreed before the first tender, stands behind the facility. If a distribution company does not pay, the facility calls in turn on its state or provincial owner, on the national government through an intercept of its transfers to that owner, on a multilateral agency, and on a donor contingency account. The order is fixed in advance, and the first calls fall on the governments that control the utility.
Liquidity, not loss, is what can break the facility. A devaluation or a fuel shock can push many distribution companies into arrears at once. In a stylized regional facility buying 2 gigawatts of solar power, with contract payments of $174 million a year, a buffer of about $57 million, a third of a year’s payments, bridges a 1-in-200-year crisis until the national layer pays (working paper, the waterfall).


Guarantee the contract, not the debt
A contract guarantee removes the whole premium; a debt guarantee removes only the lenders’ share. A debt guarantee pays lenders when the project cannot service its loan, whatever the cause, so equity still bears the buyer’s arrears and still charges for them. A contract guarantee pays the generator when the buyer does not, so equity and debt are both paid.



Table 2: A contract guarantee removes more of the premium per dollar of expected cost, at a fraction of the exposure (stylized). Base WACC 8 percent; one-year default episodes at 15 per 100 buyer-years; 60 percent of arrears recovered; debt is 75 percent of the $80 million cost, and lenders bear 30 percent of the buyer’s losses. The debt guarantee also covers construction and operating risks, at a further expected cost of $0.18 million a year. Source: working paper, Table 3.

The contract guarantee is cheaper per dollar saved because its claim is better. The facility keeps its claim on the distribution company, and in the stylized case recovers 58 cents of each dollar of arrears in present value; a debt guarantor’s claim runs against a project company that has itself not been paid, and recovers 39 cents three years later. Its worst case in one episode is a year of unpaid bills, $8.7 million, against the whole $60 million loan (working paper, the comparison).
The saving is real only if the facility collects better or makes default rarer. If investors charged nothing for risk and the facility collected no more than generators would, the guarantee would simply move the expected loss from investors to the state. Its value to society comes from better collection (at 80 percent recovery the saving rises to $3.6 per dollar), from fewer defaults by a buyer that faces one creditor and reform conditions, and from the state bearing a risk more cheaply than investors, which fails when the utility and the treasury are in trouble together (working paper, Proposition 2).
Small versions already work in Africa. Under the World Bank Group’s Scaling Solar program, a $3.5 million IDA guarantee behind the Zambian utility’s letter of credit supported a 47.5-megawatt plant financed with about $60 million, at a tariff of 6.015 US cents per kilowatt-hour (World Bank Group 2018). The African Trade Insurance Agency’s liquidity facility covers independent producers for six months of late payment (Wass 2017). The facility pools such guarantees behind one contract and one creditor.


India shows the design works, and that the buyers must be fixed
The Solar Energy Corporation of India is the working model of a payment intermediary. It is wholly owned by the central government, signs contracts with developers only after back-to-back sales to state distribution companies, and earns a margin of Rs 0.07 per kilowatt-hour. In July 2025 it had sales of about 60 gigawatts at an average Rs 2.93 per kilowatt-hour, well below the distribution companies’ average purchase cost, and was rated AAA (ICRA 2025). Its margin, 2.4 percent of the tariff, pays for itself if it lowers the cost of capital by a third of a percentage point.
Its protections are layered much as the waterfall proposes. Distribution companies must open letters of credit, and since August 2019 grid operators may schedule power only once they have (Power Line 2019). A payment security fund covers older capacity. Since October 2016 the corporation has been a beneficiary of an agreement among the central government, the states and the Reserve Bank of India under which the central bank can debit a defaulting state’s account; the corporation used it against distribution companies in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka in 2020–22 (ICRA 2025).
But the buyers were never fixed, and the center paid twice. Most state distribution companies remain financially weak, and their letter-of-credit coverage is only 68 percent (ICRA 2025). In 2020 the central government organized Rs 90,000 crore of loans to distribution companies against state guarantees so they could pay generators (CRISIL Ratings 2020), and in 2022 it let them reschedule their arrears over up to four years (Power Line 2022). Legacy arrears fell from Rs 1,39,947 crore in June 2022 to Rs 3,330 crore in March 2026 (Press Trust of India 2026). The risk moved to the center; it was not removed.
Nigeria shows the failure. Its bulk electricity trader, a single buyer, expected to collect about a quarter of its bills in 2017 and needed a central bank loan of up to N701 billion to pay generators (Okafor 2017). It had no reliable revenue and no funded layer behind it. A single buyer of that kind invites weak payment discipline and hidden liabilities, as the World Bank warned long ago (Lovei 2000); the facility avoids that by keeping procurement competitive, leaving the buyers’ obligations alive and recording its guarantees (working paper, objections).


Design the facility so the risk stays small
Write contracts in the currency the buyer earns. A dollar tariff hands the distribution company, and behind it the state, the devaluation risk of every contract, and that risk arrives in a balance of payments crisis, when every buyer is stressed at once. Where projects borrow in dollars, the facility should hold and price the mismatch in the open.
Let tariffs decline over the life of the contract. A flat 20-year price signed when solar is dear becomes a target for renegotiation as new plants get cheaper. A tariff starting at 7.7 cents and falling to 3.9 cents by year 7 has the same present value at 8 percent as a flat 5 cents, but leaves 23 percent less owed after year 7 and nearly halves the part above the cost of new solar (stylized; working paper, tariff profile).
Build national facilities in large markets and regional ones for small states. India, Nigeria and Brazil can each diversify across many distribution companies. Small states should share a facility, for example in the Economic Community of West African States; it lacks a cross-border intercept like India’s, so its multilateral layer must be stronger.
Make utility reform a condition of entry. A guarantee makes the generator whole; it does not make the utility solvent. Entry should require a published path to cost-recovery tariffs, letters of credit, an intercept agreement and loss-reduction targets, with access widening as targets are met.


The state’s exposure shrinks but does not vanish
The facility turns an implicit liability into a smaller, contracted one. States already bail out their utilities, as India did in 2020 and 2022 and Nigeria in 2017. The waterfall makes that exposure contingent on the state’s own utility failing to pay, fixes its order and cap in advance, and, with reform, makes it smaller. In the stylized regional facility the national government expects to be called for about 2.2 percent of contract payments a year, before it recovers from its own utility.
Record the guarantee at its expected cost under a published cap. International statistical standards treat expected calls under a scheme of many similar guarantees as a liability (International Monetary Fund 2014); a facility with one standard contract is such a scheme. Countries in debt distress can buy power as a service under the facility’s contracts, but a long-term take-or-pay contract is still a fiscal commitment and belongs in debt analysis, alongside the fuel bill it replaces (working paper, fiscal accounting).


What to do
Finance ministries: build or join a facility before the next tender. Use one standard power purchase agreement and sign the guarantee waterfall first; route new utility-scale renewable procurement through it, in local currency, on declining tariffs; and record the national layer at expected cost under a published cap.
Regulators and utilities: make payment security a condition of supply. Require letters of credit, enforce dispatch rules like India’s, and put distribution companies on a published path to cost recovery as the price of entry.
Development banks and donors: guarantee the facility, not the loans. Stand as the multilateral layer, pool payment guarantees of the Scaling Solar kind behind one facility, and fund the donor contingency account at the bottom of the waterfall. Once contracts are standard and guaranteed, the plants can be refinanced as a few standard securities (Brief 3.2).


Related papers in this series

Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.2: two-stage finance and synthetic sovereign bonds, which refinance the contracts this facility makes safe (Stretton 2026b).
No. 4.1: guarantee capacity earned by climate policy, which can stand behind the facility’s waterfall (Stretton 2026c).
No. 4.2: the Climate Investment Trust, a source of loss-absorbing capital for the donor layer (Stretton 2026d).
No. 4.3: sustainability-linked sovereign lending, a way to pay for the utility reforms that make the guarantee affordable (Stretton 2026a).
The working paper behind this brief: the model, proofs, calibration and the record in India, Nigeria and Zambia.

title: From Projects to Asset Classes
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The two-stage finance and tiered guarantee material was developed with Jasper Zimmermann. The full analysis, with the model, proofs and robustness checks, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Bespoke finance is expensive finance. Solar power is mostly the cost of the money that built it, and that money is dear partly because each plant is financed alone, on bespoke terms.
Split each project at commissioning. Banks finance the two-year build; once the plant runs, bond investors refinance its debt.
Pool and tranche operating plants under one standard contract. A thin first-loss layer and a mezzanine let 70 to 92 percent of the debt come from a highly rated senior “synthetic sovereign bond”.
The saving is about a fifth of the price of solar power. It is still 14 percent with the thick cushions real deals carry.
Pool across countries, publish the numbers, and keep the host’s exposure on the books. Ten-country pools need about 40 percent less cushion; the host’s guarantees remain contingent liabilities.


Bespoke finance is expensive finance
The cost of capital, not the cost of panels, now sets the price of clean power in developing countries. For a stylized solar plant costing $800 per kilowatt with a 20 percent capacity factor, power costs 3.6 US cents per kilowatt-hour at a 4 percent cost of capital and 6.5 cents at 12 percent. At 10 percent, financing is 56 percent of the price (working paper, calibration). The International Energy Agency’s survey of financiers found that the cost of capital for utility-scale solar in emerging and developing economies is well over twice that in advanced economies, and that financing can be around half or more of the cost of their solar power (International Energy Agency 2024).
Removing the risk that the buyer will not pay is the first step. The companion brief proposes a payment intermediary that buys power under one standard contract and pays generators in full and on time whatever the state-owned distribution company does, backed by a waterfall of guarantors agreed in advance (Brief 3.1).
A guaranteed contract is not yet cheap money. Each project is still financed alone, by a lender who prices the host government into every coupon and cannot sell the loan, because nobody will rate plants one at a time. Deal-by-deal blended finance mobilized only $0.75 of private money per dollar of development finance across developing countries in 2012–2015, and $0.37 in low-income countries (Attridge and Engen 2019). Pension funds and insurers have the money; what they lack is a standard, rated security they are allowed to buy (Ehlers 2014; Arezki et al. 2017).


Split each project at commissioning
A plant under construction and a plant in operation are different credits. Construction lasts about two years and needs supervision; operation lasts twenty-five, with predictable output and no fuel. Moody’s data on 6,389 project finance loans show default rates like those of speculative-grade borrowers in the first three years, falling toward single-A levels by year seven; loans that survived their first three years defaulted at under 3 percent over the next seven, and lenders recovered 80 percent on average (Moody’s Investors Service 2017).
Two-stage finance gives each phase to the investor who prices it most cheaply. Banks and development finance institutions, which can supervise construction, lend for the build; bond investors, who want long, safe cash flows, refinance the operating plant’s debt. Single-stage finance carries the construction-era price of risk through all twenty-five years of operation.
The rate on the long phase is what matters. Because operation lasts more than ten times as long as construction, a percentage point off the operating cost of capital lowers the price of power about nine to eleven times as much as a point off the construction rate (working paper, the refinancing gain).
A contingent purchase contract ties the two stages together. Before construction, the payment intermediary commits to buy the plant’s power on completion under its standard contract. The construction lender then lends against a creditworthy buyer, and the pool knows exactly what it will be offered. Developers can bid a tariff on the refinanced cost only if refinancing is assured; otherwise they add a premium for the risk that it will not come.


Pool the operating plants and tranche the pool
Operating plants’ debt is pooled and refinanced through three securities, each for a different investor. A first-loss tranche of equity absorbs losses before any debt does; its natural holder is a regional fund of the Climate Investment Trust (Brief 4.2). A thin mezzanine sits above it, held by development lenders or insurers, or replaced by a guarantee from highly rated sovereigns. The senior synthetic sovereign bond, backed by guaranteed contracts on operating plants, the cushion beneath it and that co-guarantee, is rated on the structure rather than on the host government, and is sold to pension funds and insurers.
In a large pool of operating plants, a cushion of 5 to 8 percent makes the senior bond near-AAA. A standard portfolio model, the one behind the Basel bank capital rules, sizes the cushion from three numbers: how often operating plants default, how much is lost when they do, and how much they fail together. With a 5 percent chance of default over ten years and 80 percent recovery, a near-AAA senior bond needs 4.8 percent of losses absorbed beneath it if plants fail together a little (a correlation of 0.10) and 7.7 percent if they fail together more (0.20). Halving recovery doubles the cushion (working paper, how much first loss).
The host government is the main reason plants fail together, and pooling across countries removes it. Plants in one country share a currency, a regulator, a distribution sector and a treasury, so a sovereign crisis hits them all at once. In the working paper’s illustration, a near-AAA bond on a single-country pool needs 9.1 percent subordination; on a pool spread over ten countries, 5.3 percent. That gain is available only if the plants carry the same contract: identical contracts make portfolios, and portfolios make ratings.






Figure 1: The cost of power from a stylized solar plant falls by about a fifth when its senior debt is refinanced into a tranched pool. Two-stage cases build at 12 percent and refinance the senior debt (80 percent of the plant’s cost) at the rate shown; project equity earns 12 percent. What it saves: about a fifth of the price of power
Refinancing into a tranched pool cuts the cost of solar power from 6.2 to 5.0 cents per kilowatt-hour. Table 1 compares ways of financing the stylized plant, including interest during a two-year build. Against single-stage finance at 10 percent, building at 12 percent and refinancing the senior debt into a stand-alone project bond at 8 percent saves 7 percent. Refinancing it into the pool, whose blended cost is 5.65 percent with stylized returns of 12 percent on first loss, 8 percent on mezzanine and 5 percent on the senior bond, saves 19 percent. The sponsor’s equity, a fifth of the plant’s cost, still earns 12 percent.

The saving survives the strongest objection: real deals carry much thicker cushions. The first securitization of Asian infrastructure loans, Clifford Capital’s Bayfront deal of 2018, put 30 percent of the notes beneath its most senior class (Allen & Gledhill 2018). Its pool was small (37 loans), mixed sectors and included plants still under construction, and agencies had no record to rely on. With the same 30 percent cushion, the saving is still 14 percent, because the senior bond still funds most of the pool cheaply (working paper, robustness). The 5 to 8 percent cushion is where a large, standard pool with a track record ends up, not where the first issue starts.
A sovereign co-guarantee of the mezzanine is cheap in expectation and expensive in a crisis. On a $10 billion pool it covers $460 million at an expected cost of about $6 million over ten years, but all $460 million can be drawn in a regional crisis.


Where there is no contract, guarantee the bond
Transmission lines and storage have no power contract to guarantee, and without them cheap generation buys nothing. Vietnam added 16.5 gigawatts of solar in 2019–2020, mostly in southern provinces with a weak grid, and curtailed about 364 gigawatt-hours of solar output in 2020 (Ketelsen et al. 2023). South Africa’s 2022 auction sought 3,200 megawatts of wind and awarded none, because the grid in the Eastern and Western Cape, where every wind bid was, had no room (Bellini 2022).
The first choice is to create a contract. Privately financed transmission lines, tendered and paid on availability, raised more than $24.5 billion of investment in Brazil, Chile, Peru and India in 1998–2015 (World Bank 2017). A contracted line can enter the pool like a solar plant. The rule is simple: guarantee the contract where there is one, and guarantee the bond where there is not.
For backbone lines and storage that cannot be contracted, a tiered bond guarantee does the job, conditional on reform. Behind the bonds stand the government that regulates the power system, then the national government, then a donor-backed vehicle. Guarantees go only to governments that adopt agreed reforms: the standard power purchase agreement, cost-reflective tariffs, a coal retirement schedule and workable grid connection. Because a state and its national government often fail together, the donor tier carries more than it seems: in a stylized example, raising the correlation between tiers from zero to 0.5 triples the chance that the donor is called, from 1.2 to 3.6 percent over ten years (working paper, tiered guarantees).


Local currency for domestic savers
A dollar senior bond moves currency risk to the host; a local-currency senior tranche keeps it out. Where power contracts are in local currency, the pool can issue the same senior claim in local currency, with the same cushion beneath it, for domestic pension funds, insurers and banks. Banks can sell it as a fixed-term green savings certificate. A local-currency pool cannot diversify across countries, so it needs a thicker cushion or a local-currency guarantor such as GuarantCo, rated A1 by Moody’s and AA− by Fitch (Private Infrastructure Development Group 2025).
The host government’s exposure shrinks but does not vanish. The national government stands in the guarantee waterfall behind the intermediary and in the second tier of grid guarantees. These are contingent liabilities, mostly triggered only if the government’s own utility stops paying or its own policy reverses. They should be recorded and capped, not denied.


What to do
Payment intermediaries should write a contingent power purchase agreement and a published refinancing route into every auction, so that developers bid on the refinanced cost of capital.
Development banks should sponsor regional pools of operating clean power plants under one standard contract, size the first loss with a published model at the cautious end of plausible correlation and recovery, and expect the first issues to carry thick cushions that thin as a record builds. Keep each pool to one asset type, with no re-securitization.
The Climate Investment Trust’s regional funds should hold the first-loss tranches, priced explicitly and published, with the right to sell seasoned positions so the capital recycles (Brief 4.2).
Highly rated sovereigns should co-guarantee the mezzanine layer rather than fund it, and hold explicit reserves against the correlated tail.
Host governments should contract transmission and storage where they can, and seek tiered bond guarantees, conditional on reform, where they cannot. They should record their contingent liabilities under these structures and cap them.
Central banks and financial regulators should treat the local-currency senior tranche as a high-grade asset for domestic pension funds, insurers and banks, with capital treatment that matches its structure.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
text: Working paper, version 0.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 2.1. Version 0.1 (April 2026) was a sketch; this version adds the literature, states the results as propositions with their conditions, corrects the specification of the two destination layers, and computes the worked examples and revenue estimates.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
text:
3.1 Land: the oldest rent tax
The case for taxing land rent is as old as political economy. Ricardo (1817, ch. 2) treated the rent of land as a surplus, the payment for the use of the soil’s original powers, determined by the price of its produce rather than determining it. Mill (1848, bk. 5, ch. 3) proposed taxing the future increase in rent “arising from the mere action of natural causes”, while sparing existing rents, a transition rule that Stretton and Styles (2020) revive. George (1879) made the land value tax a popular cause, on the argument that land value is created by the community, not the owner. Dwyer (2014) traces the longer history, back to the physiocrats and Adam Smith, of the view that rent is the natural base of public revenue. Modern theory gives the idea a precise form in the Henry George theorem: in a city of optimal size with optimal local public goods, aggregate land rent equals spending on those goods (Arnott and Stiglitz 1979).
The Mirrlees Review called the economic case for taxing land “very strong” (Mirrlees et al. 2011, ch. 16). Land is not produced and its supply is fixed, so a tax on its value is reflected one-for-one in a lower price: owners on the day the tax is announced suffer a windfall loss, and nothing else changes. The review recommended a land value tax for business and agricultural land, replacing business rates and stamp duty, and a tax on housing services in place of council tax. The capitalization result has one theoretical exception: when land and capital are alternative stores of wealth, a land tax pushes savings into capital, lowering the interest rate and raising wages, so part of the burden shifts from landowners to the owners of capital (Feldstein 1977). The effect strengthens the case for the tax, which then raises investment, but it qualifies the claim that landowners bear all of it.
The evidence is limited but consistent. Pittsburgh sharply raised its tax rate on land, but not on buildings, in 1979–80; building activity rose in the following decade while it fell in comparable cities, though other causes contributed (Oates and Schwab 1997). Across Pennsylvania municipalities that adopted split-rate taxes, the ratio of capital to land rose and the main effect was more housing units rather than larger ones (Banzhaf and Lavery 2010). Across OECD countries, recurrent taxes on immovable property are the taxes least harmful to growth (Arnold et al. 2011), and they are widely seen as underused (Norregaard 2013): in 2023 they raised 0.95 percent of GDP on average across the OECD (OECD 2025). Many are levied on outdated values, which the OECD names as the first thing to fix (OECD 2022).

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
section: 3.2 Corporate profit: taxing the return above normal
text:
3.2 Corporate profit: taxing the return above normal
The corporate counterpart of the land tax is a tax on profit above the normal return to capital. Brown (1948) showed that a tax on cash flow, with investment deducted immediately, takes a share of a project’s net present value and leaves the decision to invest unchanged. The Meade Committee (1978) set out the R-based and S-based cash-flow taxes. Boadway and Bruce (1984) showed that any depreciation schedule combined with a deduction for the cost of funds on the written-down value of assets gives the same neutrality, and the IFS Capital Taxes Group (1991) turned the result into the allowance for corporate equity (ACE): a deduction for a notional return on shareholders’ funds, which taxes only profit above that return. Bond and Devereux (2003) proved that the ACE is neutral under uncertainty, provided the tax rules for losses, default and wind-up are right. The Mirrlees Review recommended an ACE for the United Kingdom (Mirrlees et al. 2011, ch. 17).
Practice has been mixed. Belgium introduced a notional interest deduction in 2006, narrowed it in 2018 and abolished it for periods ending on or after 31 December 2023 (Kingdom of Belgium 2022); Italy introduced an ACE in 2011 and repealed it from 2024 (Republic of Italy 2023); Austria, Croatia and Brazil ran variants (Klemm 2007). The evidence is that an ACE reduces leverage (Princen 2012; Hebous and Ruf 2017), but that a unilateral ACE also invites multinationals to route intra-group lending into the country to claim the allowance (Hebous and Ruf 2017), and that when rates are raised to pay for it, profit shifting and discrete location choices make it less attractive for a single country than for countries acting together (Mooij and Devereux 2011). Both findings bear directly on this paper’s design.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
section: 3.3 Natural resources: high rates on location-specific rent
text:
3.3 Natural resources: high rates on location-specific rent
Resource rent taxes are the working proof that rent can be taxed at high rates under free movement of capital. Garnaut and Clunies Ross (1975) proposed a tax that carries a project’s net cash flows forward at a threshold rate of return and taxes only the surplus above it; it became the model for Australia’s petroleum resource rent tax. Boadway and Keen (2010) set out the theory. Norway taxes petroleum profit at a combined marginal rate of 78 percent, with the special tax computed on a cash-flow basis since 2022 (Norwegian Ministry of Energy and Norwegian Offshore Directorate 2025). The resource is where it is, so the rent cannot move, and the cash-flow base leaves the normal return untaxed.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
text:
3.4 Source, destination and mobile rent
A small open economy has a strong reason not to tax the normal return on capital at source, because the cost of capital is set abroad; the Mirrlees Review draws the further distinction on which this paper rests, between rents that are specific to a location (natural resources, proximity to a large market, local skills) and rents that are mobile, such as the return to a patent or a brand (Mirrlees et al. 2011, ch. 18). Location-specific rent can be taxed at source at high rates; mobile rent cannot. The evidence on mobility is strong. Discrete location choices depend on the effective average tax rate, which rises toward the statutory rate as profitability rises (Devereux and Griffith 2003). Reported profit is highly sensitive to rate differences: a meta-analysis finds that a 1 percentage point lower rate than in other countries raises reported before-tax income by 1.5 percent (Beer et al. 2020).
The proposed answer in the literature is to tax at destination. A destination-based cash-flow tax taxes sales to domestic customers less domestic costs; imports are taxed and exports exempt, as under value-added tax (VAT), so the base is where the customer is and cannot be moved by relocating production or booking profit elsewhere (A. Auerbach et al. 2017; Devereux et al. 2021). With a flexible exchange rate the currency appreciates to offset the border adjustment and trade is unaffected (A. Auerbach et al. 2017). In a model with three sources of rent, a destination-based cash-flow tax does not distort behavior, while a source-based one does (A. J. Auerbach and Devereux 2018). A second proposal, residual profit allocation by income, splits a group’s profit into a routine part, taxed at source, and a residual part, taxed where sales are made (Devereux et al. 2021). The OECD’s Pillar One adopted the same idea in Amount A, which would allocate 25 percent of the residual profit of the largest groups, defined as profit above 10 percent of revenue, to market countries; its Pillar Two sets a 15 percent minimum tax on groups with revenue above €750 million, with a carve-out of 5 percent of payroll and of tangible assets (OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS 2021). Meanwhile several countries have taxed digital revenue directly, at low rates: France at 3 percent from 2019 and the United Kingdom at 2 percent from 2020 (French Republic 2019; United Kingdom 2020).

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
text:
3.5 Market power
The evidence that rent in the corporate sector has grown is substantial but disputed. In United States firm-level data, aggregate markups rose from 21 percent above marginal cost in 1980 to 61 percent, driven by the upper tail of the distribution, and the average profit rate rose from 1 to 8 percent (De Loecker et al. 2020). Measured directly from the cost of capital, a large rise in the share of pure profit offsets the decline in the labor and capital shares (Barkai 2020). The measurement is contested: different methods give different trends, and existing methods cannot rule out stable or modestly rising markups (Basu 2019). The interpretation is contested too: concentration and high profit may reflect the superior efficiency of leading firms (Demsetz 1973), and the reallocation of sales toward the most productive “superstar” firms explains much of the fall in the labor share (Autor et al. 2020).

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
text:
3.6 What is new
Each instrument in this paper has a literature; what is missing is a design that combines them for a country that will not restrict capital movements. The land tax literature rarely discusses corporate rent, and the corporate literature treats the land tax, if at all, as a separate reform. The ACE literature shows a unilateral ACE invites shifting; the destination literature proposes replacing the corporate tax, which few governments will do at once. This paper keeps a profit tax at source, adds destination layers only where shifting is easy, presumes rent for large firms, and caps the total by the rent earned from local customers. It also computes what the combination does for firms of different kinds.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
text:
4.1 Land above a household allowance
Every household receives an allowance of land value \(A\), exempt from tax. Above it, the household pays a land value tax at rate \(\tau_L\) on the assessed site value, the value of the land without its buildings: \[
T_{\text{land}} = \tau_L \cdot \max(0,\; V_{\text{land}} - A).
\tag{1}\] For illustration, \(A\) is set at the site value of an ordinary home in a modest neighborhood, close to the median household’s holding, and \(\tau_L\) at 2–3 percent a year. Most households then pay nothing or little, while those holding land worth several times the allowance pay a meaningful rate on the excess. Land held by firms is taxed without an allowance, and the tax a firm pays is deductible from its Layer One base, so that the same rent is not taxed twice.
I have called this a “reverse wealth tax” in earlier drafts, because the allowance can be paired with a payment to households that own no land, making the schedule negative below the allowance (Stretton and Styles 2020). Here the allowance is simply a threshold, and the term is not used again.
Proposition 1 (land). If the supply of land is fixed and the tax depends only on assessed site value, not on how the land is used, the tax does not change any decision about the use of land. Its present value is capitalized into a lower land price on announcement, so its burden falls on those who own land at that date. The conditions matter. If the assessment rises when the owner builds, it becomes a tax on buildings; and if land and capital are close substitutes as stores of wealth, part of the burden shifts to capital and labor (Feldstein 1977). Capitalization is also the source of the transition problem: a household that bought its home last year bears the whole present value of the tax. Phasing the rate in, or applying it first to future increases in site value as Mill (1848) proposed, spreads that loss.
The design has three further properties. It is progressive in land wealth without being progressive in earnings. Because land cannot move, there is no exit problem: the owner can leave, but the tax stays. And because cash income and land wealth differ, owners who are rich in land and poor in cash, often pensioners, need the option to defer the tax, with interest, until sale or death (Stretton and Styles 2020).

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
text:
4.2 Market power as the default
Standard tax analysis treats market power as an exception that must be identified before it can be taxed. This paper reverses the presumption. For firms above a size threshold, the default assumption is that they earn substantial rent, and the burden of showing otherwise sits with the firm.
The reasoning starts from competition. In a competitive market, firms earn about the normal return on capital, because profit above it attracts entry. A firm that is large and stays large must therefore be earning rent of some kind, from network effects, brands, economies of scale, regulatory protection, patents or customer lock-in, or else operate in a sector whose minimum efficient scale is so large that only a few firms can exist. The second category is narrow: civil aircraft manufacturing and leading-edge semiconductor fabrication are examples. In most of the economy, large size reflects rent, not the technical necessity of scale.
The strongest objection is that large firms may be large because they are more productive (Demsetz 1973; Autor et al. 2020). It does not undo the presumption, because rent from superior productivity is still rent: a firm whose costs are lower than its rivals’ earns an inframarginal surplus at the market price, as Ricardo’s better land does. What the objection does show is that some of the rent is a return to past investment in innovation, which a tax could discourage if it were expected. The answer is not that the rent was “generated in the past”, as the first draft of this paper argued: a permanent, anticipated tax lowers the expected return to the investment that creates rent. The answer is Proposition 2. A tax on profit above a normal return, with losses carried forward at interest and investment (including research and development) deducted in full or through the allowance, leaves the expected return to risky investment unchanged, whatever the rate. Neutrality, not the past, protects innovation.
Three design choices follow from the presumption. First, the threshold does the work of a definition: firms above it are presumed to earn rent, firms below it are presumed competitive. Using the €750 million group revenue threshold of Pillar Two (OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS 2021) means the groups in scope already report the data needed. Second, carve-outs are narrow, sectoral and set in advance; firms in designated scale-driven sectors pay the conventional rate on rent instead of the higher one, and every other firm is covered. Third, the instruments reward local productive activity and tax rent separately, so that no instrument has to decide whether a firm is “really” competitive: the bill is low when local activity is high relative to sales and high when rent is high.
The threshold creates a cliff. Under the first draft, a firm below it paid 25 percent of all its profit, including the normal return, while one just above it paid nothing on the normal return and 50 percent of its rent. Giving the allowance to every firm, and phasing the higher rate in between €750 million and twice that figure, removes the cliff. Consolidation at group level, as under Pillar Two, prevents groups from splitting to stay below it.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
section: 4.3 Layer One: profit above a normal return
text:
4.3 Layer One: profit above a normal return
The first layer is an ACE. The firm deducts from its taxable profit a notional normal return on its equity, measured on the tax basis (the tax written-down value of its assets less its debt) rather than the book value, and only the residual is taxed: \[
B_1 = \pi - r_A E, \qquad T_1 = \tau_1 \max(0,\; B_1),
\tag{2}\] where \(\pi\) is taxable profit (with interest deductible, as now), \(E\) is equity on the tax basis and \(r_A\) the allowance rate. Losses, negative \(B_1\), are carried forward with interest at \(r_A\). The rate on large groups is \(\tau_1 = 50\) percent, within the first draft’s range of 45–55 percent.
Proposition 2 (neutrality of Layer One). If equity is measured on the tax basis, the allowance rate equals the rate at which the firm discounts its tax allowances, and losses are refunded or carried forward with interest at that rate, then the present value of tax on a marginal investment is zero for any rate \(\tau_1 < 1\), whatever the depreciation schedule. Appendix A gives the proof, which follows Boadway and Bruce (1984). Under uncertainty, the allowance rate that makes the tax neutral is the risk-free rate, provided the allowances themselves are certain, which full loss offset ensures (Bond and Devereux 2003). In practice the long-term government bond rate is the workable choice.
Two consequences follow. The rate can be high: a firm deciding whether to invest an extra euro faces the same decision at 30 or 55 percent, because the tax falls only on returns above what the euro had to earn to be worth investing. And the tax collected includes a share of the expected risk premium as well as rent; with full loss offset the government earns that share by bearing a matching share of the risk, so measured revenue overstates the pure rent captured.
Proposition 3 (where a high origin rate is safe). Layer One’s base stays in the country only for rent that is specific to its location. Rent that can be booked elsewhere, through transfer prices, intra-group debt or the location of intangible assets, responds to the gap between the country’s rate and other countries’ rates, and a firm choosing between discrete locations compares effective average rates, which approach the statutory rate for highly profitable projects. Proposition 2 concerns the scale of an investment that will be made in the country anyway; it does not protect the base from Proposition 3. A 25-point rise in the rate on declared rent, from today’s typical 25 percent to 50 percent, would on the semi-elasticity of Beer et al. (2020) reduce the reported base by roughly 37 percent, a linear extrapolation well beyond the range of the data but a fair warning of the order of magnitude. That is why the design does not stop at Layer One.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
section: 4.4 Layer Two: a sectoral destination-based cash-flow tax
text:
4.4 Layer Two: a sectoral destination-based cash-flow tax
The second layer addresses rent that is earned from local customers but booked abroad. Digital platforms, holders of pharmaceutical patents, some financial services and streaming services can route revenue through low-tax jurisdictions so that little profit is declared locally, however well designed the ACE. For designated sectors, a destination-based cash-flow tax is added: \[
T_2 = t_2 \max(0,\; S - C),
\tag{3}\] where \(S\) is sales to customers in the country and \(C\) is costs incurred in the country, including payroll and purchases from local suppliers; imports and payments to related parties abroad (royalties, management fees, intra-group purchases) are not deductible. Layer One is credited against Layer Two, so a firm pays the larger of the two, not both. The rate is \(t_2 = 22\) percent, within the first draft’s range of 20–25 percent.
The first draft described this layer as a tax of 20–25 percent “on in-country revenue”. Read literally, a 22 percent tax on gross revenue takes 63 percent of the profit of a platform with a 35 percent operating margin and more than all the profit of a firm with a 20 percent margin; that is why national taxes on digital revenue are set at 2 or 3 percent (French Republic 2019; United Kingdom 2020). Deducting local costs makes Layer Two a tax on the cash flow a firm earns from local customers, which is where its rent is.
Proposition 4 (the destination layer and its rate). Layer Two’s base depends on where the firm’s customers are and where its local costs are incurred, not on where its profit is booked, so transfer pricing and the location of intangible assets cannot reduce it. Because the tax is confined to a few sectors, the exchange rate does not adjust to offset it, unlike an economy-wide destination-based tax; it therefore acts within those sectors as a tax on imported inputs and related-party services at the tax-exclusive rate \(t_2/(1-t_2)\) and favors local costs at the same rate. At \(t_2 = 22\) percent the implicit charge on imported inputs is 28 percent; at 50 percent it would be 100 percent (Appendix B). The first draft gave these as \(t_2/(1+t_2)\), 20 and 33 percent, which are the tax-inclusive equivalents and understate the effect. The distortion grows faster than the rate, which is the reason to keep the rate moderate and the scope narrow: only sectors where rent clearly accrues to mobile intangibles and origin taxation demonstrably fails.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
section: 4.5 Layer Three: a sales tax with presence credits
text:
4.5 Layer Three: a sales tax with presence credits
The third layer applies to every group above the threshold. It charges a small rate on sales to local customers and gives credits for local presence: \[
T_3 = \max(0,\; \tau_s S - d_K K - d_W W),
\tag{4}\] where \(K\) is the value of tangible assets in the country, excluding land, and \(W\) is payroll in the country. With \(\tau_s = 4\) percent, \(d_K = 8\) percent and \(d_W = 25\) percent, a firm with €1 billion of local sales, €50 million of local assets and €100 million of local payroll pays €11 million, 1.1 percent of its sales; a firm with the same sales but €500 million of assets and €400 million of payroll pays nothing.
The credits are subtracted from the tax, not from the base, so their incentive is larger than it looks. For a firm with positive liability, each euro of local tangible assets cuts tax by 8 cents a year and each euro of local payroll by 25 cents; the first draft described the asset credit as worth “an extra 2–3 percent” because 8 percent exceeds a normal return of 5–6 percent, which compares a credit rate with a rate of return. Firms already at zero, which is most firms with substantial local operations, get no marginal incentive. Land is excluded from \(K\), so that buying land to shelter tax is not rewarded. The credits mirror the substance carve-out of Pillar Two, which excludes from the minimum tax a return of 5 percent of payroll and of tangible assets (OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS 2021), and the “Dyson tax” of Stretton and Styles (2020), a destination-based tax on sales less local wages and supplier costs.
Layer Three is a tax on sales that are not matched by local activity. Appendix C shows that a firm pays nothing when \(d_K K/S + d_W W/S \geq \tau_s\): payroll of 16 percent of sales is enough on its own. The firms that pay are those whose sales in the country are large relative to their local factor base.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
section: 4.6 The cap and the combined liability
text:
4.6 The cap and the combined liability
A tax on sales can exceed a firm’s profit. A fuel distributor with €10 billion of sales, payroll at 5 percent of sales and tangible assets at 10 percent pays 1.95 percent of sales under Layer Three, against a net margin of perhaps 2 percent. That would tax effort, not rent. The design therefore caps the destination layers. Let \(\rho\) be the group’s global rent margin, its worldwide profit less the allowance on its worldwide equity, divided by its worldwide sales, taken from the consolidated accounts. The total liability is \[
T = \max\Big(T_1,\; \min\big(T_1 + \max(0,\, T_2 - T_1) + T_3,\;\; \tau_1 \rho S\big)\Big).
\tag{5}\]
Proposition 5 (the cap). The destination layers never reduce a firm’s tax below its Layer One liability, and never raise its total above \(\tau_1 \rho S\), the Layer One rate applied to the rent the group would earn on its local sales if its global rent margin applied locally. A firm with no global rent pays only Layer One; a firm whose global rent margin is the same in every market pays at most \(\tau_1\) of the rent it earns from local customers.
The cap is a residual profit allocation by sales, of the kind proposed by Devereux et al. (2021) and adopted for Amount A (OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS 2021), used here as a ceiling rather than a division of the base. It needs only figures that groups above the threshold already publish: consolidated profit, equity and revenue.

title: Let Land Pay for the City
text: Working paper, version 0.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. This is paper 2.2 in the section “Tax Rent, Not Effort”; its companion, paper 2.1, sets out a land value tax above a household allowance (Stretton 2026).
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Infrastructure raises land values, and the owner did nothing to earn the rise
text:
Infrastructure raises land values, and the owner did nothing to earn the rise
The value of a plot of urban land is the capitalized value of what can be reached from it. A hectare beside a new metro station is worth more than the same hectare a day before the line opened, because the people who will live or work on it can now reach more jobs, customers and services in less time. The owner did nothing to create the gain; the public authority that built the line and the residents and firms whose presence makes access valuable did. Economists call the part of a return that requires no effort or investment from its recipient economic rent, and land value is the textbook case: the supply of land at a location is fixed, so its price is set entirely by demand, and demand is set by what the city around it provides.
The rise can be large compared with the cost of the infrastructure that causes it. A meta-analysis of 102 estimates from 23 studies finds that rail projects raise land and property values near stations, by amounts that vary widely with the type of rail, the market and the study design (Mohammad et al. 2013). Summed over every plot within walking distance of every station, the uplift can rival the cost of the line. That is why Hong Kong’s rail operator can pay for much of its network from property development (Section 4), and why a city that leaves the uplift with landowners pays for its infrastructure twice: once through the budget, and again through the higher rents that tenants pay landowners for the access the budget created.
The rise in land value is also the main way the benefits of urban infrastructure reach their final owners. Better roads, drainage and transit lower commuting costs and raise wages, but in a city where people can move, competition for the newly better locations bids those gains into rents and land prices (Arnott and Stiglitz 1979). This capitalization makes land a good tax base for infrastructure: a tax on land value reaches those who gain, roughly in proportion to their gain, without anyone having to measure each person’s benefit.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: The Henry George theorem gives the theoretical limit
text:
The Henry George theorem gives the theoretical limit
Under ideal conditions, the rents that a city’s public goods create are exactly enough to pay for them. Arnott and Stiglitz (1979) showed that in a city of optimal size, aggregate differential land rents equal spending on pure local public goods. The result is called the Henry George theorem, after the nineteenth-century American who proposed that a single tax on land could replace all others. No real city meets its strict conditions, but its message is practical: the infrastructure that makes a city productive creates a land-value base large enough to fund much of it. A city that cannot finance its infrastructure while its land values soar has a tax design problem, not a resource problem.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Two families of instruments capture land value
text:
Two families of instruments capture land value
This paper uses land value capture to mean any public instrument that recovers for the public part of the land value that public action creates (OECD and Lincoln Institute of Land Policy 2022). The instruments fall into two families, which differ in timing.
Recurrent taxes are levied every year on the value of land, or of land and buildings together. They capture the uplift gradually, as values are reassessed, and give a steady revenue that can service debt, but they depend on a working valuation roll and the political will to revalue.
One-off capture instruments recover the uplift at the moment it is created. The OECD and Lincoln Institute compendium of land value capture in 60 countries groups them into five types (OECD and Lincoln Institute of Land Policy 2022). An infrastructure levy, often called a betterment levy, is a one-time charge on the owners of land that benefits from a defined project, such as Colombia’s contribución de valorización. A developer obligation requires a developer to provide or pay for the roads, schools or open space that a project needs as a condition of permission. A charge for development rights sells the right to build more floor area than the base zoning allows, as São Paulo does with its auctioned building-rights certificates. Land readjustment pools privately held plots, returns to the owners smaller but serviced and better-shaped plots, and keeps some land for roads and for sale, as in Japan and in the town planning schemes of Gujarat, India. Strategic land management, which includes public land leasing or sale, lets a government that owns the land sell or lease it after the infrastructure has raised its value, which is the core of the Hong Kong and Singapore models.
Proposition 1 (land should pay). Where infrastructure raises land values, a combination of a recurrent land-value tax and one-off capture instruments can recover a large share of the infrastructure’s cost from those who gain from it, at lower efficiency cost than taxes on labor, capital or consumption. The share recovered rises with the quality of the valuation roll and with the extent to which the public owns or controls the land before the infrastructure is announced.
The second condition matters most in practice. Land prices move on the announcement of a project, not on its completion, so instruments that act after the announcement capture less of the uplift than instruments that act before it. A government that owns the land, or pools it at pre-project value, captures most of the gain; one that relies on a recurrent tax with infrequent revaluation captures little of it for years.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Land taxes are the least harmful taxes a government can levy
text:
Land taxes are the least harmful taxes a government can levy
A tax on land value does not reduce the supply of land, so it does not shrink the economy the way taxes on work, saving or investment do. OECD research ranks recurrent taxes on immovable property as the least damaging to long-run growth, followed by consumption taxes, personal income taxes and, most damaging, corporate income taxes (Johansson et al. 2008; Arnold et al. 2011). A tax on buildings is less benign, because it discourages building; a tax on land alone, or a lower rate on buildings than on land, keeps the growth advantage and adds the green advantages of Section 5.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Recurrent property taxes raise a few tenths of a percent of GDP
text:
Recurrent property taxes raise a few tenths of a percent of GDP
Developing countries collect far less from property than rich countries (Table 1). In 2023 the OECD average yield from recurrent taxes on immovable property was 0.95 percent of GDP, and all property taxes together, including taxes on transfers, raised 1.68 percent; the United Kingdom, Canada and the United States each collected more than 2.5 percent from the recurrent tax alone (OECD 2025). In 2009 middle-income countries collected 0.40 percent of GDP (Norregaard 2013). In Africa, the 32 countries with data collected an average of 0.38 percent of GDP from all property taxes, mostly over 2008–2013, and only South Africa’s recurrent tax exceeded 1 percent (Franzsen and McCluskey 2017). The IMF puts total property tax revenue in Sub-Saharan Africa and emerging Asia at about 0.1 percent of GDP in 2021 (Grote and Wen 2024). India, with the world’s largest urban population after China, collects municipal property tax of around 0.15 percent of GDP, a figure that has barely moved for decades (Roy 2026).

The shortfall is large. The IMF estimates that middle-income countries could raise about 0.9 percent of GDP from recurrent property taxes, more than double what they collect (Norregaard 2013), and its most recent guidance treats 1 to 2 percent of GDP as a reasonable medium-term target (Grote and Wen 2024). The World Bank estimates that low- and middle-income countries need to invest about 4.5 percent of GDP a year in new infrastructure through 2030 to meet the infrastructure-related development and climate goals, plus another 2.7 percent a year to maintain it (Rozenberg and Fay 2019). Property taxes cannot close that gap alone, but they are the main source a city can raise for itself, and they are the natural source for the urban share of the bill.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: The structure inherited from colonial rating rarely reaches land value
text:
The structure inherited from colonial rating rarely reaches land value
Most developing-country property taxes were designed for a different purpose, and their structure still limits what they can collect. Four bases are common. Annual rental value bases, inherited from British rating, tax the rent a property would fetch in a year; they are used across South Asia and in much of Commonwealth Africa, and also in Singapore and Hong Kong. Capital value bases, which tax the market value of land and buildings, are standard in Latin America and South Africa. Area-based systems, which multiply floor area by a rate per square meter that varies by zone and building type, have spread in Indian cities and elsewhere because they need no market data. Site value bases tax land alone; Jamaica has taxed the unimproved value of land since 1957 (Sjoquist 2005).
Each base has a weakness in a fast-growing city. A rental value base gives a vacant plot a low rent and so a low tax, however valuable its land, which rewards holding land idle. A capital value base taxes buildings and so discourages building. An area-based system captures none of the uplift from infrastructure unless its zonal rates are updated, which rarely happens. Only a site value base targets the land value that infrastructure creates, and it is the least used.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Coverage, valuation and collection each lose half the base
text:
Coverage, valuation and collection each lose half the base
The yield of a property tax is the product of four ratios: the share of properties on the roll, the ratio of assessed to market value, the share of the bill actually collected, and the statutory rate. In developing countries the first three are each typically between a fifth and four-fifths. A World Bank diagnostic finds that low- and middle-income countries typically have coverage of 40 to 60 percent and collection of 30 to 60 percent, against nearly 100 percent for both in OECD countries (R. Kelly et al. 2020). Valuation ratios of 20 to 80 percent are common (Grote and Wen 2024). Multiply three ratios of about one-half and the tax collects about one-eighth of what its statutory rate implies. So raising the rate is the wrong first step: it burdens those who already pay and leaves untouched those who pay nothing. Exemptions for owner-occupied homes, agricultural land, religious bodies and new buildings, often permanent, narrow the base further.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Transfer taxes do the work that a recurrent tax should
text:
Transfer taxes do the work that a recurrent tax should
Many developing countries lean heavily on taxing property sales. In India, stamp duties and registration fees on property transactions provided between 7 and 14 percent of states’ own tax revenue (National Institute of Public Finance and Policy 2019), while the recurrent municipal tax raises around 0.15 percent of GDP. Transfer taxes are easy to collect, because a buyer needs a registered deed, but they have three costs. They discourage people from moving closer to work (Section 5). They push transactions off the record, because buyers and sellers understate prices or never register, which leaves the valuation roll without market evidence. And they capture land value only when land changes hands, which may be once a generation.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Freetown shows that a poor city can reform quickly
text:
Freetown shows that a poor city can reform quickly
Freetown, the capital of Sierra Leone, shows that a city with low capacity can rebuild a property tax in about two years. Property tax already provided about 42 percent of the city council’s own revenue (Franzsen and McCluskey 2017), but the roll was incomplete and valuations arbitrary. In 2018–2019 the council piloted, on more than 11,000 properties, a points-based valuation that estimates each property’s value from a few observable features such as size, building quality and location (Grieco et al. 2019). The register then grew from about 57,000 to about 110,000 properties, and by April 2020 almost all properties in the city had been mapped and valued. The council’s estimate of potential revenue rose more than fivefold (Prichard et al. 2020). The central government asked the council to pause the reform in June 2020, and collection under the new system resumed in 2021. Freetown shows both halves of the problem: the technical work can be done fast, and politics can stop it.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: China shows the opposite risk: dependence on land sales
text:
China shows the opposite risk: dependence on land sales
China built much of its urban infrastructure for two decades by selling long leases on land owned by local governments. Land sales provided about 30 percent of local government revenue in 2021, and land sales plus land-related taxes about 38 percent (Huang 2024). Revenue from land sales reached 8.71 trillion yuan in 2021, then fell to 4.87 trillion in 2024 and 4.15 trillion in 2025 as the property market contracted (Ministry of Finance of the People’s Republic of China 2026). Local governments that had borrowed against future land sales through financing vehicles found the revenue gone and the debt still due. China has no general recurrent property tax on homes; a pilot in Shanghai and Chongqing since 2011 was never extended nationally. Land finance built a vast amount of infrastructure quickly; the lesson is that one-off land sales are a volatile base that should fund capital spending only, with a recurrent land tax as the stable complement.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Hong Kong: the rail company is also the developer
text:
Hong Kong: the rail company is also the developer
All land in Hong Kong belongs to the state, which leases it to users for fixed terms; this gives the government a direct claim on the rise in land value (Suzuki et al. 2015). Land premiums, the payments developers make for new leases or for changes to existing ones, have been a major source of public revenue. In 2017–18 they raised HK$164.8 billion, 26.6 percent of government revenue, and between 16 and 24 percent in each of the following three years (Inland Revenue Department, Hong Kong 2021). Revenue from land is also volatile: in the depressed market of 2024–25, the revised estimate was HK$13.5 billion, under 3 percent of revenue (Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region 2025).
The rail-plus-property model turns that claim into a way of financing transit. When a new line is planned, the government grants the rail operator, the MTR Corporation, the development rights for sites at and around the new stations, and charges a land premium equal to the land’s full market value without the railway: the before-rail price (Suzuki et al. 2015). MTR then develops the sites with private developers at their after-rail value, and keeps a share of the profits and often the shopping centers and offices it builds. The difference between the before-rail and after-rail values pays for much of the line. Since 2007, the government has sized the development rights for each new line to close an independently assessed funding gap; for the South Island Line (East) and the Kwun Tong Line Extension those gaps were HK$9.9 billion and HK$3.3 billion (Secretary for Transport and Housing, Hong Kong 2012).
Property makes MTR’s railway business profitable. Between 2000 and 2012, property development and related business provided 38 percent of MTR’s recurring profits (Suzuki et al. 2015). In 2024, property development contributed HK$10.3 billion of an underlying business profit of HK$17.5 billion, about 59 percent, while Hong Kong transport operations made a small loss (MTR Corporation 2025). Fares on their own also cover operating costs with room to spare: MTR’s farebox recovery ratio was 185.5 percent in 2012 (Suzuki et al. 2015), and on 2024 figures transport revenue was still about 150 percent of transport operating costs before depreciation (author’s calculation from MTR Corporation (2025)). The two sources reinforce each other: dense housing and shops above stations generate riders, and riders make that property more valuable. Cervero and Murakami (2009) found that a rail-plus-property station with transit-oriented design added about 35,000 weekday passengers, and that nearby housing sold at a premium of roughly 5 to 30 percent.
The result is one of the world’s most transit-dependent cities. In 2016 public transport carried more than 12 million passenger trips a day in Hong Kong, over 90 percent of all trips (Transport and Housing Bureau, Hong Kong 2017); in 2024 it carried about 11.7 million, of which MTR carried 5.2 million (Transport Department, Hong Kong 2025).
Hong Kong’s model also has a dark side that a developing country should study as closely as its success. A government that depends on land sales for its general budget has a fiscal interest in high land prices, and Hong Kong has released land for housing slowly; its housing is among the least affordable in the world. A recurrent land tax creates no such incentive, because it raises revenue from land already in use rather than from rationing new land.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Singapore: the state assembled the land and taxes its value
text:
Singapore: the state assembled the land and taxes its value
Singapore took a more radical route: the state acquired most of the land, and then planned, built and taxed it. In 1960 the state owned 44 percent of Singapore’s land; by 1985 it owned 76 percent and by 2005 about 90 percent (Phang and Helble 2016). The Land Acquisition Act of 1966 allowed the government to acquire land compulsorily for public purposes, and from 1973 compensation was fixed at land values on a historical statutory date, 30 November 1973, which was held for about 14 years and later moved forward several times. Only in 2007 was compensation pegged to full market value (Phang and Helble 2016). In effect, the state captured the land value that growth created by buying land at prices that excluded it.
Public ownership let Singapore plan housing and transit together. At the end of March 2025, 76.0 percent of Singapore’s resident population lived in flats built by the Housing and Development Board, the public housing agency (Housing and Development Board 2025), and 91 percent of resident households owned their homes (Department of Statistics Singapore 2026). Most of these flats are sold on 99-year leases, so the state remains the landowner. Because the Housing and Development Board and the Land Transport Authority plan new towns and rail lines together, the stations sit at the center of the towns, within walking distance of most homes.
Singapore funds transit from the budget, and the budget is supported by land in three ways. The first is the sale of state land: proceeds go into the national reserves rather than the current budget, and up to half of the expected long-term real return on the reserves can be spent each year through the Net Investment Returns Contribution, which funds about a fifth of government spending (Ministry of Finance, Singapore 2025). The second is a recurrent property tax on the annual value of property, with progressive rates: owner-occupied homes pay from 0 to 32 percent of annual value, and non-owner-occupied homes from 12 to 36 percent (Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore 2025). The third is a charge on the value created by planning permission. Since 1 August 2022 the Land Betterment Charge has taxed 70 percent of the rise in land value when the government permits a more valuable use or a higher density (Singapore Land Authority 2022; Tong 2021).
Singapore pairs this financing with one of the world’s most consistent policies of managing car use. It introduced the Area Licensing Scheme, a charge to enter the central business district, in 1975; replaced it with Electronic Road Pricing in 1998 (National Library Board Singapore 2009); and since May 1990 has capped the vehicle population by requiring a Certificate of Entitlement, bought at auction, for every new vehicle (National Library Board Singapore 2006). Its rail network was about 258 kilometers long at the end of 2023 and is planned to reach about 360 kilometers in the early 2030s (Land Transport Authority 2023). The Land Transport Master Plan 2040 aims for “20-minute towns and a 45-minute city,” with nine in ten peak-period journeys by walking, cycling and public transport completed within 45 minutes (Land Transport Authority 2019).
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: What transfers to poorer countries, and what does not
text:
What transfers to poorer countries, and what does not
The two models share four features that a developing-country city can adapt. First, the public controls the land before the infrastructure is announced, either by owning it or by being able to tax or charge its uplift, so the gain is captured at the before-infrastructure price. Second, transit and land use are planned together, so stations sit where people live and work and the land around them is allowed to be dense. Third, the uplift is captured through more than one instrument: lease premiums, development rights, betterment charges and recurrent taxes. Fourth, car use is priced and limited, so transit does not compete with free roads.
Other features do not transfer. Compulsory acquisition at historical prices, as Singapore practiced it, would be unjust and politically impossible in most developing countries today, and in weaker states it would be captured by the powerful. Hong Kong’s model needs very high land values and a competent operator able to develop property at scale. But a city that cannot buy its land can still tax its value every year, charge for the uplift that planning and infrastructure create, pool land through readjustment, and sell building rights near transit.
