crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: It pushes development inward and upward rather than outward
text:
It pushes development inward and upward rather than outward
A land value tax raises the cost of holding well-served land idle or underused. The owner of a plot near a transit line pays the same land tax whether it is empty or holds a ten-story apartment block, so the tax rewards the most intensive use the zoning allows. A tax on buildings does the opposite, because every extra story raises the bill. The best available evidence comes from Pennsylvania, where some cities tax land at a higher rate than buildings. Banzhaf and Lavery (2010) found that the split-rate tax raised the ratio of capital to land, mainly by adding housing units rather than making units larger. In the first one to two decades after adoption, growth in housing-unit density was 2 to 10 percentage points per decade higher than it would otherwise have been. Oates and Schwab (1997) found that Pittsburgh’s sharp shift toward land in 1979–80 was followed by a rise in building activity in the 1980s that fifteen comparable cities in the region did not share, while cautioning that a downtown redevelopment drive also played a part.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: It deters speculative land banking on the urban fringe
text:
It deters speculative land banking on the urban fringe
A land value tax makes it costly to hold land at the edge of a growing city in the hope of selling it later, which slows the leapfrog sprawl that characterizes fast-growing cities in developing countries. Without a holding cost, an owner of a peri-urban plot can wait for prices to rise, and development jumps past the withheld land to cheaper land further out. The city spreads, and its infrastructure and its residents’ trips both lengthen. A tax on land assessed at its value with planned infrastructure makes waiting expensive, which is why agricultural land inside a planned urban extension should be taxed at its urban-use value once infrastructure is committed. Many developing-country codes do the reverse and exempt agricultural land, which turns the urban fringe into a tax shelter for speculation.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: It funds transit and lets transit pay its way
text:
It funds transit and lets transit pay its way
Land value capture makes rail and bus rapid transit financially viable in places where fares alone cannot cover their costs, which tilts the choice between transit and roads toward transit. A road widening spreads its accessibility gains thinly along a corridor, while a station concentrates them within walking distance, where the uplift is easy to identify and charge. A city that captures land value therefore finds transit cheaper relative to roads than a city that relies on general revenue. Hong Kong’s rail network is the leading example (Section 4).
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: It replaces taxes that lock people in place
text:
It replaces taxes that lock people in place
Shifting revenue from property transfer taxes to recurrent land taxes lets households move closer to work, which cuts commuting. A transfer tax is a fine on moving. In the United Kingdom, Hilber and Lyytikäinen (2017) found that a 2 percentage point jump in the stamp duty rate cut household mobility by 35 to 42 percent, mostly by deterring short-distance, housing-related moves. Every extra kilometer a household commutes because moving is too costly adds to emissions and congestion.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: The green effect needs planning to go with it
text:
The green effect needs planning to go with it
A land value tax supplies the incentive to build compactly, but planning has to permit it. If zoning caps building heights at two stories, minimum plot sizes are large and parking requirements absorb a third of each site, the tax cannot raise density; it can only raise revenue. The plan sets where density is allowed and where infrastructure goes; the tax makes sure the allowed density is used and the uplift funds the next round of infrastructure.
Proposition 2 (property taxes on land are green taxes). A recurrent tax on land value, with buildings taxed at a lower rate or not at all, lowers the cost of compact development relative to dispersed development, raises the cost of holding serviced land idle, and gives transit a financing advantage over roads. Where planning permits higher density near transit, the tax lowers vehicle travel, energy use and emissions per resident. Where planning forbids density, the tax raises revenue but does not change urban form.
The direct evidence on density comes mostly from rich-country cities, and dense cities with poor transit still congest. The green case for the land tax is strongest as part of a package: a land tax, capture of transit uplift and planning for density near transit.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Poor cities are spreading out and losing density
text:
Poor cities are spreading out and losing density
The default path of urban growth in developing countries is sprawl, and it is expensive. Average built-up densities in a global sample of 120 cities fell by about 2 percent a year between 1990 and 2000, and cities’ land areas grew much faster than their populations (Angel et al. 2011). In Africa the result is what the World Bank calls cities that are crowded, disconnected and costly. African cities are about 29 percent more expensive than cities in other countries at similar income levels (Lall et al. 2017). About 1.12 billion people lived in slums or informal settlements in 2022, a quarter of the world’s urban population (United Nations 2024). On an unplanned fringe, roads, drains and water mains arrive late and cost more, because land must be bought back and buildings demolished.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: The green model rests on five planning choices
text:
The green model rests on five planning choices
The planning a poor city needs is not elaborate, but it has to come first. Five choices do most of the work, and each one creates land value that the fiscal instruments of Section 7 can capture.
The first is to lay out an arterial road grid ahead of growth. A grid of arterial roads about a kilometer apart, each about 30 meters wide, secured on the urban fringe before development arrives, gives the future city the rights-of-way it will need for buses, water mains, drains and power lines. Ethiopia’s Urban Expansion Initiative applied this approach, starting in four secondary cities and extending to eighteen (Lamson-Hall et al. 2019). Securing a right-of-way on farmland costs a fraction of clearing one through a built-up district.
The second is to use land readjustment to turn fringe farmland into serviced urban plots. In the town planning schemes of Gujarat, the planning authority pools the land in a scheme area, lays out roads and public spaces, keeps a share of the land for public uses and for sale, and returns serviced plots to the original owners. The law allows the authority to keep up to 50 percent of the land, for roads, open space, social infrastructure, housing for low-income groups and sale; in practice it keeps 25 to 40 percent (UN-Habitat 2013). The owners receive less land but more value, the authority funds the roads by selling the land it keeps, and no one is evicted.
The third is to build bus rapid transit first and rail later. A bus rapid transit system, with dedicated lanes, level boarding and off-board fare collection, carries large volumes at a fraction of the cost of a metro. A review of 44 systems found that most cost less than $10 million per kilometer (Hensher and Golob 2008), while fully tunneled metro lines rarely cost less than $60 million per kilometer and often several times that (Goldwyn et al. 2023). Bogotá’s TransMilenio carried about 1.8 million passengers a day on 114 kilometers of trunk lines in 2023 (Global BRT Data 2023). Dar es Salaam’s DART system won the international Sustainable Transport Award in 2018, the first African city to do so (Institute for Transportation and Development Policy 2018). A bus corridor laid on an arterial grid can later be upgraded to light rail or metro when densities justify it.
The fourth is to allow density where transit is. Zoning should permit much higher floor-area ratios within walking distance of transit stops and stations than elsewhere, mix housing with shops and workplaces, and cap or remove minimum parking requirements near transit. This is where planning and fiscal policy meet: the extra floor area is the land value, and selling it, as São Paulo does, funds the transit that makes it valuable.
The fifth is to protect the walking city. Most residents of poor cities walk, or ride a bus or minibus, because they cannot afford a car. Safe sidewalks, crossings and lighting cost little and protect the most common way people travel. The risk is that roads are widened for rising motor traffic at the expense of the people who walk.
Public health research supports this list: the eight features of urban design that Giles-Corti et al. (2016) find encourage walking, cycling and transit, including density, land-use diversity, distance to transit and parking policy, are mostly put in place by these five choices.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: The health gains are large, and they fall mostly on the poor
text:
The health gains are large, and they fall mostly on the poor
A compact, transit-based city prevents deaths on three fronts: road crashes, air pollution and physical inactivity. On each front, the burden today falls overwhelmingly on low- and middle-income countries.
Road crashes killed about 1.19 million people in 2021, and 92 percent of road deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries (World Health Organization 2023). More than half of those killed are pedestrians, cyclists and riders of motorcycles and other two- and three-wheelers, and road crashes are the leading cause of death for people aged 5 to 29. WHO’s newest data, released in July 2026, put deaths at 1.16 million in 2025 (World Health Organization 2026). The economic cost is large: in five case-study countries, the World Bank estimated that halving road deaths and injuries over 24 years could raise GDP per capita by between 7 percent (the Philippines and Tanzania) and 22 percent (Thailand) (World Bank 2017).
Air pollution kills more. Ambient fine-particle pollution caused about 4.2 million premature deaths in 2019, 89 percent of them in low- and middle-income countries (World Health Organization 2024), and household air pollution about 2.9 million more in 2021 (World Health Organization 2025). The World Bank put the health cost of fine-particle pollution at $8.1 trillion in 2019, 6.1 percent of global GDP (World Bank 2022). Transport is one of the main sources of urban air pollution, and it produced 23 percent of global energy-related CO₂ in 2019, 70 percent of that from road vehicles (Jaramillo et al. 2022).
Physical inactivity is the least visible of the three. In 2022, 31 percent of the world’s adults, about 1.8 billion people, did not get enough physical activity, up from 23 percent in 2000 (Strain et al. 2024). Inactivity was estimated to cause about 5.3 million of the 57 million deaths worldwide in 2008 (Lee et al. 2012). A meta-analysis found that walking or cycling about 11 MET-hours a week, roughly two and a half hours of brisk walking, reduced all-cause mortality by 11 percent for walking and 10 percent for cycling, with the largest gains for people who started from little activity (P. Kelly et al. 2014).
The combined effect of compact urban form is large. Stevenson et al. (2016) modeled six cities, including Delhi and São Paulo, under a compact-city scenario: land-use density and diversity each 30 percent higher, distance to public transport 30 percent shorter, and a 10 percent shift from car travel to walking and cycling. Health gains ranged from 420 to 826 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) per 100,000 people, mainly from fewer cases of diabetes, cardiovascular disease and respiratory disease. Delhi gained 620 DALYs per 100,000 and São Paulo 420. Scaled to a city of five million, Delhi’s figure is about 31,000 years of healthy life gained. These are modeled estimates for one scenario, not observed results, but they indicate the order of magnitude.
For a poor city the health gain comes less from changing behavior than from preventing a change. Its residents already walk and share transport. The green model stops the shift to motorcycles and cars, and the rise in road deaths and pollution and fall in daily activity that came with motorization in richer cities. A city that builds a bus rapid transit spine and safe streets before car ownership takes off locks in the healthy pattern; one that waits will spend decades trying to retrofit it.
Proposition 3 (the green model is within reach of poor cities). A city that secures arterial rights-of-way ahead of growth, assembles fringe land through land readjustment, builds bus rapid transit before rail, permits high density near transit and protects walking can finance a large share of its trunk infrastructure from the land value it creates, provided it has a working land tax and legal instruments to capture uplift. The health gains, from fewer road deaths, cleaner air and more daily activity, are large and accrue mostly to lower-income residents.

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Tax land more heavily than buildings, and move toward a pure land base over time
text:
Tax land more heavily than buildings, and move toward a pure land base over time
The code should define the base as the market value of land, or as the market value of land and buildings with a lower rate on the building component. A pure site-value base gives the strongest green and growth incentives, and in fast-growing cities, where many buildings are informal or unfinished, it is often simpler to value. A split-rate base is the practical route where the existing roll values land and buildings together: the code fixes a ratio, such as a building rate one-quarter of the land rate, and narrows it on a published schedule. Annual rental value bases should be converted to capital or site value, because they give a vacant plot near zero liability.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Value everything, often, by mass appraisal, and test the results in public
text:
Value everything, often, by mass appraisal, and test the results in public
Valuation is where most developing-country property taxes fail, so the code should make it a legal duty with measurable standards. It should require a general revaluation at least every five years, with annual indexation between revaluations, so values never drift for decades. It should authorize computer-assisted mass appraisal from sales, rental and land-use data, and simpler banded or points-based methods where market data are thin, as Freetown adopted. It should require the valuation authority to publish annual ratio studies against the international standard of the International Association of Assessing Officers: a median ratio of assessed to market value between 0.90 and 1.10, a coefficient of dispersion of no more than 15 percent for ordinary residential property, and a price-related differential between 0.98 and 1.03, which tests whether expensive properties are under-assessed relative to cheap ones (International Association of Assessing Officers 2013). Publishing these statistics shows taxpayers whether the roll is fair.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Put every parcel on the roll, whatever its legal status
text:
Put every parcel on the roll, whatever its legal status
The fiscal cadastre should cover every occupied parcel, whether or not it has a formal title, and the code should say plainly that being on the tax roll neither confers nor removes property rights. The code should place the duty to register on the occupier where the owner is unknown, and allow self-declaration of basic attributes, checked by sample audits.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Keep exemptions few, explicit and costed
text:
Keep exemptions few, explicit and costed
Exemptions should be limited to a small household allowance and to land used directly by government and recognized public-benefit bodies, and every exemption should be listed and costed each year. A basic allowance, a slice of land value exempt for every owner-occupied home, protects poor households better than a list of exempt categories and keeps the base broad (Stretton 2026). Blanket exemptions for agricultural land inside urban boundaries, for religious or political bodies’ commercial property, and for new buildings for many years should be removed.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Make collection easy and non-payment costly
text:
Make collection easy and non-payment costly
The code should make unpaid tax a first charge on the property, so that it must be cleared before any sale, mortgage or building permit, and should authorize, as a last resort, the sale of the property to recover long-standing arrears. Mobile payment, bills by text message, interest on arrears above the government’s borrowing rate, and a clear tax account as a condition for permits and utility connections all raise compliance at low cost. Deferral for asset-rich, cash-poor households, such as elderly owners, can be offered with the tax accumulating as a charge settled on sale or inheritance.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Let cities set rates within a national band, and let them keep the money
text:
Let cities set rates within a national band, and let them keep the money
Rate-setting should sit with the city, within a minimum and maximum set in national law. A city that sets its own rate and keeps the revenue answers to its residents for both. National transfers should not fall when a city collects more, or cities will stop trying. A vacant-land surcharge, a higher rate on serviced land left undeveloped for more than a set period, belongs in the code as an option for cities with fringe speculation.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Give cities the legal tools to capture uplift before it is capitalized
text:
Give cities the legal tools to capture uplift before it is capitalized
The code should authorize the five land value capture instruments and set the procedures for each. For infrastructure levies, it should define a benefit zone around each project, a method for apportioning the charge, and payment over several years. For development rights, it should allow cities to sell floor area above a base ratio, by auction where demand is strong. For land readjustment, it should allow a scheme area to be pooled after public consultation, with clear limits on the share of land the authority keeps, as Gujarat’s town planning law does. For public land, it should allow leasing with periodic rent review, so that the public owner shares in future increases in value, and require that proceeds from sales go to a capital fund rather than to current spending.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: Ring-fence the land revenues for capital, and publish what they buy
text:
Ring-fence the land revenues for capital, and publish what they buy
The code should send one-off capture revenues, which are lumpy and cyclical, to an urban infrastructure fund, and allow recurrent property tax revenue to service infrastructure debt. China’s experience shows the danger of using land sales to fund current spending: when the property market turned, revenue that local governments had come to rely on fell sharply (Section 3). A fund that publishes what land revenue built, and where, gives taxpayers a reason to pay.

crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
text:
“The poor will lose their homes”
The most serious objection is that a land tax can force poor households off valuable land they cannot afford to be taxed on. The answer lies in design. A basic household allowance exempts the land value of an ordinary home, so most poor households pay nothing (Stretton 2026). Deferral lets cash-poor owners accumulate the tax as a charge settled on sale or inheritance, so no one is forced to sell to pay it. And without a property tax, the same metro raises rents for tenants, often the poorest residents, while landlords keep the whole gain. A land tax with an allowance is more progressive than the status quo.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
text:
“Informal tenure makes it impossible”
A second objection is that a property tax needs clear titles, and most land in many African and South Asian cities has none. The answer is that a tax roll needs an occupier and a value, not a title. Freetown doubled its register to about 110,000 properties by mapping and valuing buildings on the ground, not by searching title records (Grieco et al. 2019). Taxing occupied property can strengthen tenure security in practice, because a tax receipt is evidence of occupation. The code should say explicitly that registration for tax does not confer or remove rights, which protects both the occupier and the state.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: “Land value capture fuels bubbles and debt”
text:
“Land value capture fuels bubbles and debt”
A third objection is that dependence on land sales ties public finances to the property cycle, as China has shown. The objection is right about land sales and wrong about recurrent taxes, which fall on the stock of land value rather than the flow of transactions and so are far more stable. The answer is to use one-off capture for capital spending only, build up the recurrent tax as the main revenue, and strictly limit borrowing against future land sales.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
section: “Compulsory acquisition and land pooling invite abuse”
text:
“Compulsory acquisition and land pooling invite abuse”
A fourth objection is that the Singapore model rested on acquiring land at below-market prices, which in weaker states becomes a license to evict the poor and enrich the connected. The objection is fair, which is why this paper recommends land readjustment and land value taxes rather than compulsory acquisition for most countries. Land readjustment leaves owners on their land, with a smaller but more valuable plot. Where acquisition is used, the code should require market-value compensation, published valuations and independent appeal.
crumbs: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City

title: Let Land Pay for the City
text:
“Cities lack the capacity”
A fifth objection is that the cities that most need this model have the least capacity to run it. The capacity required has fallen sharply. Satellite imagery, cheap smartphones for field surveys, mobile money and open-source mass appraisal software have cut the cost of building and running a fiscal cadastre; Freetown mapped and valued almost every property in the city in about two years. The binding constraint is political, not technical: a mayor has to be willing to send bills to the city’s most powerful landowners.

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text: Working paper, version 0.4, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.1.

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text:
13.1 A.1 Where the architecture sits
The two-track architecture joins four bodies of work that have mostly developed apart: the theory of unilateral policy under leakage, border carbon adjustment, intensity-based instruments, and destination-based taxation.
The theory of the split is old. Markusen (1975) showed that with an international externality the best unilateral policy combines a production tax with a trade (equivalently, consumption) tax. Hoel (1996) showed that when tariffs cannot be used, carbon-intensive tradable sectors should face a lower carbon tax. Weisbach et al. (2023) restate the result in modern form and add an extraction leg. Most directly, Stephen P. Holland (2012) proves that an intensity standard combined with a consumption tax can sometimes reach the first best under leakage when an emissions tax combined with a consumption tax cannot. Böhringer et al. (2017) show the policy-relevant version: output-based rebating plus a consumption tax on emission-intensive, trade-exposed goods can be equivalent to a border carbon adjustment. Proposition 1 is therefore an implementable statement of a known allocation result, not a new theorem. Its revenue corollary, that the tracks differ by \(t\) times carbon in net exports, is the carbon analogue of the neutrality of origin and destination bases for a uniform tax (Lockwood and Whalley 2010; Lockwood et al. 1994).
The design has close European precedents. Grubb et al. (2022) list the separation of incentives at the point of production from a charge on the use of carbon-intensive materials as one of three trade-compatible options. Pollitt et al. (2020) simulate a consumption charge on basic materials rising to about €80/tCO₂ by 2050: it cuts EU CO₂ emissions by up to 10 percent by 2050 and, because imports are charged alike, avoids leakage. Ismer et al. (2016) give the legal design of such a charge as an excise-like charge at product-specific benchmark intensity, applied equally to imports. Neuhoff et al. (2026) propose benchmark-based free allocation plus a standardized liability per tonne of material with export relief. Each is a production-plus-consumption architecture.
What this paper adds is narrower: (i) a revenue-neutral feebate with an updated benchmark in place of free allocation, so the production track needs no emissions trading system and no auction revenue and can be adopted by a developing country alone; (ii) a consumption track that runs through VAT across all goods rather than an excise on a few materials; (iii) the closed-form residual cost \(\tfrac12 t\Delta e\) and its calibration to EU default intensities for steel; (iv) the exporter best response under intensity-based destination charges; and (v) the extension of Strand’s crediting threshold to feebates, with the best response \(t = \pi\).

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text:
13.2 A.2 Leakage and competitiveness
Model-based estimates of leakage from unilateral carbon pricing range from 5 to 25 percent, with a central value of about 14 percent (Branger and Quirion 2014). Ex-post studies of the EU system find little or none at prices to date (Naegele and Zaklan 2019; Dechezleprêtre et al. 2022; Colmer et al. 2025), partly because free allocation shields industry and partly because prices were low; the evidence on relocation of investment is similar (Dechezleprêtre and Sato 2017). Pass-through of carbon costs is probably under half in most EU industrial sectors (Neuhoff and Ritz 2019), against about 70 percent for energy-cost shocks in a set of US manufacturing industries (Ganapati et al. 2020). The case for the architecture is therefore prospective: it concerns rates in the upper half of the $50–100 range the High-Level Commission set for 2030 (High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices 2017), not leakage already observed. A second leakage channel, through world fossil-fuel prices, survives any charge on goods (Branger and Quirion 2014; Weisbach et al. 2023); only supply-side measures or wider participation address it (Jakob et al. 2014).

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text:
13.3 A.3 Border carbon adjustment
Keen et al. (2022) is the reference design paper: border adjustments are the most effective domestic response to leakage, design is critical, coverage should start with energy-intensive trade-exposed sectors, and charges should be benchmarked first on domestic intensities. Mehling et al. (2019) analyze border adjustments under GATT Articles I, II:2(a), III and XX and the subsidies agreement, and recommend default values with rebuttal and credit for foreign policies, which supports the recognition of non-price instruments argued here and in Stretton (2026b). Cosbey et al. (2019) give design guidance in the same direction. On distribution, Mattoo et al. (2009) simulate border taxes on the carbon content of all merchandise imports, set at each exporter’s sectoral intensity: China’s manufacturing exports fall by about a fifth and those of low- and middle-income countries by about 8 percent. The EU’s mechanism (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023b) as amended in 2025 (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2025), with default values that carry deliberate mark-ups (European Commission 2025), deducts only carbon prices effectively paid, net of rebates, a choice examined in the companion paper (Stretton 2026b).

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text:
13.4 A.4 Intensity-based instruments and feebates
Carolyn Fischer (2001) shows that tradable performance standards, taxes with output-based rebates and output-based permit allocation are all equivalent to an emissions tax plus an output subsidy: for a given target they lean too much on intensity and too little on output. That is Proposition 4. Stephen P. Holland et al. (2009) show that intensity standards can even raise emissions where the output subsidy dominates. C. Fischer and Fox (2007) and Carolyn Fischer and Fox (2012) compare output-based rebates with border adjustment: full border adjustment is usually the most effective, but output-based rebating captures many of its gains and, in most sectors, protects output better than an import-only or export-only adjustment. The evidence from feebates in use is mixed in the expected direction. The Swedish NOx charge, refunded on output, contributed to a fall of about 40 percent in emission rates over its first seven years (Sterner and Höglund Isaksson 2006). The French bonus-malus on cars shifted purchases toward low-emission models but raised total emissions, because higher sales outweighed the shift to cleaner models (D’Haultfœuille et al. 2014). In IMF simulations, packages of feebates and regulations with the same marginal incentive achieve roughly 50–70 percent of the cuts of a carbon tax (International Monetary Fund 2019).

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text:
13.5 A.5 Destination and origin
For a uniform, broad-based tax, a switch between origin and destination bases changes price levels, not relative prices, and so has no real trade effects (Lockwood and Whalley 2010; Lockwood et al. 1994). Proposition 7 therefore rests on the non-uniformity of carbon charges across exporters’ intensities, not on the destination basis as such. VAT shows that a destination-based tax can spread country by country without an international agreement, because the gain from adopting it does not depend on partners having it (Keen and Lockwood 2010; OECD 2017); proposals for destination-based corporate taxation rest on the same logic (Auerbach et al. 2017; Devereux et al. 2021). Consumption-based accounts show that the footprints of industrialized countries exceed their territorial emissions (Peters and Hertwich 2008; Peters et al. 2011; Davis and Caldeira 2010).

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
section: 13.6 A.6 Clubs and the race to the top
text:
13.6 A.6 Clubs and the race to the top
Nordhaus (2015) shows that a club with a small uniform tariff on non-members can sustain a large coalition. The incentive in Proposition 7 differs: it comes from a charge that rises with each exporter’s intensity, not from a flat penalty. Böhringer et al. (2016) find the threat of carbon tariffs credible in a numerical game, and D. Helm et al. (2012) argue that border adjustments give exporters an incentive to price carbon themselves so as to keep the revenue.

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text:
13.7 A.7 Crediting and results-based finance
Strand (2020) derives, for a donor-supported carbon tax, a break-even payment of half the tax rate when the host keeps the reduction toward its own target, the same threshold as Proposition 6, rising to about one and a half times the rate when the credit is transferred with a corresponding adjustment under Article 6 (World Bank 2022). The case for crediting policy rather than projects rests on the poor record of project offsets: fewer than 16 percent of credits examined by Probst et al. (2024) represent real reductions, and Calel et al. (2025) find at least half of Indian wind credits non-additional. Baselines remain the hard part (Partnership for Market Readiness 2017; World Bank and Frankfurt School of Finance and Management 2017).

title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text:
13.8 A.8 Credibility and forward obligations
A government that re-optimizes each period cannot commit, so a carbon price set annually will not be believed by investors in long-lived capital (Kydland and Prescott 1977; Dieter Helm et al. 2003). Once firms have sunk low-carbon investment, governments are tempted to lower the price, and firms anticipate this (Dieter Helm et al. 2003; Brunner et al. 2012). A forward-announced legal obligation on the few large suppliers of fuel and electricity is a commitment device of the kind this literature recommends.

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
text: Working paper, version 0.4, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.4. Legal texts are as of 31 October 2026; version 0.2 was the author’s submission to the Commission’s consultation of May–June 2026 (Stretton 2026a). All CBAM amounts are in euros.
crumbs: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
text:
6.1 A liability formula
I propose that the CBAM liability per tonne of product from country \(c\) in sector \(s\) be \[
L_{c,s} = \big(\tau - r_{c,s}\big)^{+}\,\hat e,
\qquad
r_{c,s} = p_{c,s} + \rho\,\big(t^{\mathrm{sig}}_{c,s} - p_{c,s}\big)^{+},
\tag{2}\] where \(\hat e\) is embodied carbon measured at the verified country-sector average \(\bar e_{c,s}\) without mark-up, updated each year (or at a firm’s verified whole-output intensity under Section 7), \(p_{c,s}\) the sector’s average price paid, \(t^{\mathrm{sig}}_{c,s}\) its price signal and \(\rho \in [0,1]\) the recognition weight on the unpaid part of the signal. In certificates, the declarant surrenders \((1 - r_{c,s}/\tau)^{+}\hat e\) per tonne, which is how the draft regulation already converts a price paid into fewer certificates (European Commission 2026a, Art. 6). The formula is stated at full phase-in; until then the free-allocation adjustment reduces the certificates due on every import, and the formula applies to what remains.
The formula nests the current rule and the proposal. With \(\rho = 0\) and plant-level \(\hat e\), it is the top-up charge of Mehling and Ritz (2023) and the logic of Article 9: recognition is the price paid. With \(\rho = 1\), it is the full signal, \((\tau - t^{\mathrm{sig}})^{+}\bar e_{c,s}\). For a flat tax \(p = t^{\mathrm{sig}}\) and \(\rho\) is irrelevant, so countries with explicit, unrebated carbon taxes receive the same credit as now. Only instruments whose signal exceeds their average payment, feebates, output-based rebating, tradable performance standards, gain.
Proposition 5 (signal recognition). Under equation 2:
(i) Invariance. \(L_{c,s}\) does not depend on which plant supplies the EU or which plants file data.
(ii) Most competitive rate. Let unit cost be \(c(e) = c_0 + \tfrac{k}{2}(e_0 - e)^2\) as in paper 1.1, so a feebate at rate \(t\) sets intensity \(e_0 - t/k\), and consider the delivered cost of a tonne sold to the EU, \(D(t) = c_0 + t^2/2k + (\tau - \rho t)^{+}(e_0 - t/k)\). With \(\rho = 0\), \(D\) is minimized at \(t = \tau\) (Stretton 2026e, Prop. 7). With \(\rho = 1\) and \(k e_0 \ge 2\tau\), \(D\) is minimized at \(t = \tau\) as well, where the liability is zero and \(D\) is lower than with \(\rho = 0\) by \(\tau(e_0 - \tau/k)\).
(iii) Best response of the exporting country. If the country weighs the resource cost of abatement on all output against CBAM savings on the share \(\mu\) sold to the EU, its best feebate rate is \[
t^{*} = \frac{\mu\,(\tau + \rho\,k e_0)}{1 + 2\rho\mu}
\tag{3}\] (capped at \(\tau/\rho\)), which rises from \(\mu\tau\) at \(\rho = 0\) and increases in \(\rho\) whenever \(k e_0 > 2\mu\tau\).
(iv) Adoption threshold. A feebate at \(t = \tau\) is a net gain to the country if and only if \(\mu > 1/2\) when \(\rho = 0\), and \(\mu > \tau/(2 k e_0)\), half the proportional intensity cut it induces, when \(\rho = 1\).
The proofs are in Appendix B. Part (i) is immediate: every term in equation 2 is a country-sector aggregate. Part (ii) connects to paper 1.1: a charge on embodied carbon measured by country and sector already makes the exporter’s most competitive feebate rate equal to the charge, and full recognition keeps that property while adding the reward for adoption. The condition \(k e_0 \ge 2\tau\) says the feebate at the EU price cuts intensity by no more than half. If it cut more, a producer would rather pay a small residual liability than abate further. Parts (iii) and (iv) give the reason recognition matters: an exporting country bears the abatement cost on all output and wins CBAM relief only on its EU sales. Price-paid recognition makes a feebate at the EU price worthwhile only if more than half the sector’s output goes to Europe, which almost no exporter meets. Full recognition lowers the threshold to about a quarter in the calibration of Section 8.
Recognition is policy crediting paid in CBAM relief. Paper 1.1 shows that an outside buyer paying \(\pi\) per tonne abated induces a feebate at \(t = \pi\) (Stretton 2026e, Prop. 6). Recognition works the same way, but the buyer pays in forgone CBAM revenue on the EU-bound share only. The relief per tonne of the country’s output is \(\mu \rho t\,\bar e\), for abatement of \(t/k\), an implied price of \(\mu\rho k\bar e\) per tonne abated, where \(\bar e\) is the sector’s intensity after the feebate. With \(\mu = 0.1\) and the calibration below, that is about €15 per tonne of CO₂ at the country’s best response (€17 at the intensity before the feebate): cheap per tonne because the signal acts on ten times the tonnage the relief is paid on.
What full recognition gives up is the charge on average carbon in EU-bound goods. At \(\rho = 1\) and \(t^{\mathrm{sig}} = \tau\), an imported tonne from a feebate country bears no CBAM charge, while a tonne made in the EU after free allocation ends bears \(\tau\) on all its emissions. The intensity margin is priced on both sides; the average carbon cost is not. That favors imports in the EU market and, where the exporter’s intensity after abatement exceeds the EU producer’s, raises emissions on each tonne of production that moves. This is the consumption margin, which the two-track architecture assigns to a destination charge on consumption, such as a carbon component of the value-added tax (Stretton 2026e, 2026b). Paper 6.1 draws the same line: border recognition should credit the sector’s switching-margin price, because the border charge leaves the demand margin to the importer’s own price (Stretton 2026d). Until the EU prices consumption separately, recognition should be phased in, with relocation reviewed at each step (Section 11).
crumbs: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
text:
6.2 Measuring the signal
The Total Effective Carbon Price supplies the signal for price and non-price instruments alike. Paper 6.1 defines the Total Effective Carbon Price (TECP) as the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much as a given policy mix, and splits it into a fuel-switching margin and a demand margin (Stretton 2026d). For CBAM the relevant quantity is the switching-margin price of the sector: the weighted average of the price differences that instruments open up between cleaner and dirtier ways of making the same product. A feebate across steel routes at rate \(t\) scores \(t\). A fuel excise above the efficient level, or the removal of a subsidy, scores its per-tonne rate on the fuels the sector uses, weighted by how strongly their use responds; a subsidy scores negatively. A tradable performance standard scores its credit price, and a binding standard without a market scores its shadow price, the marginal compliance cost per tonne. The ingredients exist: the World Bank’s total carbon price for fuel taxes net of subsidies (Agnolucci et al. 2024), the IMF’s efficient fuel prices (Black et al. 2023) and the OECD’s effective carbon rates (OECD 2023). Recognition on this basis credits a foreign policy’s effect on emissions, not its cost to producers: a standard usually costs firms less than a tax with the same equivalent, so equal recognized signals are not equal competitive burdens, and the EU’s own producers can fairly ask which of the two is being matched.
Support measures need a test, and the right test asks whether the measure lowers the marginal cost of emitting. A support measure reduces the recognized signal if the amount a producer receives rises with its emissions or its fossil-fuel use at the margin: a fuel subsidy, an energy-price cap, a refund of carbon payments, or allowances allocated on updated emissions. Support paid per unit of output leaves the signal unchanged and lowers only the price paid, as the feebate’s rebate does. Support paid in proportion to verified spending on abatement, the case the draft’s Article 8(2) exempts, raises the signal: inaction forfeits the subsidy as well as paying the charge (Hagem et al. 2020). It should reduce neither measure. General support that offsets a sector’s carbon bill without touching its marginal cost, including the absorption of a state-owned producer’s losses, reduces the price paid but not the signal. Under equation 2 it lowers recognition only through the price-paid term, so it matters most while \(\rho < 1\), and beyond that it is a matter for subsidy discipline rather than carbon-price recognition.
crumbs: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
section: A.1 Border carbon adjustment design and recognition of foreign effort
text:
A.1 Border carbon adjustment design and recognition of foreign effort
The design literature treats recognition of foreign policy as one of a handful of core choices. Ismer and Neuhoff (2007) set out the early case that border adjustment for an emissions trading system can be made consistent with trade law if it is based on best available technology rather than actual foreign emissions. Cosbey et al. (2019), reviewing the literature for practitioners, list the regulatory choices: scope, the method for carbon content, the type and price of the adjustment, scenarios requiring modification, use of revenue, and compliance with trade and climate agreements. Mehling et al. (2019) give the most complete legal-economic analysis, tracing the Commission’s 2008 proposal that would have exempted partners taking “comparable action”; their analysis of the trade-law exceptions is the basis of Section 9. Kortum and Weisbach (2017) ask which goods, emissions and countries a border adjustment should cover, and conclude that adjustments impose high administrative costs and need stronger welfare justifications.
The two closest designs bracket this paper’s proposal. Mehling and Ritz (2023) propose a voluntary individual adjustment: a default intensity that a firm may rebut with its actual intensity, and a top-up charge on the shortfall of the foreign explicit carbon price, \(\max\{t - t_k, 0\} \times \min\{z, Z\}\). They do not include “effective” prices from non-price policies. Equation equation 2 with \(\rho = 0\) and plant-level \(\hat e\) is their rule; the paper’s generalization is to credit the signal and measure by country and sector. Neuhoff et al. (2026) go the other way: standardized values independent of process or location, free allocation at benchmark for EU producers, and a standardized liability per tonne of material, with export relief. That removes shuffling and keeps carbon-pricing incentives along the EU value chain, but by their own account creates no direct incentive for cleaner production or carbon pricing abroad. The country-sector route of Section 7 sits between the two: no plant can shuffle, and the exporting country is rewarded for its own instrument.
Recent work recommends starting simple and moving to finer measurement. Keen et al. (2022) judge border adjustments the most effective unilateral instrument against competitiveness loss and leakage, but stress that design is decisive. They recommend limiting coverage to energy-intensive, trade-exposed sectors, benchmarking initially on domestic emission intensities, and deciding explicitly how to treat partners that mitigate by other means. They show that output-based rebating of a carbon tax is a feebate, the equivalence this paper uses. Clausing and Wolfram (2023) separate free-riding by low-ambition countries from the competitive disadvantage of jurisdictions that price carbon against those that subsidize clean production, and show that one border instrument cannot address both. A feebate, which prices at the margin and subsidizes on average, sits between their two cases, which is why price-paid recognition misjudges it.
Leakage estimates bound what is at stake. Branger and Quirion (2014)’s meta-analysis of 25 studies and 310 estimates finds leakage rates of 5–25 percent without border adjustment (mean 14 percent) and 5–15 percent with it (mean 6 percent); extending the adjustment to all sectors is the most effective feature. Fischer and Fox (2012) compare border adjustment with output-based rebating as anti-leakage tools.
crumbs: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
text:
A.2 Who bears CBAM
Exposure falls disproportionately on middle- and low-income exporters with weak verification capacity. Beaufils et al. (2023) find that middle- and low-income countries for which the EU is an important market are hit hardest relative to their economies, even under conservative designs, and explore international schemes for recycling the revenue. Magacho et al. (2024) find Russia, China, Türkiye and Ukraine most exposed in absolute terms, many developing economies with more than 2 percent of exports and 1 percent of production affected, and the Western Balkans, Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Cameroon most exposed relative to their economies. Eicke et al. (2021) build a risk index that includes capacity for monitoring, reporting and verification, and find most high-risk countries in Africa. Perdana and Vielle (2022) find in a general equilibrium model that CBAM cuts leakage by about a third by 2040 but reduces welfare in the least developed countries through lower exports; exempting them raises leakage more than alternatives, while returning revenue for clean energy improves their welfare at low cost to the EU. Mattoo et al. (2009) show, for border taxes set on each exporter’s carbon content, that the burden falls heavily on poorer exporters: China’s manufacturing exports fall by about a fifth, and those of low- and middle-income countries by about 8 percent. These findings matter for recognition because the countries most exposed are those least able to file verified plant data, for which the default values and default carbon prices are the only routes.
crumbs: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
section: A.3 Resource shuffling and leakage under incomplete regulation
text:
A.3 Resource shuffling and leakage under incomplete regulation
The quantitative evidence on shuffling comes from electricity. Fowlie (2009) simulates California’s electricity market under source-based cap-and-trade and finds that exempting out-of-state producers achieves about a third of the reductions of complete regulation at more than twice the cost per tonne. Caron et al. (2015) find that California’s program without restrictions on imported electricity would raise emissions elsewhere by 45 percent of its domestic reduction; with imports in the cap and resource shuffling banned as legislated, leakage falls to 9 percent. The 9 percent assumes the ban works, and Mehling and Ritz (2023) report that it has been difficult to enforce. Fowlie and Reguant (2022) show how to calibrate output subsidies to leakage risk in incomplete carbon markets, which bears on how free-allocation benchmarks should be set. Apaydın (2026) shows the same gap between reported and real cuts in a new place: under CBAM’s electricity-accounting rules, Chinese industrial parks can report reductions of which only about a fifth to a quarter are real in some provinces.
The leading analysis of industrial goods expects less shuffling than in electricity, but offers no measurement. Mehling and Ritz (2023) judge reshuffling “perhaps most acute for electricity markets” and likely less pronounced for industrial goods, whose flows are easier to trace, and suggest a company-level point of regulation. This paper’s Proposition 6 formalizes their trade-off, and the firm-level verification route in Section 7 is their remedy. Their expectation of smaller industrial shuffling is plausible for routing that requires changing physical flows. It is weaker for routing between installations owned by one firm, which requires only that the firm choose which plant fills which order, and for selection into country-average default values, which requires nothing at all.
For steel there are scenario estimates and no measurement of routing. Assous et al. (2024) estimate CBAM fees on imports from China at 2021 trade volumes and full phase-in: €590 million with unchanged flows, €313 million if exporters supply the EU only with electric-furnace steel (half scrap and half direct-reduced or pig iron for flat products), aluminum made with 80 percent scrap and cement with 20 percent clinker, and €695 million with no reporting. They note that the Commission must monitor resource shuffling under Article 30 but has no enforcement mechanism. Hamidani (2026) tests, with monthly customs data for 52 flat-steel products in January–June 2026, whether origins with higher default-based exposure lost EU business, and finds no stable effect yet. A Crossref search on 31 October 2026 found no empirical paper on routing between scrap-EAF and BF-BOF output to the EU.

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
section: A.4 Measuring carbon prices beyond explicit ones
text:
A.4 Measuring carbon prices beyond explicit ones
Implicit carbon pricing through fuel taxes and subsidies is most of the world’s carbon price, and measures of it exist. Agnolucci et al. (2024) develop a total carbon price that adds indirect pricing, fuel excise taxes net of subsidies, to explicit carbon taxes and emissions trading, for 142 countries from 1991 to 2021. Direct pricing covers roughly a quarter of global emissions, but the global total carbon price is not much higher than in 1994, and indirect pricing still makes up “the lion’s share”. Many developing countries, especially net fuel importers, contribute substantially once indirect pricing counts. Black et al. (2023) estimate efficient fuel prices that reflect supply and environmental costs, and the subsidies implied by charging less. The OECD’s effective carbon rates add carbon taxes, fuel excise taxes and permit prices by country and sector (OECD 2023). All three measure the average price per tonne. Paper 6.1 converts any instrument, including feebates and standards, into the uniform tax that would cut emissions as much, and separates the fuel-switching margin from the demand margin (Stretton 2026d); its switching-margin price is the price signal in equation 2.
crumbs: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
text:
A.5 Intensity-based pricing and refunding
Instruments that price intensity and return revenue by output are well understood, and are exactly what price-paid recognition misses. Output-based allocation, tradable performance standards and feebates charge the full rate on emissions at the margin while returning revenue in proportion to output, so they subsidize output relative to a tax (Fischer 2001; Fischer and Fox 2012). Holland et al. (2009) show that an intensity standard can even raise emissions when its implicit output subsidy is large. Paper 1.2 of this series designs feebates for power and industry (Stretton 2026c). Hagem et al. (2020) compare refunding emission payments by output with refunding in proportion to abatement spending: expenditure-based refunding needs a lower fee than a tax for the same abatement, output-based refunding a higher one, and both tilt effort toward abatement technology rather than output. This is the economic content of the draft implementing regulation’s Article 8(2) exemption for revenue-financed decarbonization support, and the basis of the support test in Section 6.2.
crumbs: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
section: A.6 Trade law and comparable effort
text:
A.6 Trade law and comparable effort
The trade-law literature favors recognizing foreign effort and warns against treating like products differently by origin. Ismer and Neuhoff (2007) argue that a border adjustment levied as an internal charge can be defended under the GATT if it charges imports no more than domestic producers would pay with the best available technology. Mehling et al. (2019) analyze the full chain: whether a carbon border charge is an internal tax adjustable at the border, whether products differing only in how they were made are “like”, and the general exceptions of Article XX, whose chapeau forbids “arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination between countries where the same conditions prevail”. The US–Shrimp disputes are the main precedent: the Appellate Body faulted an import ban that in effect required exporting countries to adopt the same program as the United States, and later accepted a revised measure that required a program comparable in effectiveness (WTO Appellate Body 1998, 2001). For recognition, a test of comparable effect, applied by criteria any country can meet, is safer than one that credits only instruments resembling the importer’s own.
Country-level measures raise their own trade-law questions. Country-specific default values and default carbon prices treat like products differently by origin, which engages most-favored-nation treatment under Article I. Cosbey et al. (2019) and Keen et al. (2022) recommend generous defaults that individual producers can rebut with their own data. The country-sector route of Section 7 departs from this by removing the individual rebuttal for countries that opt in; its defense is that the exporting government chooses it, that the criteria are origin-neutral, and that the verification route stays open to every other exporter. Whether that defense would hold has not been tested.
crumbs: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
text:
A.7 What this paper adds
Four points stand against the literature and the legal texts. First, the default carbon price is the operative recognition route for most exporters, and the law makes it discretionary, from 2027, and confines it to countries with carbon pricing rules; for countries with only implicit pricing it is zero by construction. Second, the draft implementing regulation’s Article 8(1)(b)(ii) nets below-baseline emissions, so a feebate or output-based pricing system is recognized only on emissions above its benchmark, although its marginal signal is the full rate; Proposition 4 formalizes this. Third, plant-level measurement creates two routes to shuffling, routing under actual values and selection into country-average default values, neither of which the Commission’s anti-circumvention proposal addresses, while country-sector measurement removes both but leaves plants almost no incentive (Propositions 1–3 and 6). Fourth, a liability formula that credits the country-sector price signal is invariant to shuffling, restores the plant incentive through the exporter’s own instrument and preserves the best-response property of paper 1.1, at a cost to the level playing field that Section 6.1 makes explicit.
