13 Appendix A: Literature review

This appendix reviews the literature by theme. Where only an abstract or the bibliographic record could be checked, the text says what a work addresses rather than what it finds.
A.1 Destination and origin bases, and VAT. VAT is levied on the destination basis: the tax on a good or service accrues where it is consumed, with exports relieved and imports charged (OECD 2017). The equivalence of origin- and destination-based commodity taxes is old: for a uniform, broad-based tax, switching the basis changes price levels and exchange rates but not real allocations (Lockwood et al. 1994). Lockwood and Whalley (2010) apply the result to carbon border adjustments and argue that the policy debate confuses price-level effects with relative-price effects. The result cuts both ways for this paper. It explains why the VAT machinery adjusts for borders without extra apparatus, which is the practical case for using it. It also shows that VAT’s value component, being uniform, carries no carbon incentive and no trade advantage: everything that matters for carbon and for trade sits in the carbon component. The World Bank’s total carbon price takes the same view: Agnolucci et al. (2024) compute direct and indirect carbon prices for 142 countries over 1991–2021 and exclude general VAT because, as across-the-board consumption taxes, VATs “do not affect relative prices”; only VAT preferences on fuels enter, as subsidies. The arithmetic that a 15 percent VAT on a good embodying 0.30 kg per euro is “worth” €500 per tonne is correct, but it is not a carbon price in any useful sense.
VAT’s spread is documented by Keen and Lockwood (2010). Destination-based business taxation rests on the same logic as VAT: a tax levied where the immobile consumer is removes the incentive to shift profits or production (Auerbach et al. 2017). Shapiro (2021) adds an observation that sharpens the case for a destination charge on carbon: tariffs and non-tariff barriers are lower on dirty industries than on clean ones, which amounts to an implicit global subsidy to CO₂ in traded goods of $550–800 billion a year. The existing destination-side tax on trade already prices embodied carbon negatively.
A.2 Consumption-based accounting. Production-based inventories, which national targets use, attribute emissions to the country where they occur; consumption-based accounts attribute them to the country of final demand (Peters and Hertwich 2008). Emissions from producing traded goods grew from 4.3 GtCO₂ (20 percent of the global total) in 1990 to 7.8 GtCO₂ (26 percent) in 2008, and net transfers from developing to developed countries grew from 0.4 to 1.6 GtCO₂, more than the Kyoto Protocol’s reductions (Peters et al. 2011). In 2004, 23 percent of global CO₂ was embodied in trade, and more than 30 percent of consumption-based emissions were imported in Switzerland, Sweden, Austria, the United Kingdom and France (Davis and Caldeira 2010). Grubb et al. (2022) find that net transfers peaked around 2006 and have declined since.
Two qualifications matter. Jakob et al. (2014) argue that a tonne of imported embodied emissions is not a tonne added to global emissions, so pricing all embodied carbon at the full social cost is not first-best; trade measures should concentrate on a few emissions-intensive, highly traded industries. And Steininger et al. (2014) compare the justice and cost-effectiveness of consumption- and production-based approaches for a region acting alone. This paper therefore rests the case for a consumption charge on leakage, administration and acceptability, not on first-best optimality (Section 11).
A.3 Carbon-added taxes, footprint taxes and consumption charges. The carbon-added tax was proposed for Canada by Courchene and Allan (2008): a destination-based tax that, like a VAT, rebates the carbon tax on inputs so that only the carbon added at each stage is carried forward, with imports taxed at entry and exports relieved (Courchene and Allan 2011). McLure (2010) replied that carbon content is unobservable, that extending a credit-method tax through retail would impose compliance and administrative costs out of proportion to the gain, and that border adjustments on imports would need the same ad hoc methods as other carbon taxes; he preferred an upstream tax with border adjustments limited to a few carbon- and trade-intensive basic products. McAusland and Najjar (2015) analyze a carbon footprint tax modeled on a credit-method VAT. They find a pure version, which requires the footprint of every product, possibly too costly, and propose a hybrid in which firms either calculate their own footprints or use default footprints for their product class; because it falls on all goods consumed at home, it keeps domestic firms on an equal footing with producers in countries without climate policy. Eichner and Pethig (2015) show that a unilateral consumption-based carbon tax can produce negative leakage in general equilibrium.
A European proposal for a consumption charge on carbon-intensive materials, sometimes called a climate contribution, is the nearest policy relative. Ismer et al. (2016) set out its legal design as an excise-like charge at product-specific benchmark intensity, applying equally to imports. Pollitt et al. (2020) simulate it with the E3ME model: with the charge rising to about €80 per tonne by 2050, it cuts EU CO₂ emissions by up to 10 percent by 2050 and, because imports are charged alike, avoids leakage. Grubb et al. (2022) place the charge among three trade-compatible price options (border adjustments, a carbon-footprint consumption charge, and an excise contribution combined with free allocation). They note that a charge on actual footprints would reward exporters who decarbonize, but that tracing embodied carbon through global value chains is administratively demanding and open to fraud; defaults by product category are a feasible shortcut if they apply to imports and domestic goods alike. Neuhoff et al. (2026) restate the idea for the CBAM era: CBAM’s production-specific intensities invite resource shuffling, as foreign producers send their cleanest output to the EU; they propose a standardized liability per tonne of material, independent of process and origin, applied along the value chain with export relief.
Holland (2012) shows that, when regulation is incomplete and leakage is possible, an intensity standard combined with a consumption tax can sometimes reach the first best, and Böhringer et al. (2017) that output-based rebating combined with a consumption tax on emission-intensive, trade-exposed goods can be equivalent to a border carbon adjustment: the formal case for pairing the consumption track with an intensity-based production track. What this paper adds to the line is the chain results, the calibration for a whole household basket, the swap inside VAT, and the deduction that links the consumption track to the production track.
A.4 Border adjustment, trade law and trading partners. The design literature establishes the main choices for border carbon adjustment: sectoral coverage, the measure of embodied carbon (domestic benchmark, country default or firm data), treatment of exports, and recognition of foreign policy (Ismer and Neuhoff 2007; Mehling et al. 2019; Keen et al. 2022). Mehling et al. (2019) give the fullest legal analysis, under GATT Articles I, II:2(a), III and XX and the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures, and recommend narrow coverage, default values with a right of rebuttal and crediting of foreign policies; they leave open whether carbon intensity can differentiate like products under Article III:2. Ismer and Neuhoff (2007) argue that border adjustment at the intensity of the best available technology is defensible. Keen et al. (2022) recommend benchmarking first on domestic intensities and moving to country-specific values later, with rebuttal, and note the tension between destination-basis border adjustment and the origin-basis accounting of the Paris Agreement.
The evidence on trading partners favors one default for every origin. Mattoo et al. (2009) find that a border tax on the carbon content of imports, measured at the exporter’s own intensity across all merchandise, would cut China’s manufacturing exports by about a fifth and low- and middle-income countries’ exports by 8 percent, while a tax based on the carbon content of domestic production would do far less damage. Maliszewska et al. (2025) find macroeconomic exposure to CBAM small for most countries and high for a few; their method could size partners’ exposure to an economy-wide carbon component. Evans et al. (2021) show that a border adjustment on imports alone leaves exporters exposed and that export relief raises legal risk, which careful design can reduce; a VAT-based charge zero-rates exports by construction.
A.5 Leakage. Model-based studies find leakage of 5–25 percent without border adjustment, and some leakage survives border adjustment through the fossil-fuel price channel (Branger and Quirion 2014). Ex-post studies find no detectable leakage from the EU ETS so far (Naegele and Zaklan 2019; Dechezleprêtre et al. 2022), partly because industry was shielded by free allocation (Grubb et al. 2022). Two consequences follow. The claim that a destination charge is leakage-proof holds for the goods channel only. And the case for a consumption charge concerns the carbon prices of €100–200 per tonne in prospect, not the leakage observed at the prices of the past.
A.6 Distribution and acceptability. Household carbon is a necessity. Environmental Engel curves for the United States show household CO₂ rising with income but less than proportionally (Sager 2019), and the same holds for local air pollutants, with curves shifting down over time (Levinson and O’Brien 2019). A uniform per-tonne charge on consumption therefore takes a larger share of poorer households’ spending before revenue is returned. VAT itself is regressive against income but proportional or progressive against total spending (Decoster et al. 2010). The most directly relevant study is Feindt et al. (2021), who model a comprehensive carbon price on all goods, including imported ones, in 23 EU countries: incidence before recycling is mostly neutral, sometimes progressive, within countries, but regressive across the EU, because households in lower-income, mainly eastern, member states bear higher average burdens; relatively small transfers between member states would offset this. Section 7 reproduces both patterns with independent data.
Acceptability depends on perceptions as much as on incidence. After the Yellow Vests protests, most French respondents rejected a tax-and-dividend scheme, overestimated their own losses and wrongly believed it regressive, and information moved beliefs only slightly (Douenne and Fabre 2022). Across 20 countries, support for climate policies depends on perceived effectiveness, perceived personal losses and concern for poorer households (Dechezleprêtre et al. 2025). Carattini et al. (2018) identify five sources of resistance to carbon taxes (personal cost, regressivity, economic damage, doubts about effectiveness and suspicion of a revenue grab) and remedies including phasing, earmarking, lump-sum rebates and communication; Klenert et al. (2018) review how revenue use shapes public support. A revenue-neutral swap phased over ten years answers the revenue-grab and personal-cost concerns; presenting it as a cut in VAT on clean goods answers the effectiveness concern.
A.7 Credibility and forward commitment. Optimal plans are time-inconsistent when agents’ expectations depend on future policy (Kydland and Prescott 1977). Helm et al. (2003) apply the problem to carbon and propose delegating carbon policy to an independent agency; Brunner et al. (2012) compare commitment devices, including legislation, delegation, contracts and reputation; Nemet et al. (2017) set out remedies for credibility problems in low-carbon investment and their advantages and drawbacks. Chiappinelli and Neuhoff (2020) show that carbon contracts for difference, in which the government pays investors a fixed carbon price, improve decarbonization incentives and derive conditions under which the government is willing to tie its hands. On instrument choice, exogenous pricing through a tax or a cap with a price floor or ceiling avoids price volatility and harmful interactions with other policies (Goulder and Schein 2013). The forward obligation of Section 8 applies these ideas to ETS2: it is an application, not a new mechanism, and its novelty is the published floor fixed a decade ahead.
A.8 Feebates and the production track. Feebates price intensity without raising average costs. Sterner and Höglund Isaksson (2006) analyze Sweden’s refunded NOₓ charge, a working revenue-neutral feebate, and D’Haultfœuille et al. (2014) find that France’s car bonus-malus shifted purchases toward low-CO₂ cars but raised total CO₂ emissions, because it also raised car sales: a lesson on benchmark design. Intensity standards, the regulatory cousin of feebates, implicitly subsidize output and can even raise emissions (Holland et al. 2009); the consumption track exists to supply the output margin they miss (Stretton 2026d, 2026b).
14 Appendix B: Proofs

Setup. Stages \(k = 1, \dots, n\); \(p_k = p_{k-1} + w_k\) with \(p_0 = 0\); \(E_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} a_j\) with \(E_0 = 0\); carbon base \(C_k\) with \(C_0 = 0\); remittance \(T_k\) as in equation 1. Prices are cost plus value added; taxes are passed to the next stage, except that an exempt firm’s irrecoverable input taxes become part of its price.
Proposition 1. (i) \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} T_k = v \sum_{k=1}^{n} (p_k - p_{k-1}) + P \sum_{k=1}^{n} (C_k - C_{k-1}) = v\,p_n + P\,C_n\), because both sums telescope; nothing depends on \(C_1, \dots, C_{n-1}\). (ii) With \(C_k = E_k\), the carbon part of \(T_k\) is \(P(E_k - E_{k-1}) = P\,a_k\). (iii) The consumer pays \(p_n + v\,p_n + P\,C_n\); with \(C_n = E_n\) the carbon part is \(P\,E_n\). Under carry-forward, \(C_k = C_{k-1} + a_k\) for every \(k\) from the first verified stage on, so a verified base upstream reaches \(C_n\) and hence the consumer price.
Proposition 2. Let stage \(j\) be exempt. It remits nothing and pays \(v\,p_{j-1} + P\,C_{j-1}\) to its supplier without credit, so its price is \(p^x_j = p_{j-1} + w_j + v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1}\) when \(C_{j-1} = E_{j-1}\). (i) If \(j = n\), the consumer pays \(p^x_n = p_n + v\,p_{n-1} + P\,E_{n-1}\) and no further tax. Against full crediting, \((1+v)\,p_n + P\,E_n\), the difference is \(-v\,w_n - P\,a_n\): value added and carbon added at the exempt stage go untaxed, and upstream carbon is charged once. (ii) If \(j < n\), every later price is higher by \(\Delta = v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1}\), and stage \(j+1\) has no creditable input tax, so the taxes on later invoices are \(v\) and \(P\,C_k\) on the full values and bases. The consumer pays \((1+v)(p_n + \Delta) + P\,E_n\), which exceeds the full-crediting outlay by \((1+v)\,\Delta = (1+v)(v\,p_{j-1} + P\,E_{j-1})\). The upstream carbon \(E_{j-1}\) is charged once inside \(\Delta\) and again inside \(E_n\).
Proposition 3. With \(Q_k = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \min(q_j, P)\, a_j\) and carbon component \(P\,E_k - Q_k\) on each sale, firm \(k\) remits \((P\,E_k - Q_k) - (P\,E_{k-1} - Q_{k-1}) = (P - \min(q_k, P))\,a_k \ge 0\). Each tonne emitted at stage \(k\) bears \(q_k\) directly and \(P - \min(q_k, P)\) through the carbon component, a total of \(\max(P, q_k)\). Summed over the chain, the carbon component raises \(P\,E_n - Q_n\) and explicit prices raise \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} q_k a_k\), which equals \(P\,E_n\) when every \(q_k \le P\). For a revenue-neutral feebate the sector-average net price is zero, so it contributes nothing to \(Q\) and the consumer bears \(P\,E_n\) through the carbon component. With default bases \(C_k\) in place of \(E_k\), \(P\,C_k - Q_k\) can be negative when the default understates an ETS-heavy chain; flooring the charge at zero keeps every remittance from becoming a refund on that account.
All three results were checked symbolically for \(n = 4\) with sympy, and the worked example of Section 4 numerically, in 2.Source/check_propositions.py.






Figure 4: Value component, ETS price and carbon component remitted at each stage of the worked example in Section 4. Source: 2.Source/make_wp_figures.py.



15 Appendix C: Calibration of defaults and distribution

Data. (1) FIGARO inter-country input–output table at basic prices, product by product, 2022, million euro (Eurostat 2026b): 50 economies (45 named countries plus the rest of the world and four Western Balkan economies) by 64 CPA products, with five categories of final demand. (2) Greenhouse gas emissions by emitting country and NACE A*64 industry, thousand tonnes CO₂e, from the footprint dataset with destination “world” and all final demand (Eurostat 2026d); the CO₂-only dataset gives the last column of Table 2. (3) Household direct emissions from heating and transport (Eurostat 2026a). (4) Household budget shares by income quintile, 2020 wave, and mean expenditure by quintile (Eurostat 2025). (5) Household final consumption by COICOP purpose, 2022 (Eurostat 2026c). All were downloaded from the Eurostat API on 29 October 2026.
Model. With intermediate flows \(Z\), output \(x\) and technical coefficients \(A = Z \hat{x}^{-1}\), emission intensities per euro of output \(s = f \hat{x}^{-1}\), where industry emissions \(f\) are assigned to the matching CPA product, the multipliers are \(m = s\,(I - A)^{-1}\), in kg CO₂e per euro of final demand. The four Western Balkan economies, present in FIGARO but not in the emissions data, take the rest-of-world intensity for each product; they are a negligible share of EU purchases. Category intensities weight \(m\) by EU-27 household final consumption by origin and product. The model gives an EU-27 footprint of 3,749 Mt CO₂e for all final demand excluding households’ direct emissions, against Eurostat’s 3,743 Mt; for households alone, 2,282 Mt against 2,255 Mt; for CO₂ alone, 2,760 Mt against 2,797 Mt.
Purchasers’ prices. Household purchases of trade services (CPA G45–G47), €1.19 trillion, are 64.5 percent of household purchases of goods (CPA A–C) at basic prices, €1.85 trillion. Spreading them evenly gives a goods intensity at purchasers’ prices of \((e_g + 0.645\, e_{\text{trade}})/1.645\). Taxes on products are excluded throughout.
Sources of the footprint. Of the 2,116 Mt CO₂e embodied in taxable household purchases, 28 percent was emitted by EU power and energy-intensive industry (CPA D35, C17, C19, C20, C23, C24, a proxy for ETS coverage), 14 percent by EU agriculture, 17 percent by other EU industries and services, and 40 percent outside the EU (2.Source/footprint_sources.csv).
Distribution. COICOP 3-digit purposes are mapped to the categories of Table 2 (2.Source/distribution.py); rents, health and education services, social protection, insurance and finance are exempt. Household energy (COICOP 04.5) carries the embodied intensity of electricity and gas supply per euro of EU spending on it, 0.83 kg CO₂e per euro; fuel for vehicles (07.2) carries the supply-chain intensity of refined petroleum products per euro of spending on it, 0.25 kg per euro. Direct emissions per euro of 04.5 and 07.2 spending are computed for each member state. Simplifications: budget shares are applied to spending including taxes; every member state uses EU-wide defaults; national quintiles are averaged with household-spending weights rather than ranked EU-wide; the 2020 survey wave is combined with 2022 intensities.
Code. 2.Source/calibrate_defaults.py builds the model and writes defaults_by_category.csv, defaults_by_product.csv, basket_summary.csv and footprint_sources.csv; 2.Source/distribution.py writes the distribution files; 2.Source/make_wp_figures.py prints the fiscal numbers and draws Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3 and Figure 4. The input–output download is about 72 MB and is cached outside the repository. Setting the environment variable CCT_YEAR=2023 reruns the calibration for 2023, which gives a taxable basket intensity of 0.36 kg CO₂e per euro.

title: 1. Carbon Pricing
text:
Carbon prices stay low in open economies because one instrument is asked to do two jobs: to make producers cut emissions per unit of output, and to make buyers pay for the carbon in what they consume. A tax on domestic production charges exporters and spares imports, so governments exempt industry and hold the rate down. The papers in this section give each job its own instrument. A revenue-neutral feebate prices production intensity at the full rate at the margin, at no cost to the treasury. A carbon component of VAT and a forward obligation on fuel suppliers price consumption, imports included. Recognition at the border should credit a trading partner’s price signal, measured by country and sector, and the Total Effective Carbon Price puts every instrument on one scale. In hot-rolled steel at $80 per tonne of CO₂, a feebate raises producer prices about a third as much as a tax; payments above half the feebate rate make adoption a gain; and once importers charge by country and sector, each exporter does best with a feebate at the importer’s charge.

title: 1. Carbon Pricing
text:
1.1 Price Production and Consumption Separately
A Two-Track Architecture for Carbon Pricing in Open Economies
Carbon prices stay low in open economies because one instrument does two jobs: it pushes producers to cut emissions per unit of output, and it makes buyers pay for the carbon they use. The second job hurts exporters and spares imports. This brief gives each job its own instrument. A revenue-neutral feebate prices production at no cost to the treasury and with a small price effect. A carbon component of VAT, and forward obligations on fuel suppliers, price consumption, imports included. Climate finance above half the feebate rate makes adoption a gain, and border charges set by country turn leakage into a race to the top.

title: 1. Carbon Pricing
section: 1.2 Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin, Without the Carbon Bill
text:
1.2 Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin, Without the Carbon Bill
Decarbonizing Coal-Heavy Power and Trade-Exposed Industry
Carbon taxes stall where coal dominates power or industry competes abroad, because they charge producers for every tonne they still emit. A revenue-neutral feebate charges producers whose emissions per unit of output are above their sector’s average and rebates those below it. It gives the same incentive to switch to cleaner plants as a tax at the same rate, at no cost to the treasury. At $50 per tonne in India, Indonesia and South Africa, it raises regulated power tariffs by $0–4 per megawatt-hour, against $33–40 for a tax. In a wholesale market where coal sets the price the rise is $7–18. The benchmark’s design decides whether it works.

title: 1. Carbon Pricing
section: 1.3 Converting a VAT into a Destination Carbon Tax
text:
1.3 Converting a VAT into a Destination Carbon Tax
A Carbon Component in VAT and a Forward Obligation on Energy Suppliers in the European Union
The EU prices the carbon its factories and power plants emit but not the carbon in most of what Europeans buy, 40 percent of which is emitted abroad. This brief proposes pricing consumption instead, through institutions the EU already has. A carbon component inside VAT charges every good for its embodied carbon, imports included and exports exempt, while the value part of VAT falls by a rule that keeps revenue unchanged. A legal obligation fixed a decade ahead makes the few suppliers of fuel for homes and vehicles pay for the carbon they sell. The obligation can pass by qualified majority now; the VAT component needs unanimity.

title: 1. Carbon Pricing
section: 1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
text:
1.4 Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
Carbon Price Recognition and Scrap Shuffling under the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism
The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism charges imports for their embodied carbon, measured plant by plant, and credits only carbon prices effectively paid abroad. Both rules work against its aim of encouraging trading partners to decarbonize. Exporters can send scrap-based steel to Europe and blast-furnace steel elsewhere, saving €160–310 per tonne for Türkiye, China and India with no fall in emissions. A revenue-neutral feebate, which gives every producer the full carbon price at the margin, earns no credit. Measuring carbon by country and sector, and crediting the country’s price signal, fixes both. Recognition should rise as free allocation is phased out.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
4.1 Typology and the standard schedule
Every line is assigned to one of seven categories by its policy rationale, not by its tariff code. The categories are energy and environment (including transport and plastics); health and gambling (tobacco, alcohol, sugar-sweetened beverages, gambling); luxury; telecommunications and digital services; financial transactions; industrial inputs and legacy residuals (cement, edible oils, soap); and resources. A line that fits two categories goes to its dominant rationale: an annual vehicle levy is energy and transport, not luxury. Sorting by rationale forces an answer to the question most schedules never answer for themselves: what is this excise for? The classic objectives are revenue, external cost, discouraging consumption and charging road users (Cnossen 2005). A cement excise with none of these stated is a revenue line that has outlived its reason, and the typology puts it on the page as such.
Each national line is then mapped onto a fixed standard schedule of 30 lines. The standard schedule (version 1.0) has six fuel lines (petrol, road diesel, kerosene, aviation fuel, heavy fuel oil, lubricants), two vehicle lines (annual circulation; first registration or import), three tobacco lines (cigarettes per pack of 20, other tobacco, e-cigarettes), five alcohol lines (mainstream beer, local-content beer, traditional beer, wine and spirits, all per liter of pure alcohol), four beverage lines (soft drinks, juice, energy drinks, bottled water), and one line each for plastics, gambling, voice, data, mobile money, cement, edible oils, sugar, other inputs and luxury goods. Each standard line has a fixed physical unit. A national line with no counterpart is recorded; a standard line with no national counterpart is recorded as not covered. The rows never change within a version, so the tenth country mapped can be compared with the first without rework.
Each line is recorded on five fields. These are its category; the item as printed in the schedule; the current rate in local currency at a stated legal cut-off date; its structure and differentiation (specific, ad valorem or hybrid, and any differentiation by origin, content, user or alcohol band); and its history since 2020, with every amendment and any pending bill. A pending bill is flagged but never applied. Customs duties are excluded even where they behave like excises, and noted. Levies outside the excise law that work as excises in substance, such as road fund and fuel-price levies, are recorded as excise-like levies and counted with the excise when revenue is compared across countries, because international revenue statistics count them that way (Section 8).

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
4.2 Three comparable measures
A rate on its own is a local-currency number against a locally defined product; the diagnostic scales it three ways. Read together, the measures triangulate a line’s policy intensity. A rate that is low per unit but high as a share of price says the product is cheap; one that is high per unit but low as a share of price says it is expensive; one that is high on both but raises little revenue says the base is small or the tax is not collected.
The first measure is excise per standard physical unit, in US dollars. For line \(j\) with statutory rate \(r_j\) in local currency per legal unit,
\[
m^{U}_j = \frac{r_j \, c_j}{X \, a_j},
\tag{1}\]
where \(X\) is the exchange rate in local currency per US dollar at the cut-off date, \(c_j\) converts the legal unit to the standard unit (0.02 to turn a rate per 1,000 cigarettes into a rate per pack of 20), and \(a_j\) is the representative alcohol content for alcohol lines (5 percent for beer, 4 percent for traditional beer, 12 percent for wine, 40 percent for spirits) and 1 otherwise. For ad valorem lines, \(r_j c_j\) is replaced by the rate times a representative taxable value. This measure is the one for international comparison, because it cuts through differences in schedule architecture. Its weakness is that it hides whether a rate is specific or ad valorem, which decides how it behaves under inflation.
The second measure is excise as a share of the consumer price. With \(\tau_j\) the excise per retail unit and \(p_j\) the typical tax-inclusive retail price,
\[
m^{P}_j = \frac{\tau_j}{p_j}, \qquad \tau_j = \max\left(\tau^{s}_j,\; \theta_j \, v_j\right)
\tag{2}\]
for a “higher-of” hybrid with specific component \(\tau^{s}_j\), ad valorem rate \(\theta_j\) and taxable value \(v_j\). The binding component is reported. Where the legal base (ex-factory or import value) is not observed, the ad valorem rate is applied to the retail price and the result is labeled an upper bound. This measure is the one for domestic debate and for health targets, which are set as shares of retail price. Its weakness is that it moves with the chosen reference price, so the diagnostic reports a range where prices vary by brand or region.
The third measure is implied revenue as a share of GDP. With \(Q_j\) the annual taxed volume and \(Y\) nominal GDP in US dollars,
\[
m^{R}_j = \frac{\tau_j \, Q_j}{X \, Y}.
\tag{3}\]
This measure puts each line in macro-fiscal terms. It is also the most error-prone, because line-level volumes are rarely published. Where the revenue authority publishes collections by line, collections replace the implied figure; where it does not, the implied figure is reported next to whatever aggregate collections exist. Volumes inferred from prevalence surveys (adult smokers times cigarettes a day) include untaxed and illicit supply and are labeled upper bounds. The uncertainty is real: in Sierra Leone the implied tobacco excise runs from 0.09 to 0.17 percent of GDP depending only on whether smokers are assumed to smoke 5 or 10 cigarettes a day (Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic 2026).

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
4.3 Erosion
Erosion is measured as the real value of each specific rate since its last change. With \(P_t\) a consumer price index, a specific rate unchanged since year \(s\) keeps \(P_s/P_t\) of its real value in year \(t\). Laying out the year-by-year trajectory since 2020 makes the erosion-and-catch-up cycle visible: long periods of decline ended by a large nominal increase that is politically expensive because it looks large. A schedule whose specific rates have not moved for five years at 7 percent inflation has handed back 29 percent of their real value without any decision to do so. Rates printed in US dollars, as in Liberia, do not erode with the local currency but still lose value with US inflation. WHO recommends regular, ideally automatic, inflation adjustment of specific tobacco and alcohol excises for this reason (World Health Organization 2021, 2023a).

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
4.4 The four-level report
The report is a pyramid, read from the top and built from the bottom. Level 1 is the page a minister reads: key metrics on the three measures, headline findings, inconsistencies, peer comparison and issues for policy dialogue. Level 2 is the standard schedule, with every national line mapped to it and each standard line scored in US dollars per unit and as a share of price. Level 3 is the country’s own schedule on the five fields, with its rate trajectory. Level 4 is the raw data: the parameter sheet (exchange rate, GDP, prices, volumes, conversion factors), each with a source and a status, the line-level computations and the legislative history. Each level can be checked against the one below it, and nothing appears at Level 1 that Level 4 does not compute.
Every report ships with a workbook in a fixed layout. Its sheets are a summary, country metrics, the standard schedule in human-readable form, the same schedule in long format with one row per rate component (a higher-of hybrid has two rows), parameters, a data-quality scale and sources. US dollar values and data-quality scores are formulas, not typed numbers. Because every country’s workbook has the same columns, a regional comparison is a matter of stacking files.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
5.1 Why one spine
A corrective tax is only defensible if the damages behind it are valued consistently. An analyst who values a statistical life at one figure for air pollution and another for road accidents, or applies a 2020 carbon value to diesel and a 2030 value to coal, produces benchmarks that cannot be added and will not survive a skeptical ministry. The externality spine fixes the valuation parameters once for every country report and applies them across all components. Country data enter through quantities (fuel volumes, exposure, road deaths, vehicle stocks); the values applied to those quantities come from one table. This is what makes the components of a corrective fuel tax comparable with each other and across countries.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
5.2 The corrective fuel tax
The benchmark for road fuels is the corrective tax of the optimal-tax literature. Sandmo showed that, under standard conditions, an externality enters the optimal tax only on the good that causes it, as a term added to that good’s revenue-raising (Ramsey) tax (Sandmo 1975). For motor fuel the corrective term depends on how the fuel causes damage. Carbon and, approximately, local air pollution are proportional to fuel burned. Congestion, accidents and road damage are proportional to distance driven, so a tax per liter corrects them only in proportion to how much of the fall in fuel use comes from driving less rather than from more efficient vehicles (Parry and Small 2005; Parry et al. 2007). The IMF method puts this in operational form (Parry et al. 2014):
\[
t^{*}_f = e^{C}_f + e^{P}_f + \beta \left( e^{G}_f + e^{A}_f + e^{R}_f \right),
\tag{4}\]
where all terms are in US dollars per liter. \(e^{C}_f = \phi_f \, s^{C}\) is the carbon cost: the fuel’s carbon dioxide content \(\phi_f\) times the carbon value \(s^{C}\). On IPCC default emission factors and calorific values (IPCC 2006) and typical densities (0.745 kg per liter of petrol and 0.84 of diesel, the author’s assumption), \(\phi_f\) is 2.29 kg per liter of petrol and 2.68 kg per liter of diesel. \(e^{P}_f\) is the local air pollution cost, mostly premature deaths from fine particulates valued at the value of a statistical life. \(e^{G}_f\), \(e^{A}_f\) and \(e^{R}_f\) are the congestion, accident and road damage costs per liter. \(\beta\) is the share of the fuel-demand response that comes from reduced driving. If half the response to a fuel tax is fewer kilometers and half is better fuel economy, only half of the distance-related damage is corrected through the fuel tax; the rest is better addressed by distance charges, congestion pricing or vehicle standards. The simple sum of the five components (the “naive Pigouvian” rate) is reported beside \(t^{*}_f\) as an upper bound. Parry and Small treat local pollution from petrol cars as distance-related, because emission standards are set per kilometer (Parry and Small 2005); the diagnostic keeps the simpler fuel-based form and says so.
The corrective rate is a floor for a defensible fuel tax, not the optimal rate. equation 4 omits the Ramsey term. Where fuel is one of the few bases a government can tax well, the efficient fuel tax exceeds the corrective rate (Parry and Small 2005; Cnossen 2005). The diagnostic reports the corrective rate because it is the part of the argument that does not depend on a government’s revenue needs, and says so on the page (Section 9).
The gap is the corrective rate less the current effective rate. The current effective rate is the excise plus any fuel levies that work as excises in substance (road fund, regulator and price-stabilization levies), less any explicit subsidy per liter. Value added tax is excluded because it applies to all consumption. The gap \(g_f = t^{*}_f - \tau_f\) is reported with a range from the low and high cases of the spine. Because the current tax is not earmarked to any one damage, the gap itself cannot be split by component; what the report decomposes is the corrective rate. That decomposition matters more than the total: a diesel benchmark made up mostly of air pollution and accident costs makes a health and road-safety case for reform, not a climate case, and the case a government makes affects whether a reform survives.

text:
5.3 Valuation defaults
The spine’s defaults are set once, published with their sources and varied in a stated range. Table 1 lists them. They are defaults for the product, not recommendations: a country team may depart from one with a written justification, and the report then shows the result at the default as well.

The carbon default is a policy-anchored value well below damage estimates. USD 50 per tonne is the middle tier of an IMF staff proposal for an international carbon price floor in 2030, which set floors of USD 75, 50 and 25 for advanced, high-income emerging and low-income emerging economies among six large emitters (Parry et al. 2021). It is a negotiable floor, not a measure of damage. The leading recent damage estimate is USD 185 per tonne (2020 dollars; 5–95 percent range 44–413) at a 2 percent discount rate (Rennert et al. 2022). At USD 185 the carbon component is USD 0.42 per liter of petrol and 0.50 per liter of diesel, against 0.11 and 0.13 at USD 50. The diagnostic keeps USD 50 as its default because a ministry is more likely to accept a benchmark built on a price that governments have discussed than on a damage estimate, and it reports the social-cost case beside it so that the choice is visible.
The value of a statistical life is transferred from a base by income, and the choice of base moves the health components by a factor of up to five. For country \(c\) with income per head \(y_c\),
\[
\text{VSL}_c = \text{VSL}_{b} \left( \frac{y_c}{y_b} \right)^{\eta}.
\tag{5}\]
The diagnostic’s default takes an OECD-based ratio of 100 times income per head with \(\eta = 1\), so the value is proportional to income (OECD 2012). The global benefit-cost guidance of Robinson, Hammitt and O’Keeffe recommends instead a United States base (USD 9.4 million, 160 times income per head) with \(\eta = 1.5\) and a floor of 20 times income, and treats the OECD-based approach as a sensitivity case (Robinson et al. 2019). The two differ most where incomes are lowest. At an income of USD 800 per head the default gives USD 80,000 and the recommended approach USD 16,000, where the floor binds: a factor of five. Because air pollution and accident costs are the largest components of the diesel benchmark in lower-income countries, the report shows both.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
5.4 Health benchmarks
For tobacco, alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages, the diagnostic uses published targets instead of computing externalities. The external and internal costs of these goods (health care paid by others, harm to others, and harm to consumers who misjudge addiction or their own self-control) are harder to value per unit than fuel damages and are contested (Allcott et al. 2019; Chaloupka et al. 2019). The health literature has instead settled on targets that ministries recognize. WHO’s technical manual recommends that excise make up at least 70 percent of the retail price of tobacco products, with specific or mixed structures and regular adjustment for inflation; WHO’s monitoring indicator rates a total tax share of at least 75 percent as best practice (World Health Organization 2021). The diagnostic uses the excise target because it isolates the excise. For sugar-sweetened beverages, WHO finds that taxes that raise retail prices by 20 percent or more cut consumption roughly in proportion (World Health Organization 2016).
For alcohol the diagnostic tests consistency rather than level. Expressing every alcohol line per liter of pure alcohol shows whether a country taxes the same harmful content at very different rates across beer, wine and spirits, just as expressing fuel taxes per tonne of carbon shows inconsistent carbon pricing across fuels (Stretton 2026c). WHO considers specific taxes based on alcohol content the best design for reducing harm (World Health Organization 2023a). Consistency is a test, not a rule: where heavy drinkers favor particular products, differentiated rates can do better than a uniform rate per liter of alcohol (Griffith et al. 2019). An inversion in which the strongest drink pays least per liter of alcohol has no such defense, and the report flags it.
The health and energy lines are read on one page because they share a design question. Health and climate practitioners both favor specific rather than ad valorem rates for corrective excises, since the damage depends on quantity, not price, and both favor automatic indexation so that real rates do not erode between finance acts (World Health Organization 2021, 2023a). A diagnostic that finds unindexed specific rates on fuel, tobacco and alcohol can recommend one indexation rule that covers all three, which is cheaper politically than three separate fights.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
5.5 Depth by data
The same spine runs at two depths. With good data the report uses country-specific elasticities, air pollution attributed by source and separate urban and rural profiles. With weak data it uses pooled elasticities, global burden-of-disease estimates and congestion only for the main city, and reports direction and magnitude with a range. A finding that diesel is undertaxed in every plausible case is more useful to a ministry than a falsely precise point estimate.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
6.1 Stages
The diagnostic is produced by an AI model working to a written specification, with a country economist directing and checking each stage. The pilots used Claude (Anthropic). The process follows the report from the bottom up in five stages, with an AI review pass at the end of each and a human review before anything moves up a level (Table 2). The specification is written to be given to the model directly as context, so the method travels with the instructions rather than with the person who ran it last.



Table 2: Production stages of the diagnostic.










Stage

A1

A4

A schedule can be run whole or in five parts. A whole run covers all 30 standard lines and suits a first diagnostic or a small schedule. A sectoral run splits the work into fuel, vehicles, health (with sugar), other lines (plastics, gambling, telecommunications, financial transactions, cement and other inputs, luxury), and an overarching part that runs last. Every standard line belongs to exactly one part. The first part to run writes a common header (country, cut-off date, currency notation, exchange rate, GDP, price index, list of legal instruments) that every later part reuses unchanged. The overarching part holds what belongs to no single sector (aggregate revenue, the legal framework, the indexation rule and a reconciliation of collections across the revenue authority and the finance ministry) and stacks the four part workbooks into one.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
6.2 Quality rules
The quality rules exist because the pilots broke each of them once. Every number is computed from the parameter sheet; none is typed into the narrative. An early pilot draft carried revenue figures that did not follow from its own inputs, and the Level 4 computations caught them. Every legal line carries at least one reference to a source document, section and page: no reference, no line. An early draft misread a currency notation after a redenomination, and a later draft missed a whole finance act; the line-by-line review caught both. Rates are quoted as printed, with their currency notation. If a table cannot be read, the report says “not legible” and shows the last legible rate. The model may not rely on memory for any rate or data point.
Each figure carries a data-quality score, and a derived figure takes the lowest score of its inputs. The scale runs from 5 (matches the gazetted text or official data, quote on file) through 4 (corrected in review and now matching), 3 (confirmed only in an official secondary source), 2 (not yet verified, or estimated from published inputs) to 1 (assumption, last legible rate or data gap). The rule that a derived figure inherits its weakest input means an implied revenue figure built on a guessed volume cannot present itself as better than a guess. The workbook computes the score by formula.
A comparator comes only from another finished diagnostic. The model may not fill comparator columns from memory or web search, or analyze a second country inside the same run. To compare country A with country B, B is run and reviewed first, and its report and workbook are supplied to A’s run. Both must use the same standard-schedule version and conversion rules. Without a comparator, Level 1 benchmarks only against international references.
When the model cannot fetch a source, it stops and asks. Government websites block automated access and scanned tables cannot be read as text. Rather than fill the gap, the model lists the documents it needs with a short download script; the user runs it and uploads the files, and the model checks each one before resuming.
AI drafting speeds up the work; it does not replace the check against the gazetted text. The time saved is in reading, converting and laying out. The time that remains is in checking, and the process is built so that checking cannot be skipped. Section 8 reports how much the check found.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
7.1 Country A
Country A is fictitious; every input below is a labeled stylized number. It is a lower-middle-income economy with GDP of USD 40 billion in 2025, an exchange rate of 100 local currency units (LCU) per US dollar, and consumer prices 40 percent higher than in 2020. Its schedule has five priority lines: petrol at LCU 30 per liter, road diesel at LCU 18 per liter, cigarettes at LCU 1,500 per 1,000 sticks, beer at LCU 40 per liter, and spirits at 30 percent of an ex-factory value of LCU 600 per liter. All the specific rates were last changed in 2020. It has no excise on sugar-sweetened beverages. Retail prices, volumes and externality costs are set out in the code that produces every number in this section (2.Source/stylized_example.py).

Two-thirds of the diesel benchmark is local damage, not carbon. At the central values, carbon is 31 percent of the diesel corrective rate, local air pollution 35 percent, and congestion, accidents and road damage after the mileage adjustment 35 percent. Air pollution and carbon are close in size on these stylized inputs, so the finding that holds is not that one dominates but that local damage is twice the climate damage. A reform case for diesel built on carbon would rest on the smaller part of the argument. The report says this in its Level 1 findings, where it shapes how a reform is framed: as a health and road-safety measure first.
Closing the diesel gap would raise between 1.1 and 1.2 percent of GDP in the stylized economy. The static gain is USD 510 million, 1.27 percent of GDP. With a short-run price elasticity of −0.3 and full pass-through to a pump price of USD 1.05, diesel use falls about 7 percent and the gain is 1.11 percent of GDP; with −0.1, closer to the publication-bias-corrected estimates for gasoline (Havranek et al. 2012), use falls 2 percent and the gain is 1.22 percent (Brief 5.4 discusses why published elasticities overstate the response). The range of the gap is wide, from USD 0.02 per liter in the low case to USD 0.73 in the high case, and showing it is what stops one challenged parameter from discrediting the whole report.
The spine’s two most contested parameters move the result more than any other. Moving \(\beta\) alone from 0.35 to 0.65 moves the diesel corrective rate from USD 0.39 to 0.48 per liter. Valuing carbon at USD 185 instead of 50 moves it to USD 0.80, and petrol’s to USD 0.61, so that both fuels are undertaxed by a wide margin. The value of a statistical life moves the air pollution and accident components, together more than half (58 percent) of the diesel benchmark at central values, in proportion, and the two transfer methods of Section 5.3 differ by up to a factor of five.
The petrol result is a warning against reading the spine alone. Petrol was taxed about 40 percent above its corrective rate in real terms when its rate was set in 2020 (USD 0.42 in today’s prices against 0.30). Inflation has since brought it down to the benchmark without any decision, and unindexed it will fall further below it every year. The finding for petrol is about indexation, as it is for tobacco and beer, and one indexation rule covering every specific excise is the cheapest reform the report identifies.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
section: 8.2 What counts as an excise decides the revenue comparison
text:
8.2 What counts as an excise decides the revenue comparison
On a consistent definition both countries raise about the African mean, but the two figures rest on different evidence. Liberia’s excise law raised 0.37 percent of GDP in FY2024, about a quarter of the African mean of 1.32 percent in 2023 (OECD et al. 2025). But Liberia taxes fuel through earmarked Road Fund and refinery-company levies outside the excise law, and international revenue statistics count such levies as excises: in the OECD data, Liberia’s petroleum taxes and Road Fund fee are in the excise category, which totals 0.99 percent of GDP in 2023. Counting those levies and the motor vehicle levy, the diagnostic finds excise and excise-like levies of 1.25 percent of GDP in FY2024, close to the mean. The excise law alone describes about a third of Liberia’s system.
Sierra Leone’s collections differ from the public series by a factor of about two, and the diagnostic has not yet explained why. The diagnostic reports excise collected of 1.25–1.28 percent of GDP in 2024–25, nine-tenths of it from fuel. The OECD series records 0.57 percent in 2023, of which petroleum excise 0.34 percent and road user charges 0.15 percent, and 0.93 percent in 2021 (OECD et al. 2025). Fuel rate increases since 2023, a revision to GDP, or a difference in what is counted could each explain part of the gap. Reconciling collections across sources is one of the diagnostic’s own validation steps (Section 10.1), and for Sierra Leone it is open. Until it is closed, the Sierra Leone revenue figure should be read as the diagnostic’s estimate, not as a finding about the country’s tax effort.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
8.3 What the two runs find
Sierra Leone raises most of its excise from fuel, on a large base rather than a high rate. Petrol pays USD 0.23 per liter, 16 percent of the pump price, about twice the carbon component of USD 0.11 at USD 50 a tonne and about half of it at USD 185. The Finance Act 2026 raised fuel rates by 79 to 147 percent, and at the new rates fuel would raise about 1.6 percent of GDP on the diagnostic’s estimate. Every non-fuel line together collected only 0.10–0.16 percent of GDP, although cigarettes, beer and sugar-sweetened beverages are all on the schedule.
The Sierra Leone run finds erosion by redenomination and incoherence across alcohol lines. When rates moved from US dollars to leones in 2024, beer rates fell about 70 percent and wine rates 70–90 percent in dollar terms; the 2026 act caught up on fuel and raised cigarettes by half, to USD 0.14 a pack, still about 14 percent of the retail price against WHO’s 70 percent target. Beer is taxed under two regimes, a specific rate and ad valorem bands for local content, whose rates differ by a factor of 1.3 to 4 depending on classification; imported beer and wine pay 50 to 140 percent more than local; wine pays less than beer per liter of pure alcohol; kerosene pays 40 percent of the diesel rate. The current spirits and soft-drink rates could not be read in the published law, so the report shows the last legible 2023 rates at the lowest data-quality score, as the quality rules of Section 6.2 require.
Liberia’s excise raises little because its largest bases sit outside the excise law. Fuel carries only the levies, worth USD 0.095 per liter, 7.3 percent of the June 2026 petrol price ceiling, and below the carbon cost alone at USD 50 a tonne before any air pollution, accident or congestion cost is counted. Plastics, mobile money, cement and edible oils are outside the excise law, and aviation fuel is exempt. Cigarettes pay USD 0.50 a pack, 27 percent of the last known retail price, yet the revenue authority booked no excise on imported tobacco in FY2024 or the first quarter of FY2025.
Liberia’s alcohol rates are inverted and unstable. Spirits pay USD 7.50 per liter of pure alcohol against USD 20.00 for beer, the same inversion as in Country A: the strongest drink pays least. The local spirits rate moved from USD 2.00 to 0.50 to 3.00 per liter in 16 months. The soft-drink rate of USD 0.45 per liter is flat, with no link to sugar, and above the UK’s top rate of GBP 0.28 at any exchange rate below 1.6 dollars per pound (HM Revenue and Customs 2026). Rates printed in US dollars do not erode with the Liberian dollar, and indexation is legislated from 1 January 2027. These rates read the latest amending act’s “Proposed” column as in force, an interpretation the run leaves open.
Both runs point to collection, not legislation, as the binding constraint outside fuel. Sierra Leone’s non-fuel lines together collect only 0.10–0.16 percent of GDP, and its run lists configuring excise on imports in the customs system among the open items; Liberia’s tobacco excise cannot be traced in the accounts. In both countries the most useful next steps the runs identify are administrative: publish legible schedules, book each excise line separately, and confirm which rates are in force. No reading of the schedule alone could have produced that finding; it comes from setting implied revenue beside collections.
The two runs report the three measures and the benchmarks but do not yet include a full externality spine. The comparison of fuel rates with the carbon component is the author’s calculation from the diagnostic’s measures. Whether Sierra Leone’s USD 0.23 also covers air pollution and accidents, as the Country A diesel example suggests it would not, is the question a full spine run would answer.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
10.1 How the diagnostic is checked
Validation runs at three levels: legal text, arithmetic and collections. Every legal line is checked against the gazetted source and given a status. Every computed number can be traced through the workbook to the parameter sheet, so a reviewer can recompute any Level 1 figure. Implied and reported revenue are reconciled with published collections: if the implied figure for fuel is 1.65 percent of GDP and collections are 1.2 percent, the gap is itself a finding, pointing to exemptions, arrears, smuggling or wrong volumes, and the report says which it cannot tell apart. The comparison with the OECD’s revenue series in Section 8.2 shows why this step matters and that it is not yet complete for Sierra Leone.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
10.2 What it cannot do
The diagnostic is static. It does not model pass-through, demand response beyond a first-order correction, cross-border fuel smuggling or tobacco illicit trade. A ministry that wants revenue and emission projections should take the diagnostic’s rates and gaps into a model that has those responses, such as the Climate Policy Assessment Tool for fuels (Stretton 2026d), with the caution on its elasticities in Brief 5.4.
Implied revenue is approximate. Line-level volumes are the weakest input. Prevalence-based volumes include untaxed supply and overstate the base, and shares of consumer price move with the reference price. The data-quality score on each implied figure says how much to trust it.
Informal and home-produced goods sit outside the formal base. Opaque beer, home-distilled spirits and informally traded fuel are large in many lower-income countries. The diagnostic describes the formal base accurately and understates total consumption.
The externality spine is only as good as its weakest component. Air pollution exposure data at the spatial detail needed to attribute deaths to transport are missing in most low-income countries. Police accident records undercount road deaths, which is why WHO publishes modeled estimates by country (World Health Organization 2023b); the accident component should start from those estimates, not from police counts. Credible local fuel-price elasticities are rare, and the mileage share \(\beta\) is rarely estimated at all. The report surfaces these uncertainties as ranges and data-quality scores instead of burying them.
AI drafting introduces its own failure modes. A model can misread a scanned table, carry forward a superseded rate or produce a fluent paragraph that its own workbook does not support. The quality rules target exactly these failures. They work only if the human review is done, and no process can force a tired reviewer to read every line.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:
10.3 How a ministry uses it
The diagnostic is built to be run every year and read in a meeting. A tax policy unit can run it at each budget cycle, with the same standard schedule and the same spine, so that the change from last year shows on one page. It supplies what any budget or tax policy review needs on excise: the tax structure, the effective rates and their erosion, benchmarks against peers and targets, and the issues for policy dialogue.
The findings feed a reform sequence, which is a separate exercise. The sequence turns the diagnostic’s gaps into steps: what can be done by administrative indexation this year, what needs legislation, and what needs a compensation package first. Sequencing depends on political economy as much as on the size of each gap. Where a fuel tax is too salient to raise, other instruments can price part of the same damage: a feebate on new vehicles, as France has run since 2008, charges high emitters and rebates low ones without moving the pump price (Durrmeyer 2022; Stretton 2026b). The diagnostic’s contribution to that discussion is narrower and harder to argue with: it says where the system stands, against what, and how sure anyone can be.
The next step is a common regional table. Because every report maps onto the same 30 rows and uses the same spine, a set of country diagnostics stacks into a regional comparison with no further work, which a fiscal profile such as the indicators dashboard of paper 7.2 can then place in context (Stretton 2026a). Each new country makes the others more useful.

title: The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
text:

This version condenses and replaces a 24,800-word draft (version 0.1, kept in the paper’s folder). The method was developed and piloted with country economists on three sub-Saharan African excise schedules; Section 8 reports the two pilots that were peer reviewed, Sierra Leone and Liberia, as illustrative results from the diagnostic, not official estimates. title: 7. Analytics Tools
text:
Analysis changes policy only when the people who hold the budget can reproduce it. The two tools in this section each take data a finance ministry already holds or can download, put it on a common scale and return something sequenced enough to act on. The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic reads a whole excise schedule against the damage taxed goods do; run on Sierra Leone and Liberia, it finds fuel taxed lightly, alcohol taxed inconsistently and health excises weakly collected. The Global Fiscal Indicators dashboard gives a one-page fiscal and energy profile for 217 economies, with the year and public source of every value; it separates a revenue problem from a debt-service problem. A third tool built to the same standard, the Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool, extends the Climate Policy Assessment Tool and is described in section 6 (paper 6.5). The October 2026 reviews held both tools to their own standard and corrected a benchmark, a definition and a claim of reproducibility.

title: 7. Analytics Tools
text:
7.1 The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic
Reading an Excise System Against Its Externalities
Excise schedules grow by amendment until no one can read them whole, so few finance ministries know whether their fuel, tobacco or alcohol taxes are high or low against the damage those goods do. The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic is a short, repeatable report that maps every excise line onto a standard schedule, measures each rate three comparable ways and sets fuel taxes against one fixed set of damage values. Run on Sierra Leone and Liberia in 2026, it finds fuel taxed below or near the carbon cost alone, alcohol taxed inconsistently and health excises weakly collected. Ministries should index specific excises, book each line separately and rerun the diagnostic every budget.

text:
7.2 A Global Fiscal Indicators Dashboard for Climate-Fiscal Analysis
Eighty Public Indicators, One Country Profile, and a Build That Traces Every Number to Its Source
Climate-fiscal advice often starts from whichever number was easiest to find. The Global Fiscal Indicators dashboard puts the numbers that matter on one page for 217 economies: 80 public indicators in twelve blocks, each answering one question, scored 1 to 10, with the year and source of every value. Four middle-income economies show the payoff: Indonesia has a revenue problem and costly fuel subsidies, South Africa a debt-service problem and large unpriced pollution. A check against the IMF’s own files confirms most values and finds three compilation faults. Ministries and development banks should use such profiles to choose the next question, and should publish the builds behind them.

title: Price the Capital, Then Test the Budget
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The equations, proofs, worked example and country runs are in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
The cost of capital, not the size of the bill, decides whether clean capital pays its way in developing countries. A typical clean asset that pays its way handsomely at 6 percent stops paying above 12.6 percent.
CPAT can price this, but teams should say which cost of capital they use. Its default adds a technology premium to each country’s own rate; its optional income-group rates put lower-middle-income countries at 12.5 percent, right on the line.
What investors see and what society gets differ, and the gap is what de-risking buys. Each point off the cost of capital is worth about $36 billion a year for each year’s global clean energy investment.
A project can be worth building and still break the budget’s cash flow. In a stylized island, a solar plant worth $108 million leaves the budget $14.6 million a year short on a seven-year loan; a power purchase agreement hides a larger liability than the debt it avoids.
Ministries should test public spending with a cost of funds that rises when cash is short, and count contract liabilities as debt.


Climate models price policies but not the capital they call for
Developing countries need trillions of dollars of clean capital, and ministries’ main climate model does not price it. Developing countries other than China need $2.3 to 2.5 trillion a year of climate investment by 2030 (Bhattacharya et al. 2024). The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), built by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), tells a ministry what a carbon tax raises and cuts in more than 180 countries (Black et al. 2023). Its power model builds new plants and reports what they cost. But outside power it has no capital at all, and it has no test of whether public money should pay (working paper, what CPAT lacks).
A minister needs two answers before any of the capital is built. The first is what the capital costs to carry. For a solar plant, money is most of the price: the International Energy Agency finds that the cost of capital for utility-scale solar in emerging and developing economies is well over twice that in advanced economies (International Energy Agency 2024), and the same plant financed at 12 rather than 4 percent sells power for about 80 percent more (Brief 3.2, Stretton (2026a)). The second is whether the budget should pay, and how. A plant can pay back handsomely and still break a budget that must service a short loan.


Price investment needs three ways
The first extension turns the physical change CPAT computes into investment, and prices it three ways. Investment is new capacity times its unit cost, against a baseline: gigawatts of solar, kilometers of line, buses bought. CPAT supplies this for power; elsewhere a share-of-GDP rule fills in until a physical model, such as the open SISEPUEDE model, can replace it. The capital is then turned into an annual charge three ways: at the market cost of capital the country faces, at the World Bank’s 6 percent social rate (World Bank 2016), and at 6 percent with cleaner air and carbon counted (working paper, investment needs).
The three lenses separate the price of finance from the value of time. The market rate is what investors and households pay. The social rate is what the economy gives up by waiting. The physical need is the same in all three; what changes is the cost of carrying it and the benefits set against it. The gap between the first lens and the third is the case for public finance.
A typical clean asset pays its way at 6 percent and stops paying at 12.6 percent. Take an asset that saves 13.3 cents a year in fuel and running costs for each dollar it costs, over 25 years. That is a stylized figure, of the same order as the financial savings the SISEPUEDE model finds for Latin America (Kalra et al. 2023). Each $1,000 of it earns $43 a year at 7.5 percent, $23 at 10 percent, about $1 at 12.5 percent, and loses $22 at 15 percent (Table 1).



Table 1: A typical clean asset pays its way at 6 percent and breaks even at 12.6 percent. US dollars a year per $1,000 of capital; stylized asset saving $133 a year for 25 years. The four rates from 7.5 to 15 percent are CPAT’s optional rates for high-, upper-middle-, lower-middle- and low-income countries. Source: working paper, Proposition 1.

CPAT’s default cost of capital differs from what its documentation says, and the choice moves the verdict. CPAT’s documentation describes a cost of capital by income group, from 7.5 percent in high-income to 15 percent in low-income countries (CPAT Team 2024). The model’s default is different: each country’s own rate, built from risk-free rates and country risk premiums, plus a technology premium of about 3 points for wind and solar in a lower-middle-income country (CPAT-AI Project 2026). The income-group rates are an option. Under the option, a lower-middle-income country sits right on the break-even line; under the default, its solar asset crosses it once the country’s own rate passes about 9.7 percent. Uganda’s observed rate for renewables, 8.5 percent, is far below the 15 percent the option would give it (working paper, the cost of capital).
At the scale of global needs, the cost of capital is worth tens of billions of dollars a year. Applied to the expert group’s 2030 estimate of $2.4 trillion of investment in developing countries other than China, the same stylized asset earns $45 billion a year more than its financing costs at a 10.5 percent market rate and $131 billion at 6 percent; at 15 percent it loses $52 billion. Each point off the cost of capital is worth about $36 billion a year for each year’s global clean energy investment of $4.8 trillion (working paper, what the lenses show).
The instruments that close the gap already exist. Pricing carbon and air pollution turns society’s gains into revenue. Concessional loans substitute a lower rate for the market rate. Guaranteeing the power contract rather than the debt removes payment risk (Brief 3.1, Stretton (2026b)), and refinancing operating plants through pooled securities cuts the cost of solar power by about a fifth (Stretton (2026a)). A high cost of capital also changes what gets built: dear capital favors fossil plants over capital-heavy wind and solar (Hirth and Steckel 2016).


Test whether the budget should pay
The second extension asks what each dollar of net public money buys. For each candidate measure, compare the value to people with what the budget really pays, after removing what the private sector would have done anyway, money lost in delivery, and money that comes back as fees or fuel savings. Fund the measure if value per budget dollar beats the cost of raising a dollar of tax, about $1.20 in African evidence (Auriol and Warlters 2012). With a cost of funds of one, this is the World Bank’s usual net present value test (working paper, the rule).
Money spent is not capital built. The IMF estimates that low-income developing countries get 40 percent less from public investment than the same spending could buy, emerging markets 27 percent and advanced economies 13 percent; better investment management could close up to two-thirds of the gap (International Monetary Fund 2015). The extension charges each public measure for that loss once, and puts capital and recurrent costs on one footing, because unfunded maintenance is a main way public capital loses value (working paper, five corrections).
Revenue that comes back is worth more than its face value. Each dollar the budget recovers saves more than a dollar of tax, so who keeps a fuel saving changes the budget case but not the economic one. And pricing comes first: a carbon tax raises money cheaply, so a subsidy that a price could replace should be flagged (Brief 6.1, Stretton (2026c)).


A good project can still break the budget
In a stylized island, a solar plant worth $108 million passes every test but cash. The island has $2 billion of GDP, public debt of 85 percent of GDP and diesel power. A $120 million solar plant with batteries replaces 30 percent of its diesel and saves $20.5 million a year. At 6 percent it is worth $108 million, and it stays worth building down to oil at about $22 a barrel (working paper, worked example).
The only commercial loan, at 8 percent over seven years, leaves the budget $14.6 million a year short. Debt service and upkeep come to $24.8 million a year; the budget keeps half the fuel saving. The plant still passes the public-money test: each budget dollar buys over four dollars of value. But the cash gap lasts seven years, and headline debt rises from 85 to 91 percent of GDP (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Net cash to the budget in year one, and the debt or contract commitment each financing route creates, stylized island. Source: working paper, worked example.



Concessional finance closes the gap; a power purchase agreement hides it. A 30-year concessional loan at 1.5 percent puts $6.6 million a year into the budget from the start. A power purchase agreement with a private producer keeps the plant off the debt statistics and narrows the cash gap to $4.0 to 6.4 million a year. But its committed payments are worth 7.6 to 8.9 percent of GDP at the government’s borrowing rate, more than the 6 percent of debt it keeps off the books. A guarantee that cuts the producer’s cost of capital from 11 to 8.5 percent is worth about $31 million to the island.
A longer loan eases cash but does not make borrowing cheaper. At the government’s own rate, the seven-year and 25-year loans cost the same in present value. A model with one fixed cost of public funds even prefers the short loan. Only a cost of funds that rises in cash-short years sees the trap.


Country runs show the same pattern
Illustrative runs put 2030 mitigation investment at 4 to 5 percent of GDP in Kenya, Uganda and St Lucia. The investment-needs tool shares global totals among countries, so the results are allocations, not bottom-up estimates (Mitigation Investment Needs Model 2026). In Kenya and Uganda the extra investment is a net cost at market rates and at 6 percent, and pays only when cleaner air is counted. In St Lucia, which burns imported diesel, it pays at any rate (working paper, country runs).
In Uganda, under a fifth of the benefits of net zero reach the budget as cash. A run of the open SISEPUEDE model values Uganda’s net-zero strategy at $161 billion at 6 percent, but only 18 percent of its benefits are fuel and system savings that a budget or utility would see; the rest is health, crops and water (SISEPUEDE 2025). Such measures make a strong case for public money, financed mostly by tax, not by the savings they generate.


The method has limits that teams should state
The weakest numbers are the savings per dollar and the country cost of capital, and they matter most. The 13.3 cents of savings is stylized; country runs should use CPAT’s own fuel savings or a SISEPUEDE run. Observed costs of capital for renewables exist for a few dozen countries, and CPAT’s default premium is a judgment. Even the accounting convention matters: if savings start in year zero, as in CPAT’s own cost formula, the break-even rate is 14.8 percent rather than 12.6 (working paper, limits).


What to do
Finance ministries: ask for investment needs at your own cost of capital and at 6 percent, side by side. Ask which cost-of-capital setting the model used, and what each point off it would be worth.
Ministries and debt managers: test public measures with a cost of funds that rises when cash is short. Count a power purchase agreement’s committed payments, valued at the government’s own rate, as a liability beside debt, and compare financing routes on cash, debt and liabilities together.
Development-bank teams running CPAT: report which cost-of-capital setting and which accounting convention you used. Replace the stylized savings rate with CPAT’s own fuel savings or a SISEPUEDE run, and apply the delivery haircut once.
The CPAT team: publish the cost of capital by country and technology as open data, with sources. It is the most influential input in the model and the least measured.
