title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full analysis, with the model, proofs, calibration and literature, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Headline carbon prices miss most climate policy. They add up explicit prices per tonne, so a fuel standard, a clean-power subsidy or a revenue-neutral feebate scores nothing, and a dollar on coal counts the same as a dollar on gasoline.
Measure a policy mix by the carbon tax it is worth. The Total Effective Carbon Price (TECP) is the uniform, economy-wide carbon tax that would cut emissions as much as the actual mix. A ministry can compute it from data it already holds.
The difference is large. In a stylized economy, a mix that explicit prices rate at $21 per tonne is worth $37 in the long run ($32–38 across the evidence on elasticities) and $28 after one year.
Standards and mandates fit on the same scale. A tradable standard counts at its credit price, weighted by how much it cuts; a mandate counts through its measured effect.
Use it to pay for policies, to credit non-price policies at the border and to show governments where their mix is weak. Report it beside each instrument’s cost, never instead of it.


Headline prices measure the signal, not the result
No country prices carbon with one instrument. A typical package combines a carbon tax or emissions trading in power and industry, fuel taxes, subsidies for renewable power, a clean-fuel standard and efficiency rules. Comparing countries’ effort, paying a country for a policy or crediting its carbon pricing at a foreign border all need one number per tonne that treats a tax, a subsidy and a standard alike.
The standard measures add up prices. The OECD’s effective carbon rate adds carbon taxes, emissions trading prices and fuel taxes per tonne of CO₂ (OECD 2023). The World Bank’s total carbon price adds direct carbon pricing to indirect pricing through fuel taxes net of fuel subsidies, so it can turn negative, and weights by emissions (Agnolucci et al. 2024). Its authors state the limit: the measure describes the incentive, not the emission cuts it produces, and a version weighted by effectiveness is left for future work (Agnolucci et al. 2024).
Adding prices fails in three ways. First, it weights each price by emissions, not by how much emissions respond. A $1 tax raises the cost of coal power by 1.4 percent but the price of gasoline by 0.2 percent, so the coal tonne responds far more. Second, instruments without a per-tonne rate score zero: a renewable subsidy, a clean-fuel standard, a procurement rule, and a revenue-neutral feebate, whose average payment is nil (Brief 1.2). Third, it cannot see how an instrument works: a feebate pushes producers to switch to cleaner fuels and leaves demand almost untouched, while a tax on energy does the reverse.
Counting standards at their credit price does not fix the problem. The comprehensive carbon price of Carhart et al. (2022) adds the credit prices of standards and feed-in tariffs to explicit prices, weighted by the emissions each covers. It shows the incentive emitters face. Its authors leave the question of what the incentives achieve for future work, and the answer can differ by a factor of two, as the example below shows.


The Total Effective Carbon Price
The TECP asks what uniform carbon tax would cut emissions as much as the actual mix. A tax of $30 per tonne on every fuel is worth exactly $30. Any other instrument, priced or not, is worth the uniform tax that matches its effect on emissions, against the same baseline and over the same horizon. The concept was proposed for comparing countries and for border adjustments by Weil (2021), and the IMF computes it for the G20 with its Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), one model run per policy (Black et al. 2022).
The working paper makes it computable without a model run. Each instrument is translated into the price changes it causes on each fuel in each sector. A standard model of energy demand then splits the response into two effects: switching to cleaner fuels, and using less energy. Weights computed once per country, from the energy balance, fuel prices and two published elasticities per sector, turn any package into one number by a weighted sum (working paper, the Total Effective Carbon Price). A short correction brings the result to within 2 percent of the full model, which gives the exact value (working paper, beyond first order).
The weights show where carbon prices bite. They are large where clean and dirty fuels compete, as in power, and where carbon is a large share of the energy bill, as with coal in industry; they are small in road transport, where fuel is expensive per tonne of carbon.
The TECP has a horizon. Switching fuels needs new boilers, vehicles and power plants and takes a decade or more; using less energy happens within a year or two. So a policy that works by switching, such as a feebate, a renewable subsidy or a fuel standard, is worth less in its first years than in the long run, relative to a tax (working paper, horizon).


Standards and mandates fit on the same scale
A tradable standard is a feebate at its credit price. A low-carbon fuel standard taxes fuels above the standard and subsidizes fuels below it (Holland et al. 2009); with credits traded, every supplier faces the credit price at the margin. It therefore enters the TECP like any price instrument. A renewable portfolio standard charges every fossil megawatt-hour the same, so it does not separate coal from gas, and the TECP shows the cost of that (working paper, non-price instruments).
A standard that cannot be traded counts at the average marginal cost of compliance, weighted by how strongly each firm responds. A simple average overstates the TECP when the firms with the highest costs are also the least able to respond, which is common.
A mandate counts through its measured effect. Rules that change technology directly, such as coal-plant retirement, low-carbon cement in public works or forward obligations on fuel suppliers (Brief 1.3), are scored by the uniform tax that would cut as much. The effect must be measured against the same baseline and must be net of leakage. When some US states limited greenhouse gases per mile of new cars inside the federal fuel-economy standard, leakage to other states offset an estimated 70–80 percent of the reductions from new cars in the adopting states (Goulder et al. 2012).


A stylized mix is worth $37, not $21
The working paper scores one policy mix in a stylized three-sector economy. The economy emits 261 million tonnes of CO₂ a year: 119 from power (coal, gas and renewables), 80 from road transport (gasoline, diesel and biofuel) and 62 from industry (coal, oil and gas). The mix has a $30 per tonne carbon tax on power and industry, a $10 per megawatt-hour subsidy for renewable power and a tradable standard that cuts the carbon intensity of road fuel by 2 percent. All numbers are stylized (working paper, worked example).

The tax is worth more than its headline, because it falls where emissions respond. The explicit-price measure spreads the $30 tax over all emissions, including the 31 percent from road transport that it does not cover. But a uniform tax gets only about 6 percent of its effect from road transport, so leaving road fuel out costs little: the tax alone is worth $27, not $21. Extending it to road fuel would add only about $1.6.
The fuel standard has a high price and a small effect. Its credit price is $166 per tonne, yet it adds only about $1 to the TECP: a high price on a large, unresponsive base. Counting its credit price as a carbon price, as the comprehensive carbon price does, puts the mix at $72.
The renewable subsidy is worth $4 in the long run and $1 after one year. It works by building new capacity, which takes time, while cheaper power raises demand at once. At $79 of budget per tonne avoided, a cost-per-tonne measure would rank it the most ambitious instrument; the TECP ranks it a distant second.






Figure 1: TECP of each instrument and of the mix, split into fuel switching and using less energy, against the explicit-price measure (stylized economy; first-order calculation). The full model rates the mix at $36.9. Source: working paper; figures/make_figures.py.



The result holds across the evidence on elasticities. Drawn 2,000 times from the published ranges, the mix’s long-run TECP lies between $32 and $38 in 90 percent of draws and above $21 in every draw (working paper, calibration). Errors common to all elasticities cancel, because the TECP compares two cuts made with the same numbers. Errors in the demand elasticities alone do not: with the higher demand elasticities built into CPAT, the TECP is $33, as Brief 5.4 found (Stretton 2026a). A model that, like CPAT, applies long-run responses in the first year would also report $37 for year one, about 30 percent above the $28 that capital turnover allows.


Three uses
Climate finance can pay for policies rather than projects. A payment per tonne above half a feebate’s rate makes adopting the feebate a gain for the country (Brief 1.1). The tonnes paid for are the policy’s change in TECP times the country’s emission cut per dollar of uniform tax (working paper, uses). A country that adopts a fuel standard or a procurement rule then earns the same per tonne as one that adopts a tax. Because the TECP is a forecast, payments should be settled against observed emissions.
Border mechanisms can credit the price signal of feebates and standards. The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) reduces an importer’s charge only by the carbon price effectively paid abroad, net of any rebate (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2025). A feebate or an intensity standard pays almost nothing net, so it earns nothing, although its marginal signal is the full rate. The TECP’s switching part, computed for one sector, measures that signal for price and non-price instruments alike: a feebate across steel routes scores its rate, a tradable standard its credit price (Brief 1.4). Equal signals are not equal costs: non-price policies generally impose lower private costs on firms than a carbon price at the same shadow price (Keen et al. 2022), so recognition on this basis rewards effort, not competitive burden.
Governments can see where their mix is weak. The TECP splits by sector, instrument and effect. In the example the weak point is road transport, which responds little to any carbon price at the margin; that argues for instruments aimed at vehicle choice rather than a higher fuel price.


What the TECP does not measure
It measures abatement, not cost. Two mixes with the same TECP cut the same tonnes but need not cost the same. Per tonne, standards and subsidies generally cost more than a price (Fischer and Newell 2008; Kalkuhl et al. 2013). Report the TECP beside each instrument’s shadow price and cost.
It is only as good as its inputs. Elasticities are known to ranges; taxes may move demand more than equal market price changes; and a government that reports its own standards’ costs has reason to overstate them. The example is stylized: the TECP has not yet been computed for a real country (working paper, limits).


What to do
Finance ministries and statistical offices: compute and publish the TECP beside explicit carbon prices. The inputs are an energy balance, delivered fuel prices, emission factors and two elasticities per sector; publish the weights so that others can reproduce the number, with a range and a one-year and long-run value.
The World Bank, the IMF and the OECD: add an effectiveness-weighted series to the total carbon price and the effective carbon rate. Use one shared set of elasticities across countries, so that common errors cancel, and compare the closed-form TECP with CPAT’s model-based equivalents for the same policies.
Climate-finance facilities: pay per tonne of change in the TECP, settled against observed emissions, so that standards, feebates and taxes earn on the same basis.
The European Commission: accept the sector’s switching-margin TECP as the measure of a foreign price signal, phased in alongside the price paid, as Brief 1.4 proposes (Stretton 2026c).
Regulators: publish the marginal compliance cost of every binding standard, so that it can enter the TECP and be compared with a carbon price.


Related papers in this series

No. 1.2: feebates in power and industry (Stretton 2026d).

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.5, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full account, with the equations, the checks and the sources, is in the working paper. Country results are illustrative results from the tool, not official estimates.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
A climate investment program changes the budget, the tax base, growth and debt at once, but ministries usually see these as four unconnected numbers. The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool puts them in one open workbook for 186 countries, with every assumption visible.
How a program is financed and how well the money is spent matter more than its size. Earmarked carbon revenue and concessional finance lower the debt path; the efficiency of public investment decides the growth gain.
Whether carbon pricing can pay depends on which political limit binds. When the loss to coal and oil generators binds, a tax and a feebate cut emissions equally, but only the tax raises revenue.
For Kenya, the mitigation bill is mostly land use and non-CO₂ gases, and carbon pricing pays for little of it. Kenya was at high risk of debt distress before the program; financing terms, not the program, decide what happens next.
Use the tool to compare packages, not to forecast debt. Check its starting point against the published debt sustainability analysis, and replace its defaults with country data, efficiency first.


Climate investment decisions need one answer on debt, and usually get four
A minister asked to commit to a climate investment program wants to know what it does to debt. That answer depends on four others. How much will the program cost the budget, once private investors and utilities have paid their share? How much could carbon pricing raise to pay for it? What will the spending do to growth? And what will all of that do to debt and the risk of debt distress?
Different teams usually answer these with different models, and the numbers do not add up. The energy team estimates investment needs; the tax team estimates carbon revenue; macroeconomists run a public investment scale-up through a growth model; the debt team runs the Bank-Fund debt framework. Each uses its own calibration and its own year, and the growth model rarely sees the revenue the pricing would raise.
The stakes are large. The IMF estimates that reaching net zero mainly through spending could raise public debt by 45 to 50 percent of GDP by 2050 in a representative large-emitting country, while a mix that includes carbon pricing holds the rise to 10 to 15 percent of GDP in an indicative advanced-economy case (International Monetary Fund 2023). A ministry needs to see that trade-off for its own country, in its own numbers.


One workbook runs the whole chain for 186 countries
The tool chains four models on one set of public country data. An investment model estimates what a net zero path needs to 2050 and who pays for it, from pure public spending through utilities and contracts to pure private investment. A pricing screen finds the most emission cuts a power-sector carbon tax, a feebate or a mix can deliver within limits on political cost. Simplified, open versions of three IMF and World Bank macro models turn the financed program into paths for GDP and debt (Kumhof et al. 2010; Marto et al. 2018). A simplified version of the Bank-Fund debt framework for low-income countries rates the risk of debt distress before and with the program (International Monetary Fund and World Bank 2018) (working paper, the tool).
Only the budget’s share of the investment, and only the part above current trends, reaches the macro models. Public buildings, access grids and land use fall on the budget; a viability-gap contract puts part of a private project there too. The tool also shows the larger need once weak project delivery is allowed for, using each country’s public investment efficiency; the IMF puts the average loss to inefficiency at around 30 percent (International Monetary Fund 2015) (working paper, investment needs).
A ministry economist can run a country in an afternoon. A country selector and a handful of levers drive the workbook: the program on or off, the shares of grants, concessional loans and commercial debt, the carbon pricing mode and the use of its revenue, and the political limits. Each result is a difference from a reference path that holds the country’s 2024 fiscal position fixed, so the tool is built to compare packages, not to forecast.


How the money is raised and spent matters more than how much
Earmarking carbon revenue cuts the debt peak without costing growth. In a stylized run, public investment of 1 percent of GDP a year for ten years raises GDP by 1.5 percent by year 10 and lifts debt from 50 to 57 percent of GDP. Earmarking carbon revenue of 0.5 percent of GDP a year holds the debt peak to 53 percent, with the same growth (Figure 1) (working paper, a stylized run).






Figure 1: Earmarked revenue lowers the debt path; low efficiency lowers the growth path. GIMF-lite, stylized program of 1 percent of GDP a year of extra public investment for ten years, default illustrative calibration; values in year 10. Source: working paper, Table 3.



Low efficiency wastes the borrowing. If only half of each dollar becomes public capital rather than 70 cents, the GDP gain falls by 30 to 40 percent at every horizon and debt is unchanged: the same borrowing buys less capital. Evidence from developing economies agrees that public investment does more where it is spent well (Furceri and Li 2017).
For a low-income country, concessional finance is a debt question, not a growth question. In the low-income model, financing 30 percent of the program with grants and 30 percent with concessional loans keeps debt 2.4 points of GDP lower at its peak than all-commercial borrowing, and growth is almost the same. The growth case rests on efficiency and the return on public capital.


The binding political limit decides whether carbon pricing can pay
The tool screens carbon pricing against three political limits. The first is the visible rise in household electricity tariffs; the second is the loss to the poorest 40 percent of households; the third is the loss to coal and oil generators. The default limits are placeholders: setting them is a political judgment, and the tool shows what each choice costs in emission cuts and revenue (working paper, carbon pricing).
When the generators’ loss binds, a tax and a feebate cut emissions equally, but only the tax raises money. A feebate charges plants above a benchmark emissions rate and rebates those below it, so it changes the marginal price without raising the average tariff (Stretton 2026b). In a stylized power sector, the best tax (US$35 per tonne), the best feebate (US$38) and the best mix each cut fossil power emissions by about a quarter; only the tax raises revenue.
Rebating revenue to households does not help when generators are the binding constraint. Compensating the owners of high-emitting plants, or retiring them faster, would raise the feasible price. If generators recover less of the carbon cost than the default assumes, the feasible tax falls to US$22 per tonne and the best instrument becomes a pure feebate (working paper, a stylized run).


In Kenya, carbon pricing pays for little, and debt risk was high before the program
Kenya’s net zero program needs about 0.5 percent of GDP a year from the budget in 2030, and four-fifths of that is spending, not capital. Kenya’s power is already over 90 percent renewable (Ember 2026), so most of the incremental need is for land use and non-CO₂ gases. The direct budget need is 0.60 percent of GDP in 2030, and 0.81 percent once weak delivery is allowed for (Table 1) (Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool 2026). The program goes beyond Kenya’s NDC, which aims to cut 2030 emissions 32 percent below a business-as-usual of 143 MtCO₂e (Republic of Kenya 2020).



Table 1: Kenya: a small budget need that pricing cannot pay for, and a debt risk set by the starting position. Program financed 30 percent by grants, 30 percent by concessional loans and the rest commercially. Sources: Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool (2026); Ember (2026); International Monetary Fund (2026); International Monetary Fund (2024). Working paper, Table 5.











Tool result (illustrative)

Direct budget need, 2030
0.60% of GDP; 0.81% after the efficiency gap



Incremental need entering the macro model, 2030

A clean grid leaves little to tax. The feasible power-sector tax of US$88 per tonne applies to oil-fired plants that emitted under 1 million tonnes of CO₂ in 2024 (Ember 2026). It raises about 0.05 percent of GDP in 2030, a tenth of that year’s need and about 5 percent of the need to 2050 (working paper, Kenya).
The program adds about 7 points of GDP to debt by 2050 for a quarter of a percent of GDP. Most of the need builds no capital, so growth barely moves in the low-income model. A cross-check with the other model family gives a much larger GDP gain, 4.6 percent, because it credits energy savings and private investment; whether those happen in Kenya is the largest uncertainty. The 7 points are an addition to whatever path debt follows: the IMF already projects Kenya’s debt at 71 to 74 percent of GDP in 2025–2030 (International Monetary Fund 2026).
The published debt analysis confirms the tool’s rating and shows where it falls short. The joint IMF-World Bank analysis of December 2023 rates Kenya at high risk of debt distress with medium debt-carrying capacity, as the tool does (International Monetary Fund 2024). But its capacity indicator, 3.01, is higher than the tool’s 2.73, because the tool lacks trade data. And the shock that actually raised Kenya’s debt ratios, a falling real exchange rate in 2023–2024, is one the tool’s simplified models cannot show.


The tool compares packages; it does not replace a debt sustainability analysis
The simplified models are not their parents. They have one country, one good and a fixed real exchange rate, and they have been checked for internal consistency but not yet against the parents’ published simulations. Several inputs are income-group defaults. A result is a scenario to argue with, not a forecast, and it does not replace a calibrated IMF or World Bank model run, a debt sustainability analysis or a run of the Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT Team 2023) (working paper, limits and use).
The tool earns its keep by showing which assumptions decide the answer. In both the stylized run and Kenya, those are the financing mix, the efficiency of public investment, the political limit that binds on pricing and the starting debt position. That tells a ministry where better data would pay most.


What to do
Finance ministries: compare financing packages, not program sizes. Run the program under grants, concessional loans and commercial debt, with and without earmarked pricing revenue, and read the change in the debt path and the risk rating. Treat the levels as a reference, not a projection.
Ministries and development-bank teams: start from the published debt analysis. Where an IMF-World Bank debt sustainability analysis exists, use its capacity rating and debt path as the reference, and use the tool to see how a program would move them. Add the depreciation stress the tool cannot run.
Fix efficiency before scaling up. In Kenya, closing the gap between spending and capital created would save the budget about 0.2 percent of GDP a year; in the stylized run, low efficiency cuts the growth gain by a third at the same debt.
Design carbon pricing around the limit that binds. Where generators’ losses bind, compensate or retire high-emitting plants, or use a feebate to cut emissions without raising tariffs; where revenue is the aim, a tax is needed. Where the grid is already clean, as in Kenya, plan to finance land-use and non-CO₂ needs with grants and concessional loans, as Kenya’s NDC does (Republic of Kenya 2020).
Replace defaults with country data in order of influence. Investment efficiency and the return on public capital first, then the financing mix, then trade data for the debt test, then the pricing assumptions, ideally from CPAT runs.


Related papers in this series

Brief 6.1: the Total Effective Carbon Price, which puts a feebate and a tax on one scale (Stretton 2026c).
Brief 1.2: feebates, the full carbon price at the margin without the carbon bill (Stretton 2026b).
Paper 6.3: investment needs and the efficiency of public spending (Stretton 2026d).
Paper 7.2: the global fiscal indicators dashboard that supplies the tool’s data (Stretton 2026a).
Paper 5.1: the CPAT mitigation module, whose data and conventions the investment model follows (Stretton 2026e).

title: The CBAM Policy Tool
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. Legal texts as of 31 October 2026. All amounts are at a stylized certificate price of €80 per tonne of CO₂. The Egypt results are illustrative tool results, not official estimates. The method, the equations and the data are in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
The EU’s carbon border charge is large, and for dirty goods most of it arrives in the first year. Turkish hot-rolled steel declared at the EU’s default value owes €107 a tonne in 2026 and €252 at full phase-in, close to half its price.
Exporting governments have three levers: verified emissions data, cleaner production, and a carbon price at home that the EU deducts. For Turkish steel, data are worth €58 a tonne and a €20 domestic price another €49, which stays at home.
The right lever differs by product. For Egypt, verified data would cut the charge on steel from €193 million to €16 million a year, but on urea, the largest exposure, only from €369 million to €321 million.
A tool’s accounting must follow the EU’s rules exactly. Two fertilizer corrections changed the largest line in the Egypt results.
Run the numbers for each product before choosing a policy, and press the EU to credit price signals, not only payments.


The border charge is large and arrives early
Since January 2026, EU importers of steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity have owed a charge on the carbon in what they buy. Under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), importers buy certificates priced in line with the EU’s emissions trading system for the emissions embedded in their imports (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023b, 2025). Certificates go on sale in February 2027. Importers bringing in less than 50 tonnes a year are exempt. The charge is phased in as the EU’s own steel, cement and fertilizer plants lose their free emission allowances, by 2034 under current law (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023a).
The bill depends on three things exporting governments can influence. First, whether plants file verified emissions data: if they do not, the EU applies a default value for the country, raised by a mark-up of 30 percent from 2028 (1 percent for fertilizers) (European Commission 2025b). Second, whether plants cut their emissions. Third, whether the country levies a carbon price that the EU deducts: a price “effectively paid”, net of any rebate, can be subtracted from the charge (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2025, Art. 9).
For goods far dirtier than the EU benchmark, most of the charge applies from 2026. The phase-in only shields emissions up to a benchmark set from the cleaner EU plants; everything above it is charged in full from the start. Turkish hot-rolled steel declared at the default owes €107 a tonne in 2026, €196 in 2030 and €252 at full phase-in, against an average 2025 import price of €549 (Figure 1). The 2026 charge is already 42 percent of the final one (working paper, the charge per tonne).






Figure 1: The charge on Turkish hot-rolled steel rises from €107 a tonne in 2026 to €252 at full phase-in; verified data and a domestic carbon price each cut it by about €50. Charge per tonne at €80/tCO₂, declared at the default value; with verified data at the country average; and with a €20 domestic carbon price deducted. The dotted line shows the slower phase-out proposed in July 2026 (not adopted). Source: Commission default values; Eurostat; working paper, Table 3 and Figure 1.



The EU may slow the phase-in, but not by much. A Commission proposal of July 2026, not yet adopted, would keep 15 percent of free allocation until 2037 and end it in 2038 (European Commission 2026c). The charge on Turkish hot-rolled steel would then be €188 a tonne in 2030 instead of €196, and €236 in 2034–2037 instead of €252.


The CBAM Policy Tool turns the rules into a bill a ministry can check
The tool computes the charge for each product of one exporting country, year by year, from public inputs. It builds each product’s emissions from its energy use and chemistry, compares them with the EU’s default value, applies the phase-in and the certificate price, and deducts a domestic carbon price where the rules allow. Every input sits in a labeled cell with its source (working paper, what the tool does).
It answers the three questions a ministry asks. How large is the charge on each product each year? How much would verified data save? And what would a domestic carbon price do: how much of the fall in the charge comes from cleaner production, and how much from the deduction? With a €20 price and a 10 percent cut in emissions per tonne, the charge falls by a third, two-thirds of it from the deduction (working paper, abatement and deduction).
Its estimates of what plants emit are technology averages, not plant data. The EU will use each plant’s verified figures. The tool’s estimate shows where verification is likely to pay; plant data must confirm it. The tool computes exposure, not who bears the charge, and it is not a compliance calculator (working paper, limits).


Data and a domestic price are each worth tens of euros a tonne
Filing verified data saves at least the mark-up. A Turkish steel plant at the country average that files verified data avoids the 30 percent mark-up on the default, worth €58 a tonne at full phase-in. A cleaner plant gains more.
A domestic carbon price lowers the border charge one for one and keeps the money at home. A €20 price effectively paid on all emissions cuts the charge on Turkish hot-rolled steel by €49 a tonne, and the treasury collects the same €49. Together with verified data, the charge falls from €252 to €146 a tonne. At 2025 volumes, a €20 price on the three Turkish goods in the example would move about €127 million a year from the EU budget to Türkiye’s (working paper, worked example).
A rebated price or feebate earns no deduction under the draft rules. A feebate charges producers above their sector’s average emissions per tonne and rebates those below. It keeps the full incentive to cut emissions, but the Commission’s draft rules treat emissions below a baseline as compensation to be netted off, so the feebate earns nothing at the border (European Commission 2026b, Art. 8). Brief 1.4 argues that the EU should credit the price signal, not only the payment (Stretton 2026a).


Egypt shows the right lever differs by product
The tool’s Egypt application compares its estimates with the EU defaults for seven products, and the gaps range from enormous to nil. Table 1 and Figure 2 show the charge at full phase-in on 2025 volumes, declared at the EU default and with verified data where it pays. Across the seven products the charge falls from about €793 million a year to €480 million (working paper, Egypt).

Egypt’s steel is charged as if it came from the dirtiest exporters, so verified data are worth almost the whole charge. Egypt has no EU default of its own for steel, so the EU applies a value of about 4 tonnes of CO₂ per tonne, set from the most carbon-intensive exporters. Egypt makes steel from gas and scrap in electric furnaces; the tool puts it at 0.16–0.73. Verified data would cut the charge on Egyptian steel from €193 million to €16 million a year. The tool’s figure for gas-based steel is uncertain, but even at the EU’s own default for Iran, another gas-based producer, the charge would be €36 million (working paper, steel range).
Some of what verification “saves” on steel may be routing, not cleaner steel. A firm with both gas-based and scrap-based plants can send only scrap-based steel to Europe. Its verified figure then falls below what the country’s steel actually emits. Measuring by country and sector, as Brief 1.4 proposes, removes that gain.
For urea, Egypt’s largest exposure, the default is close to what plants emit, so data barely help. Urea is made from ammonia, and the EU counts both the ammonia’s emissions and the carbon dioxide the urea carries, which it releases when spread on fields (European Commission 2025a; De Klein et al. 2006). Counted this way, Egyptian urea emits 1.22 tonnes of CO₂ per tonne against a default of 1.39. Data save €48 million a year; €321 million remains. For urea the levers are cleaner production, such as cleaner ammonia production, and a domestic carbon price that keeps the charge at home: €20 a tonne of CO₂ on urea alone would move about €80 million a year.
Getting the accounting right changed the answer. The tool’s first Egypt results deducted the carbon dioxide in urea and counted only half the ammonia in ammonium nitrate, against the EU’s rules. They also used the tool’s own estimates of trade volumes rather than the trade Eurostat records. Corrected, the charge at default values rose from €595 million to €793 million and the remaining charge with verified data from €177 million to €480 million, and urea moved from the strongest case for data to the weakest (working paper, corrections).


What to do
Exporting ministries: run the calculation product by product before choosing a policy. Where the default is far above what plants emit, as for Egyptian steel and clinker, build verification capacity first: accredited verifiers and monitoring at the plants that sell to the EU. Where it is close, as for Egyptian urea and ammonia, the choice is between abatement and a domestic carbon price that keeps the charge at home. Where plants emit more than the default, as for Egyptian aluminum, keep the default.
Design a domestic carbon price knowing what the EU will deduct. A price effectively paid is deducted one for one; a rebated price or feebate earns nothing under the draft rules. A ministry that wants the incentive of a feebate and the deduction of a tax should know the cost of each before choosing, and can finance abatement from the revenue in ways the draft rules do not net off.
Use the 2027 revision of default values. The EU must revise its default values in 2027 at the latest (European Commission 2025b). A country with no default of its own, as Egypt for steel, or whose plants emit far less than its default, should bring documented estimates to that revision, and a country with a carbon price should engage on the default carbon price methodology the Commission is preparing (Technopolis Group 2026).
The European Commission: credit price signals, and measure by country and sector. Crediting a feebate or other non-price policy at its carbon-price equivalent (Brief 6.1) would reward the instruments exporters can adopt, and country-sector values would stop routing (Brief 1.4).
Tool builders: follow the EU’s accounting exactly, and publish the corrections. The Egypt fertilizer errors were in the method, not the data. The tool’s next version should carry the corrections, reconcile its steel factors, and report each product as a range.

title: Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.4, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full method, with the equations, the parameter sources and the proofs, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Linked climate models disagree before any policy is applied, because each starts from its own forecast of activity. CPAT, SISEPUEDE, the CBAM Policy Tool and FTT grow electricity use, travel, vehicles and industrial output from different drivers, so a ministry that links them gets four baselines.
One driver layer fixes this. Grow ten activities with population, income per person and the cost of the energy service, from one forecast and one base year, and let each model keep its own data and take the layer’s growth.
A carbon price must reach demand exactly once. CPAT and the CBAM Policy Tool already respond to prices; SISEPUEDE and FTT do not. Apply the layer’s price response only to the activities it passes to those two.
Cars grow faster than travel, so every link needs a check. Under stylized growth, cars in use rise 64 percent in ten years and travel 35 percent; left unchecked, car travel would exceed all travel within two generations.
Fix the data gaps that matter most. FTT has no car data for 21 of its 71 regions, SISEPUEDE’s country calibrations are not public, and the response of heavy industry to a carbon price rests on judgment.


Linked models disagree before any policy is applied
A ministry that asks four models about a carbon price gets four different starting points. The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), built by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), grows fuel use with total GDP and prices for more than 180 countries (Black et al. 2023). SISEPUEDE, an open model developed by RAND and the Inter-American Development Bank, grows travel, freight, household energy and industrial output with income and population (Kalra et al. 2023). The CBAM Policy Tool grows output of the steel, aluminum, fertilizer and cement that the European Union’s carbon border adjustment covers (Brief 6.2) (Stretton 2026d). The Future Technology Transformations (FTT) models decide which technologies win in power, cars, freight and heating, but take the size of each market as given (Mercure 2012; Future Technology Transformations developers 2026). Each is good at its job.
The differences are in the drivers, not just in the numbers. CPAT does not separate population from income: a country whose population grows fast gets the same fuel growth as one getting richer (working paper, CPAT). SISEPUEDE never lets prices change demand; a carbon tax changes its emissions only if the analyst writes a change into the scenario (working paper, SISEPUEDE). FTT’s demand is a fixed input file that ends in different years for different sectors (working paper, FTT). So two models can disagree about the effect of a carbon tax simply because they disagree about how much driving or steelmaking there would have been without it.
Inside CPAT, road transport is described three ways that need not agree. By default, road fuel follows CPAT’s general fuel equation. An optional engineering model tracks vehicles, electric-vehicle choice and distance driven. A third block values congestion, accidents and road damage, and it always uses the engineering model’s driving, whichever model the user selects (CPAT-AI Project 2026). A ministry reading CPAT’s co-benefits of a fuel tax should ask which road model produced them.


One driver layer puts the four models on one baseline
The layer grows ten activities with one rule. The activities are electricity generated, passenger travel, cars in use, kilometers per car, road freight, vans and trucks, home heat, steel and aluminum, cement and clinker, and fertilizers. Each grows with population, with income per person, and with the cost of the energy service it provides, through fixed elasticities. Activities that follow people, such as travel and households, grow one-for-one with population; activities that follow the economy, such as industrial output, grow with total GDP (working paper, the rule).
Every model gets the same two forecasts and the same base year. Use the IMF World Economic Outlook for GDP and the United Nations World Population Prospects for population, for every model (International Monetary Fund 2026; United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division 2024). Each model keeps its own last data point and takes the layer’s growth from there, so FTT keeps its own fleet and FTT’s power demand keeps its own level (working paper, feeding the models).
Where the models’ own values fail against the evidence, the layer replaces them. SISEPUEDE’s example data grow regional travel with income at an elasticity of 2.64, with no ceiling, and move every industrial elasticity to 1 by 2050 (Syme et al. 2026). The evidence says total travel rises roughly in proportion with income (Schäfer and Victor 2000) and that demand for steel and cement rises for decades and then levels off (Ruijven et al. 2016). Vehicle ownership grows about twice as fast as income at low and middle incomes, then saturates (Dargay and Gately 1999). The layer uses those patterns. Where no public estimate fits, as for heavy-industry output, the working paper states its values as assumptions (working paper, parameters).


Count the carbon price’s effect on demand once
A price response applied twice doubles; one never applied is lost. If the layer cuts driving because fuel got dearer and the receiving model cuts it again, the response is counted twice. If neither does, a carbon tax changes nothing in that model’s demand. Table 1 shows which model already responds and where the layer’s price response belongs.



Table 1: Apply the carbon price’s effect on demand in exactly one place for each activity. Source: working paper, concordance and Proposition 2.










Model
Does its demand respond to price?
What the layer passes




CPAT

The baseline only, as a cross-check; for road vehicles, the baseline only


CBAM Policy Tool
Yes, output of covered goods
Nothing for prices; it passes product output back to the layer


SISEPUEDE
No

FTT
No (prices move technology shares, not demand)
Activity with the layer’s price response






The layer’s price responses are modest, and mostly come through fewer vehicles. A carbon price that raises the energy cost of driving by 20 percent cuts car use by about 5 percent in the long run, 4.5 percent through fewer cars and 0.9 percent through less driving per car, in line with the review evidence (Goodwin et al. 2004). The same rise in the energy cost of freight cuts tonne-kilometers by about 2 percent (Jong et al. 2010). These are the responses SISEPUEDE and FTT otherwise lack.
The easiest double count to miss sits inside CPAT. CPAT’s engineering road model responds to the cost per kilometer itself. If it is fed vehicle numbers that already include the layer’s price response, the response is counted twice even when CPAT’s fuel equation is switched off. Feed it the baseline only, and select it as the road model whenever co-benefits are reported (working paper, propositions).
Product detail matters for heavy industry, and it does not always point the way people expect. A carbon price of 50 dollars per tonne of CO₂ raises the cost of clinker, which is cheap and carbon-intensive, by about two-thirds, and the cost of blast-furnace steel by about a sixth (stylized prices and intensities). Because clinker is hard to replace, output falls by 5 to 6 percent in both cases (working paper, worked example). A model that ties industrial energy to GDP, as CPAT does, cannot show either result.


Cars grow faster than travel, so the link needs a check
Under stylized growth, cars outrun travel within a decade. With population growing 1 percent a year and income per person 2 percent, cars in use grow 64 percent in ten years and passenger travel 35 percent (Figure 1). The share of travel by car rises by about a quarter. That is what happens in middle-income countries, and it is what FTT’s transport model needs to see.






Figure 1: Growth of each activity over ten years under one rule and one set of drivers: population +1 percent and income per person +2 percent a year (stylized), elasticities held fixed. Source: working paper, worked example.



Left unchecked, car travel would overtake all travel. At these growth rates, a car share of 30 percent of passenger travel reaches 100 percent in about 56 years. A saturating ownership curve, like the one in CPAT’s engineering road model, does not prevent this: with that curve the crossing still comes in year 54. What keeps car travel inside total travel in practice is that each car is driven less, and carries fewer people, as ownership rises (working paper, Proposition 3).
So every link should check, every year, that cars fit inside travel. The check is simple: cars times kilometers per car times occupancy must stay below total passenger travel. Where it fails, the layer lowers kilometers per car. Without the check, a model can show emissions from road transport that no plausible amount of travel could produce.


The data gaps bind as hard as the method
FTT cannot yet run its transport model for much of the developing world. Its standalone version has no car fleet data for 21 of its 71 regions, including Nigeria, South Africa, Pakistan and Kenya, and its industrial heat module ships without baseline data (Future Technology Transformations developers 2026). Its steel model runs only inside the full E3ME-FTT model (Vercoulen et al. 2023).
SISEPUEDE’s country calibrations are not public. Its open repository holds one example country, and the calibrated values in that example swing widely, including a negative income elasticity for chemical output (Syme et al. 2026). Teams using it for a country need the developers’ calibration, and should replace values that fail against the evidence.
The response of heavy industry to a carbon price rests on judgment. Output elasticities for steel, aluminum, fertilizer and cement are thin in the literature; one Brazilian estimate for steel is −0.14 (Schmidt and Lima 2006). Results that depend on them should be reported with a range.
The strongest objection is that a rule-based link is second-best. Solving the models together, as E3ME-FTT does for demand and technology, would make prices, technology and demand consistent by construction. But none of these four models was built for that, ministries run them separately, and a link with written rules is far easier to audit and maintain (working paper, limits).


What to do
Finance ministries: ask for one set of drivers before comparing model results. Before comparing what two models say about a carbon price, ask whether they used the same GDP and population forecast and the same base year, and which model carries the price response for each activity.
Teams running CPAT, SISEPUEDE or FTT: link through one layer and count the price once. Give every model the IMF and UN forecasts. Grow activities with one rule from one base year and splice them onto each model’s own data. Apply the price response in SISEPUEDE and FTT only. In CPAT, select the engineering road model whenever co-benefits are reported, and feed it the baseline only. Check every year that cars fit inside travel.
Model developers: close the gaps that block linking. Add car fleet data for FTT’s 21 missing regions. Publish SISEPUEDE’s country calibrations, or the method to rebuild them. Give CPAT one road transport story, and estimate output elasticities for heavy industry.
The CPAT-AI project: build the layer as an open table and test it on one country. Run one country through all four models from the same layer, and use the gap between CPAT’s fuel-based baseline and the layer’s activity-based one as a test of both.

title: Are CPAT’s Price Elasticities Right?
text:
5.1 Income elasticities
The base income elasticities are close for electricity and gas, low for road diesel, and high for gasoline once publication bias is considered. Table 2 compares CPAT’s base values with long-run estimates. The comparison is indicative: CPAT scales its base values with income per head, so a country’s effective elasticity can differ from the base, and several of the estimates are for a sector’s total energy use rather than one fuel.



Table 2: CPAT’s base income elasticities mostly lie in the published range. Sources: developing-economy averages and Dahl and Roman’s industrialized-economy values as reported in Huntington et al. (2019); sector energy and residential electricity from Burke and Csereklyei (2016) (2010 cross-section, 132 countries); gasoline uncorrected 0.66 and corrected 0.23 from Havranek and Kokes (2015); fuel-subsidizing economies 0.81 from Arzaghi and Squalli (2015); European Union residential 0.61 and industrial 0.76–1.08 from Csereklyei (2020). CPAT scales the base values with income per head (CPAT-AI project 2026). Source: author’s calculation, 2.Source/table_income.csv.

title: Are CPAT’s Price Elasticities Right?
text:
6.1 Timing: CPAT front-loads the response
CPAT reaches the full long-run response in the year the price changes; the evidence says it takes a decade. The documentation is explicit that “all the effects take place over the course of one year”, and the 2022 technical notes list the missing distinction between short- and long-run elasticities as a known issue: the developers “eliminated the distinction” while judging it “important, particularly for residential power demand, which is inelastic in the short term” (World Bank and International Monetary Fund 2022, sec. 3.1.8.6). The meta-analyses agree: short-run elasticities are about 0.3 times long-run ones (0.29–0.34 for energy, electricity and gasoline) (Labandeira et al. 2016; Havranek et al. 2012). The two margins in equation 1 adjust at different speeds. Usage responds within a year or two. Efficiency moves with the capital stock: the IMF’s vehicle model used alongside CPAT assumes cars turn over at 6.7 percent a year (a 15-year life) and buildings at 1.2–1.8 percent (Black et al. 2022, Annex C); stock-based models such as the International Energy Agency’s project energy use from vehicle stocks and their efficiencies (International Energy Agency 2018). Write the share of each margin’s long-run response achieved \(T\) years after a permanent price change as \(a(T) = 1 - (1-\lambda)^T\). The central case uses \(\lambda_U = 0.30\) for usage, inside paper 6.1’s range of 0.25–0.40 for the demand margin, and \(\lambda_F = 0.067\) for efficiency (Stretton 2026a). The horizon-\(T\) elasticity is \(a_U\epsilon_U + a_F\epsilon_F + a_U a_F\epsilon_U\epsilon_F\).






Figure 2: The own-price elasticity at each horizon after a permanent price rise: CPAT (dashed, full long-run response from year 1) against partial adjustment of the usage margin at 30 percent a year and the efficiency margin at 6.7 percent a year (solid). Bands span the alternative speeds of Table 3: usage complete within the year (upper edge) and, for coal in industry, capital turning over at 2 percent a year (lower edge). CPAT defaults for low- and middle-income countries. Source: author’s calculation, 2.Source/elasticity_check.py.



After one year about a fifth of CPAT’s response has happened; after five, about 60 percent. For gasoline in transport, the horizon elasticity is −0.14 after one year, −0.41 after five and −0.51 after ten, against CPAT’s −0.64 throughout (Figure 2). Across the five pairs in Table 3, 20–26 percent of the long-run response has happened after one year and 58–69 percent after five. Five years out, CPAT’s response is therefore 45 to 72 percent larger than the partial-adjustment response, and the overstatement is largest where capital is long-lived.

If usage responds fully within the year, the five-year overstatement falls to 29–52 percent; if capital in buildings and industry turns over at 2 percent a year, it rises to 67–108 percent. Phased price paths, which CPAT is meant for, reduce the error because each year’s increment has had less time to fall short; they do not remove it.
The timing error also understates near-term carbon tax revenue. A tax base that falls faster in the model than in the economy produces less modeled revenue in the first years. For a fuel subsidy reform, the same front-loading brings forward the modeled fall in consumption, and with it the fiscal and emission gains.

title: Are CPAT’s Price Elasticities Right?
section: 6.2 Structure: own-price elasticities without cross-price terms
text:
6.2 Structure: own-price elasticities without cross-price terms
Applying each fuel’s own-price elasticity to a simultaneous rise in all fuel prices overstates the cut when the estimates hold other prices constant. In the CES system of Section 3, a policy that changes fuel prices by proportions \(\pi_g\) changes use of fuel \(f\) by \[
d\ln q_f = \big[-\sigma + (\sigma-\eta)s_f\big]\pi_f + (\sigma-\eta)\sum_{g\neq f}s_g\pi_g .
\tag{3}\] A model with own-price terms only keeps the first bracket and drops the second. When the substitution elasticity exceeds the demand elasticity and other fuels’ prices also rise, the dropped term is positive: the cut in fuel \(f\) is overstated by \((\sigma-\eta)\sum_{g\neq f}s_g\pi_g\). For a uniform proportional price rise the correct response is \(-\eta\pi\) for every fuel, while the own-price model gives \([-\sigma+(\sigma-\eta)s_f]\pi\), more negative by \((\sigma-\eta)(1-s_f)\pi\). The condition is about what the estimates measure. Single-equation studies that omit other energy prices, common in the meta-analyses, pick up part of the response to the general level of energy prices, and for them the bias is smaller.
The bias is largest for minor fuels in sectors with easy substitution. In industry, with \(\sigma\) near 0.8 and \(\eta\) near 0.3 (Stretton 2026a), a fuel with a 20 percent cost share has its response to a uniform price rise overstated by 0.4 times the price change: an own-price elasticity of about −0.6 would imply a cut twice the correct \(-\eta\) response. CPAT avoids the worst of this because its end-use elasticities are close to demand elasticities, not to substitution elasticities, but the consequence is the mirror image: with almost no cross-price terms, CPAT has almost no fuel switching outside power. A carbon tax that makes coal dearer relative to gas does not move industry from coal to gas in CPAT; it cuts coal and gas each by their own elasticities applied to their own price rises. CPAT’s own panel study recommended “a more explicit analysis of the impact of cross-price elasticities”, starting with specific fuels in specific sectors (CPAT-AI project 2026).

title: Are CPAT’s Price Elasticities Right?
section: 6.3 Emission cuts and the Total Effective Carbon Price
text:
6.3 Emission cuts and the Total Effective Carbon Price
Elasticity errors move emission cuts roughly in proportion but move the Total Effective Carbon Price much less. The Total Effective Carbon Price (TECP) of a policy mix is the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much as the mix (Stretton 2026b). Because it is a ratio of two cuts computed with the same elasticities, a common error cancels. At first order the TECP is \(\tau^* = R_P/\Lambda\), where \(R_P\) is the mix’s emission cut and \(\Lambda\) the cut from a $1 uniform tax; both are linear in the elasticities (Stretton 2026a, Proposition 1). Scaling every substitution and demand elasticity by the same factor \(k\) scales \(R_P\) and \(\Lambda\) by \(k\) and leaves \(\tau^*\) unchanged. Only errors that differ across sectors or margins move the TECP, by shifting weight toward the sectors whose elasticities are most overstated.

The policy mix is paper 6.1’s: a $30 carbon tax on power and industry, a $10/MWh renewable subsidy and a 2 percent low-carbon fuel standard. With CPAT’s demand elasticities, the demand margin’s cut more than doubles and the total cut rises by about a third. In Table 4, a $30 economy-wide tax cuts the stylized economy’s emissions by 13.4 percent with paper 6.1’s central values and by 17.5 percent with CPAT-implied demand elasticities, because the demand margin’s cut rises from 4.8 to 10.8 percent of emissions while switching is unchanged. Halving CPAT’s demand elasticities, the correction Havranek and coauthors find for gasoline, brings the cut back to 13.8 percent. In CPAT itself, the end-use sectors outside power have almost no switching, so there an overstatement of demand elasticities by a factor of two overstates the cut by close to a factor of two. The power sector, where CPAT does model switching, dilutes this in the national total.
The TECP moves by about a tenth. The exact TECP of paper 6.1’s mix is $36.9 per tonne with the central calibration, $33.1 with CPAT-implied demand elasticities and $37.0 with those elasticities halved. The mix leans on switching (the subsidy and the fuel standard work only through relative prices), so raising demand elasticities raises the benchmark tax’s cut more than the mix’s and lowers the TECP. Correcting only road fuels for publication bias moves it by $1.4. For a cross-country comparison of TECPs, then, the elasticity errors found here matter less than they do for estimated emission cuts, provided the same elasticities are used for every country.
For the Total Carbon Price, which uses no elasticities, the issue is what it leaves out. The World Bank’s Total Carbon Price adds explicit carbon prices and fuel excises net of subsidies per tonne (Agnolucci et al. 2023). In the dataset kept with CPAT, which covers 155 countries from 1995 to 2022, the mean country’s Total Carbon Price in 2022 was $32 per tonne, made of $57.7 of net energy taxes, $8.4 from emissions trading and $3.5 from carbon taxes, less $36.0 of net subsidies and $1.5 of VAT concessions; 54 of the 155 countries had a negative total (CPAT-AI project 2026, All_data_TCP.xlsx). That metric weights a dollar per tonne on every fuel equally. The TECP weights it by how much it cuts emissions, which is where elasticities enter: with CPAT’s defaults, a dollar of subsidy on industrial diesel would count about 1.7 times as much as the median evidence supports.

title: Validating CPAT: Baselines, Back-Casts and Model Comparisons
section: 6.1 Price response: the same slope as Enerdata
text:
6.1 Price response: the same slope as Enerdata
CPAT’s response of emissions to a carbon price has about the same slope as Enerdata’s. The documentation runs carbon prices of $0 to $120 per tonne of CO₂ in 2030 through both CPAT power models and compares the resulting world emissions in 2030, indexed to each model’s own baseline, with Enerdata’s marginal abatement cost curves. For total CO₂, power-sector CO₂ and greenhouse gases excluding land use, it finds “good alignment” for both of CPAT’s power models (Campmas et al. 2023). Indexing to each baseline removes baseline differences, so this is a clean test of the response. A second comparison, against Enerdata’s Enerbase scenarios for 2025, 2030 and 2035, finds “similar slopes” and, for power-sector CO₂, that CPAT’s simpler “average” power model comes closer to Enerdata than its engineering power model.

title: Validating CPAT: Baselines, Back-Casts and Model Comparisons
section: 6.2 Ex-post evidence: inside a wide range
text:
6.2 Ex-post evidence: inside a wide range
CPAT’s response to a $10 carbon price is of the same order as the best cross-country estimate. The documentation ran a $10/tCO₂ step for 171 countries over 2019–2035 and computed “semi-elasticities”: the average percentage gap between CO₂ in the policy run and in the baseline, over the first five years (short term) and over the whole period (long term). Table 3 reports them.

The documentation’s comparison with the ex-post literature sets two different measures side by side. It finds CPAT “comparable” with a literature whose estimates are “minimal to modest”, 0 to 2 percent a year (Green 2021; Campmas et al. 2023). But CPAT’s figures are average level gaps, while the ex-post studies mostly estimate an annual effect, often on the growth rate of emissions, under whatever price and coverage each scheme had. On a common basis, if a $10 price slows the growth of emissions by g a year, the level gap after k years is about gk, and its average over the first N years is g(N+1)/2. CPAT’s −2.4 percent over five years then corresponds to g ≈ 0.8 percent a year, and its −6.2 percent over 17 years to g ≈ 0.7 percent a year (author’s calculation; the linear build-up is an assumption, and it overstates g for the part of CPAT’s response that is immediate). Rafaty et al. (2020), the cross-country study most like CPAT’s exercise, estimate that each dollar of carbon price slows emissions growth by 0.05 percent a year, or about 0.5 percent a year at $10, an estimate they call imprecise. CPAT is therefore of the same order as the best per-dollar estimate, and somewhat larger.
The rest of the ex-post literature is too wide to say whether CPAT over- or under-responds. Green’s review of 37 studies finds aggregate reductions of 0 to 2 percent a year (Green 2021). A later systematic review and meta-analysis of 80 causal evaluations of 21 schemes finds statistically significant total reductions of 5 to 21 percent (4 to 15 percent after correcting for publication bias), “despite the low level of prices in most instances” (Döbbeling-Hildebrandt et al. 2024). Across 142 countries, emissions from fuel combustion grew about 2 percentage points a year more slowly where a carbon price existed (Best et al. 2020). These figures are for real schemes with low coverage, generous free allocation or both, and they do not scale simply to a comprehensive $10 price; the meta-analysis names the price elasticity of emissions as an evidence gap. The ex-post evidence therefore bounds CPAT loosely rather than testing it.
The sector pattern agrees with the evidence. The power sector shows the largest long-run response in CPAT, as it does in Rafaty et al. (2020), who find most abatement in electricity and heat, and transport the smallest. This is the firmest finding of the comparison, because it does not depend on matching metrics.

title: Validating CPAT: Baselines, Back-Casts and Model Comparisons
section: 6.3 Power: the same mix as the World Bank’s planning model, smoother investment
text:
6.3 Power: the same mix as the World Bank’s planning model, smoother investment
CPAT’s engineering power model gives a generation mix close to EPM’s in most countries compared. EPM is the World Bank’s least-cost capacity expansion and dispatch model, with hourly renewable availability, ramping limits, reserves, storage and transmission constraints (Campmas et al. 2023). The comparison set CPAT’s 2030 carbon price at about $40/tCO₂ by goal seek, to approximate EPM’s carbon budgets, which are mostly 40 percent below business as usual, and compared electricity demand, generation by fuel and new investment for 14 countries in the main text (Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, South Africa, Türkiye, Ukraine, Vietnam and seven in Africa) and 20 more, all in Africa, in Appendix H. The documentation finds similar fuel types and shares in the mix, with EPM showing more wind in some countries such as Vietnam.
The models differ most on the timing of investment, and the comparison is approximate by design. EPM, as an optimization model, builds in lumps; CPAT spreads new investment over time. For developing countries, where EPM often suggests discontinuous generation and investment, the documentation finds parallels hard to draw (Campmas et al. 2023). The policies are matched only approximately (EPM’s budget looks to 2040, CPAT’s goal seek to 2030), fuel categories are mapped by hand, and storage is not compared. CPAT is therefore supported as a source of plausible mixes, not of investment schedules; a ministry needing an investment plan should use a planning model.

title: Validating CPAT: Baselines, Back-Casts and Model Comparisons
section: 6.4 Air pollution: conservative against global datasets
text:
6.4 Air pollution: conservative against global datasets
CPAT’s air-pollution module tends to understate the share of fine particles that comes from fossil fuels. The documentation compares CPAT’s ambient PM2.5 death rates with the Global Burden of Disease 2019 estimates (GBD 2019 Risk Factors Collaborators 2020), its PM2.5 emissions from transport and power with EDGAR and IIASA inventories, and its fossil-fuel share of ambient PM2.5 with the GEOS-Chem estimates of Vohra et al. (2021; CPAT Team 2023). Depending on which of CPAT’s methods links emissions to concentrations, Vohra and coauthors’ fossil share is higher than CPAT’s in 61 percent of countries (averaged intake fraction and FASST local study), 55 percent (machine learning) or 44 percent (FASST local study alone). The chapter concludes that its default configuration gives a conservative fossil contribution, so CPAT is likely to understate the health benefits of a climate policy. It adds that good agreement on baselines does not guarantee agreement on policy impacts, which need checking country by country.

title: CPAT-AI: Rebuilding a Policy Model as a Transparent, Testable Tool
text:
4.1 Legacy CPAT is the specification
Both rebuilds take legacy CPAT as ground truth, not the documentation and not anyone’s view of what CPAT should be. The legacy workbook was kept read-only, in the three versions current during the rebuild (CPAT 1.0pre_456, 459 and 465, with the proprietary data stripped), and work was done on copies (CPAT-AI project 2026c). The project proceeds block by block in five steps: replicate a block of legacy formula by formula, with the same section numbers; check it against an independent Python recomputation and against legacy’s stored results; classify every difference; release a new version only after the checks pass; and port validated blocks to Python.
The chain being replicated is the CPAT mitigation chain set out in paper 5.1 (Stretton 2026d). Policies set price signals; retail prices build up from international prices, taxes and subsidies; fuel use in 16 end-use subsectors and power responds to income, prices and efficiency; a power model dispatches plants and invests; and the results feed revenue, emissions, GDP effects and household incidence. The core is a constant-elasticity demand equation, \[
Q_{ijt} = Q_{ij,t-1}\,(1-a_{ij})\,(1+g_t)^{\varepsilon^{Y}_{ij}}\left(\frac{P_{ijt}}{P_{ij,t-1}}\right)^{\varepsilon^{P}_{ij}},
\tag{1}\] for fuel \(i\) in sector \(j\), where \(a_{ij}\) is autonomous efficiency improvement, \(g_t\) GDP growth and \(\varepsilon^{Y}\), \(\varepsilon^{P}\) the income and price elasticities. The full form, with a separate efficiency response to prices, is in paper 5.1 and in the Total Effective Carbon Price paper (Stretton 2026c). Every block of the rebuild has to reproduce equations like equation 1 exactly as legacy computes them, except where legacy does not compute what it means to. Bug L3 is an example: the income factor on the elasticity \(\varepsilon^{Y}\) was applied twice and anchored to 2023, so the effective elasticity drifted as incomes rose (CPAT-AI project 2026e).

title: CPAT-AI: Rebuilding a Policy Model as a Transparent, Testable Tool
text:
4.2 The replication rule
The rule separates two kinds of difference between what legacy does and what it should do. A bug is a place where legacy does not compute what it means to: a reference to the wrong row, a term applied twice, a dead or blank reference, a sign error, a formula that contradicts its own label. An issue is a place where legacy does what it means to, but the choice is open to question: an old data vintage, a simplification, a missing feature, a result nobody can yet explain. Bugs are fixed and never copied. Issues are copied exactly and tracked (CPAT-AI project 2026b).
Stated formally, the rule gives every difference from legacy a code. Let \(L(x)\) be what legacy computes for input \(x\), \(I(x)\) what its authors intended (read from labels, documentation and the CPAT team) and \(P(x)\) what the prototype computes. The rule sets \(P(x) = I(x)\), except where the owner has decided a departure \(D\). Since \(I(x) = L(x)\) wherever legacy has no bug, \[
P(x) \neq L(x) \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{a registered bug fix, or a registered departure decided by the model owner}.
\tag{2}\]
Claim (closure). Every difference between the prototype and legacy can be traced to a register entry, provided that three conditions hold: every difference found is registered the same day, codes are never reused, and every release is regression-tested against the previous one, so that no unregistered difference enters between releases. The first two are rules of the project (CPAT-AI project 2026b); the third is the fourth test level in Section 6. A reviewer who finds that Excel-AI and legacy disagree on a number can look up why.
Three further rules make the closure hold in practice. When in doubt whether something is a bug or an issue, treat it as an issue, replicate it and ask. Never improve legacy silently: a better method or newer data is an issue, proposed as an upgrade for the owner to decide. And any departure that is not a bug fix needs an explicit decision by the model owner, recorded with the issue (CPAT-AI project 2026b). One example: legacy computes energy subsidies for the baseline scenario only; the prototype, by the owner’s decision, computes them in every scenario, with the baseline equal to legacy (issue I110) (CPAT-AI project 2026e).
Data problems are issues, ranked by whether legacy can fix them. Where legacy reads data wrongly (a blank VAT cell read as a rate of zero), the formula fix is a legacy bug with a cell-level plan, and the data problem is an issue of priority Very high. Where no formula fix is possible because the data themselves are missing or poor, the prototype does exactly what legacy does and the issue is Extremely high. Two issues held that rank in release 1.0.2: combustion emission factors available only as base and final values, and current account data typed in for Egypt only (CPAT-AI project 2026e).
The rule also runs between the two rebuilds. Coded CPAT treats Excel-AI as its specification exactly as Excel-AI treats legacy. A bug that Python finds in the Excel prototype is never copied into Python. It is registered as a prototype bug, fixed in Python where the fix is obvious, and listed as a “known difference” that the tests check really does differ. It is then fixed in the next Excel release, after which the known difference is deleted and the two must agree again (CPAT-AI project 2026b, 2026c).

title: CPAT-AI: Rebuilding a Policy Model as a Transparent, Testable Tool
section: 4.3 Shared codes make three models comparable
text:
4.3 Shared codes make three models comparable
Every input, variable and output has one code, the same in legacy, Excel and Python. Inputs keep the names and rows of legacy’s input sheet (NameOfParameter), in legacy units, so a scenario defined for one model means the same thing in the others. Outputs carry codes that state country, module, variable, sector, fuel and scenario: egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.2 is Egypt’s total CO2 in scenario 2. A codes map lists every input with its legacy row, its name and its Python key, and Python may not invent a second name for anything that has a code (CPAT-AI project 2026b).
Shared codes turn comparison into a join. Without them, comparing two implementations of a model with 15,086 output codes means matching rows by hand. With them, a comparison is a table merge on the code and the year, followed by a tolerance check, and it can be run after every change. In the author’s judgment this is the design decision that made the rest affordable: it is what let one person check three implementations against each other every day.

title: CPAT-AI: Rebuilding a Policy Model as a Transparent, Testable Tool
section: 4.4 Excel written by code, Python written to be read
text:
4.4 Excel written by code, Python written to be read
Excel-AI is a workbook that no person typed. Python builders write it with openpyxl and recalculate it in LibreOffice, so it can be built and checked on any machine (CPAT-AI project 2026c). The norms that govern it are mechanical and checkable: every formula was at most 100 characters as Excel shows it; one formula serves a whole block of cells, so that copying, dragging or pasting it anywhere in the block gives the same result; no constant is typed into a formula (only 0 and 1 are allowed); every money unit comes from one vocabulary; and every file passes a lint check before it ships, so Excel never shows a repair prompt (CPAT-AI project 2026b). The workbook of release 1.1.0 holds about half a million formulas (497,541) (CPAT-AI project 2026a).
Coded CPAT is written so that a person with the equation list open can check every equation. Each equation of the list is one small function, named after the code of the quantity it computes, whose docstring states the equation. Names are CPAT codes (ener for fuel use, atp for after-tax prices); no number other than 0 and 1 is typed into the code; unit conversions live in one place; and a test fails if any equation in the list has no function or any function cites an equation that is not in the list (CPAT-AI project 2026b). Release 1.0.2p1.1 runs one country and two scenarios in 0.8 seconds once the baseline is cached (CPAT-AI project 2026d).

title: 5. Modelling (CPAT)
text:
Finance ministries decide on carbon taxes, fuel subsidy reform and climate investment with the help of models they cannot inspect. This section is the paper-length companion to the CPAT-AI project, which rebuilt the Climate Policy Assessment Tool so that every step can be read and tested. It states the mitigation module’s method in fourteen equations; describes the two AI-assisted rebuilds and the legacy bugs they found (231 in the register, 24 of them high priority); gathers the published validation, which supports the model for ranges and policy comparisons but not point forecasts; and checks the price elasticities that drive every result, finding most defaults within the published range and the timing of the response the larger problem. The through-line is that a model a ministry can use must be small enough to state on a few pages, built at least twice, and tested against data and other models. The extensions ministries ask for are written as modular upgrades in section 6.

5.1 The CPAT Mitigation Module: Methods in Brief
How a Finance-Ministry Climate Model Turns Prices into Fuel Use, Power Investment, Emissions and Revenue
Finance ministries use the Climate Policy Assessment Tool, built by the World Bank and the IMF, to estimate what carbon taxes and fuel subsidy reform would raise, cost and cut. Its mitigation module is simple, but its documentation runs to 57,000 words and its 2023 edition contains twenty errors. A rebuild of the model states the whole method in fourteen equations. This brief explains what the model does, why a carbon price bites on coal far more than on road fuel, why power-sector results rest on two judgment calls, and how ministries and the teams who serve them should read and improve the results.

text:
5.2 CPAT-AI: Rebuilding a Policy Model as a Transparent, Testable Tool
What two AI-assisted rebuilds of the Climate Policy Assessment Tool found, and how policy models should be maintained
Finance ministries use the Climate Policy Assessment Tool, a large spreadsheet built by the IMF and the World Bank, to judge carbon taxes and fuel subsidy reforms. Nobody had checked all of it. In October 2026 it was rebuilt twice, as a readable workbook and as a Python model, mostly by AI coding agents, under one rule: fix bugs, copy and log deliberate choices. The rebuild found 228 bugs, 24 serious enough to change standard results; the second rebuild found seven bugs in the first. Ministries should require shared variable codes, one register of known problems, a second implementation, and a named owner of every judgment.

section: 5.3 Validating CPAT: Baselines, Back-Casts and Model Comparisons
text:
5.3 Validating CPAT: Baselines, Back-Casts and Model Comparisons
What the published checks of the Climate Policy Assessment Tool show, where it fits and where it does not
Finance ministries use the Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT) to estimate what a carbon tax does to emissions and revenue. This brief sets out what the tool’s published checks show. CPAT fits its base year by construction, follows the trend of emissions in back-casts for large economies, and agrees in order of magnitude with other energy models and with the wide range of evidence on real carbon prices. Its results move most with its price elasticities: a G20 emissions cut of 29 percent can be anywhere from 7 to 39 percent. Ministries should read CPAT results as ranges, use them to compare policies, and ask for the checks to be rerun on the corrected model.

title: 5. Modelling (CPAT)
text:
5.4 Are CPAT’s Price Elasticities Right?
A Check Against the Evidence
The Climate Policy Assessment Tool, which the IMF and the World Bank use to estimate what carbon taxes and fuel subsidy reforms do, turns price changes into emission cuts through price elasticities. This brief reports a check of its defaults against the published evidence. Most are consistent, and many are cautious. Two are too high, and road gasoline is twice the estimate corrected for publication bias. The bigger problem is timing: the tool applies the full long-run response in the first year, so it overstates five-year cuts by about half and understates early revenue. Users should read near-term results as upper bounds and show a low-elasticity case.
