title: CPAT-AI: Rebuilding a Policy Model as a Transparent, Testable Tool
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full account, with the register, the tests and the sources, is in the working paper; the rebuilt models are public at https://github.com/cpmodelai/cpat_ai.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
A model that guides tax reform had never been fully checked. The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT) is a spreadsheet of over 21 megabytes with about 400 pages of documentation. Its formulas differ from row to row, so no one could audit it cell by cell.
Rebuilt twice in October 2026, it turned out to hold 228 bugs, 24 of them serious. Some changed standard results: a one-off GDP gain compounded every year, and a methane fee on farming and waste did nothing.
One rule made the rebuild trustworthy: fix bugs, copy deliberate choices and log them. Every difference from the original has a code and a reason, and every departure was decided in writing by a named owner.
Building twice caught what one build missed. The Python version found seven bugs in the rebuilt workbook. But versions built from the same reading can share an error, and agreeing models can all be wrong about the world.
Ministries should ask four things of any model they rely on: shared variable codes, one register of known problems, a second implementation tested at every release, and a named owner for every judgment.


A model ministries rely on had never been fully checked
CPAT shapes advice on carbon pricing and subsidy reform in many countries. Built by the IMF and the World Bank, it estimates what carbon taxes, emissions trading, fuel subsidy reform and related policies do to energy prices, fuel use, emissions, revenue, GDP and households, year by year, for more than 180 countries (CPAT Team 2023; Black et al. 2023). Finance ministries and development-bank teams use it to size reforms and their effects on the poor.
It is a spreadsheet, which makes it open but not checkable. Anyone can open it and see every number, and its authors chose Excel for that reason (CPAT Team 2023). But the legacy workbook is over 21 megabytes, its main sheet runs past row 18,000, and its formulas change from row to row, so checking one row says little about the next. Its documentation had also drifted from the workbook.
Large spreadsheets almost always contain errors. Studies of spreadsheet audits find errors in a few percent of cells, so a large workbook’s question is how many errors it holds, not whether (Panko 1998); no audit has found an operational spreadsheet free of them (Powell et al. 2008). Errors of this kind can move a policy debate: a spreadsheet slip, together with data choices, turned 2.2 percent average growth into a published −0.1 percent in a famous study of public debt (Herndon et al. 2014).
The cure is known; the labor to apply it was missing. Writing the model as code, testing each block, keeping one list of problems and building it twice are standard advice, and the UK Treasury asks for them of every business-critical government model (HM Treasury 2013). A policy model run by economists rarely has the software team to do them.


One rule and shared codes made a full rebuild possible
CPAT was rebuilt twice in four weeks, mostly by AI coding agents. The first rebuild, Excel-AI, is a readable workbook written by code, in which one short formula serves a whole block of cells. The second, Coded CPAT, is a Python model written from the first one’s equation list. Both are public (CPAT-AI project 2026b).
The rule separates mistakes from choices. A bug is a formula that does not compute what its authors meant, such as one that points to the wrong row; the rebuild fixes it and never copies it. An issue is a deliberate choice that is open to question, such as an old data vintage; the rebuild copies it exactly and logs it for the modelers to decide. Any other departure needs a dated decision by the model’s owner (working paper, the replication rule). So a reviewer who finds a difference between the rebuild and the original can look up why.
Shared codes make the three models comparable at every step. Every input, variable and output has one code, the same in the original workbook, Excel-AI and Python. Comparing any two is then a table join, which can be run after every change (working paper, shared codes).
Every number is checked by something that did not produce it. Each block is first shown to reproduce the original’s own results with its bugs switched back on, so the rebuild understood the method before changing it. The workbook is then checked against an independent recomputation, Python against the workbook (every one of 7,458 outputs per Egypt scenario, to one part in a billion), and each release against the last (working paper, the testing regime).


The rebuild found 228 bugs, 24 of them serious
Half of the 454 entries in the register are bugs in the original model. Table 1 gives the counts at release 1.0.2. The 24 high-priority bugs change results in standard runs; the 142 low-priority ones sit in options the standard run does not use, or in a reported number only.



Table 1: The rebuild of CPAT registered 454 entries; half are bugs in the original model. Source: CPAT-AI register, release 1.0.2, 29 October 2026; working paper, Table 1.

The serious bugs sit where formulas were copied across sectors or years. Services electricity demand grew with industry’s multiple after 2023, the largest single error in power demand. The GDP effect of recycled carbon revenue was added to the growth rate every year instead of to the level once, so a one-off gain compounded. A methane fee on farming and waste had no effect, because that methane never changed. Regulation scenarios did nothing, because a lookup never matched. “Other oil products” were priced at a floor, so their use rose about tenfold by 2030 (CPAT-AI project 2026c).
Most bugs are latent, and they fire exactly when a ministry asks a new question. A bug in an option the standard run does not use, such as the detailed road-fleet model, changes nothing until someone switches that option on. That is when a ministry is asking a question the default run does not answer.
The total is a lower bound. The register held 64 legacy bugs on 18 October 2026, 159 two days later and 228 at release 1.0.2 on 29 October (Figure 1); a day later it held 231 (CPAT-AI project 2026a). The modules not yet rebuilt, air pollution and transport co-benefits, will add more.






Figure 1: Legacy bugs in the CPAT-AI register, October 2026. The count rose as each new block of the model was rebuilt. Source: CPAT-AI task log and register; working paper, What the rebuild found.



The owners are fixing what the rebuild found, and the checks keep everyone honest. Within weeks the CPAT team marked 63 bugs fixed in its next file. A cell-by-cell check confirmed 52, found 9 fixed with caveats, and found 2 marked fixed that were not (CPAT-AI project 2026c).


Building twice catches what one build misses, but not everything
The Python build found seven bugs that the workbook’s own checks had missed. They included nominal GDP divided by a billion when the source was already in billions, and two gas price series read from each other’s rows. All seven were fixed in both models (working paper, the testing regime).
Versions built from the same reading can share the same error. Software engineers have known this for forty years: in a classic experiment, 27 programs written independently to one specification failed together far more often than chance predicts (Knight and Leveson 1986). A 2026 repeat with programs written by AI agents found the same, though voting across three versions still cut failures by about two thirds (Ron et al. 2026). CPAT-AI limits the risk by tying every block to the original’s own stored results, which no agent wrote, and by sending every fix to the CPAT team (working paper, what AI did and did not do).
Agreement between models is not proof that the model is right. The tests show that three implementations compute the same thing; they do not show that CPAT’s price elasticities are right or that its baseline fits history. That is validation, the subject of Brief 5.3 and Brief 5.4 (Stretton 2026d, 2026a).


AI agents built; a named owner decided
The agents did most of the construction. Working under written rules, through Claude Code and GitHub Copilot, they wrote the code that builds the workbook, the checks, the whole Python model and its tests, and the documents generated from the register. The project log records 241 finished tasks in four weeks (CPAT-AI project 2026a).
The people kept every judgment. Whether a difference is a bug or an issue is settled by rule, whose default is “copy it and ask”. Every departure from the original carries a dated decision by the owner, and the owner accepted each release. The checks caught agents’ errors and people’s alike: one overlong formula written by an agent stopped a release, and a cell-by-cell check found two bugs that the original’s owners had marked fixed but had not.
The evidence on AI productivity is mixed, so the safeguard is the test, not the tool. In one experiment programmers with an AI assistant finished a task 56 percent faster (Peng et al. 2023); in another, experienced developers on their own large projects were 19 percent slower with AI tools while believing they were faster (Becker et al. 2025). CPAT-AI did not depend on settling that question, because every output was tested by something its author did not write.


What it means for decisions made with CPAT
Results from earlier versions of CPAT should be read with the register at hand. A result that rests on the GDP feedback, methane fees outside energy, regulation scenarios or the detailed road model may be affected by a bug now fixed in the rebuild and, in part, in the CPAT team’s latest file. The register lists each bug, where it sits and what it changes, so an analyst can check a past run against it (CPAT-AI project 2026c).
The rebuilt models are ready for one country, not yet for all. Excel-AI and Coded CPAT shipped with complete data for Egypt only, because several of CPAT’s data tables are licensed; other countries need the full database. Air pollution and transport co-benefits are not yet rebuilt (working paper, lessons).


What to do
Ministries and agencies that commission a policy model: ask for four things. A codes map, so that any later audit or rebuild is a table join. One register of bugs, issues and departures, shared with the model’s owners. A second implementation, and a regression test on every output at every release. And a named owner who decides every departure in writing, as the UK Treasury asks of its own models (HM Treasury 2013).
The CPAT team and its users: work through the register. Apply the cell-level fix plans to the legacy file, confirm each fix independently, and rerun the published validation and elasticity checks on the corrected model for every country (Brief 5.3, Brief 5.4).
Development-bank teams running CPAT for a client: check the run against the register. Before a result goes into advice, check whether the run used any feature with a known high-priority bug, and say so in the note.
Anyone building models with AI agents: let agents build and people decide. Write the rules down, route every agent to them, keep judgments with a named person, and test every output against something its author did not produce.


Related papers in this series

Brief 5.1: the CPAT mitigation module, its methods in brief (Stretton 2026c).
Brief 5.3: validating CPAT against data and other models (Stretton 2026d).
Brief 5.4: are CPAT’s price elasticities right? (Stretton 2026a).
Brief 6.1: the Total Effective Carbon Price, which uses the same demand system (Stretton 2026b).
The working paper behind this brief: the register in full, the replication rule, the four test levels and the sources.

title: The CPAT Mitigation Module: Methods in Brief
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full method, with every equation, the corrections and the derivations, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
A finance ministry should be able to audit the climate model it relies on, and CPAT’s mitigation module is small enough to audit. The whole module fits in fourteen equations, from fuel prices to revenue and growth.
A carbon price bites where fuel is cheap and carbon-rich. At 50 dollars per tonne of CO₂, CPAT’s default responses cut industrial coal use by about a third and road fuel use by about 6 percent.
Power-sector results rest on two judgment calls. New investment is shared by a rule whose key setting was chosen “subjectively”, and the growth of wind and solar is capped; under a large carbon price the caps often decide the answer.
The rebuild found real errors, and they are fixed. Rebuilding CPAT found 231 bugs in the legacy workbook and twenty errors in the 2023 documentation; the rebuilt model and a corrected edition of the documentation fix them.
Use CPAT as a first estimate for phased reforms, and say which results depend on judgment. Replace default settings with country evidence where it exists, and fund the three upgrades that matter most.


A model ministries rely on was hard to check
CPAT answers the four questions a finance minister asks about a carbon tax. How much will it raise, what will it do to fuel prices, how far will it cut emissions, and what will it do to growth? The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), built jointly by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), answers all four for more than 180 countries. IMF staff have used it in Article IV reports, technical assistance and climate assessments, and World Bank teams in country work (Black et al. 2023; CPAT Team 2024). Its core is the mitigation module, which turns a policy into prices, fuel use, power investment, emissions, revenue and output.
Its documentation made it hard to know what the model assumes. The mitigation chapter alone runs to 57,000 words with seven appendices (CPAT Team 2024). A ministry economist who wanted to check a result had to assemble the method from tables, dashboard screenshots and equations, some of which were wrong. A model whose assumptions cannot be checked is hard to defend in a budget negotiation.
A rebuild has now stated the method in fourteen equations. The CPAT-AI project rebuilt the model twice, as a spreadsheet and in Python, wrote out every equation, and checked each against a running model (CPAT-AI Project 2026b). The working paper behind this brief states the corrected method in one place, with each correction noted (working paper, Appendix A).


The model is a short chain that every number can be traced through
Prices come first, and every part of them is explicit. The retail price of each fuel in each sector is the cost of supply, plus existing taxes, less subsidies, plus the new carbon charge and the value-added tax (VAT) on it. Because each part is separate, CPAT can report the total price signal on carbon, which Brief 6.1 turns into the Total Effective Carbon Price (Stretton 2026c). Where a country controls fuel prices, CPAT lets a floating tax or subsidy absorb world-price changes, but a positive tax never falls below its last observed level, so price rises in taxed fuels reach consumers (working paper, prices).
Fuel use then responds to income, an efficiency trend and the price. One equation covers every sector outside power. The price response has two parts: how much an existing car, boiler or furnace is used, and how efficient the stock becomes. Non-price policies such as efficiency standards and feebates act only on the second part, so they cut fuel use without raising the price paid per unit (working paper, demand).
An engineering power model meets electricity demand. It runs renewables and nuclear first, splits the rest between coal and gas on running cost, retires old plants, and shares new investment among technologies on full cost, including a charge for the storage that a high share of wind and solar needs (working paper, power).
Emissions and revenue follow by accounting, and revenue moves growth a year later. Emissions are fuel use times emission factors, calibrated to the national inventory. Revenue is fuel use times tax rates, net of the smaller base for existing fuel taxes. The change in revenue, and what the government does with it, moves output a year later through fiscal multipliers.


A carbon price bites on coal, not on road fuel
The same carbon price changes some fuel prices far more than others. A carbon charge adds a fixed amount per tonne of CO₂, so it is large relative to the price of a cheap, carbon-rich fuel and small relative to a heavily taxed one. At 50 dollars per tonne it more than doubles the price of industrial coal but adds only 10 to 13 percent to road fuel (Table 1).



Table 1: Effect of a carbon price of 50 US dollars per tonne of CO₂ with CPAT’s default elasticities for low- and middle-income countries. Pre-policy prices are stylized; emission factors are the IPCC defaults (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change 2006). Full pass-through, no VAT on the charge, output held fixed. Source: working paper, Table 1.










Fuel and sector
Price rise from the carbon charge
Fall in fuel use




Coal, industry
+118%
−36%


Natural gas, industry
+35%
−20%


Diesel, road transport
+13%
−6%


Gasoline, road transport
+10%
−6%






So most of the percentage cut comes from coal. Industrial coal use falls by about a third and road fuel by about 6 percent, for similar responsiveness. The tonnes depend on each country’s fuel mix, but a country that burns coal will find most of its cut there.
Each fuel responds to its own price alone. Outside power, cooking and road vehicles, CPAT has no fuel switching: a carbon price that raises coal more than gas cuts coal more than gas, but does not move a factory from coal to gas. The model therefore understates switching in industry and overstates the fall in total energy use. Paper 6.1 shows how a richer demand system with switching changes the result (Brief 6.1).
The responses are long-run, but the model applies them within a year. CPAT’s elasticities were set from a meta-analysis of price responses (Labandeira et al. 2017) and adjusted for developing countries, and they are long-run values. The model applies them to each year’s price change, so a sudden price jump produces its full long-run response at once (Black et al. 2023). For a carbon price phased in over several years, which is the usual design, the error is small; for a sudden shock it is not. Paper 5.4 checks the elasticities against the wider evidence (Brief 5.4).


Power-sector results rest on two judgment calls
New power investment is shared by a rule whose key setting was chosen by judgment. CPAT shares new investment among technologies by a “logit” rule: cheaper technologies get more, but every permitted technology gets something. How sharply cost differences translate into shares is set by one parameter, which the documentation says was “set subjectively at 2” (CPAT Team 2024). It has never been estimated.
The second judgment call is a cap on how fast each technology can grow. Wind and solar can each add about 2 percentage points of the power system a year in most countries. Under a large carbon price the cap, not the price, often decides how fast the system changes. A ministry reading CPAT’s power results should ask whether the caps bind.
The investment rule has an economic meaning, and a simpler alternative exists. The working paper shows that CPAT’s rule is what a planner would choose if it minimized cost while paying a penalty for concentrating investment, with the penalty worth about 22 dollars per megawatt-hour in a stylized example. Changing the shape of that penalty gives a rule with a simple formula that a ministry can check by hand, and that gives uncompetitive technologies nothing (working paper, penalty-based allocation). Figure 1 compares the two. With no carbon price CPAT’s rule still gives oil-fired power 1.4 percent of new investment at more than two and a half times the cost of solar; the alternative gives it none. At 75 dollars per tonne the alternative stops investment in coal; CPAT’s rule keeps 1 percent.






Figure 1: Shares of new power investment under CPAT’s logit rule and the proposed quadratic-penalty rule, with no carbon price and at 75 US dollars per tonne of CO₂ (stylized costs: solar 45, wind 55, gas 60, coal 65, oil 120 US dollars per megawatt-hour before carbon). Source: working paper, Table 2.



Neither rule is right in general. Both need a parameter fitted to observed investment. The case for the alternative is transparency, not accuracy, so it should be tested behind a switch before any change to the default.


The rebuild found real errors, and they are fixed
The legacy workbook had 231 bugs, and none is carried into the rebuilt model. The rebuild follows one rule: a bug, where the workbook does not compute what it means to, is fixed and never copied; an issue, where it computes what it means to but the choice is open to question, is copied and tracked (CPAT-AI Project 2026b). Some bugs changed results. The workbook added each year’s growth effect of a policy to the growth rate every year, so a one-off effect on output compounded; it sized new power plants for this year’s demand although they come online next year; and it computed the effect of efficiency regulations but never applied it.
The 2023 documentation had twenty errors, now corrected. They include a wrong sign on the electricity price markup, a wrong discount factor in the cost of power, and no equation at all for how revenue moves output. None changes the model, but a reader of the 2023 text would get these equations wrong. A corrected edition was published on 31 October 2026, fourteen errors fixed in full and six in part (CPAT-AI Project 2026a); the public site still carries the 2023 text.


Read CPAT as a first estimate for phased reforms
The strongest objection is that a model this simple should not guide fiscal decisions. It has no lags, little fuel switching, a fixed world fuel market, no trade and a power sector that rests on judgment. The answer is that its biases mostly have known signs, its price responses are checked against the evidence, and it is built for phased, medium-term reforms, where the missing dynamics matter least (working paper, limitations). Paper 5.3 sets out how its results compare with other models and with history (Brief 5.3).
Some results deserve more caution than others. The first-year response to a sudden price jump is overstated. Switching from coal to gas in industry is missed. Population growth is treated like rising income, which misstates baseline demand where populations grow fast. A carbon price in a large economy would move world fuel prices, which CPAT holds fixed. And the power path under a large carbon price is set mainly by the build-rate caps.


What to do
Finance ministries: ask for the price changes before the quantities, and for the assumptions that set them. A CPAT result is only as good as the price change behind it and the elasticity applied to it. Ask whether the base year matches national data, which defaults were replaced with country evidence, and whether the power result depends on the build-rate caps.
World Bank and IMF teams running CPAT: replace defaults with country evidence and say which results rest on judgment. Use a national power plan where one exists, country elasticities where they have been estimated, and national multipliers where available. Report results from the corrected model, and cite the corrected documentation rather than the 2023 text.
The CPAT team: fund the three upgrades that matter most. Estimate the investment rule’s parameter from observed investment, or test the quadratic-penalty rule behind a switch. Add gradual adjustment and fuel switching to the demand equation, along the lines of Paper 6.1. And extend the rebuilt model’s data from one country to all, so that ministries everywhere get the corrected method.


Related papers in this series

Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.2: how CPAT was rebuilt as a transparent, testable tool (Stretton 2026b).
No. 5.3: validating CPAT against data and other models (Stretton 2026d).
No. 5.4: whether CPAT’s price elasticities are right (Stretton 2026a).
No. 6.1: the Total Effective Carbon Price, and a demand system with fuel switching (Stretton 2026c).
The working paper behind this brief: every equation, the corrections and the derivations.

title: Validating CPAT: Baselines, Back-Casts and Model Comparisons
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full analysis, with every table, source and recomputation, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
CPAT is good enough for ranges and for comparing policies, not for point forecasts. Its published checks support the direction and rough size of what a carbon tax does, not the decimal point.
A CPAT emissions cut of 29 percent means “about 20 to 35 percent”. The price elasticities and the choice of power model drive most of the spread; ask which ones a result uses.
The evidence on real carbon prices is too wide to say CPAT over- or under-predicts. On a like-for-like basis, its response is of the same order as the best cross-country estimate.
Every published check was run on a model that has since been found to contain more than 200 bugs. The rebuilt model fixes them and runs a country in under a second, so the checks can and should be rerun.
Ask for a measure of fit with every CPAT result, and fund validation as a routine test, not a one-off study.


Why a ministry should ask how wrong the model is
A carbon-pricing decision rests on a forecast, and the forecast has an error. CPAT, built by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund, estimates the emissions, revenue, GDP and household effects of carbon pricing in more than 180 countries (Campmas et al. 2023). A typical result is that a carbon tax rising to $75 per tonne of CO₂ by 2030 cuts G20 emissions by 29 percent against the baseline (Campmas et al. 2023). If the response to the price is off by half, so are the revenue estimate and the gap to the country’s climate pledge.
CPAT’s checks exist, but they are scattered and mostly in charts. The CPAT team compared the model with history, with other energy models and with studies of real carbon prices, and published the results in a long methodology chapter (Campmas et al. 2023). The 2026 rebuild of the model added a fourth test: whether independent code reproduces it. The working paper sets all of these side by side, recomputes what can be recomputed, and corrects several numbers.
Four tests answer four different questions. Does the model match the data in its starting year? Started in the past, does it reproduce what happened next? Do other models, and studies of real carbon prices, give similar answers? Does a second, independent version of the code compute the same numbers? Passing one test says little about the others (working paper, what validation means).


What the checks show
CPAT matches the starting year because it is made to, so that match proves little. The model scales its emissions so that they equal each country’s official inventory in the base year. The scaling can also carry a data break into every later year. Egypt’s inventory jumps by almost a fifth from 2021 to 2022, and the calibrated baseline ends up 16 to 32 percent below the inventory in 2022–2024 (working paper, baseline fit). A ministry comparing CPAT with its own inventory would see this at once.
Started in 2000 and run to 2017, CPAT gets the trend of emissions right in most of the countries tested and the level right only where prices behave. The test fed in the world energy prices that actually occurred. The model’s typical error was 5 percent of average emissions for Australia, 10 percent for the United States and 14 percent for South Africa, but 26 percent for Brazil, 33 percent for the United Kingdom and 92 percent for China (Figure 1). Most of the misses come from domestic prices that the model projected badly, as where governments control prices. None of the six countries is a typical CPAT user, and none is a low-income country.






Figure 1: CPAT’s error in the level of greenhouse gas emissions when run from 2000 to 2017 with no policy, as a percentage of average observed emissions. Source: CPAT methodology, section Hindcasting; working paper, Figure 1.



Against other energy models, CPAT is of the same order. Its world baseline is close to the International Energy Agency’s and Enerdata’s, its response of emissions to a carbon price has about the same slope as Enerdata’s, and its power-sector mix under a $40 carbon price resembles that of the World Bank’s power planning model. Only the timing of power investment differs much, because the planning model builds in lumps. None of these comparisons reports a measure of fit; all are charts (working paper, comparisons).


The evidence on real carbon prices cannot yet test CPAT’s response
CPAT’s documentation compares two different measures and calls them comparable. A $10 carbon price in CPAT lowers emissions by an average of 2.4 percent over its first five years and 6.2 percent over seventeen. Studies of real carbon prices usually report how much a scheme slowed the growth of emissions each year. Put on that basis, CPAT’s response is about 0.7 to 0.8 percent a year at $10, against about 0.5 percent a year in the most comparable cross-country study, which its authors call imprecise (Rafaty et al. 2020) (working paper, ex-post evidence).
The rest of the evidence is too wide to settle whether CPAT responds too much or too little. One review finds that real carbon prices cut emissions by 0 to 2 percent a year (Green 2021). A later meta-analysis of 80 studies of 21 schemes finds total cuts of 5 to 21 percent, even though most prices were low (Döbbeling-Hildebrandt et al. 2024). Both are for real schemes with partial coverage and free permits, so neither scales simply to a comprehensive carbon tax.
One finding holds up: CPAT ranks the sectors as the evidence does. Power responds most and transport least, in CPAT and in the cross-country evidence (Rafaty et al. 2020). Rankings like this, and comparisons between policies, are what CPAT does most reliably.


The price elasticities decide the answer
No other input moves CPAT’s results as much as the price elasticities. The elasticities say how much fuel use falls when prices rise. The CPAT team changed one input at a time in a G20 run of a carbon tax rising to $75 in 2030 (Table 1). Moving the price elasticities by two standard deviations either way moves the cut from 29 percent to anywhere between 7 and 39 percent. Choosing one power model rather than the other moves it between 22 and 34 percent. Income elasticities, fiscal multipliers and GDP growth hardly matter for the size of the cut.



Table 1: A carbon tax rising to $75 cuts G20 emissions by 29 percent in 2030; the price elasticities can move that from 7 to 39 percent. Source: CPAT methodology, section Parameter Sensitivity Analysis; working paper, Table 4.









What changes
G20 CO₂ cut in 2030




Default settings
29%


Price elasticities one standard deviation higher / lower
35% / 20%


Price elasticities two standard deviations higher / lower
39% / 7%


Power model: elasticity / engineering
34% / 22%


World energy prices 50 percent lower / higher
31% / 20%


Income elasticities, fiscal multipliers or GDP growth changed
29–30%






The evidence finds most elasticities in the right range, with clear exceptions. The CPAT team’s own estimates on data for 2000–2018 find the household electricity elasticity lower than CPAT assumes (−0.1 against −0.4), and services fuels less responsive than CPAT assumes. For gasoline the picture is mixed: the team’s estimate is lower than CPAT’s, but a review of many studies puts the long-run value higher (Brons et al. 2008), so CPAT’s value sits inside the range (Campmas et al. 2023) (working paper, sensitivity; Brief 5.4).


The rebuilt model reproduces CPAT and found its bugs
Independent code reproduces CPAT’s method to many decimal places. The 2026 rebuild rewrote each block of the original Excel model in Python and required it to reproduce the original’s stored results. The road and power-price blocks match to better than one part in ten trillion, and the new Python model reproduces the rebuilt workbook to nine digits (CPAT-AI project 2026a). CPAT’s results are therefore a property of its method, not an accident of one spreadsheet (working paper, replication; Brief 5.2).
The rebuild also found 231 bugs in the original model, 24 of them serious. They include a population path for Egypt that departed from the United Nations projection and an income effect on power demand applied twice (CPAT-AI project 2026c). Every published check was run before these were fixed, so the evidence is about an earlier model. The corrected Python model runs one country in under a second, so the checks are now cheap to rerun for every country.
Outsiders can rerun the method, not every country’s numbers. Six of CPAT’s data tables are proprietary, and the public repository holds them only for Egypt, slightly perturbed (CPAT-AI project 2026b). Repeating the validation for all countries needs the full database.


How to read a CPAT number
Read a CPAT emissions cut as a range. A cut of 29 percent is best read as “about 20 to 35 percent”: the spread from one standard deviation in the price elasticities and from the choice of power model. Ask which power model a result uses.
Trust comparisons more than levels. When two policies run on the same baseline, errors in the baseline largely cancel. “Policy A cuts twice as much as policy B” is more reliable than “policy A cuts 29 percent”.
Check the elasticities where the result depends on one sector. Results driven by household electricity, services or road fuels deserve a check against national evidence. Road transport needs extra care: CPAT describes it in three ways that are not consistent with each other, and no published check compares them (working paper, where CPAT fits; Brief 6.4).
Compare the baseline with the national inventory before using it. A break in the inventory, as in Egypt in 2022, can leave the whole baseline too low or too high.


What to do
Finance ministries: ask for ranges and a measure of fit. Request every CPAT result with its sensitivity to the price elasticities and the power model, and with the baseline set against the national inventory and one other projection.
Development-bank and IMF country teams: report which settings a run uses. State the power model, the elasticities and the data vintage in every report, and flag results that hinge on household electricity, services or road transport.
The teams that maintain CPAT: make validation a routine test. Rerun the back-casts, model comparisons and sensitivity analysis on the corrected model for every country with data; report a measure of fit for each; repeat them at every release (working paper, what validation remains).
Researchers and funders: test CPAT against real carbon prices. Use cases such as Sweden and British Columbia, with the data available before each tax began, and measure the response the way the ex-post studies do, per dollar of carbon price.


Related papers in this series

Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.1: the CPAT mitigation module, its methods in brief.
No. 5.2: rebuilding CPAT as a transparent, testable tool.
No. 5.4: whether CPAT’s price elasticities are right.
No. 6.1: the Total Effective Carbon Price, the yardstick for comparing policies (Stretton 2026).
No. 6.4: activity levels across CPAT and other models, including road transport.
The working paper behind this brief: every table, source and recomputation.

title: Are CPAT’s Price Elasticities Right?
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 5.4, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full analysis, with the evidence register, the calculations and the validation protocol, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
A carbon-pricing model’s answer is set mostly by its price elasticities. In the Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT), changing them within their uncertainty moves the estimated cut in G20 emissions from a $75 carbon tax from 29 percent to anywhere between 7 and 39 percent.
Most of CPAT’s default elasticities are consistent with the evidence, and many are cautious. Eight of ten main fuel-sector values lie within the published range; two, for diesel in industry and gasoline in services, are well above it.
For road fuels, the published evidence itself overstates the response. Corrected for publication bias, the long-run gasoline elasticity is −0.31, half CPAT’s −0.64.
The bigger problem is timing. CPAT applies the full long-run response in the first year. After five years only about 60 percent of it has happened, so CPAT overstates five-year cuts by about half and understates early revenue.
Read CPAT’s near-term results as upper bounds, and show a low-elasticity case beside them. Comparisons of policies and of countries, such as the Total Effective Carbon Price, are much less affected.


Elasticities decide the size of the answer
Finance ministries use CPAT to decide carbon-tax rates and subsidy reforms, and its elasticities set the size of every estimate. CPAT, built by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, projects fuel use, emissions and revenue for more than 180 countries (Black et al. 2022). For each fuel in each sector it applies a price elasticity: the percentage fall in use when the price rises by one percent. An elasticity of −0.6 means a 10 percent price rise cuts use by 6 percent. If the true value is −0.3, the tool reports twice the cut and a tax base that erodes twice as fast.
No other parameter moves CPAT’s results as much. CPAT’s own sensitivity tests run a carbon tax rising to $75 per tonne of CO₂ in the G20. With the default elasticities, emissions fall 29 percent by 2030. Raising or lowering every elasticity by two standard deviations moves the cut to anywhere between 7 and 39 percent (CPAT-AI project 2026), as Brief 5.3 reports. A ministry that sets a rate to meet a pledge, or counts on revenue from a reform, is relying on these numbers.
The elasticities were set by the model’s builders and checked mainly against their own targets. CPAT’s documentation says its values were calibrated to one meta-analysis, a study that pools about 2,000 published estimates, and then checked against those targets and against panel estimates on the tool’s own data (CPAT-AI project 2026). This brief reports an outside check: each default against every published estimate that could be verified, keeping the figures CPAT was calibrated to apart (working paper, the evidence).


Most defaults pass, two fail
Eight of ten main fuel-sector values lie within the published range, and six are less responsive than the middle estimate. Table 1 shows CPAT’s long-run elasticity for developing countries beside the published range. For industrial electricity, CPAT uses −0.44 where the median estimate is −0.69; for industrial gas, −0.75 against −1.05. Read against the published averages, CPAT understates more responses than it overstates.



Table 1: CPAT’s long-run price elasticities against the published evidence. The median excludes the figures CPAT was calibrated to. High-income values are 0.05–0.08 smaller in magnitude, except the two “too high” pairs. Source: CPAT legacy defaults (CPAT-AI project 2026); evidence from the meta-analyses and studies listed in the working paper, Table 1 and Appendix A.

The two failures come from stretching thin evidence across sectors. CPAT’s builders set targets for each sector by adding a sector adjustment, estimated over all fuels, to each fuel’s base value. Diesel in industry and gasoline in services have almost no studies of their own, and the services adjustment rests on 61 estimates. The result is −1.06 and −1.04, beyond every published estimate for either fuel. CPAT’s own panel estimation called the industrial diesel value “high” and found services no more responsive than households (working paper, comparison). Electricity in services, built the same way, sits at the edge of the range.
Gas looks more responsive in the evidence than in CPAT, but the gap is not a reason to change the default. Cross-country studies find gas use falls by more than 1.2 percent for each 1 percent price rise (Burke and Yang 2016). But in many developing countries gas use follows pipeline building, often a government decision, and part of the measured response is switching between fuels that CPAT models elsewhere or not at all (Huntington et al. 2019).


The published evidence itself overstates the response
Journals publish large, significant estimates more readily than small or wrong-signed ones, and this inflates the averages. For gasoline, correcting for this publication bias halves the long-run elasticity, from −0.69 to −0.31 (Havranek et al. 2012). In 32 countries that subsidize fuel, where CPAT is often used to study subsidy reform, the long-run elasticity is −0.25 (Arzaghi and Squalli 2015). CPAT’s −0.64 for road gasoline matches the uncorrected averages and is twice the corrected one. The same bias may affect other fuels; it has been measured carefully only for gasoline.
Tax increases may move demand more than other price increases, which pulls the other way. In Sweden, gasoline demand responded three times as much to the carbon tax as to equal market price changes (Andersson 2019). Publication bias and this tax effect point in opposite directions, and both are documented mainly for road fuels. So the right response is not to cut the defaults but to show a second case with road fuel elasticities halved beside every central result (working paper, the strongest objection).


The bigger problem is timing
CPAT applies the full long-run response in the year the price changes; in reality it takes a decade. People drive or heat less within a year or two, but they replace cars, boilers and machines only as these wear out: about 7 percent of the car fleet a year, and 1–2 percent of buildings (Black et al. 2022). CPAT’s documentation states that “all the effects take place over the course of one year”, and its developers list the missing short-run response as a known issue, noting that household electricity demand “is inelastic in the short term” (World Bank and International Monetary Fund 2022).
After one year about a fifth of CPAT’s response has happened; after five, about 60 percent. Figure 1 shows road gasoline and industrial coal. Five years after a permanent price rise, CPAT’s response is 45 to 72 percent larger than a gradual one across the main fuel-sector pairs, and between about 30 and 110 percent under other plausible adjustment speeds (working paper, timing).






Figure 1: The price response builds up over a decade, but CPAT applies it in year 1. Own-price elasticity at each horizon after a permanent price rise. CPAT (dashed) applies the whole response in year 1; the gradual response (solid) adjusts use at 30 percent a year and equipment at 6.7 percent a year; bands show alternative speeds. CPAT defaults for developing countries. Source: working paper, Figure 2.



Front-loading overstates early emission cuts and understates early revenue. A tax base that shrinks faster in the model than in the economy yields less modeled revenue in the first years, when budgets are set. For a fuel subsidy reform the error runs the other way on timing: the modeled fall in consumption, and the fiscal gain with it, arrive too early. Phasing a price in gradually, the use for which CPAT’s documentation says the tool is best suited, reduces the error but does not remove it.
CPAT also has almost no switching between fuels outside power. A carbon tax that makes coal dearer than gas cuts coal and gas each by their own elasticities; nothing moves industry from coal to gas or electricity. CPAT’s own panel study recommended adding substitution for specific fuels in specific sectors (working paper, structure).


Comparisons hold up better than levels
Errors that affect every policy and country alike largely cancel when policies are compared. The Total Effective Carbon Price measures a policy mix as the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much (Brief 6.1). It is a ratio of two cuts computed with the same elasticities, so a common error cancels. In the stylized economy of paper 6.1, replacing the central demand elasticities with CPAT’s raises the cut from a $30 tax by about a third, from 13.4 to 17.5 percent, but moves the Total Effective Carbon Price of a policy mix by only about a tenth, from $36.9 to $33.1 per tonne (working paper, emission cuts and the Total Effective Carbon Price).
So a CPAT ranking of policies or countries is more reliable than a CPAT forecast of tonnes or revenue. The same holds for the back-casts and model comparisons in Brief 5.3: CPAT is best used for ranges and comparisons, and least reliable for near-term levels.


What to do
Finance ministries and development-bank teams using CPAT results: treat near-term cuts as upper bounds. Report cuts and revenue for the first five years with a note that the model front-loads the response, and show a case with road fuel elasticities halved beside the central result. For decisions that hinge on road transport or household electricity, check the elasticities against national evidence.
CPAT’s maintainers: fix the two outliers and the timing. Bring industrial diesel, services gasoline and services electricity into the range of the evidence for those fuels, for example by using their transport or household values. Add separate adjustment speeds for use and for equipment, and report results by year after the reform by default. Rerun the documentation’s own calibration check, which reports road gasoline at −0.77 where the defaults give −0.64.
Everyone updating a policy model: run a fixed validation protocol at every update. Keep a register of verified estimates for each fuel and sector, apart from the model’s own calibration source; classify each default; test what the differences do to a standard scenario; back-cast against past price shocks such as subsidy reforms; and publish every change with its evidence (working paper, protocol).


Related papers in this series

No. 5.2: CPAT-AI, the transparent and testable rebuild of the tool.
No. 5.3: validating CPAT against data, history and other models.
No. 6.1: the Total Effective Carbon Price, the yardstick for comparing policy mixes (Stretton 2026).

title: 6. Modular Upgrades
text:
The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT) tells a finance ministry what a carbon price raises and what it cuts, but ministries keep asking questions its core cannot answer. What is a mix of standards, subsidies and feebates worth as a carbon price? What will the EU carbon border adjustment cost exporters? What will the clean capital cost, and should the budget pay for it? How can CPAT be linked to the other models ministries use? What does a climate program do to growth and debt? This section answers each with one upgrade that reads the rebuilt model’s outputs without changing its core: the Total Effective Carbon Price, the CBAM Policy Tool, a public investment extension, a common activity layer, and the Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool. Each states its method in a few equations so that a ministry can check it, and each peer review in October 2026 changed a result: the Egypt border charge, the cost of capital CPAT assumes, the island case, the ownership check and Kenya’s debt comparison.

title: 6. Modular Upgrades
section: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
The Total Effective Carbon Price
Countries cut emissions with taxes, subsidies, standards and mandates, yet the usual carbon-price measures add up explicit prices per tonne. A fuel standard or a revenue-neutral feebate scores zero, and a dollar on coal counts the same as a dollar on gasoline. The Total Effective Carbon Price is the single economy-wide carbon tax that would cut emissions as much as the actual policy mix. It can be computed from an energy balance, fuel prices and published elasticities. In a stylized economy it rates a mix at $37 per tonne in the long run and $28 after one year, where explicit prices show $21. Crediting, border recognition and country reviews can all use it.

title: 6. Modular Upgrades
text:
6.2 The CBAM Policy Tool
Measuring Exporters’ Exposure to the EU Carbon Border Adjustment and What Domestic Policy Can Do About It
Since January 2026 the EU has charged importers for the carbon in steel, aluminum, cement and fertilizers. Exporting governments can cut the bill in three ways: by getting plants to file verified emissions data, by cutting emissions, and by pricing carbon at home so the EU deducts it. The CBAM Policy Tool computes the bill product by product and year by year. Turkish hot-rolled steel owes €107 a tonne in 2026 and €252 at full phase-in. For Egypt, verified data would cut the charge on steel by about 90 percent, but barely move it on urea, the largest exposure. The right lever differs by product, so ministries should run the numbers before choosing.

title: 6. Modular Upgrades
text:
6.3 Public Investment in CPAT
Investment Needs and the Efficiency of Public Spending
Finance ministries use the Climate Policy Assessment Tool to see what a carbon price raises and cuts, but not what the clean capital it calls for costs to finance or whether the budget should pay. This brief proposes two extensions. The first prices investment needs at each country’s cost of capital and at a social rate: a typical clean asset that pays its way at 6 percent breaks even at 12.6 percent. The second tests each use of public money against the cost of raising tax and counts cash, debt and contract liabilities. Often the budget’s problem is cash and hidden liabilities, not value.

title: 6. Modular Upgrades
section: 6.4 Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
text:
6.4 Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
One Driver Layer So Four Climate Models Can Be Linked, With the Carbon-Price Response Counted Once
Finance ministries increasingly ask several climate models the same question, and the models disagree before any policy is applied, because each starts from different levels of activity: electricity used, distance traveled, vehicles on the road, tonnes of steel and cement made. This brief shows how four models used in climate-fiscal work (CPAT, SISEPUEDE, the CBAM Policy Tool and FTT) can share one set of drivers and one growth rule, so that their baselines agree. It sets out where a carbon price’s effect on demand must be counted, and only once, and why every link needs a check that cars stay inside total travel.

title: 6. Modular Upgrades
text:
6.5 The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
Financing and Efficiency, Not the Size of the Program, Decide What Climate Investment Does to Growth and Debt
Finance ministries weighing climate investment get the budget cost, the carbon tax revenue, the growth effect and the debt test from different teams and models. The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool runs all four in one open workbook for 186 countries. In a stylized run, how a program is financed and how well public money is spent move debt and growth more than the program’s size. For Kenya, a net zero program needs 0.5 percent of GDP a year from the budget; carbon pricing on a clean grid covers about 5 percent of it. Ministries should use the tool to compare financing packages, not to forecast debt.

title: Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
section: 3.1 CPAT: fuel use driven by total GDP and prices
text:
3.1 CPAT: fuel use driven by total GDP and prices
CPAT does not model activity directly; it models fuel use, with total GDP standing in for activity. For fuel \(f\) in sector \(s\), fuel use \(F\) in year \(t\) relative to the year before is
\[
\frac{F_{sf,t}}{F_{sf,t-1}} = \left(\frac{1}{1 + \alpha_{sf} + \alpha^{+}_{s,t}}\right)^{1 + \epsilon_{U}} \Psi_t \left(\frac{Y_t}{Y_{t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{Y} inc_t} \left(\frac{p_{sf,t}}{p_{sf,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{U}} \left(\frac{p_{sf,t} + sh_{sf,t}}{p_{sf,t-1} + sh_{sf,t-1}}\right)^{\epsilon_{F}(1 + \epsilon_{U})},
\tag{1}\]
where \(\alpha\) is an autonomous efficiency gain of 0.5 or 1 percent a year, \(\alpha^+\) any additional efficiency gain assigned to a policy, \(\Psi_t\) a demand shock (1 in normal years), \(Y\) total real GDP, \(\epsilon_Y\) the income elasticity, \(inc_t\) an income-level factor, \(p\) the retail price including taxes, \(\epsilon_U\) the usage elasticity (how hard existing equipment is used), \(\epsilon_F\) the efficiency elasticity (what equipment is bought) and \(sh\) the shadow price of non-price policies (CPAT Team 2024; CPAT-AI Project 2026b, equation M3.1). Paper 5.1 explains each term (Stretton 2026e). The equations here are those of the rebuilt model, which found 231 bugs in the legacy workbook, and of the corrected edition of the documentation published on 31 October 2026 (CPAT-AI Project 2026c, 2026a).
Income elasticities are set by fuel and sector and then bent by income level. The legacy table holds 32 income elasticities, for eight fuel groups and four sectors, the same for every income group; for electricity they are 0.8 in homes and industry, 1.1 in services and 1.2 in transport (CPAT-AI Project 2026b). The CPAT team chose them so that weighted averages stay close to the sectoral estimates of Burke and Csereklyei (2016), and multiplies them by a factor of income per person that it inferred from Gertler et al. (2016), who show that household purchases of energy-using assets rise nonlinearly with income (CPAT Team 2024). The factor is a quartic in log GDP per person, normalized by the aggregate elasticity of 0.74 and capped at a log of 10, about 22,000 dollars. Recomputed from its constants, it is 1.04 at 1,000 dollars, peaks at 1.17 near 2,250 dollars, is 1.15 at 3,000 and falls to 0.61 at the cap. So CPAT’s income elasticity of household electricity is 0.92 at 3,000 dollars per person and 0.48 in rich countries.
CPAT does not separate population from income per person. Because \(Y\) is total GDP, a country whose population grows fast while income per person stagnates gets the same fuel growth as one with the reverse (CPAT Team 2024). The CPAT-AI project tracks this as issue I71 (CPAT-AI Project 2026c). In the notation of this paper, CPAT sets the population exponent equal to the income elasticity for every fuel.
Power demand is built bottom-up from the same kind of equation. Electricity demand in each sector grows with GDP, the efficiency trend and last year’s blended residential and industrial electricity price, with the combined price elasticity \(\epsilon_U + \epsilon_F + \epsilon_U\epsilon_F\) (CPAT-AI Project 2026b, equation M4.1). For homes and industry in low- and middle-income countries the legacy values are \(-0.3\) and \(-0.2\), so the combined elasticity is \(-0.44\). Generation then adds net exports, losses, statistical differences and own use, each held at its base-year share of final demand (CPAT-AI Project 2026b).
Road transport is described three times, and the three do not agree by default. The default road model is equation 1 itself. An optional engineering fleet model, legacy CPAT’s “technoeconomic” road model, projects vehicles per 1,000 people along an S-shaped Gompertz curve in GDP per person, lets buyers choose electric vehicles by a logit on the total cost of ownership, and derives fuel use from vehicles, distance and fuel economy; the user switches it on per scenario (CPAT-AI Project 2026b). A third block, the co-benefits module, values congestion, accidents and road damage per vehicle-kilometer (CPAT Team 2024). That module takes its vehicle-kilometers from the fleet model whatever road model the user selects (CPAT-AI Project 2026c, no. I100). So in a default run, fuel use and emissions follow the fuel equation while the co-benefits follow the fleet model’s driving, and the change in driving that is valued need not match the modeled change in fuel use. Industry is driven by GDP, not tonnes, and no fuel substitutes for another within an industrial subsector (Stretton 2026e).

title: Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
section: 3.2 SISEPUEDE: physical activity driven by income, with no prices
text:
3.2 SISEPUEDE: physical activity driven by income, with no prices
SISEPUEDE counts physical activity and multiplies it by energy intensity. SISEPUEDE (SImulating SEctoral Pathways and Uncertainty Exploration for DEcarbonization; the IDB report writes it SiSePuede) is an open Python and Julia framework for emissions accounting by IPCC sector, built for exploring decarbonization strategies across many uncertain futures (Kalra et al. 2023; Syme et al. 2026). Every income-driven demand grows with a factor
\[
G_t(\varepsilon, x) = \prod_{s=0}^{t-1}\big(1 + \varepsilon_s\, g_s(x)\big),
\tag{2}\]
where \(g_s(x)\) is the growth rate of driver \(x\) in year \(s\) and \(\varepsilon_s\) the elasticity, which may vary by year (the code’s “standard” elasticity; a “log” form, \((1+g)^\varepsilon\), is also available) (Syme et al. 2026). Passenger-kilometers per person grow with GDP per person and are multiplied by population, in two categories (“private and public” travel and “regional” travel). Megatonne-kilometers of freight grow with total GDP. Household energy demand for heat and for appliances grows per household with GDP per person and is multiplied by the number of households. Production of each industry (metals, cement, chemicals and others) grows with total GDP. Electricity demand is the sum of the electricity used by the end-use sectors, grossed up for transmission losses and exports, and is passed to an embedded least-cost model, NemoMod, developed by the Stockholm Environment Institute (Syme et al. 2026). Mode shares, fuel shares and energy per unit are scenario inputs.
Prices never change demand in SISEPUEDE. No price elasticity appears anywhere in the code. Fuel prices enter the costs of fuel supply and the cost-benefit accounts, not demand. Electrification or mode shift happens because a scenario says so. That is a deliberate design for finding strategies that hold up across many uncertain futures (Kalra et al. 2023), but it means SISEPUEDE cannot say on its own what a carbon tax does to demand.
The public example shows how the elasticities are set. The repository’s example country (Costa Rica, from 2015) holds the passenger-travel elasticities at 1.12 for private and public travel and 2.64 for regional travel, and the freight elasticity at 1.0, through 2050. The industrial and household elasticities start from short calibrations and move in a straight line to 1.0 by 2050. In 2025 they are 0.62 for cement, 0.75 for metals, \(-0.25\) for chemicals and 0.08 for household heat (Syme et al. 2026). A negative elasticity for chemical output, and convergence of every material to an elasticity of 1, are the kind of values a common layer should replace.

title: Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
section: 3.3 The CBAM Policy Tool: output of covered goods
text:
3.3 The CBAM Policy Tool: output of covered goods
The CBAM Policy Tool grows output of each covered good from a recent base year and cuts it along a constant-elasticity curve when a domestic carbon price raises its cost. For product \(i\),
\[
Q_{i,t} = Q^{0}_{i,t}\big(1 + \delta_{i,t}\big)^{\eta_i}, \qquad \delta_{i,t} = \frac{(1-\theta)\,\tau_t\, e_i}{p_i},
\tag{3}\]
where \(Q^{0}\) grows with IMF growth projections scaled by an output elasticity, \(\delta\) is the carbon cost share, \(\tau\) the domestic carbon price, \(e_i\) emissions per tonne, \(\theta\) the share of the carbon cost rebated per unit of output, \(p_i\) the product price and \(\eta_i\) a long-run output elasticity; a partial-adjustment block scales the response for a price in force only a few years (Stretton 2026d). In the tool’s illustrative runs the author uses judgment values of \(-0.4\) for steel and nitrogen fertilizers, \(-0.5\) for primary aluminum and \(-0.1\) for clinker; the evidence on output elasticities of heavy industrial goods is thin, and a Brazilian estimate of \(-0.14\) for steel is one of few (Schmidt and Lima 2006). The tool covers goods at the product level (steel by process route, gray clinker, ammonia, urea, ammonium nitrate, primary aluminum), which is finer than either CPAT or SISEPUEDE.

title: Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
section: 3.4 FTT: technology shares of a demand taken as given
text:
3.4 FTT: technology shares of a demand taken as given
FTT decides how demand is met, not how much there is. In each FTT model, heterogeneous agents compare technologies pair by pair on a distribution of perceived costs, and shares move by logistic substitution at a pace set by lifetimes and the speed of capacity expansion; the result is the S-shaped diffusion seen in practice rather than a least-cost mix (Mercure 2012; Mercure et al. 2016; Future Technology Transformations developers 2026). Output of technology \(i\) is its share of total demand,
\[
G_{i,t} = S_{i,t}\, D_t,
\tag{4}\]
and \(D_t\) comes from outside. Inside the full E3ME-FTT model, the macroeconometric model E3ME supplies it. In the open standalone Python version, which runs power, cars, road freight and household heat for 71 countries and regions (an industrial heat module ships without baseline data), it comes from input files (Future Technology Transformations developers 2026; Knobloch et al. 2019). Power reads an electricity demand that equals total generation in the base year, so it includes losses and own use and is net of trade (checked for five regions in 2022). Cars read the fleet in use and kilometers per car. Freight reads vans and trucks in use by size, and computes tonne-kilometers from vehicles, kilometers per vehicle and load. Heat reads useful heat demand for homes. FTT never reads passenger-kilometers, and it derives tonne-kilometers rather than reading them.
FTT’s data end in different years and have gaps. Power data run to 2022 (generation), transport to 2022, heat to 2020 and freight to 2023 (Future Technology Transformations developers 2026). The car fleet input is zero in 2022 for 21 of the 71 regions, including Nigeria, South Africa, Pakistan and Kenya (checked at commit 896a3ce). The standalone package has no steel model; FTT:Steel runs inside E3ME-FTT (Vercoulen et al. 2023). In policy runs FTT adds to power demand the change in each sector’s electricity use against its own baseline run (Future Technology Transformations developers 2026).

title: Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
text:
5.1 The rule
Each activity grows with population and income per person and responds to the cost of the energy service it provides.
\[
A_{j,t} = A_{j,0}\left(\frac{P_t}{P_0}\right)^{\beta_j}\left(\frac{y_t}{y_0}\right)^{\varepsilon_j}\left(\frac{c_{j,t}}{c^{\mathrm{base}}_{j,t}}\right)^{\eta_j},
\tag{5}\]
where \(A_{j,t}\) is activity \(j\) in year \(t\), \(P_t\) population, \(y_t\) real GDP per person, \(c_{j,t}\) the cost of the energy service and \(c^{\mathrm{base}}_{j,t}\) its baseline value. The population exponent \(\beta_j\) is 1 for activities that follow people (travel, households, cars) and equal to \(\varepsilon_j\) for those that follow the economy (freight, industrial output), because total GDP is population times income per person; kilometers per car, a per-vehicle activity, has \(\beta_j = 0\). \(\varepsilon_j\) is the income elasticity and \(\eta_j\) the price elasticity. In the baseline the last term equals 1, so the income and population terms describe the baseline alone.
The cost of the energy service is the price of energy divided by the efficiency of the equipment. For a service delivered by fuel \(f\) with price \(p_f\), including taxes and any carbon price, and equipment efficiency \(e_f\) (kilometers per unit of energy, or useful heat per unit of fuel), \(c_j = \sum_f s_f\, p_f / e_f\), where \(s_f\) is the share of the service delivered by fuel \(f\). For electricity it is the electricity price; for covered goods, the product price plus the net carbon cost per tonne. CPAT supplies the prices; FTT’s technology mix in the previous year supplies the efficiency, which avoids a loop. equation 5 is the constant-elasticity form; SISEPUEDE’s compounding in equation 2 differs from it by second-order terms, \(\ln(1+\varepsilon g) - \varepsilon\ln(1+g)\), about 0.005 percentage points a year at an elasticity of 1.2 and growth of 2 percent.

text:
5.2 One parameter set
Table 2 sets one value for each parameter, taken from the evidence where it is good and stated as an assumption where it is not.



Table 2: One parameter set for the common layer. Income elasticities are with respect to GDP per person; the electricity values are CPAT’s, with respect to total GDP. Price elasticities are long-run, with respect to the cost of the energy service. “Author’s assumption” marks a value chosen for the illustration where no public estimate fits; the CBAM Policy Tool’s values are the author’s judgment. Car numbers: the straight line approximates CPAT’s Gompertz curve with a saturation of 800 vehicles per 1,000, whose elasticity peaks at 2.2 near $4,350 per person and 90 vehicles per 1,000; the line is within 0.25 of it between 30 and 750 vehicles per 1,000. The travel and car values rest on the best evidence available. Total mobility rises “nearly in proportion with income” because people spend a roughly fixed share of income and a roughly fixed amount of time on travel (Schäfer and Victor 2000), so the layer uses an income elasticity of 1 for passenger-kilometers per person; SISEPUEDE’s example values of 1.12 and 2.64, held to 2050 with no ceiling, would let regional travel grow without bound. Vehicle ownership rises about twice as fast as income at low and middle incomes and the elasticity falls toward zero near saturation (Dargay and Gately 1999), at a saturation level that depends on urbanization and density (Dargay et al. 2007); CPAT’s fleet model draws the same shape. A sustained 10 percent rise in the real price of fuel cuts traffic by about 3 percent and vehicle ownership by about 2.5 percent in the long run Litman (2026), so the response of kilometers per vehicle is about \(-0.05\); the evidence is mostly from high-income countries.
The freight values come from one careful synthesis. Jong et al. (2010) reconcile a wide range of European estimates into a consistent set of best-guess long-run elasticities: a fuel-price elasticity of \(-0.1\) for road freight tonne-kilometers and \(-0.2\) for vehicle-kilometers, the difference being better loading and logistics. Because FTT holds kilometers per vehicle and load fixed, the layer passes the vehicle-kilometer response to vans and trucks in use.
The household and industrial values are assumptions, and the layer says so. SISEPUEDE’s own values are short country calibrations that converge to 1 by 2050, and the public example shows how noisy they are (Section 3.2). The layer instead uses round values that let material intensity fall as incomes rise, in line with projections in which steel and cement demand rise quickly for decades and then stabilize (Ruijven et al. 2016). The household heat price elasticity of \(-0.2\) sits inside the bound of Sorrell et al. (2009), who conclude that direct rebound for household energy services in OECD countries should generally be below 30 percent, and below CPAT’s residential usage elasticities of \(-0.3\) to \(-0.5\); a ministry should test both ends. Heavy-industry output elasticities are judgment values with little empirical support (Schmidt and Lima 2006).

title: Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
text:
5.3 Three propositions
Proposition 1 (the population exponent). Replacing \(\beta_j = \varepsilon_j\) by \(\beta_j = 1\) changes the growth of activity \(j\) by \((1 - \varepsilon_j)\, n\) a year in logs, where \(n\) is population growth. The choice matters only when \(\varepsilon_j \neq 1\) and population grows.
The models choose \(\beta_j = \varepsilon_j\) for every activity driven by total GDP, and CPAT for every fuel. Cross-country studies that separate population from income per person find population elasticities of emissions and energy near one in cross-sections, but widely varying ones over time; the main review cites the argument that, without indirect effects, population acts only as a scale factor with an elasticity of one (Liddle 2014). With population growing 1 percent a year, setting \(\beta_j = 1\) adds 0.4 percentage points a year to cement, 0.1 to fertilizers and 0.08 to household electricity, and takes 0.2 a year from steel. Over ten years that is 4 percent more cement (Table 3). The layer keeps the models’ choice for industrial output, which follows the economy, and uses \(\beta_j = 1\) for electricity used by households.
Proposition 2 (one price response per activity). If the layer applies \(\eta_j\) to activity supplied to a model that also applies its own elasticity \(\eta^m_j\) to the same activity or to fuel use that moves with it, the total log response to a cost change is \((\eta_j + \eta^m_j)\,\Delta \ln c\). Each activity’s response must therefore sit in exactly one model.
The proof is one line (Appendix A). The rule that follows is mechanical. Apply the price term in the layer only for SISEPUEDE and FTT, which have none. Do not apply it for CPAT or the CBAM Policy Tool, which have their own. The case that is easy to miss is CPAT’s fleet model: its usage margin is itself an activity response, because it moves kilometers per vehicle with the cost per kilometer, so feeding it price-adjusted vehicle numbers or distances counts the response twice even when the fuel equation is switched off. When the layer feeds CPAT’s road transport, it should pass the baseline only, and the fleet model should also be the selected road model, so that fuel use, emissions and co-benefits rest on one driving response (CPAT-AI Project 2026c, no. I100). The fleet model’s own distance response is the road-gasoline usage elasticity of \(-0.4\) (CPAT-AI Project 2026b), about eight times the per-vehicle response of \(-0.05\) implied by the review evidence; paper 5.4 should test it (Stretton 2026a).
Proposition 3 (the vehicle chain needs a check). Let cars grow with income elasticity \(\varepsilon_K\), kilometers per car with \(\varepsilon_k\) and population exponent 0, and passenger-kilometers with \(\varepsilon_T\), cars and passenger-kilometers with population exponent 1, and occupancy fixed. If \(\varepsilon_K + \varepsilon_k > \varepsilon_T\) and income per person grows without bound, car passenger-kilometers eventually exceed total passenger-kilometers.
The car share of travel grows by the factor \((y_t/y_0)^{\varepsilon_K + \varepsilon_k - \varepsilon_T}\), which is unbounded (Appendix A). With the values in Table 2 held fixed, the exponent is \(2.0 + 0.1 - 1.0 = 1.1\), and with income growing 2 percent a year a car share that starts at 30 percent of passenger-kilometers reaches 100 percent in year 56; one that starts at 50 percent, in year 32. A saturating ownership curve does not remove the problem. Recomputed with CPAT’s Gompertz curve (saturation 800 vehicles per 1,000, starting at 3,000 dollars per person and 42 vehicles per 1,000), car travel still overtakes total travel in year 54 from a 30 percent share, by which time ownership is 363 per 1,000, and in year 29 from a 50 percent share. Ownership can rise from tens to hundreds of vehicles per 1,000 while total travel grows a few-fold. What keeps car travel inside total travel in practice is that kilometers per car and occupancy fall as ownership rises: in high-income countries ownership responds to income more than traffic does Litman (2026). The layer therefore checks each year that cars times kilometers per car times occupancy (about 1.7 people per car, an assumption) stay below a share of total passenger-kilometers, and where they do not, it lowers kilometers per car.
crumbs: 6.4 Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT

title: Activity Levels Across CPAT, SISEPUEDE, CBAM and FTT
text:
5.4 Feeding the four models
The layer feeds each model in its own unit, spliced onto its own last data point. For a model input \(X_m\) whose last data year is \(b\),
\[
X_{m,t} = X_{m,b}\,\frac{A_{j,t}}{A_{j,b}},
\tag{6}\]
so the model keeps its own level and takes the layer’s growth. Each FTT input has its own last data year (2020 for heat, 2022 for power and transport, 2023 for freight), and equation 6 handles each separately. Because FTT adds to power demand the change in each sector’s electricity use against its own baseline run, the baseline power input and the baseline sector runs must all come from the same layer run. SISEPUEDE takes the layer’s base-year levels and elasticities in place of its own, and the price term through its demand scalars, inputs that scale transport demand, industrial energy demand and household heat and appliance energy demand (Syme et al. 2026). The CBAM Policy Tool takes its base-year output and price response from its own data and passes product-level output to the layer for the industrial rows. CPAT takes the layer as a cross-check on its baseline and, if its road transport is unified, as the baseline driver of its fleet model.
Two drivers and one base year make the four baselines comparable. Use the IMF World Economic Outlook for GDP (International Monetary Fund 2026) and the United Nations World Population Prospects for population (United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division 2024), for every model. Set base-year levels from one recent year: energy balances for electricity, national data or SISEPUEDE’s calibrated inputs for travel and freight, vehicle registrations for cars and trucks, and the CBAM Policy Tool’s latest output for covered goods. SISEPUEDE’s example inputs start in 2015 and must be rolled forward with observed GDP and population.
