title: The CBAM Policy Tool
text: Working paper, version 0.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.2. Companion paper to the Climate Fiscal AI Tools.1

title: The CBAM Policy Tool
section: 5.1 Embedded emissions from the bottom up
text:
5.1 Embedded emissions from the bottom up
Embedded emissions per tonne are built from energy use, process chemistry and electricity, in the same components the EU uses. For product \(i\) the tool computes direct emissions per tonne as \[
e_i^{\mathrm{dir}} = \sum_k h^{c}_{ik}\,\phi_k + \sum_k h^{p}_{ik}\,\phi_k + e^{np}_i + e^{no}_i ,
\tag{1}\] where \(h^{c}_{ik}\) is fuel \(k\) burned for heat (GJ per tonne), \(h^{p}_{ik}\) fuel \(k\) used as a reductant or feedstock, such as natural gas in direct reduction of iron or in an ammonia reformer, \(\phi_k\) the fuel’s CO₂ emission factor (for example 56.1 kg per GJ for natural gas and 74.1 for gas oil (IPCC 2006)), \(e^{np}_i\) non-fuel process CO₂ (limestone calcination in clinker, anode consumption in aluminum) and \(e^{no}_i\) non-CO₂ gases in CO₂ equivalents (nitrous oxide from nitric acid, perfluorocarbons from smelting). Indirect emissions are electricity use times the grid emission factor, \(e^{\mathrm{ind}}_i = u_i\,g\). The CBAM-relevant intensity is \(e_i = e^{\mathrm{dir}}_i\) for steel and aluminum and \(e^{\mathrm{dir}}_i + e^{\mathrm{ind}}_i\) for cement and fertilizers.
Precursors are integrated into the goods made from them, and CO₂ used in a product counts as emitted unless it stays bound. Urea and ammonium nitrate are made from ammonia, which the EU treats as a precursor whose emissions are embedded in the downstream good (European Commission 2025b). A tonne of urea contains 0.567 tonnes of ammonia from its molecular formula; a tonne of ammonium nitrate embeds 0.425 tonnes, half directly and half through nitric acid, itself a precursor made from ammonia. Each is multiplied by ammonia’s own intensity, and only net merchant ammonia is counted as standalone ammonia. The CO₂ that urea synthesis takes up is not deducted: the EU’s monitoring rules let CO₂ used in a product count as not emitted only where it is “permanently chemically bound so that it does not enter the atmosphere under normal use” (European Commission 2025b, Annex II point B.8.2), and urea releases it when applied to soil (De Klein et al. 2006, sec. 11.4). The Commission’s default for Egyptian urea, 1.32 tCO₂ per tonne direct, is consistent with this accounting: 0.567 times Egypt’s ammonia default of 1.96, plus the urea plant’s own fuel (European Commission 2026b).
The bottom-up intensity is the tool’s estimate of what verified data would show for a plant at the technology average. Comparing it with the default value tells a ministry where filing data pays. Where the estimate is below the marked-up default, producers gain from verification; where it is above, the default is a subsidy to the dirtiest plants and the producer keeps it. A verified declaration follows the installation’s own monitoring under the EU rules, so the estimate is a guide to where to look, not a substitute (Section 10).

title: The CBAM Policy Tool
text:
5.2 The charge per tonne
The charge per tonne is the certificate price times embedded emissions above the free-allocation adjustment, less any deducted carbon price. Let \(e_i\) be the declared embedded emissions, \(\bar e_{c,i}\) the country default before mark-up and \(m_t\) the mark-up, so that \(e_i = (1+m_t)\bar e_{c,i}\) under default values. Let \(B_i\) be the CBAM benchmark for the product’s route, \(f_t\) the CBAM factor in year \(t\) (0.975 in 2026, zero from 2034), \(P_t\) the certificate price and \(\tau^d\) the domestic carbon price effectively paid per tonne of CO₂. The charge per tonne of product is \[
C_{it} = \max\Big\{0,\; P_t\big[e_i - f_t B_i\big]^{+} - \tau^d e_i\Big\}.
\tag{2}\] The deduction \(\tau^d e_i\) is the form the Commission’s draft implementing regulation gives: the reduction in certificates equals the effective carbon price per tonne of good divided by the certificate reference price, with no adjustment for free allocation (European Commission 2026c, Art. 6). The draft was in the Commission’s adoption workflow, not adopted, on 31 October 2026; the floor at zero is this paper’s assumption. Two simplifications affect only 2026–2033: the free-allocation adjustment in Implementing Regulation 2025/2620 also multiplies by a cross-sectoral correction factor, set to 1 here; and a declarant using actual data builds the adjustment from process benchmarks and the free allocation embedded in its precursors, which the example approximates with the default benchmark (European Commission 2025d, Annex points 3–4).
Emissions above the benchmark are charged in full from the first year. Because \(f_t B_i\) is at most the benchmark, the term \(P_t(e_i - f_t B_i)\) is at least \(P_t(e_i - B_i)\) in every year. For a good whose embedded emissions are far above the benchmark, most of the charge applies in 2026 and the phase-in adds only the benchmark’s share. For a good close to the benchmark the charge starts near zero and rises with \(1-f_t\). The phase-in therefore protects efficient exporters, not inefficient ones.
The capture price is the domestic carbon price that would reduce the charge to zero. Setting \(C_{it} = 0\) in equation 2 gives \[
\tau^{d*}_{it} = P_t\,\frac{\big[e_i - f_t B_i\big]^{+}}{e_i}.
\tag{3}\] At full phase-in the capture price equals the certificate price. Before 2034 it is lower, because part of the embedded emissions is covered by the free-allocation adjustment. A domestic price at \(\tau^{d*}\) moves the whole charge from the EU budget to the exporter’s treasury while leaving EU buyers’ costs unchanged; it also raises revenue on all other sales the price covers, which for an exporter selling most of its output at home or outside the EU is the larger sum (Stretton 2026g).

title: The CBAM Policy Tool
section: 5.3 A domestic carbon price: abatement and deduction
text:
5.3 A domestic carbon price: abatement and deduction
In the policy version, a domestic carbon price changes output, emissions per tonne and the deduction. For product \(i\) with price \(p_i\) and carbon cost share \(\delta_i = (1-\theta)\tau\,e_i/p_i\), where \(\theta\) is the share of the carbon cost rebated per unit of output, output falls along a constant-elasticity curve, \(Q_i = Q^0_i(1+\delta_i)^{\varepsilon_i}\), with small elasticities \(\varepsilon_i\) for traded goods. Fuel emissions per tonne fall with a semi-elasticity, \(e^{f}_i = e^{f0}_i\exp(-\beta^{f}\tau)\), and process emissions per tonne with product-specific semi-elasticities \(\beta^{p}_i\). The fuel response is calibrated to the industrial fuel response of the Climate Policy Assessment Tool, net of its output effect, which links the tool to the elasticities checked in paper 5.4 (Stretton 2026b, 2026a); the process semi-elasticities are the tool’s assumptions. A partial-adjustment block scales the long-run responses for a price that has been in force only a few years.
The fall in the charge splits into abatement and deduction. At full phase-in, without rebates and with the domestic price covering all embedded emissions, equation 2 gives \(C = (P - \tau^d)e\). If the domestic price cuts the export-weighted intensity by a fraction \(r\), the proportional change in the charge is \[
\frac{\Delta C}{C^0} = -\,r \;-\; (1-r)\,\frac{\tau^d}{P}.
\tag{4}\] The first term is cleaner production; the second is the deduction. With \(\tau^d = €20\), \(P = €80\) and an intensity cut of 10 percent, the charge falls by 32.5 percent, of which 22.5 points come from the deduction. For a modest domestic price, the deduction does more for the border charge than abatement does. With a full output-based rebate (\(\theta = 1\)), the marginal incentive survives but, under the draft rules on compensation, the deduction disappears, so only the first term remains (Stretton 2026c). An abatement fund financed by the price keeps the deduction if it meets the draft’s four conditions for revenue-financed subsidies (European Commission 2026c, Art. 8(2)) and adds abatement.

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text: Working paper, version 0.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. Companion paper to the Climate Fiscal AI Tools. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.5.1

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
4.1 Investment needs and who pays
The investment model estimates, for each country and year to 2050, what a net zero path needs and who pays for it. It is a stock-and-flow model built to CPAT conventions: it uses CPAT’s energy data and its activity equation (Stretton 2026e), projected with income elasticities and autonomous efficiency improvement at real 2024 prices, and builds investment bottom up for road transport, buildings, industry and power, with spending lines for non-CO₂ gases, land use and other energy emissions. Paper 6.3 treats investment needs and the efficiency of public spending in depth, with a different method that shares a global estimate of all climate investment among countries (Stretton 2026d); the two answer different questions and their country totals should not be compared. Here what matters is the investment model’s output: an investment path in two scenarios and its split by payer.
Every investment line is split into five payer types, and the split decides the fiscal cost. The types run from pure public (P1, repaid by taxes: public buildings, access grids, land use), through regulated utility (P2, repaid by tariffs), contracted revenue (P3, repaid under a long-term contract with a public or regulated buyer), and viability gap (P4, market revenue plus a public top-up), to pure private (P5). The starting split of power investment comes from the country’s power market structure, coded from the power sector reform data of Urpelainen and Yang (2019), which end in 2013, and updated where they are out of date. Three pressure indices then move investment toward the budget: one for poor utility cost recovery, one for a high cost of capital, one for large explicit fossil fuel subsidies. The direct budget need in year \(t\) is
\[
N_t = I^{P1}_t + \gamma \, I^{P4}_t,
\tag{1}\]
with \(\gamma = 0.3\) the public share of the viability gap, an assumption. The tool adds two wider measures: the need adjusted for public investment efficiency, \(N_t / (1 - \epsilon)\), where the efficiency gap \(\epsilon\) comes from the country’s PEFA scores on public investment management where they exist and from income-group averages otherwise; and the need including regulated-utility investment, which becomes a contingent liability wherever tariffs do not recover costs. The IMF puts the average efficiency gap at around 30 percent (International Monetary Fund 2015).
Only the incremental need enters the macro models, split into capital and spending. The program is the net zero need less the current-trends need. Its capital part builds public capital in the macro models; its spending part (land use, non-CO₂ abatement and other annual outlays) is financed the same way but builds nothing. In many low-income countries most of the budget need is spending, not capital, and this matters for growth: spending raises debt without raising future output.

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
4.2 Carbon pricing under feasibility limits
The pricing screen asks how much abatement pricing can deliver without breaching limits on political cost. It covers the power sector only, and compares a carbon tax, a feebate (a charge on generation above a benchmark emissions intensity and a rebate below it, equivalent in this sector to output-based allocation or a tradable performance standard) and a mix of the two. The distinction that drives the screen is between the marginal and the average price. Fuel switching responds to the marginal price, which a tax and a feebate raise equally. Electricity demand responds to the average tariff, which only the tax raises, because a feebate’s charges and rebates cancel at the benchmark (Stretton 2026b). A feebate is a price-based instrument whose carbon-price equivalent is its rate at the margin, in the sense of the Total Effective Carbon Price (Stretton 2026c).
Abatement has a substitution part and a demand part. With a tax \(\tau_t\) and a feebate rate \(\tau_f\) in US dollars per tonne of CO₂,
\[
A^{\text{sub}} = s_{\max}\left(1 - e^{-(\tau_t + \tau_f)/\tau_{s}}\right), \qquad
\Delta p = \frac{\phi \, e_{\text{avg}} \, \tau_t}{p_{\text{res}}}, \qquad
A^{\text{dem}} = |\varepsilon| \, \Delta p,
\tag{2}\]
and total abatement as a share of baseline fossil power emissions is \(E = 1 - (1 - A^{\text{sub}})(1 - A^{\text{dem}})\). Here \(s_{\max}\) is the largest share of fossil output that cleaner supply can displace by about 2030, \(\tau_s\) is the price at which switching is well under way (at \(\tau_s\) it has reached 63 percent of its maximum; calibrated from coal and gas prices and heat rates), \(\phi\) is the pass-through of carbon costs to tariffs (set by power market structure), \(e_{\text{avg}}\) is the average grid emissions intensity, \(p_{\text{res}}\) is the residential tariff and \(\varepsilon\) is the price elasticity of electricity demand. A feebate gets the same substitution as a tax at the same rate, with no tariff rise.
Three limits stand in for political feasibility. The first is the visible price: the first-year rise in the residential tariff, \(F_1 = \Delta p / n\) for a phase-in over \(n\) years. The second is the household loss: the net burden on the bottom 40 percent as a share of their consumption, \(F_2 = b_{40}\,\Delta p\,(1 - \min(\rho / (\phi \, r \, q_{40}), 1))\), where \(b_{40}\) is their electricity budget share, \(\rho\) the share of revenue rebated to them, \(r\) the residential share of sales and \(q_{40}\) their share of residential use; \(\phi r q_{40}\) is the share of revenue they pay, so a rebate of that share leaves them whole. The third is the concentrated loser: the net payment by coal and oil generators as a share of their revenue,
\[
F_3 = \frac{\tau_t \, e_{\text{hi}} (1 - \phi) + \tau_f (e_{\text{hi}} - e_{\text{avg}})}{p_{\text{w}}},
\tag{3}\]
where \(e_{\text{hi}}\) is their emissions intensity and \(p_{\text{w}}\) the wholesale price. The first term is the tax cost they do not recover; the second is the feebate’s net transfer away from high emitters. The first term assumes each generator recovers the share \(\phi\) of its own carbon cost, as under a cost-plus contract. If instead every generator receives the same price increase, the grid-average pass-through \(\phi e_{\text{avg}} \tau_t\), the unrecovered cost is \(\tau_t(e_{\text{hi}} - \phi e_{\text{avg}})\), larger, and the limit binds sooner (Section 7). The screen searches tax and feebate rates from 0 to 200 US dollars per tonne for the mix with the most abatement that satisfies all three limits, and reports which limit binds. The default limits (10 percent for \(F_1\), 0.5 percent for \(F_2\), 15 percent for \(F_3\)) are placeholders, not recommendations. Choosing them is a political judgment; the tool’s job is to show what each choice costs in abatement and revenue.
Revenue links pricing to the budget. Carbon tax revenue is the tax rate times fossil power emissions, as a share of GDP; a feebate raises nothing. The tool can earmark pricing revenue for the climate program, which lowers its debt financing. The financing gap the dashboard reports is the incremental budget need less feasible pricing revenue.

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
5.1 Why simplified models
The parent models are the right tools, but they cannot be run in one pass for every country. GIMF and DIGNAD need country calibrations that take weeks, run in specialist software and are maintained by small teams. A ministry economist cannot open them, change an assumption and watch the debt path move. The lite models keep the mechanisms that matter for a financed public investment program (households that do not fully discount future taxes, productive public capital, an efficiency wedge, a debt-elastic borrowing premium, a fiscal rule) and drop the rest. They are written in Python, solved under perfect foresight with a sparse Newton solver, and calibrated from public data with income-group defaults where data are missing. Table 2 sets out what each keeps and drops.

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
5.2 GIMF-lite
GIMF-lite keeps the feature of GIMF that matters most for debt-financed investment: households do not fully discount future taxes. Each household survives each year with probability \(\theta\), so its planning horizon is \(1/(1-\theta)\), 20 years at \(\theta = 0.95\), and its labor income declines over its life at rate \(\chi\) (Blanchard 1985; Kumhof et al. 2010). Human wealth is then discounted at a rate above the government’s borrowing rate:
\[
HW_t = (1-\psi)\left[(1-\tau_L) w_t l_t + tr_t\right] + \frac{\theta\chi}{1+r_t} HW_{t+1},
\tag{4}\]
and these households consume a fixed share of financial plus human wealth. A share \(\psi\) of households are liquidity constrained and spend current income. Because \(\theta\chi < 1\), government debt is net wealth to households alive today: Ricardian equivalence fails, and in the long run higher public debt crowds out private capital and net foreign assets.
Public capital raises output, with an efficiency wedge. Production is \(y_t = A\,(1+sav_t)\,KG_{t-1}^{\alpha_G}\,K_{t-1}^{\alpha}\,l_t^{1-\alpha}\), and public capital accumulates as \(KG_t = (1-\delta_G)KG_{t-1} + s\,IG_t\), where only a share \(s\) of each dollar of public investment becomes capital. The output elasticity \(\alpha_G\) is calibrated from an assumed return on public capital; since \(\alpha_G\) equals the return times the ratio of public capital to output, a return of 15 percent with public capital of two-thirds of GDP gives an elasticity of 0.10, close to the meta-analytic average of 0.106 and the long-run estimate of 0.12 for core public capital (Bom and Ligthart 2014). The climate program enters as extra public investment, extra spending that builds no capital, extra private investment and net energy cost savings (\(sav_t\), entered as a value-added gain). A fiscal rule sets the path of the debt ratio, letting a share of the program be debt financed and closing the rest, including interest, with transfers or the labor tax:
\[
B_t - B_{t-1} = d\,(IG^{x}_t + G^{x}_t - R^{x}_t) - \lambda_B (B_{t-1} - \bar{B}),
\tag{5}\]
where \(B\) is debt as a share of GDP, \(IG^{x}\), \(G^{x}\) and \(R^{x}\) are the program’s extra public investment, extra spending and earmarked revenue, \(d\) is the debt-financed share and \(\lambda_B\) is the speed of return to the debt target \(\bar B\).

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
5.3 DIGNAD-lite, DIGNAR-lite and DIGNAD-R
DIGNAD-lite is the model for low-income and concessional borrowers. It keeps DIGNAD’s split between savers, who borrow abroad at a debt-elastic premium, and hand-to-mouth households, who spend current income. It has two public capital stocks: standard capital and adaptation capital, which costs more and is destroyed less by disasters (Marto et al. 2018). The government borrows concessionally at a low fixed rate and commercially at \(r^c_t = r^{*} + \eta\,e^{(d^c_t - \bar d)}\), and a fiscal rule raises the consumption tax and cuts transfers as commercial debt rises. Programs are financed in stated shares of grants, concessional loans and commercial debt, the choice that matters most for low-income countries (Buffie et al. 2012).
DIGNAR-lite adds resource rents for fossil exporters. Rents are an endowment; the government takes a share and savers the rest (Melina et al. 2016). A permanent fall in rents on a global net zero path is a permanent fiscal and income shock, so the model solves for the steady state at the final rent level and imposes a firmer fiscal rule. In the integrated run, rents start at the country’s latest fossil rents and fall 80 percent by 2050, with a government take of 50 percent; both are assumptions.
DIGNAD-R puts DIGNAD-lite into spreadsheet formulas so the user can see what moves. It makes the equations recursive, so they run in Excel without a solver and respond at once to the assumptions: disaster size, grant and concessional shares, the pricing earmark, the fiscal rule. It treats every country as a DIGNAD-type economy, has one fiscal instrument and leaves out energy savings, so for upper-middle and high-income countries it sits below the integrated run. The tool shows both on purpose: read the integrated run for the number and DIGNAD-R for the mechanism.

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
5.4 LIC-DSF-lite
The debt test follows the structure of the Bank-Fund framework. Debt-carrying capacity comes from the Composite Indicator, a weighted sum of 10-year averages (five years of history, five of projection) of the country’s CPIA score, real growth, import cover of reserves and its square, remittances and world growth. Capacity is weak below 2.69, medium from 2.69 to 3.05 and strong above 3.05. Four external indicators are compared with thresholds that depend on capacity: the present value of external public debt to GDP (30, 40 and 55 percent for weak, medium and strong) and to exports (140, 180, 240), and external debt service to exports (10, 15, 21) and to revenue (14, 18, 23). The present value of total public debt is compared with a benchmark of 35, 55 or 70 percent of GDP (International Monetary Fund and World Bank 2018, Tables 5–7). The 2018 guidance note remains in force, as modified by a 2024 supplement (International Monetary Fund and World Bank 2024).
Debt follows the standard dynamics, with a valuation term for foreign-currency debt. With \(d_t\) public debt as a share of GDP, \(i\) the nominal interest rate, \(g\) real growth, \(\pi\) the change in the GDP deflator, \(pb_t\) the primary balance and \(\alpha\) the share of debt in foreign currency, which changes value with the depreciation rate \(\varepsilon_t\),
\[
d_t = \frac{(1 + i_t)(1 + \alpha\,\varepsilon_t)}{(1+g_t)(1+\pi_t)}\, d_{t-1} - pb_t + sfa_t,
\tag{6}\]
where \(sfa_t\) collects other stock-flow adjustments. With \(\alpha\varepsilon_t = 0\) this is the textbook recursion \(d_t = (1+\lambda_t)d_{t-1} - pb_t\) with \(1+\lambda_t = (1+i_t)/((1+g_t)(1+\pi_t))\) (Escolano 2010). New borrowing is on the terms of the country’s creditor mix. The lite version applies the standard stress tests and a disaster test and rates risk mechanically: a breach in the baseline is high risk, a breach only under stress is moderate, no breach is low. It then shifts the baseline by the growth and primary-balance deviations the macro model produces, so the rating before and with the program can be compared. Because the lite macro models hold the real exchange rate fixed, the program’s effect on the valuation term is zero by construction.

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
9.1 What the tool is not
The lite models are not their parents. GIMF-lite has one country and one good, so it cannot show spillovers, the terms-of-trade effect of lower fuel imports, or the zero lower bound. DIGNAD-lite has no real exchange rate and no domestic debt. Neither has yet been benchmarked against its parent’s published simulations (Section 6). The calibrations are illustrative: four inputs to the live model (public investment, the return on public capital, the hand-to-mouth share and grants) are income-group defaults, not country estimates. A result from the tool is a scenario to be argued with, not a forecast, and it does not substitute for a calibrated GIMF or DIGNAD run, an IMF or World Bank debt sustainability analysis, or a CPAT run.
The debt test is simplified. Exports and imports, the denominators of two of the four external indicators and, through reserve cover, an input to the Composite Indicator, are assumptions because the build has no country trade series yet; Kenya shows how much that matters. Debt-carrying capacity uses the Composite Indicator only where a CPIA score exists and defaults to medium elsewhere. The coefficients, cut-offs and thresholds follow the 2018 guidance note (International Monetary Fund and World Bank 2018) and should be kept in line with its 2024 supplement (International Monetary Fund and World Bank 2024). There are no realism tools, no judgment, no market financing module and, because the real exchange rate is fixed, no depreciation channel from the macro models.
The energy side has its own simplifications. The investment model has no price response, and power follows target dates rather than least cost. The payer typology rests on power market codes that end in 2013 for most countries, updated by judgment, and the public share of the viability gap is an assumption. The pricing screen covers power only, has no dynamics, ignores indirect effects on households, and its priors (heat rates, displaceable share, pass-through, budget shares) should be replaced by CPAT runs (CPAT Team 2023) or country data before any number is quoted. Energy savings enter only GIMF-lite; pricing revenue covers power only; and the tariff rise is not fed back into the macro models.
The two macro families disagree most on the channels that matter most. Energy savings and private investment drive most of GIMF-lite’s long-run gain and are absent from DIGNAD-lite. Which channels to credit is an open decision, and the tool shows both answers rather than hiding the choice.

title: The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool
text:
9.2 How to use it
Use the tool to compare packages for one country, not to forecast or rank countries. The baseline is a fixed reference, so the useful outputs are differences: debt with and without the program, with and without earmarked pricing revenue, under concessional or commercial financing, at higher or lower efficiency. A ministry economist sets the country, switches the program on, tries the financing and pricing levers, and reads the change in the debt path and the risk rating. The highlighted input cells show which assumptions are doing the work.
Check the starting point against the published analysis before reading the change. Where an IMF-World Bank debt sustainability analysis exists, its capacity rating, its Composite Indicator and its debt path are the reference; the tool’s own debt test is a consistency check on its inputs, as Kenya shows.
Treat a large cross-check gap as a finding. Where the two model families disagree, the honest statement is that the answer depends on whether energy savings, private investment and employment respond, and the next step is evidence on those, not a choice of model.
Replace defaults with country data in order of influence. The stylized run suggests the order: investment efficiency and the return on public capital first, then the financing mix, then the trade data behind the debt test, then the feasibility limits and the pricing priors. Each replacement is one input cell, and the build records the source of every input.

text:
Footnotes


The lite models are simplified re-implementations written from the published descriptions of the parent models cited in the text; they are not endorsed by, and do not reproduce, the IMF or World Bank tools. The stylized run uses the tool’s default illustrative calibrations. The Kenya run reports illustrative results from the tool, with income-group defaults where country data are missing; they are not forecasts or official estimates, and the public figures quoted beside them are from the sources cited. title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
Working paper, version 0.4, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.1. Version 0.2 (May 2026) and earlier versions carried an error in the fuel-switching elasticity; Appendix E sets out the correction.
Keywords: carbon pricing; effective carbon price; carbon price equivalent; non-price instruments; energy demand; policy crediting. JEL: H23, Q41, Q48, Q54, Q58, C43.
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
A.1 Price-signal metrics
The effective carbon rate and the total carbon price aggregate prices on a fuel-by-sector grid and weight them by emissions. The OECD’s effective carbon rate is the sum of fuel excise taxes, explicit carbon taxes and emissions trading prices, computed for each fuel and sector and aggregated by emissions; the net rate deducts fossil-fuel subsidies (OECD 2023). It deliberately excludes non-price instruments and does not weight by responsiveness, a point Parry, Black, and Roaf (2021, n. 26) make explicitly. The World Bank’s total carbon price for 142 countries over 1991–2021 sums direct pricing, carbon taxes and trading weighted by coverage, and indirect pricing, fuel excises, consumption subsidies and deviations from standard VAT, measured by a price-gap method (Agnolucci et al. 2024, 2023). Indirect pricing is 87 percent of the global total in 2021, the global average is barely above its 1994 level, transport is priced highest and coal and gas are barely priced. Compared with the OECD’s net rate, the total carbon price is broadly aligned for OECD countries but often far off, sometimes of opposite sign, for poorer countries. Its section 6.4 proposes “effectiveness-weighted total carbon pricing”, weighting by fuel- and sector-specific mitigation elasticities, and section 6.3 notes that border credit rests on average rather than marginal prices. The World Carbon Pricing Database documents explicit instruments by IPCC sector for national and subnational jurisdictions from 1990 (Dolphin and Xiahou 2022), which maps onto the TECP’s sector dimension.
One econometric study estimates how emissions respond to an aggregate effective carbon price. D’Arcangelo et al. (2022) estimate in a large cross-country panel that a €10 rise in the effective carbon rate cuts fossil CO₂ by 3.7 percent in the long run, that broadening coverage to unpriced emissions delivers two thirds of the potential effect, and that responses vary with sectoral structure. This is an external check on \(\Lambda\): the example’s 0.61 percent per dollar per tonne is of the same order as their 0.37 percent per euro.
The IMF’s price-gap estimates measure distance from efficient prices. Efficient fuel prices include supply costs, environmental costs and forgone consumption taxes. Global fossil-fuel subsidies so measured were $5.9 trillion in 2020, 8 percent explicit and 92 percent implicit (Parry, Black, and Vernon 2021), and $7 trillion in 2022 (Black, Liu, et al. 2023); earlier estimates are in Coady et al. (2019). The fuel-demand responses behind these estimates use constant-elasticity curves. An implicit subsidy is a gap to an efficient price, not a policy price, and only the explicit part belongs in the TECP’s cells, as in the World Bank measure. Critics of price-gap methods note that they confuse market power and distribution costs with taxes and that reference prices are hard to set in large countries (Agnolucci et al. 2024, sec. 6.2); the TECP inherits these problems in its inputs.

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
section: A.2 Implicit carbon prices of non-price policies
text:
A.2 Implicit carbon prices of non-price policies
The older meaning of “effective carbon price” is cost per tonne abated. The OECD’s 2013 study estimates the cost per tonne of policies in 15 countries and five sectors, across taxes, trading, feed-in tariffs, capital subsidies and regulations, and finds market instruments consistently cheapest and capital subsidies and feed-in tariffs among the most expensive (OECD 2013, abstract). Marcantonini and Ellerman (2015) compute the net cost of German feed-in tariffs for wind and solar in 2006–2010, divide by CO₂ abated, and add the allowance price: tens of euros per tonne for wind and hundreds for solar. Gillingham and Stock (2018) survey static costs per tonne of standards, mandates and subsidies, which run from negative to several hundred dollars, and argue that static cost can mislead where learning and spillovers lower future costs (abstract). Against these, the TECP is a marginal emissions-equivalence measure: the TECP of German solar support is the uniform tax that would cut as much CO₂, far below its average cost.
Instrument-level studies decompose standards into implicit taxes and subsidies. Fischer and Newell (2008) rank US power-sector instruments by cost for a given cut: an emissions price, a performance standard, a fossil-output tax, a renewable portfolio standard, a renewable production subsidy and research subsidies. Each decomposes into implicit taxes and subsidies by technology; a portfolio standard is a small fossil-output tax with a larger renewable subsidy, no conservation incentive and a slightly lower electricity price. Holland et al. (2009) show that a low-carbon fuel standard taxes high-carbon fuel and subsidizes low-carbon fuel, can in principle raise emissions, and in simulation is costly: an average carbon cost of $307–2,272 per tonne for a national standard cutting carbon intensity 10 percent, against $60–868 for an efficient policy with the same cut. Goulder et al. (2016) show that a clean energy standard, an implicit tax on dirty and subsidy to clean generation, distorts factor markets less than emissions pricing because it is a smaller implicit tax on factors of production, and that this can make it cheaper for small cuts. These results are the TECP’s margin decomposition in other words: instruments with small or negative extensive prices deliver less abatement per dollar of shadow price.
Overlapping and supply-side effects limit any static equivalence. Goulder et al. (2012) find that state limits on greenhouse gases per mile nested inside federal fuel-economy standards cause leakage to other states that offsets 70–80 percent of the reductions from new cars in adopting states. Kalkuhl et al. (2013) show in a general-equilibrium model with fossil-resource owners that renewable subsidies without carbon pricing raise mitigation costs by a multiple, and that small deviations from the second-best subsidy raise emissions sharply through extraction paths.

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
section: A.3 Carbon price equivalents and comparing effort
text:
A.3 Carbon price equivalents and comparing effort
The carbon price equivalent was defined in law and economics before the IMF computed it. Weil (2021) proposes the “carbon price equivalent” as a metric for comparing mitigation effort across jurisdictions: the carbon price that, applied in an otherwise neutral policy environment, would produce the same aggregate emissions as the jurisdiction’s actual mix, or equivalently the allowance price of a cap-and-trade system whose cap matched observed emissions. He argues for it on grounds of justice and efficiency, proposes it for border adjustments of domestic carbon taxes and regulations, and discusses the neutral baseline, currency conversion, production against consumption emissions and spillovers. He does not compute it or give a method that separates margins.
The IMF defines the carbon price equivalent and computes it for the G20. Black et al. (2022) define the carbon price equivalent of a policy as the carbon price that yields the same emissions reduction, with economy-wide and sectoral versions. Their method builds a business-as-usual path in CPAT, simulates the policy or target, and finds the matching price. For the G20 in 2030, explicit pricing gives modest equivalents except about $50 per tonne or more in Canada, France, Germany, Italy and the United Kingdom; power-sector renewable and coal phase-out targets imply sectoral equivalents above $150 in ten cases; all policies combined exceed $150 in six cases; existing fuel taxes imply about $5–40 in most cases, with the question whether they should count left open. Vehicle and building responses come from capital-turnover models with 15-, 55- and 85-year lives. Renewable targets are modeled as a subsidy plus an electricity tax, intensity standards as an output-rebated carbon charge and vehicle standards as a shadow price on efficiency. Their Annex B stresses that equal emissions do not mean equal costs or competitiveness effects. CPAT itself models non-price policies through a shadow price on the efficiency margin only and splits elasticities into usage and efficiency margins calibrated to Labandeira et al. (2017; Black, Parry, et al. 2023; World Bank and International Monetary Fund 2022).
The IMF’s price-floor proposal asks for effectiveness weighting. Parry, Black, and Roaf (2021) propose a floor among six large emitters at $50 per tonne, or $25, $50 and $75 differentiated by income, which would cut energy CO₂ 23–24 percent below the 2030 baseline. It admits “non-pricing approaches with equivalent emissions impacts”. Its compliance metric expresses fuel taxes in CO₂ terms and weights fuel taxes and explicit prices by their relative effectiveness at reducing economy-wide CO₂ compared with a comprehensive carbon price, and it would bind on the increase from a benchmark year, because fuel taxes are set for other reasons. The October 2019 Fiscal Monitor describes the same weighting, CO₂-equivalent fuel taxes and direct carbon prices weighted by their relative effectiveness, and refers to first-pass estimates of effective carbon prices for 135 countries published separately (International Monetary Fund 2019, Box 1.2).
Comparisons of national effort need replicable metrics. J. E. Aldy and Pizer (2016) survey metrics, from emissions and intensity to explicit and implicit prices and costs, and conclude that none is comprehensive, measurable and universal, so a dashboard is needed. Implicit prices estimate average abatement cost, are model-derived and are high both for costly policies and for those that abate little. They call for an economy-wide average carbon price that weights explicit and implicit prices. J. E. Aldy et al. (2017) propose ex ante and ex post review of pledges and show that rankings change with the metric; with four integrated assessment models, J. Aldy et al. (2016) find marginal abatement costs of Paris pledges differing by two orders of magnitude across countries. Model dispersion of this size is why a TECP needs a band.

section: A.4 Energy demand elasticities, interfuel substitution and adjustment
text:
A.4 Energy demand elasticities, interfuel substitution and adjustment
Own-price demand elasticities are well studied; substitution elasticities outside industry are not. Labandeira et al. (2017) meta-analyze own-price elasticities of energy demand by fuel and sector. As reproduced in the CPAT technical notes, long-run means are about −0.62 residential, −0.51 industrial, −0.72 commercial and −0.44 transport; by fuel, −0.51 for electricity, −0.57 for natural gas, −0.53 for gasoline and −0.39 for diesel, with “adjusted” values of −0.37, −0.68, −0.77 and −0.44 (World Bank and International Monetary Fund 2022). These are CPAT’s reproduction of the meta-analysis, partly adjusted; the authors’ own summary of their global meta-analysis gives larger long-run means, −0.65 for energy, −0.69 for electricity, −0.85 for natural gas, −0.72 for gasoline and −0.60 for diesel, with short-run means about 0.3 times as large (Labandeira et al. 2016). All are demand elasticities. Stern (2012) meta-analyzes interfuel substitution elasticities among coal, oil, gas and electricity in 47 studies of industry, manufacturing and the whole economy, with no power-generation, transport or residential samples. At the level of the industrial sector, the oil–coal, oil–gas, oil–electricity and gas–electricity elasticities are significantly greater than one, the coal–gas and coal–electricity elasticities are imprecise, and substitution is more constrained at the macro level. For a single CES nest every such elasticity equals \(\sigma\), so differences across pairs are evidence against one \(\sigma\) per sector. Serletis et al. (2010) estimate sectoral interfuel elasticities for OECD and developing countries in models with fossil fuels only and find them consistently below one. Papageorgiou et al. (2017) estimate a nested CES on sectoral data for 26 countries and find the elasticity between clean and dirty energy inputs significantly above one (abstract), the relevant nest for power generation with renewables.
Published elasticities are biased upward in magnitude. Havranek et al. (2012) find that published gasoline price elasticities average about −0.23 in the short run and −0.69 in the long run, but that correcting for selective reporting gives −0.09 and −0.31. Meta-analytic means should therefore be treated as upper bounds on responsiveness, and a calibration needs a bias-corrected case.
Taxes move demand more than equal price changes. Davis and Kilian (2011) find small OLS price elasticities for US gasoline, about −0.1 nationally, but larger instrumental-variable estimates exploiting tax changes; their preferred estimate is that a 10-cent tax rise cuts vehicle CO₂ by about 1.5 percent. Li et al. (2014) find that US consumers respond more strongly to gasoline tax changes than to equal changes in tax-exclusive prices. Andersson (2019) finds that Sweden’s carbon tax cut transport CO₂ by almost 11 percent and that its elasticity was three times the price elasticity (abstract). A TECP calibrated to price elasticities therefore understates taxes relative to instruments whose price wedges reach buyers as ordinary price changes (Section 8).
Partial adjustment links short- and long-run elasticities. The Nerlove identity, adjustment speed equals the ratio of short- to long-run elasticity, gives 0.29–0.34 a year from the authors’ own meta-analytic means for energy, electricity, gasoline and diesel (Labandeira et al. 2016) and 0.29 for gasoline from bias-corrected estimates (Havranek et al. 2012). That is the demand margin. For fuel switching, capital turnover sets the pace: CPAT uses vehicle turnover of 6.7 percent a year and slower rates for buildings (Black et al. 2022, Annex C). For non-OECD calibration, country-specific road-fuel elasticities (Dahl 2012) and a review for industrializing economies (Huntington et al. 2019) are the next sources to use; paper 5.4 assembles them into a register by fuel and sector (Stretton 2026a).

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
section: A.5 Uses: border adjustment, price floors and crediting
text:
A.5 Uses: border adjustment, price floors and crediting
The economics of border adjustment separates environmental equivalence from cost equivalence. Keen et al. (2022) show that non-price policies impose only the efficiency cost of abatement on firms, not the payment on remaining emissions, so they “generally impose markedly lower private costs on firms than carbon pricing (at equivalent shadow prices)”. Charging imports the shadow price is then not a competitiveness response, and exemptions for non-price effort are justified on cooperation or leakage grounds rather than competitiveness. Mehling et al. (2019) anticipate adjusting border charges for effective carbon prices, explicit and implicit, computed from energy taxes by carbon content, average abatement cost times mandated reductions, or “economic models to identify the carbon price needed to achieve mandated emission reductions in a sector”, with third-party verification. Cosbey et al. (2019) review design choices. The EU’s mechanism deducts only the carbon price effectively paid, net of rebates and compensation (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023; European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2025, Art. 9), and so does not recognize feebates or standards; paper 1.4 proposes recognizing the price signal (Stretton 2026b).
No source found in this review measures policy-level crediting by a carbon-price equivalent. Results-based climate finance pays for verified reductions, mostly by project. The crediting argument of paper 1.1 (Stretton 2026d) pairs the two.
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
A.6 What is new here
The concept of a carbon price equivalent, the idea of weighting by responsiveness, the counting of standards at their marginal incentive and the representation of standards by shadow prices all precede this paper (Weil 2021; Black et al. 2022; Parry, Black, and Roaf 2021; Carhart et al. 2022; Fischer and Newell 2008; Black, Parry, et al. 2023). What this paper adds is: a closed-form, linear-in-policy TECP whose weights belong to the economy and can be published, with a corrected derivation from the CES cost function; a decomposition of every instrument into a switching and a demand margin; an exact and second-order version with a rule for when the closed form suffices; a theory of non-price instruments with identification assumptions; and a calibration that cites each source only for what it estimates, with an uncertainty band. The main objections a referee will raise are also in the literature: calibration fragility, especially of demand elasticities (Serletis et al. 2010; Havranek et al. 2012), tax salience (Li et al. 2014; Andersson 2019), the difference between emission and cost equivalence (Keen et al. 2022; Goulder et al. 2016), and the failure of additivity under leakage and binding caps (Goulder et al. 2012). Section 8 and Section 11 address each.

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
B.1 Proposition 1
From equation 3, \(\ln q'_{fs} = \ln q_{fs} - \sigma_s\ln P_{fs} + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)\ln(C'_s/C_s)\). At the baseline, \(\partial\ln P_{fs}/\partial\pi_{gs} = \delta_{fg}\) and, by Shephard’s lemma, \(\partial\ln C_s/\partial\pi_{gs} = s_{gs}\). So \(d\ln q_{fs} = -\sigma_s\pi_{fs} + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)\bar\pi_s = -\sigma_s(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) - \eta_s\bar\pi_s\), which is equation 4. The cut is \(R_P = -\sum_{f,s}E_{fs}\,d\ln q_{fs} = \sum_s\big[\sigma_s\sum_f E_{fs}(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) + \eta_s E_s\bar\pi_s\big]\). By equation 6, \(\sigma_s(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) = \sigma_s(x_{fs} - \kappa_s)\,\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs}\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs}\) and \(\eta_s\bar\pi_s = \eta_s\kappa_s\,\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s = \tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{ext}}_s\tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s\), which proves (i). For (ii), a $1 tax gives \(\pi_{fs} = x_{fs}\) and \(\bar\pi_s = \kappa_s\), so \(\tau^{\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \tau^{\mathrm{ext}}_s = 1\). Since \(E_{fs} = X_s s_{fs}x_{fs}\), \(\sum_f E_{fs}(x_{fs} - \kappa_s) = X_s\big(\sum_f s_{fs}x_{fs}^2 - \kappa_s^2\big) = X_sV_s\), and \(E_s\kappa_s = X_s\kappa_s^2\). So \(\Lambda = \sum_s X_s(\sigma_sV_s + \eta_s\kappa_s^2)\), positive whenever some sector has \(\eta_s > 0\) and positive emissions, or \(\sigma_s > 0\) and \(V_s > 0\). (iii) follows by dividing by \(\Lambda\); the weights sum to \(\Lambda/\Lambda = 1\). (iv) A tax \(\tau\) gives \(\pi_{fs} = \tau x_{fs}\), so both prices equal \(\tau\) and \(R_P = \tau\Lambda\).
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
B.2 Proposition 2

\(\sum_f s_{fs}\sigma_s(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s) = \sigma_s(\bar\pi_s - \bar\pi_s) = 0\). At a cost minimum the elasticity of the CES aggregate with respect to each input equals its cost share, so \(d\ln Q_s = \sum_f s_{fs}\,d\ln q_{fs}\) and the switching term contributes nothing to \(Q_s\). For a uniform tax, \(\sum_f s_{fs}\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = \sigma_s(\kappa_s - \kappa_s) = 0\). (ii) With equal prices \(p\) per unit of service, \(s_{fs} = w_{fs}\), \(x_{fs} = e_f/p\) and \(\kappa_s = \bar e_s/p\), so \(\sum_f q_{fs}\tilde\varepsilon^{\,\mathrm{int}}_{fs} = (\sigma_s Q_s/p)\sum_f w_{fs}(e_f - \bar e_s) = 0\).
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
B.3 Proposition 3

The CES is homothetic, so from any taxed price vector the response to a further tax has the form of Proposition 1 with cost shares, carbon per dollar and spending evaluated at that point: \(R'(\tau) = \sum_s X_s(\tau)[\sigma_sV_s(\tau) + \eta_s\kappa_s(\tau)^2] > 0\). \(R\) is continuous and strictly increasing, so \(R(\tau^*) = R_P\) has at most one solution and bisection finds it. As \(\tau \to \infty\) every emitting fuel’s quantity goes to zero when \(\eta_s > 0\). If a zero-carbon fuel exists and \(\sigma_s > 1\), the cost index stays bounded and \(q_{fs} \propto P_{fs}^{-\sigma_s}C_s^{\sigma_s - \eta_s} \to 0\). Otherwise every emitting fuel’s price and the cost index rise in proportion to \(\tau\), so \(q_{fs}\) falls like \(\tau^{-\eta_s}\); \(\sigma_s = 1\) is the Cobb–Douglas limit of the same argument. So \(R\) ranges over \([0, E)\) for \(\tau \ge 0\), and over negative cuts for taxes down to the level at which a price reaches zero. At a finite horizon, \(R_T(\tau)\) is increasing in the example and the script checks the bisection, but monotonicity is not guaranteed in general because partially adjusted quantities are off the CES optimum.
Expand equation 3 to second order. With \(u_{fs} = \ln P_{fs} = \pi_{fs} - \pi_{fs}^2/2 + O(\pi^3)\), \(\ln(C'_s/C_s) = \frac{1}{1-\sigma_s}\ln\sum_f s_{fs}e^{(1-\sigma_s)u_{fs}} = \bar u_s + \tfrac{1-\sigma_s}{2}\mathrm{Var}_s(u) + O(\pi^3) = \bar\pi_s - \tfrac12\bar\pi_s^2 - \tfrac{\sigma_s}{2}V^\pi_s + O(\pi^3)\). So \(\ln(q'_{fs}/q_{fs}) = L_{fs} + \tfrac12[\sigma_s\pi_{fs}^2 - (\sigma_s - \eta_s)(\bar\pi_s^2 + \sigma_sV^\pi_s)] + O(\pi^3)\), and \(q'/q = 1 + \ln(q'/q) + \tfrac12 L_{fs}^2 + O(\pi^3)\). Summing \(-E_{fs}\) times the second-order terms gives equation 11. For the TECP, write \(R(\tau) = \Lambda\tau + \tfrac12\Gamma\tau^2 + O(\tau^3)\) and \(R_P = R^{(1)}_P + R^{(2)}_P + O(\pi^3)\). Substituting \(\tau = \tau^*_{(1)} + \delta\) with \(\delta\) of second order, \(\Lambda\delta + \tfrac12\Gamma(\tau^*_{(1)})^2 = R^{(2)}_P\) to second order, which is equation 12; the residual is of third order. (iii) is the condition \(\delta = 0\).
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
B.4 Proposition 4
Let the sector choose \(q\) to minimize \(\sum_f p_{fs}q_{fs}\) subject to \(F(q) \ge Q_s\) and \(\sum_f(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}})q_{fs} \le 0\). With multipliers \(\mu\) and \(\lambda\), the first-order conditions are \(p_{fs} + \lambda(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}}) = \mu\,\partial F/\partial q_{fs}\), identical to those of minimizing \(\sum_f[p_{fs} + \lambda(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}})]q_{fs}\) subject to \(F(q) \ge Q_s\). Service demand responds to the cost index at these prices. Decentralized, each unit of fuel \(f\) sold creates \(\bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}} - e_f\) credits, negative for fuels above the standard, worth \(\lambda\) each; competitive trading equalizes every supplier’s marginal compliance cost at \(\lambda\) (Montgomery 1972), and with full pass-through the delivered price is \(p_{fs} + \lambda(e_f - \bar e^{\,\mathrm{std}})\). This proves (i) and (ii). (iii) Both routes produce the same cut in the same model, and Definition 1 depends only on the cut. (iv) A clean-share requirement \(\sum_f(\theta - c_f)q_{fs} \le 0\), with \(c_f = 1\) for clean and \(0\) for fossil units, has the same structure, with price changes \(\lambda(\theta - c_f)\).
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
B.5 Proposition 5
Applying Proposition 4 firm by firm, firm \(i\) under its own binding standard chooses as if it faced a feebate at its own shadow price \(\mu_i\) around its own standard. To first order its cut is \(\mu_i\) times its cut per dollar of such a feebate, \(E_ir_i\mu_i\). Summing over firms and dividing by \(\Lambda\) gives the first expression in equation 13. Write \(\bar r = \Lambda^F/E\) and \(\bar\mu_E = \sum_iE_i\mu_i/E\) with \(E = \sum_iE_i\). Then \(\sum_iE_ir_i\mu_i = E[\bar r\bar\mu_E + \mathrm{Cov}_E(r,\mu)]\), which gives the second expression. (ii) is the case \(\mathrm{Cov}_E = 0\). (iii) A tradable standard with the same cut has, by Definition 1, the same exact TECP, and by Montgomery (1972) it achieves the cut at least cost.
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
B.6 Corollaries
Corollary 1. With \(\Delta p_{fs} = t(e_f - \bar e_s)\), \(\pi_{fs} = t(x_{fs} - \bar e_s/p_{fs})\) and \(\bar\pi_s = t(\kappa_s - \bar e_s\sum_gs_{gs}/p_{gs})\), so \(\pi_{fs} - \bar\pi_s = t[(x_{fs} - \kappa_s) - \bar e_s(1/p_{fs} - \sum_gs_{gs}/p_{gs})]\), and dividing by \(x_{fs} - \kappa_s\) gives the stated intensive price. It equals \(t\) for all \(f\) if and only if \(1/p_{fs} = \sum_gs_{gs}/p_{gs}\) for all \(f\) (given \(\bar e_s > 0\)), that is, all prices are equal. Then \(s_{fs} = w_{fs}\), \(\kappa_s = \bar e_s/p\) and \(\bar\pi_s = 0\).
Corollary 2. Replacing \(\sigma_s\) and \(\eta_s\) by \(a^I_s(T)\sigma_s\) and \(a^X_s(T)\eta_s\) in Proposition 1 scales each sector’s switching and demand terms, in the policy’s cut and in \(\Lambda\) alike. With common speeds, \(R_{P,T} = a^I\Lambda^I\tau^*_I + a^X\Lambda^X\tau^*_X\) and \(\Lambda_T = a^I\Lambda^I + a^X\Lambda^X\); dividing and writing \(\omega = \Lambda^I/\Lambda\) gives equation 10. The first-order response at horizon \(T\) follows from equation 5 because the switching and demand terms of equation 4 are the long-run changes in \(\ln h_{fs}\) and \(\ln Q_s\), of which fractions \(a^I_s(T)\) and \(a^X_s(T)\) have occurred.
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
C.1 The CES system
With the aggregator equation 1, the unit cost is \(C_s = (\sum_f\alpha_{fs}p_{fs}^{1-\sigma_s})^{1/(1-\sigma_s)}\) and conditional demand \(q_{fs} = Q_s\alpha_{fs}(p_{fs}/C_s)^{-\sigma_s}\). Cost shares are \(s_{fs} = \alpha_{fs}(p_{fs}/C_s)^{1-\sigma_s}\), so calibrating \(\alpha_{fs}\) to observed shares and normalizing \(C_s = 1\) at the baseline gives equation 3, in which the \(\alpha_{fs}\) no longer appear. With service demand \(Q_s \propto C_s^{-\eta_s}\), fuel demand is \(q_{fs} \propto p_{fs}^{-\sigma_s}C_s^{\sigma_s - \eta_s}\). Version 0.2 wrote the exponent as \(\sigma_s + \eta_s\) with \(\eta_s\) negative; the two are the same. Year-by-year simulation applies equation 3 relative to the previous year’s quantities and prices, so the cost shares update as the mix changes.
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
C.2 The elasticity matrix
Differentiating gives \(\varepsilon_{ff} = -\sigma_s + (\sigma_s - \eta_s)s_{fs}\) and \(\varepsilon_{fg} = (\sigma_s - \eta_s)s_{gs}\) for \(g \ne f\). Holding the service fixed (\(\eta_s = 0\)), these are the Hicksian elasticities \(-\sigma_s(1 - s_{fs})\) and \(\sigma_s s_{gs}\). Each row sums to \(-\eta_s\): a proportional rise in all prices cuts every fuel by the demand elasticity. Cross-price elasticities are proportional to the other fuel’s cost share, and \(s_{fs}\varepsilon_{fg} - s_{gs}\varepsilon_{gf} = 0\) in the Hicksian case (symmetry). The matrix is the isoelastic form the TECP uses to first order; version 0.2’s Appendix A.6 stated it correctly, but its semi-elasticities in A.7 did not use it.
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
section: C.3 Local equivalence and where the forms diverge
text:
C.3 Local equivalence and where the forms diverge
The isoelastic form \(d\ln q_f = \sum_g\varepsilon_{fg}\pi_g\) is the first-order expansion of the CES at the baseline. It holds cost shares fixed; the CES lets them move. Version 0.2 stated that the linear form is accurate for price changes under about 20 percent. Section 6 gives a sharper answer for the TECP: the relevant comparison is the curvature of the policy’s cut against the benchmark tax’s, which the second-order term measures directly. For emission cuts themselves, as opposed to the TECP, the linear form is poor well before 20 percent when a cheap, dirty fuel faces a large tax, as coal does in the example’s industry.
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
C.4 Partial adjustment
The fast speed belongs to the demand margin, which needs no new capital, and the slow speed to fuel switching, which follows the turnover of vehicles, boilers, furnaces and plants. The adjustment is applied to the two CES components, \(\ln h_{fs}\) and \(\ln Q_s\) (equation 5), rather than to energy shares and total energy, so the switching margin stays on the isoquant at every date and the horizon TECP of Corollary 2 follows directly. Adjusting in logs keeps quantities positive and makes the horizon elasticities \(a(T)\) times the long-run ones, which is what the identity \(\lambda \approx \varepsilon^{SR}/\varepsilon^{LR}\) assumes. The half-life of adjustment is \(\ln 2/\ln(1/(1-\lambda))\), about 1.6 years for the demand margin at \(\lambda^X = 0.35\) and 10 years for switching at \(\lambda^I = 0.07\). Speeds may differ by sector and by fuel pair; switching between gasoline and diesel vehicles is faster than between gas boilers and heat pumps.
crumbs: 6.1 Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts

title: Measure Carbon Pricing by the Emissions It Cuts
text:
C.5 Technical efficiency
Expressing quantities in useful energy multiplies each fuel’s quantity by its conversion efficiency \(\varphi_{fs}\) and divides its price and emission factor by \(\varphi_{fs}\). Spending, emissions, cost shares and carbon per dollar are unchanged, so \(\Lambda\), the weights and every TECP are unchanged. Efficiency matters for the interpretation of Proposition 2(ii), where “equal prices” means equal prices per unit of useful energy, and for the substitution elasticity, which should be estimated over useful energy where an efficient fuel replaces an inefficient one, as electricity replaces gasoline in vehicles.

title: Public Investment in CPAT
text: Working paper, version 0.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version for policy makers is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.3. Companion paper to the public CPAT-AI repository, https://github.com/cpmodelai/cpat_ai.1

title: Public Investment in CPAT
text:
4.1 Capital from physical change
Investment is new physical capacity times a unit capital cost, measured against a baseline. For country \(c\), sector \(s\), technology \(j\), year \(t\) and scenario \(S\),
\[
I^{S}_{c,s,t} = \sum_{j \in s} \Delta Q^{S}_{c,j,t}\; k_{j,t}\; p_{c,s}, \qquad k_{j,t} = k_{j,0}\, g_j^{\,t-t_0},
\tag{1}\]
where \(\Delta Q\) is new capacity including replacements (gigawatts of solar, kilometers of line, vehicles sold, buildings retrofitted), \(k_{j,t}\) is the unit capital cost with a learning or trend factor \(g_j\), and \(p_{c,s}\) is the country’s price level for investment goods relative to the source of \(k\), from the International Comparison Program’s purchasing power parities for gross fixed capital formation. Incremental investment is the difference from the baseline run, \(\Delta I_{c,s,t} = I^{S}_{c,s,t} - I^{B}_{c,s,t}\). Both are reported, because totals compare with the expert group and the International Energy Agency, and increments compare with country climate and development reports and SISEPUEDE.
In power, CPAT already supplies \(\Delta Q\); elsewhere a share-of-GDP rule fills the gap until a physical model exists. CPAT’s capacity additions by technology plug straight into equation 1. For buildings, industry, transport infrastructure, land use and adaptation, the fallback is
\[
I_{c,s,t} = \theta_{s,\,\mathrm{inc}(c)}\; \mathrm{GDP}_{c,t},
\tag{2}\]
with \(\theta\) calibrated by sector and income group on studies that do model capital: Rozenberg and Fay (2019) for infrastructure (4.5 percent of GDP a year in low- and middle-income countries in their preferred scenario, in a range of 2 to 8 percent) and the expert group’s totals by country group (Bhattacharya et al. 2024). The fallback is only as good as its calibration. Where SISEPUEDE has been run, its physical changes replace it.

title: Public Investment in CPAT
text:
4.2 The cost of capital
Capital becomes an annual charge through the capital recovery factor, and the rate in that factor decides the answer. Over asset life \(n_j\) at rate \(r\),
\[
A_{c,j,t} = I_{c,j,t}\,\mathrm{CRF}(r_{c,j}, n_j), \qquad \mathrm{CRF}(r,n) = \frac{r}{1-(1+r)^{-n}}.
\tag{3}\]
This is the end-of-year convention of project finance: the first payment falls a year after the asset is built. CPAT’s levelized cost instead sums discounted output from year zero, which is equivalent to dividing the factor by \(1+r\); the choice moves results by a few points of the cost of capital, as shown below. For the financial case, \(r\) is the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) for that country and technology,
\[
\mathrm{WACC}_{c,j} = \frac{D}{V}\big(r_f + \pi_c + \pi_j\big)(1-\tau) + \frac{E}{V}\,k^{E}_{c,j},
\tag{4}\]
where \(r_f\) is the risk-free rate, \(\pi_c\) the country premium, \(\pi_j\) the technology premium, \(D/V\) and \(E/V\) the debt and equity shares, \(\tau\) the tax rate and \(k^E\) the cost of equity. This has the same structure as CPAT’s default setting. Observed costs of capital for renewable projects exist for a few dozen countries (46 in Steffen 2020); elsewhere \(\pi_c\) comes from sovereign spreads and the formula is calibrated to the observed level. For the economic case, \(r\) is the social rate, 6 percent in World Bank guidance, which puts the plausible range at 2 to 10 percent (World Bank 2016).
The financial case nets the capital charge against fuel and operating savings; the economic case adds co-benefits and carbon.
\[
N^{F}_{c,t} = \sum_j \big(\Delta F_{c,j,t} - \Delta OM_{c,j,t} - A_{c,j,t}(\mathrm{WACC})\big),
\tag{5}\]
\[
N^{E}_{c,t} = \sum_j \big(\Delta F_{c,j,t} - \Delta OM_{c,j,t} - A_{c,j,t}(r_s)\big) + CB_{c,t} + P^{C}_t\,\Delta E_{c,t},
\tag{6}\]
where \(\Delta F\) is fuel saved, \(\Delta OM\) the change in operating cost, \(CB\) local co-benefits (air pollution, road safety, congestion), \(\Delta E\) avoided emissions and \(P^C_t\) the shadow price of carbon: $50 to 100 a ton in 2030 on the range recommended by the High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices (High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices 2017), which World Bank appraisal follows (World Bank 2024). equation 5 is what investors and households see; equation 6 is what society gets. CPAT already computes \(\Delta F\) at retail and at supply-cost prices, and its air pollution and road transport modules compute most of \(CB\), so the economic lens reuses outputs the tool has.
The three lenses separate two jobs the discount rate is often asked to do at once. Lens (a) prices capital at each country’s WACC: the cost of financing. Lens (b) prices it at 6 percent everywhere: the social value of time. Lens (c) uses 6 percent and adds co-benefits and carbon. The physical investment need is the same in all three. What changes is the cost of carrying it and the benefits set against it.
Proposition 1 (break-even cost of capital). Let an asset cost one dollar, last \(n\) years and save \(b\) dollars a year in fuel and operating costs from the end of its first year. Its financial case \(N^F\) is positive if and only if \(\mathrm{WACC} < r^*\), where \(r^*\) solves \(\mathrm{CRF}(r^*, n) = b\); \(r^*\) exists and is unique when \(b > 1/n\). For \(b = 0.133\) and \(n = 25\), \(r^* = 12.6\) percent.
The break-even rate falls exactly where CPAT’s income-group option puts lower-middle-income countries. The proof is in Appendix A. The value \(b = 0.133\) is stylized: it gives a benefit-cost ratio of 1.70 at 6 percent over 25 years, the same order as SISEPUEDE’s financial results for Latin America, where fuel and other financial savings exceed $1.3 trillion of investment by $700 billion at 7 percent (Kalra et al. 2023). Against the income-group rates, each $1,000 of such capital nets $43 a year at 7.5 percent, $23 at 10 percent, about $1 at 12.5 percent and loses $22 at 15 percent (Figure 1). Under CPAT’s default setting, a lower-middle-income country’s solar asset carries a premium of 2.9 points, so it crosses the break-even once the country’s own rate exceeds about 9.7 percent. Under CPAT’s year-zero convention the break-even rate is 14.8 percent rather than 12.6: the convention alone is worth two points, which is why the extension must use one convention with the core model.






Figure 1: Saving less capital charge for the stylized asset of Proposition 1, per $1,000 of capital, against the cost of capital (25-year life, end-of-year capital recovery factor). Dots mark CPAT’s optional income-group rates. Source: author’s calculation (2.Source/make_figures.py).

title: Public Investment in CPAT
text:
4.3 What the lenses show
At market rates the world gains from its climate investment, but developing countries barely do. Table 1 applies the lenses to one year’s investment at the 2030 levels reported by the expert group, with the same stylized savings rate for every group, so that the differences come from the cost of capital alone. It is an illustration of scale, not an estimate: with one savings rate, it is Proposition 1 applied to three numbers.

Investment is the midpoint of the 2030 ranges in Bhattacharya et al. (2024). Savings are a stylized 13.3 cents a year per dollar of capital for every group. Market rates are illustrative values consistent with the gap reported by International Energy Agency (2024) and Steffen (2020); the high case is a stress. “Net” is savings minus the capital charge, equation 5.
