In developing countries the margin is thin and turns negative in a stress. At 10.5 percent, $2.4 trillion of investment earns $45 billion a year more than it costs to finance; at 15 percent it loses $52 billion. Financing at 10.5 rather than 6 percent costs $87 billion a year more for each year’s investment, and the penalty accumulates as vintages build up. At 6 percent the same investment earns $131 billion. Co-benefits widen the gap further: in SISEPUEDE’s Latin American results, avoided pollution and other health, safety and productivity gains ($1.5 trillion) exceed the fuel savings ($0.9 trillion), and counting them raises the net benefit from $0.7 trillion to $2.7 trillion (Kalra et al. 2023).
The gap between lens (a) and lens (c) is the case for public finance, and the series’ de-risking papers are tools for closing it. A private investor in a developing country sees a thin margin or a loss; society sees a large gain. Three instruments bridge the gap. Pricing carbon and air pollution turns co-benefits into revenue, which is CPAT’s home ground. Lending on concessional or multilateral terms substitutes a lower rate for the market rate. And cutting the risk premium in equation 4 lowers the WACC itself: guaranteeing the power purchase contract rather than the debt removes payment risk (Stretton 2026d), and refinancing operating plants’ senior debt through pooled, tranched securities at a blended cost of about 5.65 percent, against single-stage finance at 10 percent, cuts the cost of solar power by about a fifth (Stretton 2026c). In the terms of Proposition 1, these instruments move a country from above \(r^*\) to below it. The extension tells a ministry how much each point is worth: about $36 billion a year, near 6 percent, for each year of the $4.8 trillion of clean energy investment the expert group projects for 2030 (Bhattacharya et al. 2024). The IEA’s comparable figure for emerging and developing economies alone is about $150 billion a year of financing costs per point, on their whole clean energy capital stock rather than one year’s investment (International Energy Agency 2024).
A high cost of capital also changes what gets built. Low-carbon technologies are more capital-intensive than fossil plants, so a high cost of capital favors fossil fuels and a country with dear capital needs a higher carbon price to reach the same decarbonization (Hirth and Steckel 2016; Ameli et al. 2021). Running CPAT’s logit investment choice with country rates from equation 4 makes the physical needs in equation 1 respond to finance.

title: Public Investment in CPAT
text:
5.1 The rule
For each candidate use of public money, compare what people get with what the budget really pays. Let \(W_j\) be the present value of benefits of measure \(j\) to everyone other than the budget, net of their own costs, and \(F_j\) the present value of its net cost to the budget, after revenue that comes back. Then
\[
\mathrm{ENPV}_j = W_j - F_j, \qquad \mathrm{MVPF}_j = \frac{W_j}{F_j}, \qquad NB_{\lambda,j} = W_j - \lambda F_j,
\tag{7}\]
where ENPV is the economic net present value, MVPF is the marginal value of public funds (Hendren and Sprung-Keyser 2020) and \(\lambda\) is the marginal cost of public funds: the cost to the economy of raising one more dollar of tax. Fund measure \(j\) if \(\mathrm{MVPF}_j > \lambda\), equivalently \(NB_{\lambda,j} > 0\). If \(F_j \le 0\) the measure pays for itself and is funded whenever \(W_j \ge 0\); the binding problem is then financing, not value. When the budget binds, rank by MVPF.
The cost of public funds is about 1.2 in developing countries, and higher where taxes distort more. For 38 African countries, raising a marginal dollar through the existing mix of five taxes costs on average $1.20, and $1.10 through each country’s cheapest instrument, often the value added tax (Auriol and Warlters 2012). For proportional tax changes in Scandinavian and northern continental European welfare states, where the participation margin matters, estimates center around 2 (Kleven and Kreiner 2006). The extension defaults to 1.2, uses 1.1 where the marginal tax is value added tax, and applies 1.5 to 2.0 as a stress where the macro-fiscal and debt models say the country cannot borrow more.
Proposition 2 (the rule nests World Bank practice and prices revenue returns at \(\lambda\)). (a) With \(\lambda = 1\) and no budget limit, \(NB_{\lambda,j} = \mathrm{ENPV}_j\), the usual economic net present value test. (b) Shifting a dollar of present value from beneficiaries to the budget, for example by keeping part of a fuel saving in the utility, leaves \(\mathrm{ENPV}_j\) unchanged and raises \(NB_{\lambda,j}\) by \(\lambda - 1\).
Revenue returns belong in the denominator, not the numerator. A user fee is a transfer in economic analysis; counting it as a benefit as well as a saving double-counts. But every dollar the budget recovers saves \(\lambda\) dollars of taxation, not one. The same logic puts CPAT’s pricing policies on the spending ladder. A carbon tax or fuel subsidy reform raises money at a low welfare cost per dollar, so it is the natural first source of funds. A spending measure that a price could achieve more cheaply is flagged “price first”: with costly public funds, the best subsidy is smaller than the gap between social and private returns, and smaller still when most subsidized units would have happened anyway, whereas a tax raises money on those same units. Paper 6.1 shows how to measure what such prices cut, as a Total Effective Carbon Price (Stretton 2026e).

title: Public Investment in CPAT
section: 5.2 Five corrections between a project’s value and its claim on the budget
text:
5.2 Five corrections between a project’s value and its claim on the budget
First, public money pays only the gap the private sector will not cover. The investor’s net present value is computed at the market WACC and private prices, including taxes. For a purely public asset the budget pays the full cost; for a viability-gap measure it pays \(\max(0, -NPV^{priv}_j)\); for utility and contracted routes it pays nothing up front and carries a contingent liability; for purely private investment it pays nothing. Benefits are scaled by an additionality share \(a_j\), the part that would not have happened without the measure.
Second, money spent is not capital created. Pritchett (2000) showed that cumulated public investment spending is a poor measure of public capital. The IMF estimates the average public investment efficiency gap, the shortfall of outcomes from what the same spending could buy, at about 30 percent across 134 countries: 40 percent in low-income developing countries, 27 percent in emerging markets and 13 percent in advanced economies. Stronger public investment management could close up to two-thirds of the gap (International Monetary Fund 2015). The extension carries an efficiency \(s_j\), the share of public spending that becomes effective capital, and an execution rate \(e_j\), the share of the budget actually spent:
\[
C^{\mathrm{eff}}_j = C_j\Big[(1-\pi_j) + \frac{\pi_j}{s_j}\Big], \qquad K^{\mathrm{eff}}_{j,t} = (1-\delta_j)K^{\mathrm{eff}}_{j,t-1} + s_j\, e_j\big(I^{\mathrm{plan}}_{j,t} + \mathrm{backlog}_{j,t-1}\big),
\tag{8}\]
where \(\pi_j\) is the public share of the capital cost and \(\delta_j\) the depreciation rate. Efficiency raises the cost of a unit of public asset; execution delays benefits but loses no money, because unspent appropriations stay in the budget. This is the efficiency-adjusted public capital of the growth and debt-investment-growth literature (Gupta et al. 2014; Berg et al. 2012). The haircut applies once: never also to unit costs taken from the country’s own outturns, which already contain its inefficiency.
Third, efficiency frontiers convert into parameters. Frontier studies measure how far each country’s health and education outcomes fall short of the best achieved for the same spending, across 140 countries (Herrera and Pang 2005) and across 38 African countries, which score lower on average than Asian and Latin American ones (Gupta and Verhoeven 2001). Outcomes of measures costed from international norms are scaled by the country’s score; those costed from local outturns are not.
Fourth, capital and current spending go on one footing. Each capital outlay becomes an equivalent annual cost with its recurrent costs added:
\[
\mathrm{EAC}_j = K_j\,\mathrm{CRF}(r, n_j) + r^{rc}_j K_j,
\tag{9}\]
where \(r^{rc}_j\) is the recurrent-cost coefficient: operations, maintenance and staffing per dollar of capital a year. Recurrent costs are large in aggregate: on top of investment of 4.5 percent of GDP, keeping infrastructure in low- and middle-income countries running adds 2.7 percent of GDP a year (Rozenberg and Fay 2019). By sector the coefficients differ widely; as illustrative values, the extension uses about 1 to 2 percent for solar and single digits for roads, and 10 to 20 percent for clinics and schools because of staffing. The rate \(r\) is the social rate for the economic view, the government’s borrowing rate for the fiscal view, and the market WACC for private and contracted routes. Underfunded maintenance is a measure in its own right, funded before new building of the same asset class, because unfunded recurrent costs are one of the main ways public capital in low-income countries loses value (Adam and Bevan 2014).
Fifth, the financing route changes the fiscal ledger, the debt statistics and the liabilities, and the extension runs each measure under six of them. These are a commercial loan, a concessional loan, a utility balance sheet, an independent producer under a power purchase agreement (PPA) with or without a guarantee, a viability-gap contract and a grant. The yearly net fiscal flow is
\[
F_t = \mathrm{capex}_t - \mathrm{loans}_t + DS_t + OM^{pub}_t + PPA_t + SUB_t - FEE_t - \theta\, SAV_t + XL_t - PIG_t + \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{CALL}_t],
\tag{10}\]
with debt service \(DS\), public operation and maintenance \(OM^{pub}\), contract payments \(PPA\), subsidies \(SUB\), fees \(FEE\), avoided fuel cost \(SAV\) of which the budget or state utility keeps a share \(\theta\), fuel excise lost \(XL\), earmarked corrective revenue \(PIG\), and expected guarantee calls. For a PPA the tariff and the liability are
\[
T = \frac{\big(K + PV_w(\mathrm{rep})\big)\,\mathrm{CRF}(w, n) + OM}{E}, \qquad L^{PPA} = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{T E}{(1+i_g)^t},
\tag{11}\]
where \(w\) is the producer’s WACC, \(\mathrm{rep}\) mid-life replacements, \(E\) annual energy and \(i_g\) the government’s borrowing rate.
Proposition 3 (tenor is not price). (a) If a loan’s rate equals the government’s borrowing rate \(i_g\), the present value of its debt service at \(i_g\) equals the principal whatever its tenor, so the fiscal net present value at \(i_g\) does not depend on tenor; tenor changes only the timing of cash. (b) If budget costs are discounted at a social rate below the loan rate, the present value of debt service rises with tenor, so a rule with one constant \(\lambda\) ranks the shorter loan above the longer one. (c) Only a cost of public funds \(\lambda_t\) that is higher in cash-short years can reverse that ranking.
Proposition 4 (a power purchase agreement is debt in disguise). Let the producer’s WACC \(w\) exceed \(i_g\) and the PPA be take-or-pay over the asset life. (a) Without mid-life replacements, \(L^{PPA} > K + PV_{i_g}(OM)\): the committed payments, valued at the government’s rate, exceed the cost of building and running the plant. (b) With replacements, \(L^{PPA} > K + PV_{i_g}(OM) + PV_{i_g}(\mathrm{rep})\) if and only if \(\big(K + PV_w(\mathrm{rep})\big)\,\mathrm{CRF}(w,n)/\mathrm{CRF}(i_g,n) > K + PV_{i_g}(\mathrm{rep})\). The excess is the financing premium the country pays for keeping the asset off its headline debt.
Debt rules see only part of this. The proofs are in Appendix A. In the joint IMF and World Bank framework for low-income countries, once the stock of public-private partnership capital exceeds 3 percent of GDP, a stress test adds 35 percent of that stock to public debt (International Monetary Fund and World Bank 2017). Public-private partnerships do not free public funds; any case for them rests on efficiency gains large enough to beat the financing premium (Engel et al. 2013).

title: Public Investment in CPAT
text:
5.3 From measures to a portfolio
Ranking by MVPF within an affordable envelope gives an allocative frontier across sectors. Measures are ranked by MVPF and cumulative fiscal cost is plotted against cumulative value. Mutually exclusive variants of one measure keep only the efficient ones; indivisible projects need a knapsack:
\[
\max_{x} \sum_j x_j\, NB_{\lambda,j} \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_j x_j F_{j,t} \le E^{*}_t \;\;\forall t, \qquad \sum_{j \in g} x_j \le 1 \;\;\forall g, \qquad \sum_j x_j I_{j,t} - I_{t-1} \le \Delta I^{\max},
\tag{12}\]
where \(x_j\) is 1 if measure \(j\) is funded (or a share if divisible), \(g\) indexes families of exclusive variants, \(E^*_t\) is the fiscal envelope that the macro-fiscal and debt models say is affordable, and \(\Delta I^{\max}\) caps the speed of scale-up, which matters most where absorptive capacity is low. Climate measures sit on the same ladder as health, education, roads, water and cash transfers, each on a “sector card” with a unit cost, outcome per dollar and recurrent-cost coefficient, sharing one discount rate, value of a statistical life and shadow price of carbon. A cash transfer, with an MVPF near 1, is the benchmark to beat. The cut-off MVPF is itself a diagnostic: well above \(\lambda\) means the envelope is too tight; below it means the envelope is too loose.
The chosen portfolio then goes back to the macro-fiscal models, which return the envelope and \(\lambda\). Public capital by sector, its efficiency, the financing shares and the contract liabilities pass to the debt-investment-growth and debt sustainability models of paper 6.5 (Stretton 2026g), which return the debt path and the affordable envelope. Non-market benefits such as health enter \(W\) but never GDP, so the macro model does not count them twice.

title: Read the Excise Schedule Whole, Against the Damage It Should Price
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 7.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full method, the stylized calculations and the country results are in the working paper. Country results are illustrative results from the diagnostic, not official estimates.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Most finance ministries cannot say whether their excise taxes are high or low against the damage the taxed goods do. Schedules grow by amendment for decades, in mixed units and currencies, and fixed-amount rates lose value with every year of inflation.
The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic reads a schedule whole and puts every line on one scale. It maps each line onto 30 standard lines, measures it three comparable ways, and sets fuel taxes against one fixed set of damage values and health taxes against World Health Organization targets.
For diesel, the case for higher taxes is mainly about health and road safety, not climate. In a stylized economy, two-thirds of the damage a liter of diesel does is local air pollution and road use.
Sierra Leone and Liberia tax fuel lightly, alcohol inconsistently, and collect little from health excises. Liberia’s fuel levies are below the carbon cost alone, and it booked no excise on imported tobacco in FY2024.
Index every specific excise, book each line separately, and run the diagnostic every budget. The binding constraint outside fuel is collection, not legislation.


Excise schedules are rarely read whole
Excises matter more for policy than their revenue suggests. Across 37 African countries, excises raised 1.3 percent of GDP on average in 2023 (OECD et al. 2025). But they are the main price instruments a government has for carbon emissions, air pollution, road deaths, tobacco and alcohol, and finance acts change them almost every year.
A typical schedule is a record of decades of separate decisions, not a policy. It began with a few goods easy to tax at the port, then grew line by line: a tobacco increase pushed by the health ministry, a levy on mobile money, a cut for local beer, a rate left in a redenominated currency. Each change made sense when it was made. Together they rarely add up to anything a minister chose, and no one reads the whole document.
Fixed-amount rates lose value silently. A specific excise, set in currency per liter or per pack, loses about 29 percent of its real value over five years of 7 percent inflation without any decision to cut it. When a government finally catches up, the nominal increase looks large and is politically expensive, so the cycle repeats.
Ministries lack a standard way to compare their rates with what the rates are for. International work compares fuel prices with efficient prices for 170 countries (Black et al. 2023), and the World Health Organization (WHO) sets targets for tobacco and alcohol taxes (World Health Organization 2021, 2023). Neither reads a country’s own tax law line by line, and neither covers all excises on one page.


The diagnostic puts every excise line on one scale
Each line is classified by what it is for and mapped onto a standard schedule of 30 lines. The lines cover fuels, vehicles, tobacco, alcohol, soft drinks, plastics, gambling, telecommunications, mobile money and a few legacy items such as cement and edible oils, each in a fixed unit: a liter of fuel, a pack of 20 cigarettes, a liter of pure alcohol. Because the rows never change, the tenth country can be compared with the first without rework (working paper, typology).
Each rate is measured three ways, because each answers a different question. Dollars per standard unit compares countries. Share of the consumer price serves domestic debate and health targets, which are set as shares of price. Revenue as a share of GDP shows what the line is worth to the budget. A line that is high on the first two but raises little is a line that is not collected (working paper, three measures).
Fuel taxes are compared with a benchmark built from one fixed set of damage values. The benchmark adds up, per liter, the cost of carbon, local air pollution, congestion, accidents and road damage, using the method the International Monetary Fund uses for efficient fuel prices (Parry et al. 2014). The same values apply to every country, so the parts can be compared with each other and across countries. Tobacco, alcohol and sugary drinks are compared with WHO’s published targets instead.
The diagnostic measures and does not decide. It reports each gap with a range. Whether to close it, how fast and with what compensation is a decision for government, and keeping the two apart lets a ministry accept the numbers while it argues about the policy.
An AI model drafts the report, and a country economist checks every line against the law. The model works through five stages, from reading the legal texts to the one-page summary. Every number is computed from a parameter sheet and carries a score for how well it is verified, and a figure built from a weak input inherits the weak score. The check is essential: in the two country runs, the line-by-line review corrected 16 and 14 of 49 entries (working paper, the strongest objections).


For diesel, the damage is mostly local
In a stylized economy, diesel is taxed at less than half its corrective rate. Figure 1 shows a fictitious lower-middle-income country. Diesel carries a tax of USD 0.18 per liter against a corrective rate of USD 0.43, with a range of 0.20 to 0.91. Closing the gap would raise about 1.1 to 1.2 percent of GDP in that economy (working paper, stylized example).






Figure 1: In the stylized economy, two-thirds of diesel’s corrective tax is local damage, not carbon. US dollars per liter; whiskers show the low-to-high range; dashed lines show the current tax. Stylized numbers, not a real country. Source: working paper 7.1, Table 4 and Figure 1.



Carbon is only a third of the diesel benchmark. At a carbon value of USD 50 a tonne, carbon accounts for 31 percent of the corrective diesel tax; local air pollution accounts for 35 percent, and congestion, accidents and road damage for the rest. A reform argued on climate grounds alone would rest on the smaller part of the case. Framed as a health and road-safety measure, it rests on the larger.
Petrol in the example is taxed exactly at its benchmark, but only because inflation has eroded it. Its rate was 40 percent above the benchmark in real terms when it was set in 2020 and has not changed since. Without indexation it will fall below the benchmark from now on. The lesson is about indexation, not about petrol.
Two choices move every fuel result, and the diagnostic shows both. Valuing carbon at USD 185 a tonne, the leading recent estimate of climate damage (Rennert et al. 2022), rather than USD 50 nearly quadruples the carbon part and raises the diesel benchmark to USD 0.80. The method used to value lives in low-income countries can change the air pollution and accident parts by a factor of up to five (Robinson et al. 2019). A finding that diesel is undertaxed under every plausible choice is worth more to a ministry than a precise number under one (working paper, valuation defaults).
The benchmark is a floor, not a target. Where fuel is one of the few things a government can tax well, the right fuel tax is above the damage it causes, because fuel also pays for the state. A rate below the benchmark is too low on any view; a rate above it may still be right.


Sierra Leone and Liberia: light fuel taxes, inconsistent alcohol taxes, weak collection
The diagnostic has been run on the 2026 excise law of both countries and checked line by line. Table 1 gives the main results. They are illustrative results from the diagnostic, not official estimates.



Table 1: Sierra Leone and Liberia, 2026: fuel taxed lightly, alcohol inconsistently. Illustrative results from the Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic, not official estimates. Sources: Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic (2026); African mean and OECD figures from OECD et al. (2025); carbon cost is the author’s calculation; WHO target from World Health Organization (2021).

What counts as an excise decides how a country compares. Liberia’s excise law raised only 0.37 percent of GDP in FY2024, because fuel is taxed through earmarked road and refinery levies outside it. International statistics count such levies as excises, and on that basis Liberia raised 1.25 percent, close to the African mean. Sierra Leone’s reported 1.25–1.28 percent for 2024–25 is about twice the figure in the OECD’s data for 2023; the diagnostic’s own reconciliation of collections has still to explain the difference (working paper, revenue).
Fuel is lightly taxed in both countries. Liberia’s levies of USD 0.095 per liter are below the carbon cost alone at USD 50 a tonne, before any air pollution or accident cost is counted. Sierra Leone’s USD 0.23, 16 percent of the pump price, is about twice that carbon cost and about half the carbon cost at USD 185.
Both countries tax alcohol inconsistently, and Liberia taxes the strongest drink least. Liberia taxes spirits at USD 7.50 per liter of pure alcohol against USD 20.00 for beer, and its local spirits rate moved three times in 16 months. Sierra Leone taxes wine below beer per liter of alcohol and runs two beer regimes whose rates differ by up to four times. WHO regards taxes based on alcohol content as the best design for reducing harm (World Health Organization 2023).
Health excises are on the books but collect little. Sierra Leone’s non-fuel excises together collected 0.10–0.16 percent of GDP, although cigarettes, beer and sugary drinks are all taxed; its cigarette excise is about a fifth of WHO’s target. Liberia’s revenue authority booked no excise on imported tobacco in FY2024 or early FY2025. Some current rates could not even be read in the published law.


What to do
Finance ministries: index every specific excise under one rule. One automatic inflation adjustment covering fuel, tobacco and alcohol is cheaper politically than three separate fights, and it ends the cycle of silent erosion and expensive catch-up. Liberia has legislated it from 2027; Sierra Leone has not.
Revenue authorities: book each excise line separately and publish legible schedules. A tax that cannot be traced in the accounts cannot be managed, and a rate that cannot be read in the law cannot be enforced. Reconcile collections across the revenue authority, the finance ministry and international statistics every year.
Tax policy units: run the diagnostic every budget cycle, and argue diesel on health. With the same standard schedule and the same damage values, the change from last year shows on one page. Where diesel is undertaxed, lead with air pollution and road deaths; where a pump-price rise is too visible, a feebate on new vehicles prices part of the same damage without it (Brief 1.2).
Development partners and analysts using AI: never publish an unreviewed excise review. The model saves time in reading and arithmetic, but a third of its entries needed correction. Require a source reference for every line and a review against the gazetted law.


Related papers in this series

The working paper behind this brief: the method, the stylized calculations, the country results and the strongest objections.
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 6.1: the Total Effective Carbon Price, which measures carbon pricing by the emissions it cuts (Stretton 2026c).
No. 1.2: feebates, the full carbon price at the margin without the carbon bill (Stretton 2026b).
No. 5.4: why published price elasticities overstate how fast fuel use responds (Stretton 2026a).

title: A Global Fiscal Indicators Dashboard for Climate-Fiscal Analysis
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 7.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full account, with the build rules, the scoring, the check against the publishers and the sources, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Climate-fiscal advice often fixes on the wrong constraint because the right numbers take days to gather. Debt, tax, capital spending, the cost of capital, fuel subsidies and the power mix sit in a dozen databases with different names, units and years.
One page can show them all, for 217 economies, with the year and source of every number. The Global Fiscal Indicators dashboard arranges 80 public indicators in twelve blocks, each answering one question, and scores each from 1 to 10.
The profile separates problems that call for different levers. Indonesia collects tax of only 10 percent of GDP and spends 3 percent on explicit fuel subsidies; South Africa collects 25 percent but pays 19 percent of its revenue in net interest.
A first view is only as good as its compilation. Checked against the IMF’s own files, most values hold, but three faults appear: a mislabeled interest measure, a denominator that reverses a reading, and a modeled renewable share far from observed generation.
Use the profile to choose the next question, not to issue a verdict, and publish the build. The next step for the tool is a carbon-pricing block.


Advice goes wrong when the first number found frames the problem
Before advising on carbon pricing, subsidy reform or climate investment, an adviser needs to know which constraint binds. A country that cannot raise revenue needs different help from one that raises plenty but spends a fifth of it on interest, or one that has money but cannot execute capital budgets. Each calls for a different climate-fiscal lever: broaden the tax base, reform subsidies, price pollution, or fix public investment before scaling it.
The numbers that reveal the constraint are scattered. Debt and interest are in the IMF’s World Economic Outlook, taxes in the IMF’s revenue database, fuel subsidies in the IMF’s subsidy estimates, capital budget execution in World Bank budget data, public investment management in PEFA assessments, and the cost of capital in academic datasets (International Monetary Fund 2026a, 2026b; Black et al. 2025). Assembling them takes a day for one country and a week for a region, and the next analyst starts again.
Each existing database answers one part of the question. The cross-country fiscal space database measures debt sustainability and market access for up to 200 countries (Kose et al. 2022). The IMF’s Climate Change Indicators Dashboard brings climate indicators onto one platform (International Monetary Fund 2021). Neither puts fiscal space, the capacity to spend, the cost of capital and the energy-fiscal position side by side.


Twelve questions on one page
The dashboard is organized around the questions an adviser asks, not around datasets. Four assessment blocks carry the diagnosis: can the country pay for it (fiscal space), can it build it (public investment management), what does capital cost it, and who finances it and with what risk. Three context blocks explain it: how much fossil and climate money runs through the budget, whether the country sells or buys fossil fuels, and how its power is generated. Five appendices hold reference material, such as retail energy prices and the starting point of the macro-fiscal models (working paper, what the dashboard assembles).
Every value is traceable to a public file and a year. A script turns about twenty public downloads into one long table, with the source file and year on every row. Nothing is filled in: a missing value stays missing, and the profile counts the gaps. The build stops if its configuration asks for an indicator the data do not supply, a rule adopted after an earlier version lost indicators without anyone noticing (working paper, the build pipeline). The build itself is not yet public; every input is.
Scores rank each country against all others, and there is deliberately no overall index. Each indicator is rescaled from 1 to 10 between the 5th and 95th percentile of all economies, so that a few extreme values do not squeeze everyone else into the middle. Scores of 7 and above read Good, below 4 Bad. There is no defensible way to weigh fiscal space against delivery capacity, and the standard handbook on composite indicators warns that a single index “may disguise serious failings in some dimensions” (OECD and European Commission Joint Research Centre 2008). Within each block the dashboard shows a simple average, which is a reading aid only: the analyst should look at the weakest indicator and the count of missing values (working paper, scoring).
The same data feed the scenario tool, so the profile and the model agree. The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool, which links a climate investment program and carbon pricing to growth, revenue and debt, reads the same panel (paper 6.5) (Stretton 2026d). A correction in one reaches the other on the next build.


Four economies, four different problems
The profile separates a revenue problem from a debt-service problem. Table 1 shows selected indicators for Colombia, Indonesia, Morocco and South Africa in 2024, with the score each assessment indicator receives against all economies, and Figure 1 shows the main contrasts. These are illustrative readings from public data, not assessments of any country.

Indonesia’s problem is revenue, and its subsidies are a large claim on it. Its debt, 40 percent of GDP, is the lowest of the four. But it collects tax of only 10.1 percent of GDP, below the 12¾ percent that IMF research identifies as a tipping point for growth (Gaspar et al. 2016), so net interest still takes 15 percent of revenue. Explicit fuel subsidies cost 3.0 percent of GDP, about 30 percent of tax revenue, and gasoline sells for 0.57 dollars a liter, below its supply cost (Black et al. 2025). The useful questions are about subsidy reform and the tax base, not about debt limits (working paper, the comparison).
South Africa’s problem is debt service, and its largest climate-fiscal lever is pricing pollution. It collects the most tax of the four, 25.2 percent of GDP, but net interest takes 18.9 percent of revenue, the most of the four. It pays no explicit fuel subsidies, but its unpriced environmental costs from fossil fuels, which the IMF calls implicit subsidies, are 12.9 percent of GDP, the largest of the four; 84 percent of its electricity comes from fossil fuels (Ember 2025). The lever is pricing those costs; the constraint is that debt service limits how much public money can go into the transition at the same time.
Morocco and Colombia sit in between, for different reasons. Morocco pays the least interest relative to revenue, 7.9 percent, yet spends 1.9 percent of GDP on explicit subsidies while charging the highest gasoline price of the four, so its subsidies sit on other fuels. Colombia’s fiscal position is moderate, and its excises, at 1.06 percent of GDP, are as small as Indonesia’s, which an excise diagnostic could examine line by line (Brief 7.1) (Stretton 2026c).


A first view is only as good as its compilation
Checked against the IMF’s own files, most values hold. Tax revenue, net interest and the excise shares in Table 1 reproduce exactly from the IMF’s revenue database and its October 2026 fiscal data. Gross debt matches for three countries; Morocco’s was revised from 67.7 to 67.0 percent of GDP after the dashboard’s August download (working paper, the check).
Three faults turned up, each of a kind any compilation can carry for years. First, the indicator the dashboard calls “interest-to-revenue” is net interest, and its filter drops the countries that earn more interest than they pay, the strongest fiscal positions. Second, the dashboard’s excise measure, excises as a share of total revenue, ranks Colombia lowest of the four because its revenue is high, not because its excises are low; as a share of GDP, the measure paper 7.1 uses, Colombia’s excises equal Indonesia’s. Third, the renewable share of electricity the dashboard holds is a modeled series that differs from observed generation by 5 to 19 percentage points: for Colombia, 79.9 percent against 61.4 percent observed (Ember 2025).
Subsidy shares depend on the GDP figure used. The dashboard divides the IMF’s dollar estimates by the IMF’s World Economic Outlook GDP and gets 12.9 percent of GDP for South Africa’s implicit subsidies; the IMF’s own table says 11.9 percent (Black et al. 2025). Both are defensible; a profile must say which it uses.
Traceability is what made the check quick. Because every value names its source and year, the check took an afternoon. A compilation without that record would have carried the same faults into advice and into the models that read it.


Carbon pricing is the gap to fill first
A climate-fiscal dashboard without carbon prices misses the main climate-fiscal lever. The dashboard does not yet read carbon prices. Three public measures exist: explicit carbon taxes and trading prices (World Bank 2026), the OECD’s effective carbon rates, which add fuel excises (OECD 2023), and the World Bank’s total carbon price, which also nets out fuel subsidies (Agnolucci et al. 2024). Each can be added through the dashboard’s routine for new sources.
The Total Effective Carbon Price would complete the picture. It expresses a country’s whole policy mix, including standards and feebates, as the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much (Brief 6.1) (Stretton 2026b). Beside the fiscal blocks, it would show not only whether a country can afford the transition, but how hard its current policies already push.


What to do
Finance ministries and development-bank country teams: start climate-fiscal work with a one-page profile, and read it for the next question. Find the binding constraint (money, delivery, the cost of capital or financing) before choosing between subsidy reform, carbon pricing, tax measures or investment. Read the weakest indicator in each block and its year, not the block average.
Teams that compile cross-country indicators: record the source file and year of every value, never impute, and check against the publishers. Label derived measures by what they compute. Report ratios on the denominator the related literature uses, such as excise revenue as a share of GDP. Prefer observed series to modeled ones, and label modeled ones.
The dashboard’s owners: fix the three faults, add carbon pricing, and publish the build. Rename the interest measure and keep net creditors; add excise revenue as a share of GDP; read the renewable share from observed generation; add explicit, effective and total carbon prices; and release the code so that anyone can rerun it (working paper, limits).

title: Converting a VAT into a Destination Carbon Tax
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full analysis, with the proofs, the input–output calibration and the legal detail, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Europe prices the carbon it emits, not the carbon it consumes. Forty percent of the carbon in what EU households buy subject to VAT is emitted outside the Union, where neither the Emissions Trading System nor the border mechanism reaches most of it.
Put a carbon component inside VAT. Every business charges a price per tonne of the carbon embodied in what it sells and deducts what it paid on its inputs, as it does for VAT. Imports pay at the border; exports leave free.
Use one published default per product category, the same for every origin, and let sellers prove a lower figure. That treats like products alike and rewards clean exporters.
Cut the value part of VAT each year by last year’s carbon receipts. The swap then raises no extra revenue, whatever the pace of decarbonization.
Oblige fuel suppliers now; negotiate the VAT component next. A forward obligation on the few suppliers of heating and road fuel can pass by qualified majority; the VAT component needs unanimity.


Europe prices what it makes, not what it buys
EU carbon pricing stops at the factory gate and at the border of six sectors. The Emissions Trading System (ETS) prices power and heavy industry where they emit. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) charges imports of cement, iron and steel, aluminum, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen for their embodied carbon (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023b). Nothing prices the carbon in an imported shirt, phone or sofa.
Much of the carbon in European consumption is emitted abroad, and imports carry more of it per euro. On the working paper’s input–output calculation from Eurostat data for 2022, households’ VAT-taxable purchases embodied 0.41 kg CO₂e per euro, and 40 percent of that carbon was emitted outside the EU. Goods imported from outside the EU carried about 1.7 times as much carbon per euro as the same mix of goods made in the EU: 0.76 against 0.45 kg (working paper, defaults).
A price on production misses that carbon and handicaps European producers. It makes goods dearer to make in Europe than to make elsewhere for sale in Europe. A price on consumption falls equally on domestic and imported goods and spares exports, so moving production abroad does not avoid it.
This brief is the consumption track of the series’ two-track architecture (Stretton 2026d). Production is priced separately, by a revenue-neutral feebate on emissions intensity (Brief 1.2).


A carbon component inside VAT prices consumption wherever the carbon was emitted
VAT already reaches every good sold in Europe, on the destination basis. Imports pay it and exports are relieved of it (OECD 2017). But it charges value, not carbon, so it gives no reason to choose the cleaner good.
The carbon component makes part of VAT follow carbon. Each registered business charges, on its sales, a carbon price per tonne of the good’s embodied carbon, and deducts the carbon component on its purchases. Its net payment is the carbon price on the carbon added at its own stage, and the final buyer pays it on the whole supply chain. The invoice and the return gain a column, not a new administration.
An example shows the chain at work (stylized, 2032, carbon price €100 per tonne). A steel mill emits 400 kg making steel and pays €32 under the ETS; an appliance maker adds 100 kg and a retailer 20 kg. The carbon component raises €20 along the chain: €8 from the mill (€40 less the €32 already paid), €10 from the maker, €2 from the retailer. With the ETS payment, the 520 kg bear exactly €100 per tonne (working paper, the VAT chain).
Every tonne bears one price. The carbon component deducts any carbon price already paid upstream, under the ETS, CBAM, the fuel obligation below or a recognized foreign scheme (Stretton 2026a). A revenue-neutral feebate earns no deduction, because on average it charges nothing net; it supplies the incentive at production, and the carbon component supplies the price at consumption.
Electricity carries its generation carbon to the final user through the same chain. Power is sold on a VAT invoice. The generator’s invoice states its carbon and the carbon price it has already paid, so the household pays the full consumption price on electricity’s carbon, net of what was paid upstream.
The weak points are VAT’s own. Banking, insurance, rents, health and education, 31 percent of household spending, are exempt from VAT, and exemption breaks the carbon chain too. They are low-carbon, so little carbon escapes.


Defaults the same for every origin, open to rebuttal
Most firms would apply a published default, as they now apply a VAT rate. The Commission would publish, each year, a default intensity for each product category: the average for EU production of that category. Domestic goods carry it through the chain; imports carry the same default, whatever their origin. Only firms that want to pay less need to measure anything, which answers the oldest objection to a carbon-added tax, that every firm would need a carbon footprint for every product (McLure 2010; McAusland and Najjar 2015).
One default for every origin treats like products alike and avoids a trade fight. It is the strongest position under the trade rules for internal taxes (Mehling et al. 2019). Charging imports at each exporter’s own intensity would cut China’s manufacturing exports by about a fifth (Mattoo et al. 2009) and invite exporters to send only their cleanest output to Europe (Neuhoff et al. 2026). The cost is generosity to imports at first: like for like, the EU default charges imports about 60 percent of their embodied carbon.
Rebuttal turns the defaults into an incentive. A seller that verifies a lower intensity pays on its own figure, and each buyer down the chain carries that figure forward, so the saving reaches the shop price. A €100 imported phone in 2032 pays €2.80 at the electronics default of 0.28 kg per euro; an exporter that verifies 0.15 kg pays €1.50 and gains €1.30 a phone over its rivals. Verification should cover a whole plant, not single consignments (working paper, rebuttal).


A rule, not a schedule, keeps the swap neutral
A fixed schedule of VAT cuts would gamble with over €100 billion a year. Suppose the value part of VAT fell from 15 to 10 percent by 2037 while the carbon price rose €20 a year to €200 per tonne. If the basket’s carbon fell to 0.15 kg per euro the swap would lose €120 billion a year in 2037; if it stayed at 0.41 it would gain €119 billion (working paper, fiscal design).
Each member state should cut its value component each year by the previous year’s carbon receipts. The rule needs no forecast and moves no money between member states. Starting from 15 percent, the value component ends between 10.8 and 12.7 percent in 2037, depending on whether the basket’s carbon per euro falls 3 or 7 percent a year (Figure 1). The carbon component then replaces about a fifth of the value component in the central case.



Table 1: Total VAT rate (percent) under the neutrality rule, central case: carbon price rising €20 per tonne a year from 2027 to €200 in 2037; basket carbon per euro falling 5 percent a year from 2022. Clean goods get cheaper and carbon-intensive goods dearer, while the average tax barely moves. In the central case a good at 0.10 kg per euro pays 13.8 percent in 2037 and one at 0.80 kg per euro 27.8 percent, against 15 percent for both today (Table 1). Clean goods then breach the EU’s 15 percent floor on the standard rate, so the floor must be restated or the path must start from each member state’s own standard rate, all of which are 17 percent or more (Mengden 2026).






Figure 1: The neutrality rule. Left: value component of VAT when it falls each year by the previous year’s carbon receipts, for three rates of decline in the basket’s carbon per euro, against a fixed path. Right: total rate on goods of given carbon intensity in the central case. Source: working paper, Figure 2.





The swap is mildly regressive; returning the fuel obligation per household fixes it
The carbon component itself takes almost the same share of every household’s budget. At €200 per tonne it takes 5.5 percent of spending for the poorest fifth and 5.3 percent for the richest, on 2022 intensities in 22 member states (working paper, distribution).
Poorer households gain less from the VAT cut, because more of their budget goes on exempt rent. Net of the national value cut, the poorest fifth pays 0.4 percent of spending more and the richest 0.2 percent less. Because each member state recycles its own receipts, no money moves between them; one EU-wide cut would instead cost Bulgaria, Poland and Slovakia 0.7–0.8 percent of household spending, the pattern other studies find (Feindt et al. 2021).
Returning the fuel obligation’s receipts as an equal sum per household more than offsets the regressivity. The poorest fifth then gains 1.2 percent of spending and the richest loses 0.3 percent.


Fuel for homes and vehicles needs a forward obligation
VAT cannot reach the carbon in heating and road fuel. That carbon is released when the fuel is burned, after the last sale: 691 Mt CO₂e from EU households’ heating and transport in 2022. At €200 per tonne it is worth €138 billion a year, or €310 per resident.
A few large firms supply that fuel, and they decide the assets that lock in emissions for decades. Refiners, fuel importers and gas suppliers plan refineries, pipelines and networks. A tax reset every budget does not move that investment, because a government cannot bind its successors and firms discount its promises (Kydland and Prescott 1977; Helm et al. 2003).
The obligation should be ETS2 with a price floor rising for a decade. Each supplier surrenders one unit for each tonne of CO₂ in the fuel it sells, with a floor rising €20 a year to €200 per tonne in 2037, in step with the VAT component. That adds about €40 per MWh to gas and €0.54 per liter to diesel by 2037. ETS2, the EU’s new trading system for buildings and road fuel, already puts the obligation on fuel suppliers (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023a), but its start has been put back to 2028 (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2026), and it releases extra allowances when the price passes €45 per tonne (in 2020 prices) while setting no floor. A published floor, which the law may raise but not lower before 2037, gives suppliers a price they can bank on.


The obligation can pass now; the VAT component needs unanimity
A carbon component of VAT changes the harmonized VAT system, which needs a unanimous Council. Article 113 of the Treaty requires unanimity for turnover taxes, and the environmental legal basis reserves “provisions primarily of a fiscal nature” to unanimity too (European Union 2016). CBAM passed by qualified majority as a certificate scheme, not a tax, and Poland has asked the Court of Justice to annul even that, on the ground that it is primarily fiscal (Court of Justice of the European Union 2023) (working paper, legal basis).
A coalition of member states could start nationally, if it designs the charge per tonne. EU law lets a member state levy taxes that are not turnover taxes (Council of the European Union 2006). A charge per tonne of embodied carbon, rather than a percentage of price, has a defensible claim to that status; a second percentage on the VAT invoice probably does not.
The fuel obligation can be adopted by qualified majority now. It is a compliance scheme like ETS2, of which it would be an amendment.


What to do
The Commission should propose the forward obligation now, as an amendment to ETS2 that publishes a price floor rising to €200 per tonne in 2037, with receipts returned per household.
The Commission should obtain a formal legal opinion on the carbon component covering Articles 113 and 192(2)(a) of the Treaty and Articles 97 and 401 of the VAT Directive, and begin building a default schedule at the level of customs product codes, with a procedure for verified rebuttal.
Finance ministries should adopt the neutrality rule for any swap: cut the value component each year by the previous year’s carbon receipts, member state by member state.
A willing coalition should not wait for unanimity. It can legislate a national charge per tonne, coordinated on defaults and verification, and test it before others join.

title: Feebates: The Full Carbon Price at the Margin, Without the Carbon Bill
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full analysis, with the model, proofs and calibration, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
A carbon tax charges producers for every tonne they still emit, and that bill, not the incentive, is what stalls it. In coal-heavy power and in industry that competes abroad, governments exempt the biggest emitters or keep the rate low.
A feebate keeps the incentive and drops most of the bill. Producers dirtier than their sector’s average pay; cleaner ones are rebated. The payments cancel, the treasury neither gains nor loses, and every tonne cut is still worth the full rate.
Power plants are run and built exactly as under a tax. What consumers pay depends on how power is sold: almost nothing extra where a single buyer sets tariffs at average cost, and much less than a tax, but not nothing, in a wholesale market.
The benchmark decides whether a feebate works. It must fall as the sector cleans, cover all fuels, and measure a dominant state utility against everyone else’s average.
Coal-heavy countries should legislate a feebate at the rate they would have wanted for a tax. Importers should credit it at the border.


A carbon tax charges for the whole bill, not just the change
A carbon tax sends two signals, and only one of them cuts emissions. It makes coal dearer than gas and gas dearer than solar, so power companies run and build cleaner plants. It also charges every producer for each tonne it still emits, which raises the sector’s average cost and moves that carbon bill to the treasury. The first signal is the policy. The second is a transfer, and in coal-heavy power and trade-exposed industry it decides whether the policy survives.
In coal-heavy power the bill is enormous. Coal is cheap per unit of energy and rich in carbon. At $50 per tonne of CO₂, a tax adds $4.73 per gigajoule to coal bought at $2.50, a rise of 189 percent, using standard emission factors (IPCC 2006) and illustrative fuel prices. A tax at that rate on India’s power sector would collect about $70 billion a year from generators (working paper, country cases).
Concentrated losses on organized producers are the classic recipe for defeat (Olson 1965). Canada shows the pattern: it set its consumer fuel charge to zero from 1 April 2025 but kept output-based pricing for industry, which charges only emissions above a benchmark (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2026). Visibility matters more than true incidence: in France after the 2018–19 protests, 70 percent of households would have gained from a carbon tax with a dividend, but only 14 percent believed they would (Douenne and Fabre 2022).


A feebate keeps the incentive and drops most of the bill
Each producer pays or receives the carbon price on the gap between its emissions per unit of output and its sector’s benchmark. A coal plant above the benchmark pays a fee on each megawatt-hour; a solar plant below it receives a rebate. With the benchmark set at the sector’s average, fees pay for rebates exactly, so the treasury neither gains nor loses. A tax whose revenue is returned to producers in proportion to output, called output-based rebating, is the same instrument (Fischer 2001).
Every tonne a producer cuts is still worth the full carbon price. Cutting emissions per unit of output lowers a fee or raises a rebate by exactly the rate, as under a tax. What disappears is the charge on the average producer’s remaining emissions. The IMF describes the instrument for power in these terms (International Monetary Fund 2019) and has proposed it for industry in Mexico (Black et al. 2021).
The price of the design is a weaker signal to use less of the product. Because average costs barely rise, buyers have little reason to consume less. The IMF finds that packages of feebates and regulations achieve 50–70 percent of the emission cuts of a carbon tax with the same incentive at the margin (International Monetary Fund 2019). In power that loss is small, because demand for electricity responds little to its price in the short run, and partly welcome, because cheap clean power is what draws transport and heating away from oil and gas.


Power plants are run and built as under a tax
A feebate and a tax at the same rate put plants in the same order of dispatch. The benchmark shifts every plant’s cost by the same amount, so the cheapest plant under a tax is the cheapest under a feebate, and coal is switched to gas at the same carbon price (working paper, the power-sector model). The UK’s carbon price on generators cut power-sector emissions by 20.5–26 percent a year over 2013–2017 (Leroutier 2022); a feebate at the same rate keeps that signal.
The choice between new clean and new coal capacity is also the same. The benchmark cancels when the two are compared, so a feebate steers investment as strongly as a tax. The cost of capital matters more than the choice of instrument: in the working paper’s illustrative example, raising the cost of capital from 6 to 12 percent raises the carbon price at which new clean capacity beats new coal from $8 to $29 per tonne (working paper, investment). Financing costs for renewables are markedly higher in developing countries (Steffen 2020), so cheaper finance complements the feebate.
The feebate tightens by itself as the grid cleans. As clean output grows, the average falls, so the fee on each megawatt-hour of coal rises toward the full tax without any vote to raise the rate. In the working paper’s simulation starting from India’s 2024 mix, the net fee on coal rises from $11 to $38 per megawatt-hour over 25 years at a rate of $50.


What consumers pay depends on how power is sold
Where a single buyer sets tariffs at average cost, a feebate barely moves them. Fees and rebates cancel inside the buyer’s pool, so the tariff rises only by the cost of switching to cleaner plants. In 2024 generation mixes at $50 per tonne, that is $1.3 per megawatt-hour in India, $3.7 in Indonesia and nothing in South Africa, which has no gas to switch to, against $33–40 for a tax (Table 1). Most power in the three countries is sold this way today: in India short-term trading was about 12.5 percent of generation in 2023–24 (Central Electricity Regulatory Commission 2024).
The protection depends on the buyer netting fees against rebates. If coal generators pass their fees through their contracts while clean generators keep their rebates, the feebate’s tariff effect rises to $6–13 per megawatt-hour. The buyer, not the contracts, should collect fees and pay rebates.
In a wholesale market where coal sets the price, a feebate raises the price by much less than a tax, but not by nothing. Every generator is paid the price of the last plant needed. If that plant is coal, dirtier than the average, its fee is added to the price: $7.5–18 per megawatt-hour in the three countries, against $47 for a tax. In a market a feebate is in effect a tax whose revenue is handed back to consumers per megawatt-hour; generators earn exactly what they would under the tax (working paper, uniform-price market). South Africa legislated in 2024 for a competitive wholesale market (Republic of South Africa 2024), so this is its relevant future case.

Low tariffs last only if electricity’s own consumption charge stays low. The series’ companion briefs pair a production feebate with a charge on what households consume (Brief 1.1, Brief 1.3). Applied to electricity at the full rate, that charge would put the household price back where a tax would. The charge on electricity can rightly be set lower while the grid is coal-heavy: what matters for climate is that households choose electricity over oil and gas, which bear their own charge, and power is barely traded, so a low rate causes no leakage (working paper, why power belongs on the production track).


The benchmark decides whether a feebate works
The benchmark must fall as the sector cleans. France’s car feebate kept fixed thresholds while buyers moved to rebated models: sales of those models rose from 20 percent of the market to nearly 50 percent, and a scheme meant to balance cost the state about €285 million in 2008 (D’Haultfœuille et al. 2014). A benchmark recomputed each year from last year’s average, with any shortfall carried into the next year’s rebate rate, keeps the scheme in balance.
A dominant state utility pays its fees largely to itself. A firm with most of the market lowers the average when it cuts its own emissions, so it sees only part of the rate. Eskom, which supplies over 86 percent of South Africa’s needs (Eskom 2026), would face about $7 of a $50 rate; NTPC, with 24 percent of India’s generation (NTPC Limited 2026), about $38. Measuring each large firm against the average of all the others restores the full rate. For dispatch the remedy is simpler: the system operator ranks plants by cost plus the full carbon rate (working paper, benchmark design).
One benchmark across coal and gas keeps the switching signal. Separate benchmarks per fuel would reward efficiency within each fuel and nothing between them. In China’s power-sector trading system, using three benchmarks instead of one raises the cost per tonne of reducing emissions by 18 percent (Goulder et al. 2022). If coal owners must be compensated, a time-limited payment tied to closures does it without blunting the signal.
New plants should be measured against the benchmark but kept out of it for their first few years. A large new plant then faces the full rate, its early rebates are known when it is financed, and a new coal unit cannot raise the benchmark and dilute the fee on existing coal. The cost is a small deficit while clean entrants are excluded, recovered the following year. The EU’s free allocation to industry works the same way: benchmarks come from existing installations’ data, and new installations draw on a reserve (European Commission 2026).


Industry: protect exporters, then add the consumption charge
In industry a feebate removes most of the competitiveness cost of a carbon price. In the companion working paper’s calibration for hot-rolled steel at $80 per tonne, a tax raises producer prices by 21–43 percent for most exporters, a feebate by 7–14 percent (Brief 1.1). Output-based rebating captures many of the gains of a full border adjustment for key manufacturing sectors (Fischer and Fox 2012).
Working systems already price industry against benchmarks. Canada’s output-based pricing system charges facilities above a standard per unit of output and credits those below it (Government of Canada 2019). With standards set at 80–95 percent of the average, it raises net revenue. It survived the end of the consumer charge, but in May 2026 its price path was cut from C$170 to C$115 per tonne in 2030 (International Carbon Action Partnership 2026). The EU’s free allocation gives each installation allowances equal to a best-performer benchmark times its output level (European Commission 2026), and it is being phased out for the sectors covered by the border mechanism between 2026 and 2034 (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023).
Border rules do not yet credit feebates. The EU’s border mechanism deducts only a carbon price effectively paid abroad, net of rebates (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2025), so the average exporter under a revenue-neutral feebate earns no deduction. Crediting the feebate at its carbon-price equivalent, the tax that would cut emissions as much, would fix this (Brief 1.4, Brief 6.1).


The record supports the incentive and the benchmark warnings
Sweden’s refunded charge on nitrogen oxides is the clearest test. From 1992 large combustion plants paid about $5,000 per tonne of nitrogen oxides, and almost all the revenue went back to them in proportion to the energy they produced. Mean emission rates fell about 40 percent between 1992 and 1998, at a charge level that a tax could not have reached politically (Sterner and Höglund 2000; Sterner and Höglund Isaksson 2006).
France’s car feebate and Canada’s industrial system carry the warnings. France’s fixed benchmark turned a balanced scheme into a subsidy that raised total car sales, so its net effect on emissions was negative (D’Haultfœuille et al. 2014). Canada’s rate was cut when politics turned. A benchmark that tracks the average and a rate set by published formula guard against both.


What to do
Coal-heavy countries that sell power through a single buyer: legislate a power feebate now. Set it at the rate you would have wanted for a carbon tax, have the buyer collect fees and pay rebates, recompute the benchmark each year by formula, measure any firm with more than about a fifth of output against the others’ average, and pay for coal closures with time-limited transfers rather than separate coal benchmarks.
Countries liberalizing their power markets: keep long-term contracts for existing plants while the feebate beds in. A wholesale market passes the fee of the marginal coal plant to consumers; contracts that return the rents of clean generators to consumers limit it.
All adopters: keep the consumption charge on electricity low while the grid is coal-heavy, and run the same instrument for steel, cement, aluminum and fertilizer. Add the consumption charge on goods when the VAT system can carry it (Brief 1.3).
The EU and other importers: credit feebates at the border at their carbon-price equivalent. Development banks can lend against the predictable rebates that clean entrants will earn.

title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.4, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. Legal texts as of 31 October 2026. All CBAM amounts are in euros. The full analysis, with the model, proofs, calibration and legal texts, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
The EU’s border charge on carbon rewards exporters for routing clean steel to Europe, not for making cleaner steel. Because carbon is measured plant by plant, a steelmaker can ship its scrap-based output to the EU and save hundreds of euros a tonne with no fall in emissions.
It credits carbon taxes paid but not the price signal that cuts emissions. A revenue-neutral feebate gives every producer the full carbon price on each tonne it cuts, yet earns nothing, because the average producer pays nothing net.
Measure by country and sector, and credit the country’s price signal. One value per exporting country and sector removes the gain from routing; crediting the country’s own price signal restores the incentive each plant loses.
Recognition is worth hundreds of euros a tonne to the most carbon-intensive exporters. Opting into this rule with a feebate at the EU price would remove India’s €445 per tonne charge on hot-rolled steel.
Phase recognition in as free allocation to EU producers is phased out, and review relocation at each step.


Two rules undercut the mechanism’s second purpose
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is the first border charge on embodied carbon at scale. Since January 2026, EU importers of iron and steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity owe certificates for the carbon embodied in what they buy, priced in line with the EU Emissions Trading System (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023b, 2025). Free allocation to EU producers is phased out as the charge comes in, by 2034 under current law (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023a) and by 2038 under a Commission proposal of July 2026 (European Commission 2026b). At €80 per tonne of CO₂ and full phase-in, the charge on a tonne of hot-rolled steel declared at the Commission’s default value is €445 from India, €331 from China and €252 from Türkiye.
The mechanism has two purposes, and its rules serve only the first. The first is a level playing field: imported steel should bear the same carbon cost as EU steel, and no tonne should be charged twice. The second is to encourage exporting countries to cut their own emissions. Two rules undercut the second. Embodied carbon is measured plant by plant, from verified installation data or from a country default value raised by a mark-up of up to 30 percent (European Commission 2025a). And the charge falls only by a carbon price “effectively paid in a third country”, taking into account “any rebate or other form of compensation” (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2025, Art. 9(1)).


Exporters can cut their bill without cutting emissions
Plant-by-plant measurement lets a steelmaker choose which plant supplies Europe. Steel made from scrap in an electric arc furnace emits far less than steel made from iron ore in a blast furnace: about 0.3 against 2.2 tonnes of CO₂ per tonne, counting direct and indirect emissions (International Energy Agency 2020). A producer with both can send the scrap-based steel to the EU and keep selling blast-furnace steel elsewhere.
In a stylized exporter, the carbon the border sees falls by three quarters while emissions do not change. Take a producer making 10 million tonnes a year, 8 million in blast furnaces and 2 million from scrap, and selling a tenth of its output to the EU at €80 per tonne of CO₂. Shipping only scrap-based steel to Europe cuts the embodied carbon on EU-bound steel from 1.68 to 0.40 million tonnes of CO₂ and the bill from €134 million to €32 million a year (Figure 1). Its emissions stay at 16.8 million tonnes (working paper, shuffling model).






Figure 1: Route shuffling in a stylized steel exporter (10 Mt a year, 8 Mt by blast furnace at 2.0 tCO₂/t, 2 Mt from scrap at 0.4 tCO₂/t, 1 Mt sold to the EU, €80/tCO₂, full phase-in; all numbers stylized). Sending scrap-based steel to the EU cuts the carbon the border sees by 76 percent (A) while the exporter’s emissions do not change (B). The charge falls if each plant is measured, but not if the country and sector are (C). Source: working paper, Figure 1.



Scrap is limited, so the cut is mostly relabeling. The supply of scrap is set by how much steel reaches the end of its life (International Energy Agency 2020), so scrap used for Europe’s steel is replaced elsewhere by ore-based steel. The same move works for aluminum (Assous et al. 2024).
The stakes are of the same order as the charge itself. At €80, supplying Europe from scrap rather than at the country’s average saves €310 per tonne of hot-rolled steel for India, €223 for China and €162 for Türkiye (Table 1). Sandbag puts the bill on imports from China at €313 million a year if exporters reroute, against €590 million if they do not (Assous et al. 2024). The law asks the Commission to report on “resource shuffling” from 2028 but gives it no tool to stop it (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023b, Art. 30), and its December 2025 anti-circumvention proposal does not reach routing between plants (European Commission 2025b).


The rules credit payments, so a feebate earns nothing
The price paid and the price signal are different things. The price paid is what a producer hands over, on average, after rebates. The price signal is what each extra tonne of CO₂ per tonne of steel costs it, which is what drives investment in cleaner plants. For a flat carbon tax the two are the same. For a revenue-neutral feebate they diverge completely: each producer pays the carbon price on emissions per tonne above its sector’s average and is rebated below it, so every producer faces the full price at the margin while the average producer pays nothing (Brief 1.2).
The Commission’s draft rules net out exactly the rebate that makes a feebate work. The draft implementing regulation of May 2026 counts emissions “below an emission intensity baseline” as compensation to be deducted (European Commission 2026a, Art. 8(1)(b)(ii)). A feebate therefore earns no credit, although a carbon tax at the same rate, which produces the same cuts, would earn all of it. Returning revenue to industry is what makes a high carbon price passable in a large emitter, and it is what removes recognition (Brief 1.1).
The default carbon price, the only route for most exporters, covers explicit prices only. An exporter that declares default values can claim a reduction only through a yearly default carbon price, which the Commission “may” set from 2027 and only “where a carbon price was set by the rules applicable in the third country” (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2025, Art. 9(4)). A consortium led by Technopolis is preparing the methodology for 2026–2028 from an inventory of emissions trading systems and carbon taxes (Technopolis Group 2026). For a country that prices carbon through fuel taxes, subsidy reform or a feebate, the default is zero, although such pricing has been measured for 142 countries (Agnolucci et al. 2024).


Measure by country and sector, and credit the country’s price signal
A single value for each exporting country and sector removes the gain from routing. If every tonne of hot-rolled steel from a country is charged at that sector’s verified average, updated each year, it no longer matters which plant ships it. Neuhoff et al. (2026) propose standardized values for all producers, and note that these give producers abroad no direct incentive to cut emissions.
On its own, a country average leaves each plant almost no incentive. A mill that cuts its emissions lowers the average for all its country’s exporters, so it keeps only a sliver of the reward. A mill with a tenth of its country’s output, selling a tenth of that to the EU, keeps €0.80 of each €80 it saves the country. A value fixed for years, like today’s default values, gives no incentive at all.
A domestic price signal supplies the missing incentive, and crediting it rewards the country for adopting one. A feebate at the EU price gives every plant the full €80 per tonne on all its output, not only the tenth sold in Europe. The proposed rule is that importers pay the EU price less a recognized foreign price, on the country-sector average carbon content, where the recognized price adds to the price paid a weight on the unpaid part of the signal (working paper, liability formula). The charge does not depend on which plant ships, and a feebate at the EU price stays the exporter’s lowest-cost choice. Mehling and Ritz (2023) proposed the same top-up for explicit carbon prices only.
Recognition changes what an exporting country would choose for itself. A country selling a tenth of its steel to the EU would choose a feebate of €8 under today’s rules and €21 with full recognition, because it bears the cost of abatement on all its output but gets relief only on EU sales. A feebate at the full EU price pays for itself once more than 24 percent of output goes to the EU, against half today (working paper, calibration).
The signal can be measured for any instrument, price-based or not. The Total Effective Carbon Price expresses a tax, feebate, subsidy reform or standard as the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much (Brief 6.1). It credits a policy’s effect on emissions, not its cost to producers.
Where an exporter has no price signal, firm-level verification should stay. Firms there should be measured on the whole output of all their plants making the good, so that they cannot pick which plant ships, as Mehling and Ritz (2023) suggest (working paper, design trade-off).


Recognition is worth hundreds of euros a tonne
Recognition matters most to the most carbon-intensive exporters, who have the most to gain from a feebate. For India, opting in with a feebate at €40 cuts the charge on hot-rolled steel by €274 a tonne: €103 from dropping the mark-up and €171 from recognition (Table 1). At €80 the charge disappears. For a country shipping 1 million tonnes a year to the EU, each €100 a tonne is €100 million a year.

The cost is a weaker level playing field, so phase it in
Full recognition would let a feebate country’s steel enter without a carbon charge while EU steel pays on all its emissions. Both would face the full price at the margin, but only EU producers would pay for their remaining carbon. That favors imports, and raises emissions where the imported steel is still dirtier (working paper, objections and limits). The full answer is a separate charge on consumption that falls on imported and EU-made goods alike (Brief 1.3).
Recognition should therefore rise as free allocation falls. Setting the recognition weight each year to one minus the factor that governs free allocation gives 2.5 percent in 2026, about half in 2030 and full recognition from 2034, or later if the phase-out is extended. Relocation should be reviewed before each step.
Recognizing a feebate’s signal needs an amendment. The law defines a carbon price as a “monetary amount paid” (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023b, Art. 3(29)) and nets rebates. The Commission can drop the mark-up and state which support measures reduce recognition by implementing act; crediting the signal itself needs Article 9 amended (working paper, legal pathway). Under trade law, crediting comparable effect by criteria any country can meet is easier to defend than crediting only instruments that resemble the EU’s own (Mehling et al. 2019). Governments have reason to overstate their price signal; published measures, computed by an independent body and updated yearly, limit the risk.


What to do
The European Commission should open its default carbon price method to consultation and widen it. Build it on the World Bank, IMF and OECD measures, set it by country and sector, and let it cover feebates and non-price policies measured as carbon-price equivalents.
It should offer a country-sector route in the 2027 revision of default values. Exporters whose sector has a recognized price signal would be charged at the verified sector average, updated yearly, without the mark-up. Elsewhere, firms would verify the whole output of all their plants.
It should state which support measures reduce recognition. Support paid for verified abatement should reduce nothing; output-based rebates should reduce only the price paid; support that rises with emissions or fuel use should reduce both.
It should propose amending Article 9 to credit the price signal, phased in with free allocation, and measure shuffling from installation-level declarations matched to customs data.
Exporting countries should consider a sector-wide feebate. It prices every tonne at a rate a tax could not reach politically, costs the treasury nothing and is the instrument these changes would reward (Brief 1.2).
