title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full analysis, with the model, proofs and calibration, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
One carbon price cannot do two jobs in an open economy. It should cut emissions per tonne of what a country makes, and it should make buyers pay for the carbon in what they use. Asking one tax to do both puts the cost on exporters and lets imports off, so governments keep the rate low.
Price production with a revenue-neutral feebate. Firms pay on emissions per tonne above their sector’s average and are rebated below it. The treasury neither gains nor loses, every firm still saves the full carbon price on each tonne it cuts, and prices barely move.
Price consumption at the destination. A carbon component of VAT charges imports and home-made goods alike and exempts exports; a forward-announced obligation covers fuel for homes and vehicles.
Pay for policies, not projects. A climate-finance payment per tonne above half the feebate rate makes adopting the feebate a gain for the country.
Charge imports by country and sector, and credit non-price policies. Exporters then do best by matching the importer’s charge at home: a race to the top.


One price, two jobs
Carbon prices are too low and too narrow to meet the Paris goals. Explicit carbon prices cover about 28 percent of global emissions, at an average of about $19 per tonne of CO₂ where they apply; averaged over all global emissions, the price is about $5 (World Bank 2025). The High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices judged that prices of at least $50–100 per tonne by 2030 are consistent with the Paris temperature goals (High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices 2017).
Part of the gap is built into the instrument. A carbon tax or an emissions trading system covers what a country produces. It does two jobs with one rate. It rewards each firm for cutting emissions per tonne of output, which is what the climate needs. And it raises the price of carbon-intensive goods, so that buyers use less of them. In a closed economy one rate does both jobs well.
In an open economy the second job undermines the first. The price rise falls on exports, which compete against unpriced foreign supply, and spares imports, which replace home production. Some of the fall in home output is then replaced by foreign production, which is leakage, not abatement: model studies put leakage under unilateral pricing at 5–25 percent of the emission cut (Branger and Quirion 2014), and the loss of output is concentrated in energy-intensive, trade-exposed industries such as steel and cement. Governments respond by exempting heavy industry, handing out free permits or keeping the rate low (Keen et al. 2022).
A border charge on imports fixes only half the problem. The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) charges imports for their carbon (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023b). It protects the home market, but exports still carry the full carbon bill, and the mechanism credits only an explicit carbon price paid abroad, not other policies that cut emissions.


The proposal: two tracks
The production track prices emissions per tonne, not the carbon bill. Each covered sector, such as steel, cement, aluminum or power, has a benchmark: its average emissions per tonne of output. A firm above the benchmark pays the carbon price on the difference; a firm below it receives a rebate on the difference. Because the benchmark is the average, payments cancel out. The treasury neither gains nor loses, and the sector’s average cost barely moves. But each firm still saves the full carbon price on every tonne of CO₂ it cuts, exactly as under a tax. Canada’s output-based pricing system for industry works on the same principle (Government of Canada 2019), and the IMF has proposed the same formula for industry in Mexico (Black et al. 2021).
The consumption track charges what the country uses, wherever it was made. Every good bought at home carries a charge for the carbon embodied in it, collected as a carbon component of VAT. Imports pay it at the border, home-made goods pay it along the VAT chain, and exports are exempt, exactly as VAT already works (OECD 2017). The value part of VAT can be cut as the carbon part rises, so the total rate barely moves at first while its base shifts from value to carbon (Brief 1.3).
Fuel for homes and vehicles needs its own instrument. Its carbon is released after the last sale, so no charge on goods reaches it. A few large firms dominate its supply: fuel importers, refiners and gas suppliers. They take on a legal obligation for the carbon in what they sell, announced years ahead and rising on a published path, so that the firms that plan long-lived capital know the price they will face.
A common yardstick lets every policy be compared. A feebate has no “price paid”, and a standard or a procurement rule has no rate at all. The carbon-price equivalent expresses any of them as the uniform carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much (Brief 6.1). It is what lets a country that regulates, or uses a feebate, earn the same credit at a foreign border and the same climate finance as a country that taxes.
Together the two tracks give the full carbon price signal, without leakage. The feebate gives producers the full incentive to cut emissions per tonne. The consumption charge makes buyers pay for carbon, and because imports pay alike there is nothing to gain from buying abroad. The two rates can differ: the production rate can be high because it does not raise average costs, and the consumption rate can be set by what households will accept (working paper, the equivalence result).


What the feebate costs: steel
A feebate raises the producer price by the cost of the abatement only. A tax charges firms for every tonne they still emit; a feebate does not. So a feebate at a given rate raises costs by roughly a third as much as a tax at the same rate. The working paper calibrates this to the EU’s default emission values for hot-rolled steel, which differ widely by exporting country (working paper, calibration).



Table 1: Rise in the producer price of hot-rolled steel. Intensities are the EU’s default values (European Commission 2025); the base price of $600 per tonne and the cost of cutting emissions (a 48 percent cut in intensity at $80) are stylized. Source: working paper, Table 1.

Carbon tax at $80/tCO₂

The most carbon-intensive exporters gain most from choosing a feebate. Their carbon bill under a tax, which the feebate avoids, is largest. For most exporters a feebate at a rate close to the EU’s carbon price raises costs by a single-digit percentage.
The saving has a price: a feebate alone does not discourage consumption. Because it does not raise the average price much, it gives buyers little reason to use less steel, and to cut the same tonnes on its own it would need a higher rate than a tax (working paper, the output margin). The consumption track supplies that missing signal, on the consumption base where it causes no leakage.






Figure 1: Carbon-related cost added to a tonne of steel at $80 per tonne of CO₂ (stylized home producer at Türkiye’s default intensity, foreign supplier at China’s). Under the two tracks, exports carry only the cost of the abatement itself. Source: working paper, Figure 1.





Pay for policies, not projects
Climate finance can make a feebate a gain for the adopting country. Suppose a climate-finance facility pays a price per tonne of reduction below the country’s unpriced baseline. A feebate cuts emissions at an average cost of about half its rate, because the cheapest cuts come first. So any payment above half the feebate rate more than covers the cost, and the country’s best choice is a feebate rate equal to the payment (working paper, crediting). A World Bank analysis of payments for a donor-supported carbon tax finds the same half-the-rate threshold (Strand 2020).
Paying for a sector-wide policy avoids the weaknesses of project credits. Project credits pay for single installations whose additionality is contested. A feebate moves the intensity of a whole sector, which can be measured, and its rebate already rewards the clean plants a project would fund. The baseline is the hard part, as in all results-based finance; crediting the measured change in sector intensity from a verified pre-policy level limits the room to inflate it.
The threshold assumes the country keeps the reduction toward its own target. If the buyer counts it instead, under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, the country must also be paid for the carbon, and the break-even payment rises to about one and a half times the feebate rate (Strand 2020).


From leakage to a race to the top
When importers charge for carbon by exporting country and sector, exporters gain by pricing carbon at home. If the EU or another importer charges for the carbon in steel at a value set for each exporting country and updated from verified data, no single mill can lower its country’s charge, but a national feebate can. An exporter’s lowest delivered cost then comes from a feebate at the same rate as the charge in its markets (working paper, best response).
Competition then rewards the cleanest producers. Under carbon taxes without border charges, a country that raises its price loses market share. Under the two tracks, a country that raises its feebate toward its markets’ charges gains share. In the working paper’s simulation of a steel import market with eight exporters, a charge of $100 per tonne cuts the average carbon content of imports by about 28 percent if exporters do nothing, through the mix of suppliers alone, and by about 70 percent if each responds with a feebate.
Today’s EU rules block half of this. The CBAM deducts only a carbon price “effectively paid” abroad, net of any rebate (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2025), so a revenue-neutral feebate, which rebates on average all it charges, earns no credit, and measuring each plant separately lets exporters send clean steel to Europe and dirty steel elsewhere. The companion brief proposes measuring the foreign price signal by country and sector and crediting non-price policies as carbon-price equivalents (Brief 1.4).


Making it work
The feebate needs data that exporters to the EU are already learning to collect. It needs, for each sector, output, emissions measured at the plant and a benchmark rule. The CBAM already defines how plant emissions are measured in six sectors, and EU importers who want to pay less than the default values (European Commission 2025) must obtain those data from their suppliers (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023b). Updating the benchmark each period to the sector average removes windfalls for firms that were already clean.
The consumption charge rides on the VAT system. Countries without a working VAT cannot run it yet. They can still run the feebate, which is where most of their emissions are, and add the consumption charge later.
Trade rules are a design constraint, not a barrier. A charge levied equally on imported and home goods, with exports exempt, follows the logic of border adjustment of internal taxes under the GATT; whether carbon intensity can distinguish otherwise like products is unsettled (Mehling et al. 2019). A sector-wide feebate is not tied to exporting, but its rebate leg needs careful drafting under the subsidies rules (working paper, implementation).
The VAT carbon charge’s effect on poorer households must be measured before rates are set. Because the value part of VAT falls as the carbon part rises, the net effect depends on how much more carbon-intensive poorer households’ spending is, not on the carbon price as such (working paper, objections and limits).


What to do
Developing-country exporters: start with a production feebate. It prices carbon at a rate a tax could not reach, costs the treasury nothing, and, once importers recognize it, earns credit at the border. Begin with the sectors that already report plant emissions for the EU.
The EU and other importers: credit the policy, measured by its effect. Set border charges by exporting country and sector, update them from verified data, and credit feebates and non-price policies at their carbon-price equivalent. As free allocation is phased out (by 2034 under current law (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2023a)), add a carbon component inside VAT so that home consumption pays the same charge as imports.
Development banks and climate-finance facilities: pay for policies. Offer a price per tonne for verified cuts in sector intensity, above half the feebate rate the payment is meant to induce. The adopting country then gains, and the payment buys a whole sector’s change rather than a single project.

title: 2. Other Tax and Fiscal Policy
text:
Governments that let capital and people move freely find it hard to tax mobile income at high rates, so they give up on high rates altogether. This section argues that the constraint binds only on the wrong base. Economic rent, income above what keeps an asset or a firm in use, can be taxed heavily without driving anything away if the tax reaches it where it cannot leave: at origin where the rent is tied to the place, and at destination where it follows the customer. The section’s paper, Rent Tax, combines a land value tax above a household allowance with a tax at 50 percent on large firms’ profit above a normal return, two destination layers that follow the customer, and a cap that stops any firm paying more than half the rent it earns from local customers. Its revenue estimates, built from sourced inputs, are 1.0–2.7 percent of GDP from land and 2.3–6.3 percent from the corporate layers. A second paper, Let Land Pay for the City, applies the land tax to fast-growing cities in developing countries: a recurrent land value tax plus capture of the uplift that infrastructure creates can fund much of their transit and services, and because the tax rewards compact building it is also a green tax. The book Plucked! gives the longer argument for UK tax and benefits.

title: 2. Other Tax and Fiscal Policy
text:
2.1 Taxing Rent, Not Effort
A Simple Design for Land and Corporate Taxation Consistent with Free Movement of Capital and People
Free movement of capital and people has pushed governments to give up on high taxes on mobile income. This brief argues that they can still tax rent, the income above what is needed to keep an asset or a firm in use, provided they reach it where it cannot leave. It proposes a land value tax above a household allowance and a corporate package that presumes large firms earn rent: a high rate on profit above a normal return, destination-based layers that follow the customer, and a cap. An asset-light foreign platform’s tax rises from 1 to 50 percent of its local rent; firms that invest and employ locally pay nothing on their normal return.

title: 2. Other Tax and Fiscal Policy
section: 2.2 Let Land Pay for the City
text:
2.2 Let Land Pay for the City
Property Taxes, Public Land and Land Value Capture to Fund Green Urban Infrastructure in Developing Countries
Cities in Africa and Asia will add about 2.5 billion people by 2050, and most of the roads, transit, water and drainage they will need is not yet built. Building it can raise the value of urban land by more than it costs, yet developing countries collect recurrent property taxes worth only a few tenths of a percent of GDP, against about 1 percent in advanced economies. This paper argues that land should pay for the city. A recurrent tax on land value, together with capture of the one-off rise in land value that new infrastructure creates, can fund a large share of urban infrastructure. Hong Kong and Singapore show the model at scale: public ownership of land and rail-plus-property development let mass transit pay much of its own way. A property tax that falls mainly on land is also a green tax. It rewards compact building, penalizes idle land on the urban fringe and makes transit viable, and the compact, walkable city it supports brings large health gains from fewer road deaths, cleaner air and more physical activity. The paper sets out how a poor city can adapt the model, the planning it needs, and a best-practice outline for a property tax and land value capture code.

title: Taxing Rent, Not Effort
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 2.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full analysis, with the propositions, the literature, the worked examples and the revenue arithmetic, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Free movement caps the rate on income that can move, not on rent that cannot. Governments have given up on high rates because profit and wealth leave. Rent, income that would be earned anyway, can be taxed heavily if the tax reaches it where it cannot leave.
Tax land above a household allowance. Land cannot move. A tax of about 2.5 percent a year on site value above the value of an ordinary home’s site falls on large holdings, not on ordinary homeowners.
Presume that large firms earn rent, and tax only the rent. Exempt a normal return on equity and tax the profit above it at 50 percent. Investment is not discouraged, because the marginal project pays nothing.
Follow the customer where profit is shifted. For a few sectors, tax local sales less local costs; for all large firms, charge a small tax on local sales with credits for local assets and payroll. Cap both so that no firm pays more than half the rent it earns from local customers.
Start with property taxes and an allowance for corporate equity, then add the destination layers. European Union law, as the Court of Justice has applied it, allows most of the design; the payroll credit needs careful drafting.


High rates on mobile income have been given up
Free movement of capital and people has made high taxes on mobile income hard to sustain. The European Union removed restrictions on capital movements between member states in 1990 (Council of the European Communities 1988). Before that, under the Bretton Woods system, most countries kept their capital accounts relatively closed (Obstfeld and Taylor 2004), and capital that could not leave could be taxed. Once it could leave, it did.
The retreat shows in the numbers. Twelve OECD countries taxed net wealth in 1990; four did in 2017 (OECD 2018). About 36 percent of multinational profits are shifted to tax havens, and reallocating them would raise the profits declared in high-tax European Union countries by about 20 percent (Tørsløv et al. 2023). Wealth, meanwhile, has concentrated: in the United States the top 0.1 percent held 22 percent of wealth in 2012, up from 7 percent in 1978 (Saez and Zucman 2016).
The usual response, lower rates, gives up more than it needs to. What a country can charge depends on the base. A base that can leave sets its own rate. A base that cannot leave, or that earns its income from the country’s own customers, does not.


Rent can be taxed at high rates if the tax reaches it where it cannot leave
Rent is income above what is needed to keep an asset, a worker or a firm in its current use. A tax on rent changes nothing anyone does, so its rate can be high. Economists from Ricardo and Mill to the Mirrlees Review have made the case for taxing it (Mirrlees et al. 2011).
Not all rent stays put. Rent from a mine or from a well-located site cannot move. Rent from a patent or a brand can be booked anywhere. The Mirrlees Review draws exactly this line: rent specific to a location can be taxed at source, mobile rent cannot (Mirrlees et al. 2011). The design therefore taxes location-specific rent where it arises, and mobile rent where the customer is (working paper, the design).
Natural resources prove the point. Norway taxes petroleum profit at a marginal rate of 78 percent, on a base that exempts the normal return (Norwegian Ministry of Energy and Norwegian Offshore Directorate 2025). The oil is where it is.


Tax land above a household allowance
A land value tax is the cleanest rent tax there is. Land is not produced, so taxing its value does not reduce its supply or change how it is used; the tax is reflected in a lower land price, and owners on the day it is announced bear it (Mirrlees et al. 2011). Where Pennsylvania cities taxed land more heavily than buildings, building and housing density rose (Oates and Schwab 1997; Banzhaf and Lavery 2010).
An allowance keeps the tax off ordinary homes. Each household’s land is exempt up to an allowance close to the site value of an ordinary home; above it, the household pays about 2.5 percent a year on site value. Most households pay little; large holdings pay a lot. Business land is taxed without an allowance.
The tax needs three safeguards. Sites must be valued regularly, since many property taxes rest on values decades out of date (OECD 2022). The rate should be phased in, because the fall in land prices on announcement hits recent buyers hardest. And owners who are rich in land but poor in cash should be able to defer the tax, with interest, until sale or death (working paper, land).


Presume that large firms earn rent, and tax only the rent
Large firms should be presumed to earn rent unless they show otherwise. In a competitive market, profit above the normal return attracts entry and is competed away. A firm that is large and stays large earns rent from network effects, brands, scale, patents or regulation, unless its industry can only support a few firms, as in civil aircraft or leading-edge chips. Markups in the United States rose from 21 percent above marginal cost in 1980 to 61 percent (De Loecker et al. 2020), although the measurement is disputed (Basu 2019).
Rent from being more efficient is still rent. Some firms are large because they are better (Autor et al. 2020). Their surplus over rivals is rent too, like the surplus of better land. What matters is not to discourage the investment that made them better, and the design achieves that by taxing only profit above a normal return (working paper, market power as the default).
Layer One taxes profit above a normal return at 50 percent. Each firm deducts a notional return on its equity, an allowance for corporate equity, and pays tax only on the profit above it. A marginal investment earns just the normal return and so pays no tax at any rate; only the surplus is taxed (Boadway and Bruce 1984; Bond and Devereux 2003). Belgium ran such an allowance from 2006 to 2023 and Italy from 2011 to 2023 (Kingdom of Belgium 2022; Republic of Italy 2023). Every firm gets the allowance; groups with revenue above €750 million, the threshold of the OECD’s global minimum tax (OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS 2021), pay 50 percent on the profit above it, and the rest 25 percent.


Follow the customer where profit is shifted
A high rate at origin alone would drive declared profit abroad. A 1 percentage point lower rate than in other countries raises the profit a multinational reports by about 1.5 percent (Beer et al. 2020). Raising the rate on declared rent from 25 to 50 percent could therefore cut the declared base by more than a third. The working paper’s arithmetic shows that Layer One alone would raise about what today’s corporate tax raises, not more (working paper, revenue).
Layer Two taxes local cash flow in sectors where rent is easily shifted. For designated sectors, such as digital platforms and pharmaceutical patents, firms pay 22 percent of sales to local customers less local costs; royalties and fees paid to related firms abroad are not deductible, and Layer One is credited against it. The base is where the customers are, so moving profit or patents abroad does not reduce it, as in the destination-based cash-flow tax proposed by Devereux and coauthors (Devereux et al. 2021). The rate stays moderate and the list short, because a tax confined to a few sectors acts as a 28 percent charge on their imported inputs.
Layer Three charges sales that are not matched by local activity. All groups above the threshold pay 4 percent of local sales, less credits of 8 percent of local tangible assets and 25 percent of local payroll. A firm with payroll of 16 percent of its sales pays nothing; a remote seller with €1 billion of local sales, €50 million of local assets and €100 million of payroll pays €11 million. The credits work like the payroll and asset carve-out in the OECD’s global minimum tax (OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS 2021).
A cap stops the destination layers from taxing effort. Without it, a fuel distributor with thin margins could pay more in sales tax than it makes in profit. The destination layers can raise a firm’s tax only up to 50 percent of its global rent margin times its local sales: half the rent it would earn locally at its worldwide margin (working paper, the cap).


The design taxes rent and spares effort
In five worked firms, the design taxes rent at about half and the normal return at zero. The table shows tax as a share of the rent each firm earns from local customers (working paper, five firms).

Figure 1: Tax as a percent of the rent each firm earns from local customers. Source: working paper, Figure 1.



The foreign platform goes from almost nothing to half its local rent. It books its profit where its patents are, so today it pays 5 on rent of 335 (€ million). Layer Two, capped, raises its tax to 168.
The design is weakest for foreign sellers outside the designated sectors. Their tax rises only from 4 to 13 percent of rent, because Layer Three is deliberately small. Closing the gap means either a longer list of designated sectors or a higher sales charge, and both have costs.
Firms that invest locally pay nothing on their normal return. The domestic manufacturer’s allowance removes its normal return and its local assets and payroll remove Layer Three; it pays half its rent, more in total than today, but nothing on the return that rewards its investment.
The revenue is real but not unlimited. The land tax could raise 1.0 to 2.7 percent of GDP, one to three times what recurrent property taxes raise across the OECD today; the corporate layers 2.3 to 6.3 percent of GDP, against 3.75 percent from corporate income tax today (OECD 2025). The low end is Layer One alone, after profit shifting; the high end requires the destination layers to recover rent now shifted abroad (working paper, revenue).


The law allows most of the design
The Court of Justice has upheld steeply progressive taxes on turnover that fall mainly on foreign firms. In 2020 it held that Hungary’s turnover taxes on telecommunications and retail were compatible with freedom of establishment, because turnover is a neutral criterion and a fair indicator of ability to pay (Court of Justice of the European Union 2020); in 2021 it held that Poland’s progressive retail tax was not state aid (Court of Justice of the European Union 2021).
The payroll credit is the main legal risk. A remote seller earns no credit for its staff abroad, which could be challenged as a restriction on services within the European Union. Under trade rules, relief for domestic but not foreign labor is the main objection raised against destination-based cash-flow taxes; a sales charge combined with a separate payroll subsidy has the same effect without that objection (Auerbach et al. 2017). Layer Two should give no export rebate (working paper, law).
Land raises no free-movement issue at all. It cannot move, and the tax applies alike to resident and foreign owners.


What to do
Finance ministries: replace recurrent property taxes with a land value tax above a household allowance. Value sites regularly, tax business land in full, phase the rate in and allow deferral for cash-poor owners.
Give every firm an allowance for corporate equity, and tax large groups’ rent at a higher rate. Measure equity on the tax basis, carry losses forward with interest, and phase the higher rate in above €750 million of group revenue so that there is no cliff.
Add the destination layers, with the cap. Confine the destination-based cash-flow tax to a short list of sectors where profit is easily shifted, apply the presence-credited sales charge to all large groups, and cap both by half of sales-apportioned global rent.
European Union members: act together where possible. Each layer works for one country alone, but a common allowance and common destination layers would leave less room to shift profit or serve a market from next door.

title: 3. Finance and Risk
text:
Clean power is cheap to build in most developing countries and expensive to finance, because investors price risks the project cannot control: a distribution company that may not pay, a plant that may not be finished, a currency that may fall and a state that may change the rules. Each risk has a different cheapest holder. This section of papers argues for removing payment risk at its source with a payment intermediary that guarantees the power contract rather than the debt, and then turning projects into a few standard securities: construction loans held by development banks, and pooled operating plants refinanced through first-loss equity and senior synthetic sovereign bonds. In stylized calibrations, the payment premium adds about 11 percent to a solar tariff, a contract guarantee removes it for about half its value in expected public cost, and refinancing the senior debt of pooled operating plants cuts the levelized cost of solar power by about a fifth (14–19 percent). The host state’s exposure becomes smaller, contingent and contracted, but it does not disappear, and the gain is real only where the structure improves collection or makes default rarer.

title: 3. Finance and Risk
section: 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
text:
3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
Removing offtaker risk at source in developing-country power markets
Solar power is cheap to build in developing countries but dear to finance, because investors price the risk that a state-owned distribution company will pay late or not at all. A payment intermediary facility buys power under one standard contract, pays generators in full and on time, and collects arrears itself, behind a guarantee waterfall agreed in advance. Guaranteeing the contract removes the whole risk premium, about two dollars of saving per dollar of expected cost in a stylized case; guaranteeing project debt removes under a third of it. India’s Solar Energy Corporation shows the design works, and its buyers’ arrears show it needs utility reform.

title: 3. Finance and Risk
text:
3.2 From Projects to Asset Classes
Two-Stage Finance and Synthetic Sovereign Bonds for Clean Power
Clean power plants in developing countries are financed one at a time, on bespoke terms, so each lender prices construction, payment, currency and sovereign risk together for the life of the loan. This brief proposes turning them into a few standard securities. Banks finance construction against a contingent purchase contract; once plants operate, their debt is refinanced into pools that issue first-loss equity, a thin mezzanine and a senior synthetic sovereign bond. Pooling across countries under one contract keeps the cushion thin, and refinancing cuts the price of solar power by about a fifth. Standardization, not subsidy, lowers the price.

title: From Projects to Asset Classes
text: Working paper, version 0.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. title: From Projects to Asset Classes
text:
4.1 The structure
Two-stage finance gives each phase of a plant’s life to the investor who prices it most cheaply. In stage one, a developer builds the plant with its own equity and a construction loan from a bank or a development finance institution. The lender supervises a bounded, project-specific risk over about two years. In stage two, once the plant operates, its senior debt is refinanced by a pool of operating plants, which funds itself by issuing tranched securities. The sponsor, or a buyer of its stake, keeps the project’s equity beneath the debt. In the calibration the senior debt is 80 percent of the plant’s cost at commissioning, the gearing Time and Chance assumes for investment-grade clean power debt (Stretton 2026g, ch. 15).
The contingent power purchase agreement links the two stages. Before construction, the payment intermediary facility commits to buy the plant’s power on completion under its standard power purchase agreement (Stretton 2026b). The construction lender then lends against a plant with a contracted, creditworthy buyer waiting for it, rather than against a merchant project. The pool knows in advance what it will be offered: identical contracts, identical documents and an identical buyer. That is what turns the refinancing from a negotiation into a take-out.
The structure creates five standard securities, each for a different investor.

Construction loan. Two to three years, floating rate, held by banks and development finance institutions, secured on the plant and the contingent power purchase agreement.
First-loss tranche. Equity in the pool that absorbs portfolio losses before any debt does. At scale its natural holder is a regional fund of the Climate Investment Trust (Stretton 2026e, 2026f).
Mezzanine. A thin layer between the first loss and the senior bond, held by development finance institutions or by insurers seeking yield, or replaced by a sovereign co-guarantee of the same layer.
Senior synthetic sovereign bond. A long-dated bond backed by guaranteed contracts on operating plants, a first-loss tranche and a co-guarantee from highly rated sovereigns, rated on that structure rather than on the host sovereign. Its buyers are pension funds, insurers and, if eligible, central banks.
Local-currency senior tranche. The same senior claim, denominated in the host currency and sold to domestic banks, pension funds and retail savers (Section 8).

The cash waterfall puts bondholders first. Payments under the standard power purchase agreement flow from the intermediary to each plant’s debt service account and from there to the ring-fenced pool, which pays senior interest and principal, then mezzanine, then the first-loss tranche. The bondholder is therefore exposed to the intermediary’s payment and to a diversified set of operating plants, not to any one developer (Stretton 2026g, ch. 7). Behind the intermediary stands the guarantee waterfall of the companion paper: the distribution company, its subnational owner, the national government, a multilateral agency and a donor contingency account (Stretton 2026b).

title: From Projects to Asset Classes
text:
4.2 Proposition 1: the refinancing gain
Let a plant cost \(C\) per kilowatt, take \(B\) years to build with capital drawn evenly, run for \(T\) years and produce \(E\) kilowatt-hours per kilowatt a year at operating cost \(m\). Under single-stage finance one cost of capital \(r_1\) applies throughout. Under two-stage finance the construction phase costs \(r_c\), and in operation the plant’s cost of capital is \(r_o = g\,r_d + (1-g)\,r_e\), where a share \(g\) of its capitalized cost is senior debt refinanced at \(r_d\) and the rest is project equity earning \(r_e\). With the capital recovery factor \(\mathrm{CRF}(r,T) = r/(1-(1+r)^{-T})\), the LCOE is
\[
\mathrm{LCOE}(r_c, r_o) = \frac{C(1+r_c)^{B/2}\,\mathrm{CRF}(r_o,T) + m}{E},
\tag{1}\]
and single-stage finance is the special case \(r_c = r_o = r_1\).
Proposition 1 (refinancing gain). (a) Two-stage finance lowers the LCOE if and only if \((1+r_c)^{B/2}\mathrm{CRF}(r_o,T) < (1+r_1)^{B/2}\mathrm{CRF}(r_1,T)\); when \(r_c = r_1\) this holds if and only if \(r_o < r_1\). (b) The ratio of the LCOE’s sensitivity to the operating cost of capital and to the construction rate is \(\frac{2(1+r_c)}{B}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{CRF}'(r_o,T)}{\mathrm{CRF}(r_o,T)}\), which for \(r_c = 12\) percent, \(B = 2\), \(T = 25\) and \(r_o\) between 6 and 10 percent lies between 8.6 and 10.6; a point off the refinanced debt rate is worth \(g\) times as much as a point off \(r_o\). (c) The gain is passed to consumers only if the refinancing terms are known when the tariff is bid; otherwise the developer adds a premium for refinancing risk.
The proof is in Appendix A. Part (b) is the heart of the matter. Construction lasts two years and operation twenty-five, so the rate that applies to the long phase dominates the tariff. Single-stage finance carries the construction-era price of risk into the operating years, because the lender cannot shed the risk it priced at the start. A plant built at 12 percent and refinanced at 8 percent stops paying for construction risk the day it is commissioned. Part (c) is why the contingent power purchase agreement and a standing take-out matter: in a competitive auction developers bid the tariff they can finance, and they can bid on the refinanced cost only if refinancing is assured.
The refinancing gain does not shrink when world interest rates rise. If construction finance costs 12 percent and the operating plant 8 percent, the four-point gap is worth at least as much whether the world’s safe rate is 2 or 5 percent. Higher rates raise the financing share of the tariff, from 30 percent at a 4 percent cost of capital to 41 percent at 6 percent (Table 1), so they make the gap more valuable, not less.

title: From Projects to Asset Classes
text:
4.3 Proposition 2: how much first loss
Model a pool holding the senior debt of \(n\) operating plants, each with a ten-year probability \(p\) of defaulting to the pool and loss given default \(\lambda\). Plant \(i\) defaults when a latent variable \(X_i = \sqrt{\rho}\,Z + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_i\) falls below \(\Phi^{-1}(p)\), where \(Z\) is a common factor, \(\varepsilon_i\) is idiosyncratic and both are standard normal. The parameter \(\rho\) is the correlation of the latent variables: how much plants fail together. “Default to the pool” means a shortfall that the guarantee waterfall behind the intermediary did not cover: a crisis that exhausts the waterfall, curtailment, a change in law, a plant that underperforms. As \(n\) grows, the fraction of the pool lost converges to
\[
L(Z) = \lambda\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(p) - \sqrt{\rho}\,Z}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right),
\tag{2}\]
the large homogeneous pool of Vasicek (2002). A senior tranche that attaches at \(K\), so that it loses only once pool losses exceed \(K\), defaults with probability \(\Pr[L > K]\).
Proposition 2 (first-loss size). In the large homogeneous pool, the senior tranche has default probability at most \(\alpha\) if and only if its attachment point is at least
\[
K^*(p, \rho, \lambda, \alpha) = \lambda\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(p) + \sqrt{\rho}\,\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right).
\tag{3}\]
\(K^*\) is proportional to \(\lambda\), increasing in \(p\) and decreasing in \(\alpha\). Whenever \(p < 1/2\) and the senior target is stricter than the average plant (\(\alpha \le p\)), \(K^*\) is increasing in \(\rho\).
The proof is in Appendix A. \(K^*\) is the subordination needed: the first-loss tranche plus the mezzanine, or plus a co-guarantee of the mezzanine layer. Three features matter for policy. Subordination scales one for one with loss given default, so recovery rights, which the guarantee waterfall preserves by keeping the claim on the distributor alive (Stretton 2026b), halve the cushion when they halve the loss. Subordination is far above expected loss when correlation is high: at \(p = 5\) percent and \(\lambda = 20\) percent, expected loss is 1 percent of the pool, but a near-AAA senior at \(\rho = 0.2\) needs 7.7 percent. And correlation, not default probability, is the parameter a sponsor can most change, by choosing what goes into the pool. The large-pool formula is a lower bound: a real pool of a few dozen plants keeps some idiosyncratic risk and needs more (Section 6).
The co-guarantee from highly rated sovereigns substitutes for part of the subordination, at a low expected cost. A guarantor that covers the mezzanine layer, losses between the top of the first-loss tranche and \(K^*\), makes the senior bond as safe as if the mezzanine were funded. The guarantor’s expected loss is the expected loss of that layer, which is small because it is drawn only in the correlated tail (Section 5). The guarantor lends its rating at the cost of a reserve against the tail, and spends it only if the tail occurs (Stretton 2026g, ch. 14).

title: From Projects to Asset Classes
section: 4.4 Proposition 3: standard contracts let pools diversify across host countries
text:
4.4 Proposition 3: standard contracts let pools diversify across host countries
The host sovereign is the main source of correlation. Plants in one country share a currency, a regulator, a distribution sector and, behind the guarantee waterfall, a treasury. When the host sovereign is in crisis, they are stressed together. Write the latent variable of a plant in country \(c\) as \(X_i = \sqrt{\rho_g}\,Z + \sqrt{\rho_c}\,Y_c + \sqrt{1-\rho_g-\rho_c}\,\varepsilon_i\), where \(Z\) is a global factor (world interest rates, the dollar) and \(Y_c\) a host-country factor, independent across countries. A pool confined to one country has correlation \(\rho_g + \rho_c\). A pool spread equally over \(N\) countries, each holding many plants, loses \(L_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{c=1}^N L_c(Z, Y_c)\).
Proposition 3 (diversification across host countries). As \(N \to \infty\), \(L_N\) converges almost surely to the one-factor loss with correlation \(\rho_g\), and the subordination needed for a senior target \(\alpha\) converges to \(K^*(p, \rho_g, \lambda, \alpha)\), which is strictly below the single-country requirement \(K^*(p, \rho_g + \rho_c, \lambda, \alpha)\) whenever \(\rho_c > 0\), \(p < 1/2\) and \(\alpha \le p\).
The proof is in Appendix A. Diversification across host countries removes the host-country factor, but not the global one. Three countries capture about two-thirds of the gain and ten capture nearly 90 percent (Table 5). The result assumes the plants in different countries can be pooled at all, and that is where standardization does its work. A pool can be rated as homogeneous only if its assets carry the same contract, the same documents and comparable loss given default. Bespoke contracts force investors and rating agencies to analyze each asset, which makes the pool effectively small, and a small pool keeps its idiosyncratic risk (Gordy 2003). Identical contracts make portfolios; portfolios make ratings. A regional payment intermediary, which buys power from several countries under one standard power purchase agreement, produces exactly the homogeneous, multi-country pool that Proposition 3 rewards (Stretton 2026b).

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
section: 4.1 The cost of capital sets the tariff
text:
4.1 The cost of capital sets the tariff
A solar plant costs \(I\) per kilowatt up front, costs \(F\) per kilowatt a year to run, and produces \(E\) kilowatt-hours per kilowatt a year for \(T\) years. At a real weighted average cost of capital (WACC) \(r\), its levelized cost is \[
\mathrm{LCOE}(r) = \frac{I\,a(r) + F}{E}, \qquad a(r) = \frac{r}{1 - (1+r)^{-T}},
\tag{1}\] where \(a(r)\) is the capital recovery factor. Since \(F\) is small, the tariff rises almost in proportion to \(a(r)\). The plant is the stylized plant used throughout this series: \(I = \$800\), a 20 percent capacity factor (\(E = 1{,}752\)), \(F = \$12\) and \(T = 25\), with capital spent at commissioning. Paper 3.2 adds interest during a two-year construction period (Stretton 2026c).
crumbs: 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
section: 4.2 Offtaker default and the premium in the tariff
text:
4.2 Offtaker default and the premium in the tariff
Offtaker default. The generator sells its output to one offtaker at a contracted tariff \(P\) per kilowatt-hour, giving contracted payments of \(A = PE\) a year. The offtaker falls into default episodes, which arrive at intensity \(\lambda\) per year. In an episode the offtaker withholds all payments for \(D\) years; at the end it pays a fraction \(R\) of what it withheld, and the contract resumes. Episodes do not depend on the plant’s own performance. Investors value the contract at the rate \(r_0\), which prices every risk except the offtaker’s, and they price episodes at a risk-neutral intensity \(\lambda^Q = m\lambda\), with \(m \ge 1\) the market price of default risk.
Two quantities summarize the process. The long-run share of time the offtaker spends in arrears is \[
\varphi(\lambda) = \frac{\lambda D}{1 + \lambda D},
\tag{2}\]
A payment withheld at a random point of an episode and paid at its end keeps, at the time it fell due, a fraction of its face value equal to \[
\tilde R = R\,\frac{1 - e^{-r_0 D}}{r_0 D}.
\tag{3}\]
The generator therefore expects to receive a fraction \(1 - h\) of every contracted dollar, where the offtaker haircut is \[
h = \varphi(m\lambda)\,(1 - \tilde R).
\tag{4}\]
Proposition 1 (offtaker premium). In the stationary regime, the break-even tariff for a generator exposed to the offtaker is \[
P^{*} = \frac{\mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)}{1 - h},
\tag{5}\] so the offtaker premium in the tariff is \(\mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)\,h/(1-h)\). It rises with the frequency \(\lambda\) and length \(D\) of episodes and with the price of risk \(m\), and falls with the recovery rate \(R\). It is equivalent to raising the WACC to \(r^{*}\), where \(\mathrm{LCOE}(r^{*}) = P^{*}\).
The proof is in Appendix A. The stationary regime averages over the offtaker’s states; a contract that starts in a normal period does slightly better, which matters little when \(\lambda D\) is small. The intuition is that a generator who expects to collect 90 cents of each contracted dollar must charge 11 percent more. Two features matter for policy. First, frequent short delays cost little if they are fully recovered: the haircut depends on \(1 - \tilde R\), so an offtaker that is often late but always pays in the end carries a small premium. What investors charge for is long arrears and losses on recovery. Second, every term in \(h\) is something an intermediary can change. A facility with liquidity shortens the episode the generator experiences to zero; a facility with powers to intercept transfers raises \(R\); and a facility that is a repeat creditor of the offtaker can lower \(\lambda\) itself, because the offtaker cannot play one generator off against another.
crumbs: 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
section: 4.3 Guarantee the contract or guarantee the debt
text:
4.3 Guarantee the contract or guarantee the debt
A public guarantor can cover the generator’s contract or the project’s debt. Under a contract guarantee the facility pays the generator the contracted amount during every episode and recovers from the offtaker itself a fraction \(R_F\) of what it paid, at the end of the episode. What it does not recover passes to the layers of the waterfall (Section 4.4), so the expected cost of the guarantee is borne by the facility and its guarantors together. Under a debt guarantee the guarantor pays the project’s lenders when the project fails to service its debt, from any cause, and recovers a fraction \(R_D\) by subrogation against the project company, \(D_D\) years later. Let \(g\) be the share of capital financed by debt.
The two guarantees remove different parts of the risk. A contract guarantee removes the whole haircut \(h\), because the generator is paid in full. A debt guarantee removes only the part that would fall on lenders. Write that part as \(\theta h\), with \(0 \le \theta \le 1\). When the equity cushion and debt service reserve absorb every episode, \(\theta = 0\): the lenders were never at risk, and the guarantee removes nothing from the tariff. \(\theta\) rises with leverage and with the length of episodes. A debt guarantee also covers non-payment from other causes, such as construction failure or plant breakdown, whose expected cost to the guarantor I write as \(\psi \ge 0\) per unit of contracted payments. The model holds \(r_0\) fixed and so does not credit the tariff reduction that cover of those other risks may bring; the comparison below is therefore made on the offtaker risk alone.
Let the facility’s recovery value be \(\tilde R_F = R_F\,\frac{1 - e^{-r_0 D}}{r_0 D}\), on the same footing as the generator’s \(\tilde R\), and the debt guarantor’s be \(\tilde R_D = R_D\,e^{-r_0 D_D}\).
Proposition 2 (contract versus debt guarantee). Under the assumptions of Proposition 1:
(i) Coverage. The tariff under a contract guarantee is \(P_C = \mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)\); under a debt guarantee it is \(P_D = \mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)/(1 - (1-\theta)h) \ge P_C\), with equality only if all offtaker losses fall on lenders (\(\theta = 1\)). One contract guarantee covers every project selling to the guaranteed offtaker.
(ii) Expected cost. Per unit of contracted payments, the expected annual cost of the contract guarantee to the facility and its guarantors together is \(c_C = \varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_F)\), and their exposure in any one episode is bounded by the arrears \(AD\). The debt guarantor’s expected cost is \(c_D = \theta\varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_D) + \psi\), and its exposure is bounded only by the outstanding debt.
(iii) Efficiency. The offtaker loss removed per unit of expected cost is \[
\frac{h}{c_C} = \frac{\varphi(m\lambda)}{\varphi(\lambda)}\cdot\frac{1 - \tilde R}{1 - \tilde R_F}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{\theta h}{\theta\varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_D)} = \frac{\varphi(m\lambda)}{\varphi(\lambda)}\cdot\frac{1 - \tilde R}{1 - \tilde R_D}
\tag{6}\] for the contract and, on the offtaker risk alone, the debt guarantee. The contract guarantee is at least as efficient whenever \(\tilde R_F \ge \tilde R_D\), that is, whenever the facility recovers at least as much from the offtaker, in present value, as a debt guarantor recovers from the project company. It removes at least its expected cost whenever \(m \ge 1\) and \(\tilde R_F \ge \tilde R\), with equality when \(m = 1\) and \(\tilde R_F = \tilde R\).
The conditions are the substance of the result. The recovery condition \(\tilde R_F \ge \tilde R_D\) holds whenever the facility keeps a claim on the offtaker and the debt guarantor’s claim runs against a project company whose only asset is an unpaid contract, recovered later. It fails if the facility cannot enforce its claim, which is why the waterfall and the intercept matter.
The equality case in (iii) separates transfer from gain. When investors charge no premium for default risk (\(m = 1\)) and the facility collects no better than generators would (\(\tilde R_F = \tilde R\)), the contract guarantee removes exactly its expected cost: it moves the expected loss from investors to the facility’s guarantors and creates nothing. Everything above that comes from three sources, which have different welfare meanings. Better recovery, the factor \((1-\tilde R)/(1-\tilde R_F)\), is a real resource gain: a repeat creditor with letters of credit and an intercept collects more than dispersed generators. Fewer episodes, a lower \(\lambda\) because the offtaker faces one creditor and reform conditions, is also real; in equation 6 it lowers \(c_C\) and \(h\) together, and its benefit appears as a lower tariff. The price of risk, the factor \(\varphi(m\lambda)/\varphi(\lambda)\), is a gain to society only if the state is better placed to bear the risk than investors are. It is not when the offtaker’s default is correlated with the state’s own fiscal distress, as it often is, and Section 8 returns to that point.
A debt guarantee is not always worse. Where there is no contract to guarantee, as for transmission lines or factories, a guarantee on the bond is the only option, and the series treats it in Paper 3.2 (Stretton 2026b). Where the offtaker is sound and the main risk is construction, a guarantee targeted on construction finance is better than either. The proposition says that where offtaker payment is the binding risk, the guarantee should attach to the payment.

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
section: 4.4 The facility under a guarantee waterfall
text:
4.4 The facility under a guarantee waterfall
The facility holds a portfolio of contracts with \(M\) offtakers, paying \(A\) a year in total. Behind the offtakers stand layers \(k = 1, \dots, K\): the subnational owner, the national government, a multilateral agency and a donor contingency account. When an episode leaves arrears unrecovered from the offtaker, the shortfall passes down the layers in order; layer \(k\) pays in full with probability \(q_k\), independently of the layers above it, and otherwise passes the shortfall on. The facility holds a liquidity buffer \(B\) to pay generators while it waits for a layer to provide funds, which takes up to \(H\) years. Episodes across offtakers are correlated through a common factor: each offtaker enters an episode within a year with probability \(p = 1 - e^{-\lambda}\), and the latent variables driving episodes have pairwise correlation \(\rho\).
Proposition 3 (expected calls and insolvency remoteness). (i) The expected annual call on layer \(k\) is \[
C_k = \varphi(\lambda)\,A\,(1 - \tilde R_F)\; q_k \prod_{j<k}(1 - q_j),
\tag{7}\] and the facility’s own expected loss is \(\varphi(\lambda)A(1 - \tilde R_F)\prod_{k=1}^{K}(1 - q_k)\), which is zero if the last layer is funded and certain (\(q_K = 1\)). The calls sum to the expected cost \(c_C A\) of Proposition 2.
(ii) In a large portfolio, the facility can pay generators in full at confidence \(1 - \varepsilon\) if \[
B \ \ge\ A\,H\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(p) + \sqrt{\rho}\,\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)
\tag{8}\] and the last layer’s committed capacity covers the shortfall that reaches it at the same confidence. Under these conditions the facility is insolvency-remote: every loss is borne by a contracted layer, never by generators.
Part (i) shows where the cost of the guarantee falls. Each layer’s expected cost depends on the reliability of the layers above it, so a reliable intercept by the national government (\(q_2\) near one) makes the multilateral and donor layers cheap. The independence assumption flatters the upper layers: a state government whose utility has defaulted is itself likely to be short of cash, so in practice the \(q_k\) fall together in a crisis and expected calls shift down the waterfall toward the national, multilateral and donor layers. Part (ii) is the standard large-portfolio result (Vasicek 2002) applied to arrears rather than losses. It treats the share of offtakers entering an episode in a stressed year as the share in arrears at once, an approximation that is close when episodes last about a year. It is about bridging, not final cost: the buffer pays generators until a layer provides liquidity, while part (i) gives who finally pays. It shows why diversification has limits: when offtaker defaults are driven by a common shock, such as a devaluation or a fuel price spike, the buffer must be sized for the share of offtakers in arrears at the same time, not for the average. The calls \(C_k\) are expected payments, not final losses. A national government that pays a utility’s arrears acquires a claim on its own utility; whether it collects is a question of utility reform, not of the facility’s design.

text:
5.2 How much the offtaker costs
The central case assumes a WACC of 8 percent for every risk except the offtaker’s, one default episode every six to seven years (\(\lambda = 0.15\)), episodes lasting a year (\(D = 1\)), recovery of 60 percent of withheld payments (\(R = 0.6\)), and a price of risk \(m = 2\). All five are stylized. They describe a weak but not failed utility, one that is regularly late and eventually pays most of what it owes. The value of \(m\) reflects the finding that default risk carries a premium in bond prices (Driessen 2005); I do not claim a point estimate, and report \(m = 1\) alongside.
In the central case the offtaker is in arrears 23 percent of the time at the risk-neutral intensity, a withheld dollar is worth 58 cents in present value, and the haircut \(h\) is 9.8 percent. The break-even tariff rises from 4.96 to 5.50 cents per kilowatt-hour, an offtaker premium of 0.54 cents or 10.8 percent, equivalent to a WACC of 9.4 percent instead of 8. Table 2 and Figure 2 show how the premium varies. A utility with 25 episodes per 100 years that pays back only 30 percent of what it withholds adds 4 percentage points to the WACC; one that is late as often but pays back 90 percent adds 0.6 points. Episodes of six months halve the central-case premium, and episodes of two years nearly double it. Without a price of risk (\(m = 1\)) the premium falls to 5.8 percent of the tariff.

The decomposition in Proposition 2(iii) shows where the contract guarantee’s $2.0 comes from. The price-of-risk factor is \(\varphi(0.30)/\varphi(0.15) = 1.77\) and, in the central case, the recovery factor is 1. All of the gain is therefore investors’ price of risk, which the state takes on at its actuarial cost. With \(m = 1\), the guarantee saves the offtaker $0.51 million at an expected cost of $0.48 million: a near-pure transfer. If the facility recovers 80 percent rather than 60, the recovery factor rises to 1.83 and the saving to $3.6 per dollar, and that part is a real resource gain. The exposures differ by an order of magnitude. The guarantors’ worst case in one episode is a year of unpaid bills, $8.7 million, much of which they recover. The debt guarantor’s worst case is the loan, $60 million at financial close. That difference is the difference between a guarantee priced at expected loss with a cap and one that must be capitalized at face value.

Three results follow. The donor account at the bottom is cheap, $0.1 million a year, because the national layer is reliable; if the national government’s intercept worked only half the time, the donor’s expected cost would rise two and a half times. The facility’s own expected loss is zero with the donor account and 0.06 percent of payments without it, well within a trading margin like India’s. And the expected calls on the subnational and national layers, about 5 percent of payments, are the price of the offtakers’ unreliability, paid by their owners rather than by consumers through a risk premium on every project.
Liquidity, not loss, is what can break the facility. Each offtaker enters an episode in a given year with probability 13.9 percent. If episodes are driven by a common factor with correlation 0.3, the share of offtakers in arrears in a 1-in-200 year is 65 percent. A facility that must wait six months for the national layer then needs a buffer of $57 million, a third of a year’s payments or about $28,000 per megawatt (equation 8). With correlation 0.1 the stress share falls to 39 percent; with 0.5 it rises to 85 percent. For comparison, India’s Solar Energy Corporation asks developers in newer tenders to deposit Rs 5 lakh per megawatt toward its payment security fund (ICRA 2025), about $6,000 at roughly Rs 85 per dollar; it relies on letters of credit and the intercept for the rest. The African Trade Insurance Agency’s facility covers six months of an independent producer’s operation and debt service (Wass 2017), the same order as the six-month bridge assumed here.

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
text:
5.5 India in the model
The Solar Energy Corporation of India earns a trading margin of Rs 0.07 per kilowatt-hour on a weighted average sale tariff of Rs 2.93 (ICRA 2025), or 2.4 percent of the tariff. In the model the margin pays for itself if the intermediary lowers the WACC by 0.32 percentage points, under a quarter of the central-case offtaker premium. Applied to the corporation’s roughly 60 gigawatts of sale agreements, at the stylized plant’s capacity factor, the central-case premium would cost about Rs 3,300 crore a year, against a margin of about Rs 740 crore. These numbers are illustrative: wind contracts have different capacity factors, and the counterfactual premium for Indian state distribution companies is not observed. The IEA reports that the cost of capital for utility-scale solar in India is about 50 percent higher than in the European Union and names non-payment by state-owned distribution companies as a key driver (International Energy Agency 2024). A direct comparison of tariffs in the corporation’s auctions with those in auctions run by state distribution companies on their own credit would test Proposition 1. I have not found public data clean enough to do it here.

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
section: 6.1 India’s Solar Energy Corporation: the waterfall works, the buyers were not fixed
text:
6.1 India’s Solar Energy Corporation: the waterfall works, the buyers were not fixed
The Solar Energy Corporation of India is the clearest working example of a payment intermediary facility. It is wholly owned by the central government. It signs power purchase agreements with developers only after it has signed back-to-back power sale agreements with state distribution companies on similar terms, so it carries no demand risk. In July 2025 it had sale agreements for about 60 gigawatts at a weighted average tariff of Rs 2.93 per kilowatt-hour, which the rating agency ICRA describes as well below the distribution companies’ average power purchase cost (ICRA 2025).
Its payment security is layered, much as Section 4.4 proposes. Each layer can be checked against public sources:

Letters of credit. Distribution companies must open letters of credit for the corporation, which earns its Rs 0.07 margin subject to their opening (ICRA 2025). A Ministry of Power order of 28 June 2019, effective 1 August 2019, made letters of credit mandatory under power purchase agreements and instructed load dispatch centers to schedule power only once they were in place (Power Line 2019).
Payment security fund. A fund financed from central budgetary support, penalties recovered from developers and interest covers capacity awarded under batches I, III and IV of phase II of the National Solar Mission. Under bidding guidelines amended in October 2019, developers in later tenders deposit Rs 5 lakh per megawatt toward it. The fund does not yet cover other schemes (ICRA 2025).
Tripartite agreement. Since October 2016 the corporation has been a beneficiary of the tripartite agreement among the central government, the state governments and the Reserve Bank of India (ICRA 2025; Kenning 2017). Under it, a central utility owed money can ask the central government to instruct the Reserve Bank to debit the defaulting state’s account and credit the utility. All but two states and union territories have signed it. The corporation last invoked it in fiscal years 2021 and 2022, against distribution companies in Andhra Pradesh and against HESCOM in Karnataka (ICRA 2025).
Sovereign support. The central government injected Rs 1,000 crore of equity in March 2022 (ICRA 2025).

Older drafts of this paper said the corporation draws on credit lines with the Reserve Bank of India. The public record does not support that. The Reserve Bank’s role is that of a debiting agent under the tripartite agreement, which works through the state’s own account rather than through central bank credit.
The design has done what Proposition 2 needs. ICRA rates the corporation AAA, citing its sovereign parentage, the tripartite agreement and its collection record (ICRA 2025). The agreement’s value lies as much in deterrence as in use: a state that defaults on the corporation risks a debit to its own account, so the corporation is paid ahead of generators that sell to the state directly. That is the higher recovery \(R_F\) on which the real gain in Proposition 2 depends.
The failure is upstream. The same rating report notes that most state distribution companies remain financially weak, with losses above approved levels and tariffs below cost, that delays from Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka were once large, and that distribution companies’ letter-of-credit coverage is only 68 percent (ICRA 2025). Across the sector the central government has had to act twice. In May 2020 it announced a Rs 90,000 crore liquidity scheme, under which two public finance companies lent to distribution companies against receivables backed by state guarantees so that they could pay generators (CRISIL Ratings 2020). In June 2022 the Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules let distribution companies pay their accumulated arrears in up to 48 monthly installments (Power Line 2022), with no surcharge accruing on the rescheduled dues while installments are paid on time and the surcharge falling due on the whole amount after a default (Arora et al. 2022). Legacy arrears under the rules fell from Rs 1,39,947 crore on 3 June 2022 to Rs 3,330 crore on 27 March 2026, according to a written reply in Parliament (Press Trust of India 2026).
India’s record therefore confirms both halves of the argument. The intermediary and its waterfall moved the risk away from generators and lowered tariffs. But the risk moved to the central government; it was not removed. The center organized liquidity in 2020 and restructured arrears in 2022, and in both cases most of the money came back because the center could reach the states. That is the waterfall working as Proposition 3 describes, with the national layer paying when called and recovering over time. It is also a warning that a waterfall without utility reform turns into a standing line of credit.

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
section: 6.2 Nigeria’s bulk trader: a single buyer with nothing behind it
text:
6.2 Nigeria’s bulk trader: a single buyer with nothing behind it
Nigeria created the Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading company (NBET) under its 2010 roadmap for power sector reform as a single buyer that purchases power from generators and on-sells it to distribution companies (World Bank Group 2024). In form it is a payment intermediary. In the terms of Proposition 3 it lacked what makes one work: recovery from its buyers, an intercept and a funded layer behind it.
The revenue never arrived. In 2017 the government arranged a central bank loan of up to N701 billion through the Ministry of Finance, repayable by the trader over ten years, so that it could pay generators and gas suppliers; at the time the trader expected to collect on average about a quarter of its invoices from the distribution companies (Okafor 2017). In June 2020 the World Bank approved a $750 million credit for Nigeria’s power sector recovery, aimed among other things at reducing the sector’s annual tariff shortfalls (World Bank 2020). An intermediary that collects a quarter of its bills is a conduit for subsidy, not a credit enhancement.
The country’s first project-financed independent power plant shows what happens when guarantees attach to debt as well as to the contract. For the 459-megawatt Azura-Edo gas plant, which reached financial close in December 2015, the World Bank provided guarantees of $238 million: a payment guarantee of up to $120 million backing the trader’s payment security obligations under the power purchase agreement, and a guarantee of up to $118 million that allowed a commercial debt tranche, alongside political risk cover from the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (World Bank Group 2024). Because the government would not give a sovereign guarantee, it signed a put-and-call option agreement instead. If the power purchase agreement ends early, the project company can put the plant to the government, which must pay a price that at a minimum covers the outstanding debt. The World Bank Group’s case study describes this as support “with no negative impact on FGN’s balance sheet” (World Bank Group 2024).
That description shows exactly the accounting problem Section 8 addresses. The payment guarantee is a contract guarantee in the sense of this paper, capped and tied to the trader’s obligations. The put option is a debt guarantee with a delay: its trigger is the failure of the contract, and its payout is the face value of the debt. In the terms of Proposition 2, it has the large maximum exposure of a debt guarantee and none of the recovery of a contract guarantee, since once the government owns the plant there is no one left to recover from. It is a contingent liability of the state and should be recorded as one.

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
section: 6.3 Zambia and the regional liquidity facility: contract guarantees at small scale
text:
6.3 Zambia and the regional liquidity facility: contract guarantees at small scale
Smaller instruments in Africa already guarantee the contract rather than the debt. Under the World Bank Group’s Scaling Solar program, Zambia tendered two plants on standard power purchase and government support agreements in 2016; the 47.5-megawatt West Lunga plant was awarded at 6.015 US cents per kilowatt-hour on a 25-year fixed-price contract with the state utility ZESCO, then the lowest solar tariff in Sub-Saharan Africa (World Bank Group 2018). ZESCO had to provide payment security by letter of credit, and could do so only with an IDA payment guarantee behind it; every bidder in the first round asked for one. For West Lunga the guarantee was $3.5 million, using less than $1 million of Zambia’s IDA allocation, against about $60 million of investment (World Bank Group 2018). That is a contract guarantee sized to a few months of arrears, not to the debt.
The African Trade Insurance Agency’s Regional Liquidity Support Facility does the same across borders. Launched in 2017 with €63.2 million, half a German grant through KfW and half the agency’s own guarantees, it gives a commercial bank cash collateral to open a standby letter of credit for an independent power producer, covering up to six months of operation and debt service if a state-owned buyer pays late (Wass 2017). It is a regional liquidity buffer in the sense of equation 8, without the layers below it. Both instruments show that multilateral contract guarantees work and are cheap relative to the investment they support. What neither does is pool many contracts behind one standard agreement, collect arrears as a repeat creditor or bind a national intercept in advance, which is what the facility adds.
crumbs: 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
text:
7.1 Tariff profile: declining, not flat
A flat real tariff for 20 years locks the offtaker into the price of the year the contract was signed. If the cost of new solar halves, the offtaker pays double the going rate for the rest of the contract, and its government comes under pressure to renegotiate. Renegotiation is itself a form of default, so a flat tariff raises \(\lambda\).
A declining tariff reduces the exposure without changing the present value. At an 8 percent discount rate, a tariff that starts at 7.74 cents and falls in a straight line to 3.87 cents by year 7, then stays flat, has the same present value over 20 years as a flat 5 cents (stylized). By year 7 the value of the payments still due is 23 percent lower under the declining tariff, 30.6 against 39.5 cent-kilowatt-hour-years. If the cost of new solar falls from 5 to 2.5 cents over the same seven years, the part of the remaining payments above new-build cost is 45 percent lower, 10.8 against 19.8. Earlier drafts proposed a tariff of 6 cents falling to 3 cents as equivalent in present value to a flat 5 cents; at 8 percent it is worth 22 percent less, so developers would not accept it.
The declining tariff therefore saves nothing in present value. What it buys is a contract that stays close to the market price and so is less tempting to break, and a smaller outstanding obligation for the guarantors in later years. The cost is a higher starting tariff, which falls on the offtaker when solar is still a small share of its purchases. The facility should index the decline to a conservative published path rather than to forecasts of technology costs.
crumbs: 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
text:
7.2 One currency rule
Contract in the currency the offtaker earns. A distribution company earns local currency. A tariff in dollars hands it, and behind it the state, the devaluation risk of every contract, and that risk arrives when the state can least bear it, in a balance of payments crisis. In the model it makes \(\lambda\) and the offtakers’ correlation \(\rho\) rise together, which is the worst case for the buffer in equation 8.
Where projects are financed in foreign currency, the facility, not the offtaker, should decide how the mismatch is held, and it should be priced in the open. It can buy hedges from specialist providers where they exist; index only the share of the tariff that pays for imported equipment, for a limited period; or fund the contracts from domestic savings, which removes the mismatch at source. Paper 3.2 sets out a local-currency senior tranche for domestic savers (Stretton 2026b). The rule excludes one practice: a hard-currency tariff whose currency risk is never priced because the state’s guarantee hides it.
crumbs: 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
text:
7.3 National or regional
Large markets should build national facilities. India, Nigeria and Brazil each have enough distribution companies, and enough procurement, to diversify across offtakers and to justify a specialist institution. A national facility can rely on a domestic intercept like India’s tripartite agreement, which gives the national layer a high probability of paying.
Small states should share a regional facility. A facility serving, for example, the members of the Economic Community of West African States would spread the fixed costs of standard contracts, procurement and collection across many projects, and diversify across offtakers whose utilities fail for different reasons. But a regional facility has a weaker national layer. No regional facility has an intercept as direct as India’s, so \(q_2\) is lower and the multilateral and donor layers bear more (equation 7). Members can strengthen it by depositing letters of credit or reserves with the facility, by agreeing to offset arrears against transfers they receive from regional institutions, and by giving the facility’s claims the same seniority as their obligations to multilateral lenders.
crumbs: 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
section: 7.4 Countries in debt distress: energy as a service
text:
7.4 Countries in debt distress: energy as a service
A country that cannot borrow more can still buy clean power. The facility, or a private developer under its standard contract, owns and finances the plant, and the state’s utility buys the electricity per kilowatt-hour. The state replaces an open-ended, foreign-currency fuel bill with a fixed and, under a declining tariff, falling local-currency one.
This changes the form of the state’s obligation, not its existence. A long-term take-or-pay power purchase agreement is a fiscal commitment, and a guarantee behind it is a contingent liability. Earlier versions of this proposal described the arrangement as outside the debt stock and protected by the World Bank Group’s preferred creditor status; neither claim survives scrutiny, and this paper drops both. The defensible claim is narrower: the commitment is smaller than the fuel bill it replaces, its terms are fixed and known, and it falls due only if the state’s own utility fails to pay. Debt sustainability analysis should count it, and should also count the fuel import bill it removes.
crumbs: 3.1 Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt: A Payment Intermediary for Clean Power
text:
7.5 Conditionality on utility reform
A guarantee makes the generator whole; it does not make the utility solvent. India’s arrears show what happens when the waterfall is not matched by reform: the national layer pays repeatedly, and a contingent liability becomes a recurrent one. A country that will not put its utility on a path to cost recovery is asking the guarantors to insure a certain loss rather than a risk.
Entry to the facility should therefore be conditional, and access should widen as the conditions are met. The conditions follow from the model. A published path of tariffs toward cost recovery, and an explicit budget transfer for any subsidy that remains, lower the frequency of episodes \(\lambda\). Letters of credit and an intercept agreement raise the recovery \(R_F\) and the national layer’s probability \(q_2\). Targets for collection and loss reduction lower \(\lambda\) over time. Because cheap solar lowers the utility’s cost of supply, reform and the facility reinforce each other: the facility makes the tariff path shorter, and the tariff path makes the facility cheaper. Sustainability-linked sovereign lending, discussed in Paper 4.3 (Stretton 2026a), is one way to pay for the reforms.

The treatment of small and debt-distressed states draws on the solar payments intermediary proposal developed by Evie Davey. The two-stage refinancing that Paper 3.2 develops came with Jasper Zimmermann. Errors are mine.↩︎
