title: The Climate Investment Trust: Hold Capital, Lend Its Strength
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The regional fund design draws on joint work on two-stage clean energy finance with Jasper Zimmermann. The full analysis, with the model, proofs and calibration, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Climate money spent once buys little policy. Cash rewards on the needed scale will not be voted, and governments cannot borrow against promised payments.
Hold the money instead, behind guarantees. A Climate Investment Trust stands second behind the guarantees that reward climate policy: the government first, the Trust second, a AAA-rated backer last. A guarantee saves the borrower the whole spread but costs only the expected loss.
On the development banks’ record, each donor dollar delivers about 80 dollars of interest savings; without their preferred-creditor status, 2.7. Holding the cautious buffer costs much of the gain until the Trust has its own record.
Accounts for future generations make the reward stick. Each country’s account grows when it acts and shrinks when it retreats, can be pledged now and is drawn after 2050; a feebate between accounts costs nothing net.
Launch it as insurance first. Publish the rules, book the Trust’s claims through a development bank, and add investment later.


Climate money is spent once
The reward for national climate policy has to come from outside, and cash on the needed scale will not come. Cutting emissions pays off for the world; the cost falls on the government that cuts. Fossil carbon dioxide emissions were about 37.8 billion tonnes in 2024 (Friedlingstein et al. 2026). Paying $100 a tonne for a 10 percent cut would cost about $380 billion a year, and paying against negotiated baselines rewards countries that wait. Even modest pooled funds are hard to raise: the Tropical Forest Forever Facility launched in November 2025 with $6.7 billion of pledges against a $25 billion target for its sponsor capital (Barber et al. 2025).
Guarantees deliver a large reward cheaply, if someone holds the capital behind them. A guarantee from a AAA-rated institution saves a government the whole credit spread on its borrowing, perhaps 3 percentage points a year, but costs the guarantor only the losses it expects, a few hundredths of a percent a year on the development banks’ record. The Trust holds the capital that absorbs those losses.


A trust separates who pays, who decides and who benefits
Donors fund the Climate Investment Trust and hold its votes, a development bank manages it, and the beneficiaries are future generations. The formal beneficiaries are the post-2050 populations of participating countries, each through a national beneficiary account. A global account holds what no country has yet earned and meets the first guarantee calls.
Countries benefit long before 2050, because an account is an asset. A balance that cannot yet be drawn can still be pledged as collateral, which lowers the rate a country pays on green borrowing.
A deduction from an account can be enforced where a charge on a sovereign cannot. The Trust credits accounts for policy kept and deducts for policy reversed. A payment to a government can be reversed by the next government; an account held for the country’s future population, which grows when it acts and shrinks when it retreats, builds a constituency for persistence (Stretton 2026g).


One pool does three jobs
First, the Trust stands second behind policy guarantees. A government that commits to a policy, such as annual auctions of guaranteed-price contracts for clean power, gives a guarantee. It takes first loss by indemnifying the guarantor, as under existing multilateral guarantees; the Trust pays if it does not, and recovers over time; a development bank or highly rated sovereign stands behind the Trust and is touched only if the buffer runs out. This is the buffer behind the guarantee capacity of Brief 4.1, in which a country’s notional capitalized value caps the guarantees development banks provide on its green borrowing (Stretton 2026e).
Second, the Trust and its regional funds invest, with the buffer kept apart. Through a separate investment function, the Trust co-invests with pension and sovereign wealth funds in clean energy before financial close and sells once plants are connected and refinanced. Private investors pay it a quarter of their returns and vote only on investment. Regional funds set up with regional development banks hold the first-loss tranche of pools of operating plants, beneath the senior bonds of Brief 3.2, where a large pool needs a cushion of 5 to 8 percent and the first real deals carried about 30 (Stretton 2026c). The buffer itself stays in high-grade bonds, because clean power equity loses value in the same crises that trigger guarantee calls.
Third, the Trust credits its surplus to national accounts by performance. A base allocation rewards joining. A feebate between accounts rewards performance: accounts are credited for emissions intensity below the participants’ average and debited above it, so the transfers cancel and cost the Trust nothing (working paper, allocation rule). The same accounts can deliver the reward in sustainability-linked lending, as collateral or guarantee capacity rather than a few basis points (Brief 4.3).


Holding beats spending, on conditions that can be checked
A buffer supports exposure many times its own size because guarantee calls do not all come at once. The development banks’ sovereign loans defaulted at 0.77 percent a year over 1984–2024, and the banks recovered 95.1 percent of the amounts in default (European Investment Bank 2025). If the Trust stands behind 20 equal guaranteed programs with losses like that, and calls are moderately correlated, a buffer of 0.5 percent of exposure keeps the chance of exhausting it in any year to 1 percent. On paper, $5 billion could support about $1 trillion of guarantees (working paper, buffer and leverage).
Each donor dollar held delivers the spread saved divided by the Trust’s expected loss: about 80 on the banks’ record. A dollar paid out is gone. A dollar held is consumed only by losses, while the guarantees it supports save borrowers money every year. With a 3-point spread saving and expected losses of 0.038 percent a year, the ratio is about 80; a fund that pays out delivers one (Figure 1, panel A). This holds when the buffer earns what donors would earn elsewhere. If it earns 2 percent a year less, the ratio is 63.
The record belongs to the banks, so the Trust should not assume it. Governments in distress keep paying development banks because they treat them as preferred creditors, a practice that is informal, with no binding legal status (G20 Expert Panel on Multilateral Development Banks’ Capital Adequacy Frameworks 2022). A new trust standing behind market debt might not be treated so well. In a stress case, guarantees are called at 3 percent a year and the Trust loses 37 cents on each dollar called, the average creditor loss in sovereign restructurings over 1970–2010 (Cruces and Trebesch 2013). The buffer must then be 9.25 percent, $5 billion supports $54 billion of guarantees, and each dollar delivers 2.7. A middle case, with a 10 percent loss, gives 10.
Prudence has a price: holding the stress-case buffer cuts the reward to about 13 per dollar until the Trust has a record. A Trust that holds a 9.25 percent buffer while its losses follow the banks’ record supports $54 billion, not $1 trillion. The capital is safe, but it does little work: at a 2 percent carry each dollar delivers about 13. Building a record fast, with many small programs and every call and recovery published, is how the Trust earns the right to hold less.
A called guarantee needs cash before the money comes back. On the banks’ record almost everything called is recovered, but only later. If the buffer must pay a year’s debt service on each call itself, $5 billion supports about $390 billion rather than $1 trillion. A liquidity line from the AAA backer, repaid from recoveries, lets the buffer be sized for losses alone.






Figure 1: The Trust’s leverage and growth (stylized). Panel A: present value of interest savings per donor dollar, for a fund that pays out and for a buffer fund in the stress, middle and base (development bank record) cases, at a 3-point spread and no carry; log scale. Panel B: Trust capital over 25 years from $5 billion at launch, holding the stress-case buffer (9.25 percent of exposure) with no guarantee fee, under the banks’ loss record or stress-case losses, with $95 billion of private co-investment or none. Source: working paper, Figures 2 and 3.





The loss record decides whether the Trust grows
A Trust that holds the stress-case buffer grows on its own yield if its losses follow the banks’ record. A 9.25 percent buffer earning 3.5 percent net of costs loses only 0.4 percent of its capital a year to expected calls at the banks’ loss rate. With no fee and no other income it grows by about 3 percent a year, to $10.7 billion after 25 years. If losses are at the stress level it shrinks by 8.5 percent a year, and holds steady only with a guarantee fee of about 0.8 percent of exposure, which still leaves the borrower 2.2 of its 3-point saving (working paper, growth).
Fees on private co-investment make it grow faster, but the private money is the least certain number. With $95 billion of private equity earning 10 percent and paying a 25 percent fee, the Trust earns $2.4 billion a year and reaches $34 billion after 10 years on the banks’ record, or levels off near $28 billion in the stress case. That sum of private equity, from the author’s earlier proposal, is an upper case: the closest working vehicle, Climate Investor One, raised $850 million for development and construction equity (FMO 2019). With $10 billion the Trust barely grows.



Table 1: Indicative scale of the Climate Investment Trust. Launch capital $5 billion: $1 billion of donor grants and $4 billion of country stakes financed by development policy loans, costing participants about $40 million a year to carry. Account balances, not the Trust’s income, limit the feebate between accounts. No deduction can exceed a balance. In a stylized power sector of ten countries, a $5 billion Trust can carry a feebate of about $8 per tonne; after 10 years of growth, $31 to $57 per tonne (working paper, the feebate between accounts). The most carbon-intensive countries join only at low rates while the Trust holds the cautious buffer, so entrants need a transitional benchmark that starts at their own intensity and converges to the average on a published schedule.


Precedents show each piece works
Development banks show that thin capital suffices for sovereign risk. The 2022 G20 review urged them to stretch their capital, including with hybrid capital (G20 Expert Panel on Multilateral Development Banks’ Capital Adequacy Frameworks 2022), and in May 2024 the IMF let members channel up to SDR 15 billion (about $20 billion) into it (Plant 2024). The Trust applies the same logic outside the banks’ balance sheets.
The IMF’s Resilience and Sustainability Trust shows donor capital lent rather than given, protected by a reserve account. Approved in April 2022 with loan, deposit and reserve accounts (International Monetary Fund 2022), it lends at 20 years (International Monetary Fund 2025b) and had pledges of $48.9 billion by July 2025 (International Monetary Fund 2025a). Its resources are owed back to contributors; the Trust’s accounts belong to beneficiaries.
The Tropical Forest Forever Facility shows sponsors taking a junior position to pay for a stock. It targets $25 billion of sponsor capital, repaid over 30 years after a 10-year grace period, beneath up to $100 billion of senior debt, and pays about $4 per hectare of standing forest a year from the spread it earns, with at least 20 percent for Indigenous peoples and local communities (Government of Brazil 2025). It rewards a stock, as Brief 4.1 proposes, but pays out each year and insures nothing.


What decides whether it works
Whether governments repay the Trust as they repay development banks decides which case it is in. The Trust’s claims on governments should be booked through a development bank, rank with the government’s obligations to it, and be published call by call (working paper, design questions).
Governance decides whether the Trust buys good policy. A fund that absorbs losses will be asked, one plausible request at a time, to absorb losses it should not. Rules should be published before money arrives and changeable only by super-majority, every balance should be public, and beneficiary countries should have a voice on rules but no vote on investments.
The price of second loss decides whether the Trust crowds in or subsidizes. Every point of guarantee fee preserves capital and takes incentive back from the borrower, so the fee should be published and set by rule.


What to do
Donors and a development bank should launch the Trust as a buffer behind policy guarantees. Start with the guarantee capacity of Brief 4.1, hold capital in high-grade bonds, arrange a liquidity line from the AAA backer, and book the Trust’s claims through the bank so that they keep preferred-creditor treatment.
They should publish the allocation rule, the guarantee fee and the exhaustion target before raising money. Hold the stress-case buffer at launch and release capacity as the Trust’s own loss record builds.
Countries should borrow to fund stakes only where the guarantees their stakes secure are worth more than the loan’s cost. Guarantee capacity should rise with a country’s stake.
Investment, private co-investment and regional first-loss funds should follow once the buffer has a public record. Regional funds should hold the first-loss tranches of the pools in Brief 3.2, priced openly, with the right to sell seasoned positions so the capital recycles.

title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The full analysis, with the model, proofs, calibration and code, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Climate finance pays for the flow and ignores the stock. It pays for tonnes avoided against baselines nobody can observe, years after the political cost is paid, and almost nothing to countries that kept their forests or leave coal in the ground.
Give each country a climate balance instead of a cheque. The balance opens at a low price per tonne of carbon stock and is debited at a higher, uniform price for every tonne emitted above an agreed allowance. It is never paid out: it sets how much of the country’s green borrowing development banks will guarantee.
A guarantee is worth far more than it costs. The country saves the whole spread; the guarantor bears only the expected loss. On the development banks’ record, each dollar of expected loss buys about $80 of interest saving; about $27 counting only the country’s net gain, and 2.7 in a stress case.
Use two prices: a low one for the stock, a uniform one for each tonne. For a forest country with Guyana’s stock, a $5 billion balance and a $50 debit price make each tonne emitted cost the country about $30, at a donor cost of about 40 cents a tonne.
Fund the buffer, not the reward. Each $1 billion a year of incentive needs about $13 million a year of expected losses and a $0.16 billion buffer that donors keep ($370 million and $3.1 billion in the stress case).


Climate finance pays for flows and ignores stocks
Countries are paid for tonnes avoided against a reference level, not for what they have kept. Guyana’s forests store about 19.5 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent on some 18 million hectares (Government of Guyana 2022). Guyana sells credits for avoided emissions: 33.47 million for 2016–2020, and a contract under which Hess buys 2.5 million credits a year to 2030 for at least $750 million (Department of Public Information, Guyana 2023), about $50 million a year. The stock counts only through a contested adjustment to the reference level worth less than 0.05 percent of the stock a year (Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market 2026).
Paying for flows has three costs. Baselines get inflated: most forest-conservation projects evaluated claimed reductions far above any measurable effect (West et al. 2023). Payment arrives years after the political cost is paid, so it guards against reversal more than it starts reform (Angelsen 2017). And a country that never cleared has little to sell.
Donors will not pay cash for stocks on the scale they would justify. Ecuador asked the world for $3.6 billion to leave an Amazon oil field unexploited and had raised about $13.5 million when it abandoned the plan in 2013 (Hernández Rentería 2020). The new Tropical Forest Forever Facility pays about $4 per hectare of standing forest a year from the returns on a bond portfolio, and deducts 100 to 200 hectares’ payment for each hectare cleared (Government of Brazil 2025). At Guyana’s density, that deduction is under $1 per tonne released.


A balance that the stock opens and emissions draw down
A notional capitalized value is a climate balance held for each country. It opens at a stock price times the verified carbon stock. Each year it is debited at a debit price for every tonne emitted above an agreed allowance path, and credited for every tonne below. Land-use emissions count like any others, so clearing a hectare is debited as the carbon it releases.
The balance sets guarantee capacity, not a payment. Capacity is the most that development banks will guarantee, at any one time, of the country’s eligible green borrowing: clean power, grids, forest enforcement. A buffer fund, the Climate Investment Trust of Brief 4.2, stands behind the guarantees. Countries that borrow little receive interest on the balance in a trust account instead.
Every tonne emitted shrinks the balance, so the incentive acts from the first year. The debit must follow actual emissions; a draw-down set by a forecast would change nothing at the margin (working paper, Proposition 2).
The opening balance is what makes the debit enforceable. No sovereign will pay a fine for exceeding a benchmark, but it can lose part of a balance it already counts as its own (Stretton 2026e, ch. 5). Because the balance is fixed at entry from a verified stock, a country cannot raise it by threatening to clear, the weakness of paying owners to conserve (Harstad 2016).


A guarantee is worth far more than it costs
The borrower saves the whole spread; the guarantor bears only the expected loss. Development bank loans to sovereigns defaulted at 0.77 percent a year over 1984–2024 and recovered 95.1 percent (European Investment Bank 2025), an expected loss of 0.04 percent a year, while the same sovereigns pay spreads of several hundred basis points. Gabon’s insured 2023 debt-for-nature bond paid 6.1 percent and was rated Aa2 (African Sovereign Debt Justice Network 2023), when its 2031 bonds yielded about 10 percent (Smith 2023).
On that record each dollar of expected loss buys about $80 of interest saving. At a 3-point spread saving, 3 divided by 0.038 is about 80. A buffer of 0.5 percent of exposure, held and invested rather than spent, keeps the chance of exhausting it at 1 percent a year (working paper, Proposition 1).
Part of that saving is not a gain to the country. A country that borrows under a guarantee backed by its own counter-indemnity gives up the option to default on that debt. Counting only the risk premium in the spread, about a third of it (Longstaff et al. 2011), the ratio is about 27, still far above the 1 of a grant.
A new facility might not inherit the banks’ preferred-creditor status, so plan for a stress case. If 3 percent of guarantees were called each year and 37 cents on the dollar lost, the average haircut in sovereign restructurings (Cruces and Trebesch 2013), the ratio would be 2.7, or 1.9 counting only the net gain. The facility can price on the record and hold the stress-case buffer until it has a record of its own; if that buffer costs 2 percent a year to hold, the ratio falls to about 13. It also needs a liquidity line, because calls must be paid before recoveries arrive.






Figure 1: A guarantee is worth many times what it costs. Ratio of interest savings to the guarantor’s expected loss, for three spread savings; dashed, the country’s net gain at a 3-point spread. Base case (development bank record), middle and stress cases marked; log scales. Source: working paper, Figure 3.





Two prices: a low one for the stock, a uniform one for each tonne
One price cannot both size the balance and price the margin. Priced at $100 a tonne, Guyana’s stock would be a $1.95 trillion balance, far above anything it would borrow, so capacity would never bind and an extra tonne would cost nothing. Sized to a $5 billion borrowing need with a single price, the stock is priced at $0.26 a tonne, and a tonne emitted costs the country only 15 cents (working paper, two prices).
A low stock price sets how much each country starts with; a uniform debit price sets what each tonne costs. Disputes over the stock and the allowance then change only how much a country gets, a matter for negotiation, not how hard it is rewarded at the margin.
In a stylized forest country, each tonne emitted costs about $30. Give a country with Guyana’s stock a $5 billion balance, a $50 debit price and emissions of 15 million tonnes a year against an allowance falling to zero in 2050. It saves $150 million a year while it keeps its balance. Each tonne emitted costs it $30 in lost interest savings ($50 × 3% ÷ 5%), or $32,500 per hectare cleared. Donors hold a $25 million buffer and expect to lose about $2 million a year: 40 cents per tonne of incentive, or $11 in the stress case (working paper, a forest country).
Business as usual drains the balance; action keeps it. On business as usual the balance runs out in 2042; cutting emissions to 3 million tonnes by 2037 keeps it, which is worth about $1 billion to the country.






Figure 2: A per-tonne debit drains the balance under business as usual. Stylized forest country with a $5 billion opening balance, a $50 per tonne debit and an allowance falling to zero in 2050. Source: working paper, Figure 1.



The $30 holds only while capacity binds and the scheme has no end date. Balance above what the country borrows is idle, so a surplus must flow to a trust account where it still has value; and a scheme ending in 2050 would cut the price of a tonne emitted in 2027 to about $20.


Big incentives need borrowers, not big donations
The incentive scales with what a country borrows, not with its stock. At a 3-point saving, each $1 billion a year of incentive needs $33 billion of guarantee capacity (Table 1). Large, lower-rated forest and coal countries gain most; for an investment-grade borrower saving 1 point, the guarantee form is weak.



Table 1: What a big incentive needs, at a 3-point spread saving. Base case: development banks’ sovereign loss record, an expected loss of 0.038 percent a year and a 0.5 percent buffer. Stress case in brackets: 1.11 percent a year and a 9.3 percent buffer. Source: working paper, Table 5.

Guarantees deliver what cash cannot. Multilateral forest funds pledged about $400 million a year from 2008 (Government of Brazil 2025); Uruguay’s $350 million sustainability-linked loan can save it at most about $12.5 million (Brief 4.3). A guarantee scheme delivering $1 billion a year costs donors about $13 million a year on the banks’ record.
Coal reserves need a narrower rule. Crediting all of Indonesia’s reserves, about 78 billion tonnes of CO₂ (BP 2021), would reward owning coal. Credit only reserves legally retired, at a low price that allows for leakage (Harstad 2012), and debit combustion emissions like any others (working paper, coal).


Declining capacity pays for acting now
Falling technology costs reward waiting. A government weighing a reform that costs money up front gains from waiting a year by the interest on that cost plus the fall in technology costs. For a stylized $1 billion coal-to-renewables reform cutting 5 million tonnes a year, acting now needs an incentive of $20 a tonne, or $32–37 allowing for uncertainty (Dixit and Pindyck 1994). Without an incentive, the government never acts (working paper, Proposition 3).
Capacity that declines as fast as technology costs fall is the cheapest way to make acting now pay. It concentrates the reward where it changes the decision. In the example it halves donors’ cost of the $20 incentive, from $25 million to $13 million in present value on the banks’ record ($740 million to $370 million in the stress case). Paid in cash, the same incentive would cost $1 billion.
Energy and forests need different schedules. Once clean power is cheaper than coal the energy incentive can phase out; a standing forest keeps an opportunity cost, so its incentive needs a permanent floor.


The risks are real but can be bounded
Moral hazard is bounded. Capacity is capped by the balance, only green borrowing is covered, and a call on a guarantee becomes a debt to a development bank.
The host’s liability shrinks but does not vanish. Its exposure becomes smaller, contingent and contracted, but stays its own; and other creditors, now standing further back, may charge more (Chamon et al. 2022). Donors’ buffer must be sized to stressed, correlated losses, and published.
Stocks that were never at risk still deserve a low price. The balance is cheap, because it is capacity costed at expected loss; it is what makes the per-tonne debit enforceable; and it does not dilute the incentive at the margin, which the debit price alone sets (working paper, risks).
Fairness needs a corrective. Low-stock countries earn balance every year they emit below their allowance; a per-capita floor on the opening balance would add more. Forests near tipping points (Lovejoy and Nobre 2018) warrant a higher debit per hectare, not a higher stock value.


What to do
Development bank shareholders: create rules-based guarantee capacity, allocated by notional capitalized value. Set it outside country lending envelopes: an opening balance from each country’s verified stock at a low, uniform stock price; an allowance path to net zero; a uniform debit price of $30–70 a tonne; capacity sized to bind on eligible borrowing, declining about as fast as clean technology costs fall, with no end date; and any surplus passed to a trust account.
Donors: fund the buffer, not the reward. Hold it in a trust that invests it (Brief 4.2), sized to the stress case until the facility has its own loss record, and report the budget saving and the net gain together.
Forest and coal countries: negotiate allowances, not baselines. Seek credit for legally retired reserves at a low price, and write the allowance path into sustainability-linked loans as the performance indicator (Brief 4.3).

title: Codify Sustainability-Linked Sovereign Lending, Then Give It Scale
text:
Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. The design that pays the reward through an intermediary comes from joint work with Marcello Estevão and Nils Zimmermann (Estevão et al. 2024). The full analysis, with the model, proofs and calibration, is in the working paper.

Key messages
Read the full working paper → · Slides (pptx)
Sustainability-linked debt pays governments for national climate results, but each deal is handmade and small. Uruguay’s $350 million World Bank loan, the first sovereign loan of its kind, can save the country at most $12.5 million.
Codify it. Publish a menu of indicators that national statistics already report, baselines set at each country’s own Paris pledge plus a margin, verification by a named verifier and a price per tonne of CO₂.
Pay the reward from outside. When a bond’s coupon moves with results, investors charge for the expected step when they buy, so the government pays for its own reward. An intermediary that lends on a fixed coupon and refunds interest for verified results brings outside money.
An interest margin is too small. A 100 basis point step-down on $1 billion is worth $77 million over ten years, against $772 million for a stylized coal reform.
Make guarantee capacity the prize. $3.3 billion of capacity is worth $772 million to the government and costs the funder about $10 million on development banks’ loss record, or $286 million on market-like losses.


Sustainability-linked sovereign debt exists, and it is small
Sustainability-linked debt pays a government for results, not for projects. A green bond finances a named solar park. A sustainability-linked bond or loan leaves the money unrestricted and changes its price according to key performance indicators: measured national outturns such as emissions per unit of output or the area of native forest. That makes it one of the few instruments that rewards national policy, which is where the large emission cuts lie.
A handful of governments have used it since 2022, each in its own way. Chile issued the first sovereign sustainability-linked bond in March 2022: $2 billion over 20 years, with a coupon step-up of 12.5 basis points for each of two missed targets from 2034 (Cleary Gottlieb 2022). Uruguay followed in October 2022 with the first step-down as well: its coupon rises 15 basis points for each lower target it misses and falls 15 for each higher target it meets, on emissions intensity and native forest area (Oriental Republic of Uruguay 2023). Thailand sold Bt30 billion (about $874 million) in November 2024 with steps of 2.5 basis points (IFR 2024), and Slovenia €1 billion in June 2025 with steps of 50 (Republic of Slovenia 2025).
Uruguay’s World Bank loan is the clearest model. Approved in November 2023, the $350 million loan’s rate falls by 50 basis points a year in 2028–2032 if the methane intensity of beef cattle is at least 33 percent below 1990, one point beyond Uruguay’s first Paris pledge, and by 100 basis points in 2033–2037 at 36 percent, one point beyond its second. There is no penalty for missing. The United Nations Development Programme verifies the national inventory, and a World Bank fund for global public goods pays the reward (Ministry of Economy and Finance, Uruguay 2023; World Bank 2023).
The rewards are tiny next to the cost of policy. Uruguay’s reward is capped at $12.5 million, 3.6 percent of the loan and about $8 million in present value (working paper, Uruguay). South Africa’s transition plan alone identifies $98 billion of financing needs over five years (UK Government 2022).


Why it does not scale
Every deal is bespoke. Each issuer picks its own indicators, baselines and step size, and pays lawyers, verifiers and reviewers to defend them. The market’s voluntary standard, the International Capital Market Association’s Sustainability-Linked Bond Principles, sets out how to disclose these choices, not what they should be (International Capital Market Association 2024). The usual step of 25 basis points is, in World Bank staff’s words, “the arbitrary market norm” (Stewart and Ul Haq 2023; Climate Bonds Initiative 2024).
Targets are easy. Corporate issuers miss their targets only 14–39 percent of the time (Feldhütter et al. 2024). A reward paid whatever the government does changes nothing; only the extra chance of meeting the target because of the policy counts (working paper, minimum reward).
Rewards arrive late. Emissions data take years to compile and verify. Uruguay’s methane result for 2025 is verified only in 2028, and the last reward is applied in 2037, fourteen years after the loan was approved (Ministry of Economy and Finance, Uruguay 2023). A finance minister heavily discounts a reward paid to a successor.
A bond whose coupon moves with results gives the government no money. Investors who can see the target charge for the expected step when they buy the bond; studies find bond prices track the size of the penalty, with no mispricing (Feldhütter et al. 2024; Lefournier 2023). Once the bond is sold the government still gains from meeting the target, so the bond is a commitment device, but the government has paid for its own reward and a premium for the uncertainty. That cannot pay for a reform that costs the country more than it gains, which is the case for most mitigation. Uruguay’s bond can lower its coupon by up to about $40 million in total, three times the loan’s reward, but bondholders priced that in (working paper, who pays).


Codify: indicators, baselines, verification and a price
A codified instrument is a contract written once and used many times. Each new loan then chooses only which indicators apply and how much debt is linked. The World Bank Group’s own reform roadmap already proposes “standardized approaches” to interest buy-downs and performance-based incentives (World Bank Group 2022).
Indicators should be outturns that national statistics already report. “Methane per kilogram of beef” is an outturn; “methane strategy adopted” is a process step. Outturns are hard to meet on paper, leave the government free to choose the cheapest policy, and convert to tonnes. The working paper gives a starter menu of eleven indicators in six sectors (working paper, indicator menu), most already used in a sovereign deal.
Baselines should be set by rule. Uruguay’s rule is worth copying: the target is the country’s own unconditional Paris pledge plus a fixed margin, so the government cannot negotiate a soft baseline (Ministry of Economy and Finance, Uruguay 2023). A peer-based floor protects against weak pledges.
Verification should check the national inventory, not commission new surveys. Uruguay’s verifier reviews the same inventory the country reports under the Paris Agreement, smoothed over five years to remove weather noise (Ministry of Economy and Finance, Uruguay 2023). One verifier and one method per indicator class turns verification into a routine service.
The reward per unit of outperformance should be published and stated per tonne. The reward for one point of an indicator equals the tonnes that point implies times a notional carbon price. That lets a funder compare a forest indicator in one country with a power indicator in another, and puts sustainability-linked lending on the same scale as policy crediting, the payment per tonne cut by a policy (Brief 1.1; Brief 6.1).


Pay the reward from outside
Investors should hold a fixed coupon, and a public partner should pay the reward. In the design developed with Marcello Estevão and Nils Zimmermann, a trusted intermediary backed by guarantees from a coalition of advanced economies issues fixed-coupon bonds at a low rate and lends the money to governments as sustainability-linked loans at a somewhat higher fixed rate (Estevão et al. 2024). When verified indicators are met, it refunds part of the interest already paid. Development agencies monitor the indicators and give technical help.
The government gets money from outside, and the risk lands where it is cheapest to bear. A pension fund charges a premium to hold a coupon that moves with a country’s methane statistics. An intermediary lending to many countries diversifies that risk and can bear it near cost (working paper, Proposition 2).
A missed target should cost the government its refund, not pay bondholders a premium. A step-up hands money to investors who did nothing to earn it and does nothing to put the country back on track.


The size problem
Even a well-designed sustainability-linked loan pays too little to change a large policy. A rebate cannot exceed the interest bill. Table 1 compares rewards with a stylized reform that retires 2 gigawatts of coal ten years early, avoiding 11.4 million tonnes of CO₂ a year at a net cost of $100 million a year: $772 million in present value.

A 100 basis point step-down on $1 billion is worth $77 million, under $1 per tonne avoided. Matching the reform’s cost at that step needs a $10 billion loan, nearly thirty times Uruguay’s.
Even waiving all interest falls short. At 6 percent, waiving every dollar of interest on $1 billion for ten years is worth $463 million. The loan would need to exceed $1.7 billion and carry no interest at all (working paper, the interest bound).






Figure 1: Interest-rate rewards are an order of magnitude too small; guarantee capacity is not. Present value at 5 percent over ten years, US$ million, log scale. Solid bars: value to the government; hatched bars: cost to the funder. Source: working paper, Figure 1.





Give it scale: make guarantee capacity the reward
A guarantee delivers a large incentive at a small cost. The borrower values it at the whole spread it saves, while the guarantor pays only its expected loss and the cost of holding a buffer. Meeting the indicators should earn guarantee capacity: the maximum outstanding guarantee exposure that multilateral development banks will provide on the country’s eligible green borrowing. Under the notional capitalized value of Brief 4.1, meeting indicators adds to that capacity (Stretton 2026d); under the Climate Investment Trust of Brief 4.2, it credits the country’s beneficiary account, which it can pledge as collateral now (Stretton 2026e).
In the stylized reform, $3.3 billion of capacity pays for the reform. On borrowing that saves 300 basis points it is worth $772 million to the government. If the guarantor’s losses match development banks’ record on their own sovereign loans, the base case shared with Briefs 4.1 and 4.2, its expected cost is about $10 million and a $16 million buffer is held, not spent: about 80 dollars of incentive per dollar of cost (working paper, the coal reform).
The multiple is lower if governments treat the guarantor like a market creditor. Development banks’ record reflects their status as preferred creditors, which governments keep paying even in a crisis. If a new guarantor’s claims are treated like market debt, its losses look like the stress case: an expected cost of $286 million with a $310 million buffer, 2.7 dollars of incentive per dollar, still better than cash. At a 200 basis point saving, the multiples are 53 and 1.8. A new facility should price on the record but hold the stress-case buffer until it has its own; if that buffer costs 2 percent a year to hold, the multiple on the record falls to about 13 (working paper, the strongest objection).
The government’s exposure does not disappear. It becomes smaller, contingent and contracted, because a called guarantee is a debt the country owes back to the guarantor (Brief 3.1). And guarantee capacity is worth most to a government that will actually borrow for clean investment.
The two routes fit in one contract. The sustainability-linked loan supplies the indicator, the baseline, verification and the price; the guarantee supplies the size. One verification can trigger both the refund and the extra capacity. Kenya’s planned sustainability-linked loan, reported in July 2026 to carry a World Bank credit enhancement, would be a first step toward combining the two (Muiruri 2026).


What to do
Multilateral development banks: publish a codified sovereign sustainability-linked loan. It should contain an indicator menu, baselines at each country’s Paris pledge plus a published margin, verification rules based on national inventories, and a price per tonne. Offer step-downs on that schedule, as the World Bank did for Uruguay, without negotiating each deal from scratch.
Advanced economies: back an intermediary that lends on a fixed coupon and refunds interest for verified results. Investors then hold a plain asset and the incentive sits with a public partner. Do not count market bonds with moving coupons as climate finance for the borrower: they buy commitment, not reform.
Donors: make guarantee capacity, not the interest rebate, the main prize, and fund the buffer behind it. The rebate is the signal; the guarantee is the incentive. Every reward must be additional to the country’s existing concessional finance, or it pays nothing.

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text: From Plucked!, by Stephen Stretton and Gordon Styles.

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
Summary
The purpose of this section is to take you on a second whirlwind tour of ideas in economics. This time, rather than travelling through history, we shall introduce these ideas through stories set on an imagined group of islands, which we will term ‘The Economic Archipelago’ (informally, the ‘Tea Islands’).

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
Specialization and Trade
Then a small group of fishermen discover something. They decide firstly, that they are only going to fish, and no longer participate in gathering berries. Whilst they like eating nuts and berries, they argue that they can catch enough fish and trade some of the fish with others for nuts and berries. They also split up tasks between themselves. Some of them make nets, others build bigger boats. They can catch more fish by splitting up tasks in this way. By collaborating and specializing they can double their productivity. Whereas before they could only make 500 grams of food per day, now they collectively can produce 1kg of food per day per fisherman.
They now have some choices. They could catch fish all day (8 hours) and sell what they don’t personally require for their own needs (the ‘surplus’), saving this return or spending it on some luxuries. Another option is to cut down working hours by working only 4 hours per day. In the shorter working day they can still produce enough food to live on. In both cases we would say that the fishermen in the firm have higher hourly wages than before - twice what they were making before they decided to specialise. These higher wages reflect their higher productivity.
This improvement in wages was generated by the fishermen and their initiative, and they are the beneficiaries of the new way of working. The economy has grown, but so far the additional prosperity has gone entirely to those fishermen. The price of fish relative to berries is unchanged. One kg of fish still sells for one kg of berries.

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
Competition
At first, the benefits of improvements are captured by those that made the improvement. Our group of fisherman now live a life of relative luxury. Everyone else’s material conditions are pretty much as they were before. The rest of the island’s population does notice, however, that the fishermen who specialised seem to be getting richer.
Pretty soon, some other islanders realise what the fisherman have done. They then follow suit, and adopt the new methods. Then even more fishermen notice what is going on and pile in as well. Fortunately the seas are plentiful. Once each fisherman has replicated the new improved double-productivity setup, they can all sell their surplus fish.
But then something strange happens. Because the islanders only want to buy a certain quantity of fish, and now much more fish is being caught, the fishermen have to compete with each other to attract customers. So, they start to undercut each other in order to win market share. The price of fish in terms of berries starts to fall.

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
The Labour Theory of Value
To what price will the price of fish fall? It continues to fall until the point at which, under the new circumstances, it only just makes sense for workers to go fishing in the new fishing-conglomerates - i.e. when the wages from fishing in the new improved setup equilibrate to the wages for going gathering. In other words, the price of fish relative to berries will fall until it makes the same sense for someone to fish as to go collecting berries. This assumes of course that there is still value in eating some berries, perhaps for a varied diet.
So now, the cost of fishing is expected to fall. In these new, changed circumstances, 1kg of fish (taking one day to collect) buys 0.5kg of berries (also taking one day to collect). This is the new, cheaper price of fish relative to berries.

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
Widely Shared Prosperity?
If we add some numbers, we can make the improvement clearer.
At the end, people fish for a day to get one kilo of fish and perhaps go collecting for a day for half a kilo of berries. Two thirds of the people fish, and one third of the people collect berries. This is a change from the fifty-fifty split before the improvement in collective capabilities.
The total average food production is (2/3)x1 + (1/3)x(1/2) = 5/6 or about 0.82kg. Thus the real wages per day have increased, from 0.5kg per eight-hour working day to 0.82kg of food per eight-hour day.
This is an example of the basic model of division of labour and competition. Let’s now extend this model to the situation in which there is scarce land that is privately owned.

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
Differential Rent
Imagine the island is split into two domains of differential rabbit productivity. On the east side of the island, rabbits are plentiful, and a full day of hunting will yield 8kg of rabbits. On the west side, rabbits are less plentiful and only 4kg per day can be hunted. The landlord rents out both plots, but the rent charged on each must differ. Assume for now that the wage a person can make is still 1kg per day when fishing. Thus the landlord can charge 3kg of rabbits for residence on the less productive plot and 7kg of rabbits per day for residence on the more productive plot. As above, if the landlord attempted to charge more in rent, then their tenant would simply leave and return to fishing.

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
Absolute Rent
Let’s say that for some reason, there’s a series of storms and the fishermen find it hard to catch fish. The landlords however have some spare resource - stored dried food - that they have accumulated over many years. They sell this food to the fishermen. In exchange the fishermen sell their boats to the landlords and rent them back. Now there is no rent-free way of earning a living. Either the islanders pay rent for a boat and fish, or they pay rent to stay on the island and hunt rabbits. In this situation, we say that land and other ways of earning a living are ‘absolutely scarce’. They have been bought up by the wealthy landlords.
The amount of the landlord’s revenue which comes from renting out boats versus the amount which comes from renting out hunting-rights to the rabbit hunters, will depend on the absolute scarcity of land and the absolute scarcity of labour.
In our current scenario of abundant labour (many islanders available to work), of the original 8kg of rabbits, only 1kg is retained by the hunter; the other 7kg are paid as rent for access to the landlord’s hunting-grounds. The residual wages are not set at what the hunters can earn in a rent-free existence, but rather, the minimum that will keep them alive.
In a scenario of scarce labour, this could change. This would require that the labourers (in this case, rabbit-hunters) have a choice of landlords to work for. If there are several islands with landlords and rabbits, but too few rabbit-hunters available to hunt all the rabbits produced by the islands, then the landlords will be forced to compete for the time and effort of the hunters. If they don’t, they will receive no rent at all. In this case, the rabbit-hunters might be able to negotiate a deal with a landlord in which they retain two rabbits per day and pay the landlord only six rabbits (again assuming the hunter is able to bag eight rabbits a day).
All this depends, of course, on the original rate of rabbit-hunting remaining sustainable; i.e. the fecundity of the rabbits and the available rabbit food on the islands must be such that the hunters’ productivity of 8 killed rabbits per day doesn’t overwhelm the ability of the rabbits to regenerate their populations. Also the rabbits’ numbers mustn’t get so high that they eat all the available greenery and cause a mass starvation. A dynamic equilibrium between rabbit population and the population of hunters is what’s best for all concerned.

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
Capital
Let’s say that our Robinson Crusoe sets aside some of his wages, in order to save for the future. He works for a bit and creates some rabbit traps. He has to invest some time in making them, but once he has done so, his productivity doubles from 1 rabbit per hour to 2 per hour; or from 8 rabbits per day to 16. It takes him one day to build the traps. The traps double his daily productivity to 16 rabbits per day. We can say that it increases his productivity by 8 rabbits. Each trap lasts 10 working days (80 hours) before having to be completely replaced.
Does this investment make sense? Let’s work it out. There’s an original investment of 8 hours of time to create the trap, and this leads to 8 extra rabbits per day for 10 days. This is a total of 80 extra rabbits. I give up 8 rabbits in one day to construct my trap, and I get back 80 rabbits. Let’s say that I borrow the resources to make the traps, so I borrow 8 rabbits to pay the rent and feed myself during the day I make the traps.
Thus my profit is 72 rabbits (assuming I continue to work a full day) each 10 day cycle. This is a profit of more than 7 rabbits per day, once the cost of my investment is taken into account.
At last Robinson Crusoe is happy! He is a great believer in hard work. He is working full days to pay the rent, and will continue to work full days. He can invest his time and create the traps, and reap the reward. After having paid back the time invested, there will be a surplus too! He can sell the spare rabbits to passing tradespeople or to Man Friday, and can build up assets.
We are assuming that Crusoe has some financial buffer, some wealth to tide him over for the day that he is building his trap and therefore not hunting. If rent is payable daily, he might be able to delay paying rent, he might be able to borrow some rabbits or other resources to pay rent, or he might invest his own stock of wealth until the investment pays back.
Everything is going swimmingly well. He invests his time and he makes a surplus, and soon enough he’s selling the spare rabbits to passing tradespeople and building up a store of value.
But there’s a catch. Man Friday comes round and observes what is going on. He takes some photos. And soon enough, some adverts go up in the Archipelago Gazette, the local newspaper for the islands. It’s only after getting a copy from a trader on a passing ship that Crusoe sees them. The adverts say the following: ‘Make a fortune hunting rabbits! Earn 16 rabbits per day.’ He also reads the small print: ‘Requires 8 rabbits investment to make traps; Rent: 14 rabbits per day.’
14 Rabbits! He’s only paying 7 at the moment! What’s coming? Sure enough, some visitors soon come around, friendly enough. The next day Man Friday invites Crusoe round for dinner again…. “About the rent”… he says. “I know you are enjoying staying here, but the market is changing. Market rents are going up. I had an offer the other day for someone to pay double what you are paying. Of course, I prefer to go with you, since I know you’re a good reliable chap, so I won’t chuck you out as long as you pay what the market is saying. It’s only 14 rabbits per day. You still make a healthy 2 rabbits profit.”1
So, Crusoe is back in his original position. He works an 8-hour day, and after rent, is again only left with 1kg rabbits in wages, enough for him to live on. He can’t seem to get ahead! It sure seems like the concept of private property is the fundamental problem here, but as we will see, abolishing property causes its own problems…

title: Chapter 3: Desert Island Economics
text:
Getting to Dream Island
Let’s now work out solutions to the problems we’ve encountered in our archepelago. It’s easiest to solve problems before they get started - to set things up well from the start.
The problem of the landlord (Man Friday for example), extracting ever increasing rent from the islanders, for which he does no work. The first solution is a land value tax (LVT) - a tax on rent. With LVT, a landlord is taxed according to the surplus of each piece of land. He makes no unearned money. There’s no such thing as a landlord any more, really. Land can still be purchased, but the person who owns and occupies it has to pay rent to the central authority. In other words, rent (money collected from tenants in excess of the landlord’s costs) now accrues to the central authority, not to a private landlord. In our island archipelago, the central authority might be a democratic council elected on a one-person-one-vote basis.
What does the central authority do with the taxes received (in our story: with the rabbits harvested)? There are two options: (1) The government could provide public services by paying people living on the island with rabbit-meat rations for doing useful things that benefit everyone. (2) The government could distribute rabbit-meat directly to the population, without requiring work in exchange.
What about over-hunting? A limited number of permits could be issued by the central authority, with fines and penalties levied against those who are caught ignoring the rules. Hunting rabbits could be constrained. Or put another way, a tax could be levied on hunting rabbits. On propertied land, it can be expected that the landowners/renters in charge of the land will themselves look after the rabbits on their own plots. If rabbits run freely between plots, there needs to be a joint solution agreed between all the land-owners or set by the central authority that constrains hunting.

text:

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text: From Plucked!, by Stephen Stretton and Gordon Styles.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Why Do We Need Tax?
The first question to address is why we should tax at all. Taxes are traditionally unpopular policies, often seen by the public as a ‘tax grab’ on private assets and wealth. So let’s give an overview of the key positives that taxation policies can have.
The simplest answer to this question is that tax is imposed in order to fund public spending. Government spending usually takes the form of investments in public infrastructure, or on social provisions like housing, healthcare, and public education. Investment in these public goods is often economical only on a large scale – it’s not often that one individual can be responsible for a public park, for example, or for a university. The pooling of resources allows for these public goods to be supplied to a cross-section of society that would otherwise be unable to access them.
It’s worth noting that the provision of public goods does not come exclusively from government sources. Artists, writers, community activists, and philanthropists can all be said to provide public services. Cafés which offer public restrooms, private enterprises which fund local newspapers, non-government cooperative agencies and institutions such as charities all provide public goods and services. However, the benefit of governmental provision lies in its ability to prioritise and maintain these services through democratic decision making, rather than relying on private benefactors.
But why doesn’t the government just print money to pay for these goods? The reasons include legitimacy and inflation. Money is effectively a transferable IOU of value from the institution that has issued it (generally a bank). In other words, money is a scorekeeping system for keeping track of promises to deliver a specified quantity of value (a specified number of British pounds). If the government prints and spends a great deal of money without subsequently taking money back out of circulation, too many £-denominated IOUs will end up in circulation, and the legitimacy of these promises will become compromised. People will stop believing that all these promises to deliver value will be fulfilled, and will begin demanding more points in the game of circulating £-denominated IOUs for any given amount of work delivered in exchange. A rabbit might cost £20 instead of £10.
Put more simply, if the government printed money and put it into circulation through spending on an excessive scale, and failed to remove some of the money already in circulation by harvesting taxes to offset new spending, this would cause inflation which would devalue the currency already in circulation. This can lead, in extreme cases, to hyperinflation and fiscal chaos, whereby money loses its worth, making it increasingly difficult for people using the government’s designated currency to pay for their private consumer goods or other obligations. This would also limit the ability of the government to invest in public goods and assets. Without a solid basis of assets, a public body is unable to guarantee that it will be able to deliver services to the public on a long-term basis. This is why tax revenue is so important.
In addition to taxation, there are several other ways in which a government can raise revenue. However, taxation revenue is one of the core methods of supplying a government with the necessary funds for its activities. This is in line with Beveridge’s principles of levying taxes as part of a comprehensive policy package of funding ongoing public services.
As noted, an additional reason for taxation is to maintain fiscal order and control inflation. The difference between tax revenue and government spending is a major factor in a nation’s economic growth and inflation paradigm. This is not a focal point of our analysis in this text. However, the macroeconomic influence of the public spending balance, and the size of its deficit, is widely seen to be important. Governments must manage their cumulative debt-to-GDP for reasons of international credibility in support of appropriate exchange rates with other nations’ currencies.
Yet the difference between tax revenues and government spending does not in itself constrain the government’s ability to source financing for public projects, or the extent to which fiscal policy can be used to boost a national economy after a recession. At the end of the day, a government that owns its own currency system and has a central bank is a government that need never worry about being able to fund projects or budgets. The real constraint on public spending is simply the availability of idle resources - i.e. qualified people available to be employed - and not, in fact, any limit on the amount of money available to a government. The government can always create any amount of money it might need to fund investments or programmes, and it can also always levy taxes in amounts it deems appropriate to rebalance the stocks and flows of money and debt within different sectors of the national economy (albeit within practical limits of political feasibility).
Another reason for using taxation is to emphasise the ‘social contract’ between a citizenry and their government. This is effectively a ‘deal’ by which the government is contracted to enact the aims and goals of those they represent. Taxation can be thought of as a method of enforcement of these designated responsibilities. It is, admittedly, not always the case that this is explicitly recognised by members of a government, but the ‘I pay for your salary’ argument can go far when shoring up a citizen’s right to complain or to lobby for the specific actions of a representative body. In nations whose governments are funded mostly by sales of natural resources, not by tax revenues (petrostates like Saudi Arabia or Venezuela are examples), governments become distributors of unearned largesse rather than accountable representatives of the citizenry; this generally has pernicious political and economic results.
By establishing a stakeholder-shareholder model in which governments are servant representatives of the people who pay for the governors’ services with their tax contributions, we change the status of the citizen in society to that of co-proprietor, as well indirect decisionmaker (through the medium of elected representatives). The citizenry thus becomes the collective sovereign as well as the natural recipient of any ‘dividends’ from natural wealth. In this worldview, we also change the status of the private landowner to that of a consumer of national resources (through temporary occupation of a patch of the sovereign’s land), rather than an outright sovereign owner. The shift in dynamics if this outlook is adopted may have considerable impacts on future resource management in the UK.
As already touched on, there are also several social objectives that can be achieved with the careful implementation of taxation. Redistributive policies are a large component of public spending, sharing the wealth that is created in a society through income, housing, and healthcare provisions. Another reason that taxation can be useful is to correct for monopoly pricing and externalities, or to change behaviour in some way that is designated as socially beneficial. Behavioural economists have only very recently started to explore the nudging and norm-changing effects of taxation. Their ideas will be explored later in this chapter.
Of course, noble objectives remain mere concepts until they are realised. In the world of policy, it is sometimes best to think of noble goals as akin to ‘spectres’ that haunt the messy reality of designing and implementing policy. In this, we draw from Derrida’s ideas of the influence of justice in law – never actually achievable, but rather existing as an influencing ideal that pushes the development of law (Glendinning 2016). The same can be said for the objectives of taxation. The ability of taxation regimes to tackle inequality and social bads will only ever be as good as the reality of such policies as they are implemented in practice. We will expand on this later - for now, we want to draw attention to the significance both of the influencing ideas and also their implementation.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Deciding What to Tax
Taxes can be applied to a range of goods and services. We will, going forward, term these targets as the ‘tax base.’ These can cover a very wide range, e.g. duties on imports, taxes on profits, taxes on incomes over some threshold, or consumption taxes, e.g. on luxury expenditures whose demand is insensitive to price, or on ‘bads’ such as tobacco products.
Deciding which tax base to use can often be determined by the objective of the policy. In the current system, raising revenue is predominantly achieved through income taxes. This helps redistribute aggregate economic income from those with high incomes to those with low incomes. Taxes can also be applied to the unearned increment on scarce resources that are limited in supply or monopolised - for example, land, fossil fuels, or endangered fish. And taxes can help disincentivise environmental and health bads - activities that damage our common resources or our health.
Overall, we could tax four different types of activities: 1. Cash Flow: Income, profit, capital gains, value added (sales tax). 2. Rents: Land, property, resources. 3. Finance: Money balances, bank balance sheets, transactions. 4. Environmental Health and Social Damage: Fossil fuels, greenhouse gas emissions, alcohol, tobacco, sugar, salt.
But how do we decide which tax base to use? One solution is to create a decision framework based on selected principles of justice and benefit. We define these as the preconditions of practicality, benefit, and fairness. The questions we can ask ourselves to build this decision framework will help shape the ultimate design of the tax policy and the schedule of assets that we decide to tax.
The first order of deciding the tax base should be efficiency. We can ask the question of whether the private value of a good reflects its social value. Where private value is greater than social value, taxes can be levied to drive these two values to equivalence. If there is a need for more revenue after taxing this value difference, we could then continue to prioritise efficiency by taxing things that are fixed in supply. Such a mechanism would avoid the distortionary incentives that taxation levied on income or wealth can have.
We could also choose to select a tax base on grounds of equity. By focusing on tackling private value inflation, we would begin to reduce the rate of growth of inequality in the UK (Piketty 2014) by reducing the windfall gains associated with returns on capital and wealth, as opposed to income. In doing so, we could enhance justice in the system. However, care must be taken to ensure that existing asset values are not changed so dramatically as to cause injustice during the transition process. One way in which to achieve this is by focusing asset value taxes on future increases in private value above the social value, rather than on the existing allocations.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
section: What are the Objectives of Reform?
text:
What are the Objectives of Reform?
It seems clear that what we choose to tax, and at what level, depends on the purpose of the tax itself.
If the goal is to reduce inequality, then taxes can be applied to private assets and high incomes. Such taxes target the accumulation of wealth to both recapture societal contributions to its formation, and to ensure inequality does not grow excessively. Some argue that these taxes must be designed to target oligarchic and monopolistic control of assets. We define Oligarchy as ‘rule by the few,’ specifically by the rich, where disproportionate power is held by a small number of wealthy people who control the majority of a nation’s assets. Assets can often be synonymous with political power, leading to a society based primarily on the principle of ‘one pound, one vote’ rather than ‘one person, one vote.’ Oligarchic groups can gain a distortive influence on the tax code so that it better suits their interests. This poses problems for the majority.
Another area where the tax system could potentially be used to benefit society is with environmental protection. Environmental taxes can help to ensure that the global environment is less damaged by our economic activities. Pollution is often considered a negative environmental externality. It’s good for society to internalise these costs, and thereby incentivise producers to reduce them, by adding a cost to the producers of ‘negative externalities’ in the form of a tax; this is an example of taxing ‘bads’ to disincentivise their production.
It is not just in the levying of the tax that this mechanism can be beneficial. It’s possible to arrange financial flows from taxes on ‘bads’ such that the beneficiaries of the tax (those who benefit from spending of the revenues raised) directly correspond with the stated social aims behind the tax policy. This can bring a ‘double dividend’ of impact. For example, taxing polluting fuels and using the revenues to subsidise clean energy could potentially accelerate the development and implementation of clean energy provision in a country. Moreover, if a tax looks to have regressive impacts (i.e. hits the poorest in society at a disproportionate level - consumption taxes and heating-fuel taxes can have this effect), some of the revenues from such a tax could be given as a rebate to those most negatively affected to ensure that the policy retains political viability, as well as a broadly positive impact. We see this in the form of modern welfare benefits in the UK, despite the well-publicised problems in the system. These will be explored in a later chapter which explores the history and functionality of the UK welfare system.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Beneficial (Not Harmful)
To be beneficial is to do good overall. There are multiple ways in which different taxes might be said to ‘do good,’ and people may reasonably disagree on what ‘good’ means. However, all taxes must have some legitimate claim to be beneficial. Most would agree that a tax is beneficial if it pays for valued public services. For example, taxation that pays for our National Health Service, our emergency services, our roads, schools, and public transport, is generally considered necessary and beneficial. This is evidenced by a recent survey of British citizens (PWC 2017) which found that the majority would be willing to pay more tax if it leads to improvements in the quality of the NHS.
More contentiously, taxation may be said to be doing good by redistributing income (or at least ensuring that the rich contribute more), helping to alleviate poverty, and reducing large wealth disparities. The proceeds of taxation may be also used to ensure a minimum standard of living by providing an income ‘safety net.’ This is evident in countries which have adopted the ‘welfare state’ ideology, whereby taxes levied on income are used to create a cushion for those at the lower income spectrum.
As we’ve noted, taxes can also be used to discourage antisocial and harmful behaviour by individuals and companies. They may do this by compelling those who cause harm to society through their economic activity to pay for that harm.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Fair (Just)
There are three ways in which we think taxes must be fair. Taxes must demonstrate consistency, progressivity, and transitional justice.
As seems obvious, the first condition is that taxes must be fair by being consistent. Similar persons, companies and situations should be treated identically. There should be no special exemptions or ‘sweetheart deals’ for favoured individuals or companies. This seems obvious. In practice however, this principle is often flouted, usually to the advantage of powerful companies or individuals.
Related to this idea of fairness are concepts of accountability and transparency. Taxes must not just be fair but must be perceived to be fair. Taxes should therefore be clear and transparent, such that it is apparent to everyone what the proper tax burden should be for each income bracket. These issues are particularly topical in Britain today. In early 2017, the Parliamentary Public Accounts Committee expressed concern that HMRC’s “lack of transparency” concerning high net worth individuals “has eroded public trust in a fair tax system.” (Committee of Public Accounts 2017)
Another, perhaps more controversial kind of fairness concerns progressivity. A progressive tax is a tax in which those who have more, pay more. UK income tax is thus a progressive tax regime, since richer citizens pay more proportionally than poorer citizens. We think this is fair - however, this viewpoint is not uncontroversial in some quarters.
Fairness is also relevant to our discussion of economic rents and land values. When land values increase because of work performed by society as a whole, by our definition, it would be fair if all citizens benefit. It would seem unfair for only some few people to benefit. Similarly, it would seem unfair if only a few people benefited from the country’s natural resources - resources which were not created by any person, but which form part of the nation’s unearned endowment.
Finally, it is important to achieve fairness during the transition from the existing system to the new system. This is necessary not only for reasons of justice, but also for the political feasibility of reforms: If their transitional consequences are seen as unfair, they will be unpopular, and subject to defeat or reversal.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Practical (Smoothly functioning)
If a tax was fair and intended to do good, but couldn’t be implemented without requiring masses of paperwork, prohibitive costs, or extreme social controls, then no matter the benefit, the tax would not be justifiable. Taxes must be practical to implement.
When considering whether a tax is practical, we might consider how close it is to a theoretical ideal. Ideally, a tax should be simple to implement and administer. It should have low collection and compliance costs. This means that it should not cost the government huge sums to collect, and it should also be simple for taxpayers to comply. The less paperwork, time-consuming research, and confusing rules are involved, the better. Taxes which are automatically collected are more practical in this regard than those which require excessive amounts of form-filling and record-keeping.
One pertinent drawback from overcomplication of tax policy is tax evasion. This has been a particularly hot topic in recent years. There is a difference between tax avoidance and evasion. Tax avoidance is the legal dodging of tax; tax evasion is the illegal dodging of tax. A tax which is easily evadable or avoidable is impractical, because it will not function to increase public revenues. It may also require significant resources to be wasted chasing up non-complying ‘tax cheats.’ Moreover, it’s important to avoid an international ‘race to the bottom’ where countries compete to reduce tax rates on companies and the super-rich. Ensuring that taxes are as intelligently and efficiently designed as possible, within a holistic policy package, will help to reduce this risk.
Another aspect of practicality is predictability. Individuals and companies must be able to predict future expenses in order to manage their financial planning. In a similar vein, taxes must be clearly defined, so that taxpayers can plan their affairs while knowing exactly how much tax they can expect to pay. This emphasises the need for steady transitions and well communicated policies when applying any policy change.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Principles in practice
How shall we think about these principles in a practical sense? As mentioned above, ideals remain mere dreams until they are successfully realised. Practicality, benefit and fairness become ideals to aim at when designing any new tax policy, without becoming restrictive principles which limit the development of any policy. The perfect should not become the enemy of the good.
No system will be perfect, but the strategic design of any new policies to prioritise clearly defined purposes and visible benefits sits at the heart of success. Incorporating this insight into a framework for guiding reform is our final task in this chapter.
So, what does all this mean for our new tax system? Having discussed historical ideas of what we should tax, outlined practical considerations for why we should tax, and touched on the guiding principles that should lie behind the design of any new policy, the clearest takeaway is that there is a lot to consider! It’s no wonder taxation has a bad reputation. The complexity of designing a successful policy results from the sheer number of considerations that must be made to try to achieve the multiple goals of raising revenue, tackling social norms, managing monopoly, and preserving equality, all while keeping things sufficiently simple and so circumventing a Kafkaesque bureaucratic nightmare scenario.
We can find our way out of this maze. By rearranging and summarising the above into a clearer decision-tree format, we can begin to pull together the threads of a decision framework that we can use to link taxation in principle with taxation in practice.
It’s clear from the foregoing that consideration of taxes can be subdivided into establishing the objectives and targets of the policy, and the guiding characteristics of the policy design itself. In our framework, we term these distinctions as the functional and qualitative requirements of the tax system. We outline these below.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
section: Functional Requirements of Tax and Welfare System
text:
Functional Requirements of Tax and Welfare System
In simple terms, three major functions of the tax and welfare system can be identified:

Raise Revenue: (Pay for government services)
Ration Scarce Factors and Economic Bads: (Share limited resources, minimise environmental and health harm, and ensure the economy develops beneficially)
Correct Maldistribution: (Redistribute income fairly, provide a safety net for those in need; help people into work; and ensure that the distribution of income is equitable)

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Qualitative Requirements of Taxation System
Similarly, we can identify three main non-functional requirements:

Useable: (Simple, with clear justification, objectives and low compliance and collection costs)
Economically Efficient: (Non-distortive, applied to a secure tax base, and with low capacity to evade/avoid)
Equitable: (Transparent, fair, and internationally cooperative)

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Qualitative Requirements of Welfare System
We can also apply a similar mindset to the use of tax revenue in the case of the welfare system.
A welfare system should be:

Useable: (Simple, integrated, value for money, with the use of modern technology)
Efficient: (Providing incentives for going to work, and for skills development)
Equitable: (Fair, without stigma)

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Theory Of Change
How do we change the tax system? We need to maximise the effect whilst minimising resistance to changes. This is true in two areas in particular: Environmental/energy policy and housing policy. If we want to have a big effect, we need a big incentive. We must use financial incentives to promote forms of entrepreneurship which will provide public benefit. But big changes tend to have big losers, and therefore suffer strong political resistance.
What can individuals and groups do to promote a better tax and welfare system? Economic justice campaigners seek to eliminate the evident unfairness of the current taxation and benefits system. Environmental and housing tax campaigners seek to use the tax system to make the private sector work for greater public good. Simplicity campaigners seek a simpler, more usable system. We propose to combine these motivations to propose a fair, beneficial, and simple tax and social security system. It provides a rallying point for key ideas that could be implemented immediately.

title: Chapter 5: Tax in Principle
text:
Tax Theories of Change
How do we change a complex, entrenched system like the UK’s tax regime? This book deals with tax reform with two distinct approaches. The first is a ‘blank slate’ approach. This considers how we would define a tax and welfare system in an ideal world where both efficiency and fairness are achieved easily.
The second approach takes into account issues of incremental improvement and transition. In other words, what practical politically feasible changes could be made right now to make the system more beneficial and fair?
So what does practicality look like? Often in policy, it is synonymous with political feasibility. Previously, we mentioned the idea of political realism and transitional justice. Changes must not seem unfair; nor must they have obvious losers.
